blocks.text: People picture Bondi as a beach; I see a stage - where surf lifesaving was born, where giant kites fill the sky each spring, and where the world's largest fun run comes pouring over the hill. These are the ten biggest events that, to me, turned an ordinary bay into the most famous beach on earth.

items.label: Oldest institution
items.value: Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club

blocks.text: The moments that made Bondi Bondi
Some are grand and global, others gloriously silly - but together they're why Bondi feels the way it does when you reach the promenade.
1. The birth of surf lifesaving

The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club is recognised as the world's oldest surf life saving club, and it changed how the country goes to the beach. It long celebrated a 1906 founding, though its own historians later settled on a formal establishment date of 21 February 1907. Either way, this is where the reel, line and red-and-yellow flags began.
2. Bondi Icebergs (club formed 1929)

That emerald pool at the southern end, waves crashing over the lane ropes, is the most photographed corner of Bondi. The Icebergs Club was formed in 1929 by local lifesavers wanting to stay fit through winter - hence the rule about swimming through the cold months. The pool is still a working ocean bath, so check the Icebergs website for current public-swim times and prices.
3. City2Surf comes over the hill

First run in 1971, the City2Surf pours 14 kilometres from the Sydney CBD down to Bondi Beach and has grown into the world's largest fun run. If you've never watched the finish, do it - tens of thousands of runners cresting the hill on a winter Sunday.
4. Sculpture by the Sea

In 1997 someone dotted the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk with sculptures for a single day. It's now the world's largest free-to-the-public outdoor sculpture exhibition, drawing huge crowds each spring. Dates shift year to year, so confirm this season's run on the Sculpture by the Sea site before planning.
5. Festival of the Winds
My personal favourite. First held in 1978, this Waverley Council event has been Bondi's most colourful day ever since - the whole beach turned upward to giant kites, music and multicultural stalls.
6. Beach volleyball at the Sydney 2000 Olympics
For the Sydney 2000 Games, a temporary stadium rose on the sand and the world watched Olympic beach volleyball at Bondi. Locals argued about it, but it cemented Bondi's image as Australia's beach.
7. Bondi Rescue hits the screen (2006)

When the reality series following Bondi's lifeguards began airing in 2006, it carried the beach into living rooms worldwide. Half the visitors I meet came because they watched it - and yes, the lifeguards really are that busy.
8. The pink bikini fundraiser (2007)
In 2007 a mass beach shoot packed the sand with women in pink bikinis for a record-setting breast-cancer fundraiser. Peak Bondi: a serious cause wrapped in something wonderfully over-the-top.
9. The graffiti (art) wall

The long sea wall along the promenade doubles as a legal, ever-changing art canvas - layers of murals painted by locals and visiting artists for decades. It's one of the few places where you can watch a piece being made and see it painted over within the month.
10. Bondi as a place to gather
From climate and community rallies to spontaneous dawn services, Bondi has become the beach Sydney comes to when it wants to be together. That, more than any single day, is what shaped it.

The big free events - Festival of the Winds, Sculpture by the Sea and the City2Surf finish - all bring road closures and packed buses. Leave the car at home: take the train to Bondi Junction, then a bus or walk down to the sand.

blocks.title: Dates move - always double-check
blocks.text: Annual events shift their dates every year, and some founding dates are still debated by the institutions themselves. The official organisers are linked in the sources below; confirm this year's programme with them first.

items.q: What is the oldest event or institution at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, the world's oldest surf life saving club. It long marked 1906 as its founding year, though its historians later settled on a formal date of 21 February 1907.

items.q: When is the City2Surf and where does it finish?
items.a: It runs in winter and finishes at Bondi Beach after 14km from the Sydney CBD. First held in 1971, it's now the world's largest fun run. Check the official City2Surf website for this year's date and entry.

items.q: What is the Festival of the Winds?
items.a: Bondi's annual kite festival, first held in 1978 and now presented by Waverley Council. Expect giant kites, live music and multicultural food stalls, usually in early spring - confirm the date on the council's events page.

items.q: Can I still see Sculpture by the Sea at Bondi?
items.a: Yes. It runs each spring along the free Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk and began in 1997. Dates change annually, so check the Sculpture by the Sea website before you go.

items.q: Is the Bondi graffiti wall legal?
items.a: The promenade sea wall is a long-standing public art space where murals are painted openly and change constantly. It's one of Bondi's most photographed backdrops, but the artwork is temporary by design.

blocks.text: Ten events, one beach - and the list keeps growing. Stand on the promenade during any of them and you'll feel why this place matters.

blocks.text: Every August, tens of thousands of people run 14km from the Sydney CBD out to my front yard - Bondi Beach - in the City2Surf, and yes, if you want to actually enjoy it rather than survive it, now is a very good time to start training. The good news? You don't need to be an athlete. This is a fun run first and a race second, and plenty of people walk large chunks of it and still finish grinning.

I live at the finish line, so I've watched years of runners come pouring down the hill onto Campbell Parade - elite club runners, mates in matching costumes, parents pushing prams, someone dressed as a banana. The City2Surf has a way of turning a Sunday into one of the best days on Bondi's calendar.

items.label: When
items.value: A Sunday in August - check the official site for this year's date

blocks.text: The course (and that hill)

The route starts in the city near Hyde Park and winds out through East Sydney, Kings Cross, Rushcutters Bay, Double Bay and Rose Bay before the harbour views open up on the eastern side. It's a genuinely beautiful course - you're never far from the water for the second half - but it is not flat, and anyone telling you otherwise hasn't run it.

The famous test is Heartbreak Hill: a long climb up New South Head Road from Rose Bay toward Vaucluse, hitting around the halfway mark when your legs are just starting to ask questions. They don't call it Heartbreak for nothing. My honest advice - don't try to be a hero on the hill. Shorten your stride, keep it steady, and remember it's followed by a long, generous downhill toward Dover Heights and Bondi.

blocks.title: Where the training pays off
blocks.text: If you train one thing specifically, make it hills. Heartbreak Hill breaks people who've only ever run flat. A weekly hill session - even just repeats up a local street - changes your whole race.
How I'd actually train for it

You don't need a complicated plan. If you can already jog 3–5km, you've got a solid base and a couple of months of consistent running will get you comfortably to 14km. The principle is simple: build your long run gradually, add a bit of hill work, and don't increase your weekly distance too fast.

items: Run 3 times a week - one easy short run, one hill or interval session, one longer run.
Grow your long run by roughly 1–2km a week, not more, until it reaches around 12–14km.
Practise on hills. Bondi to Tamarama and back, or the Bondi to Bronte coastal path, are perfect local grinders.
Do at least one run in the shoes and socks you'll wear on the day - blisters at 10km are miserable.
Ease off in the final week. A rested body beats a tired, over-trained one every time.

blocks.text: Train on the actual finish. Run the Bondi to Rose Bay direction along New South Head Road a couple of times and you'll know exactly what Heartbreak Hill feels like - and how sweet that downhill run into Bondi is on race day.
Race-day logistics

Runners set off in staggered waves from Hyde Park across the morning, faster groups first, with your start group based on the predicted time you enter. Roads across the eastern suburbs close for the event, so driving is a bad idea. Take the train into the city for the start, and plan how you'll get home from Bondi, because the buses and streets get very busy once everyone finishes.

blocks.title: Check the official details before you commit
blocks.text: Entry fees, closing dates, exact wave times and the road-closure map change each year. Confirm everything on the official City2Surf site and Transport for NSW before race day rather than trusting last year's numbers.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and where does it finish?
items.a: It's 14km, starting near Hyde Park in Sydney's CBD and finishing right here at Bondi Beach. That means Bondi turns into one big finish-line party for the day.

items.q: When is the City2Surf held?
items.a: It's run on a Sunday in August each year. The exact date shifts year to year, so always confirm on the official City2Surf website before you plan around it.

items.q: Do I need to run the whole way?
items.a: Not at all. It's a fun run, and plenty of people walk the hills or the whole course. If you can walk 14km, you can complete the City2Surf.

items.q: How hard is Heartbreak Hill?
items.a: It's a sustained climb from Rose Bay toward Vaucluse at about the halfway point - the toughest stretch of the course. Train on hills beforehand and pace yourself up it, and you'll be fine.

items.q: How should I get to and from the event?
items.a: Take public transport. Roads across the eastern suburbs close for the run, so drive nowhere near it - catch the train into the city for the start and check Transport for NSW for getting home from Bondi.

blocks.text: So - time to start training? Honestly, yes. Lace up, get a few hills in your legs, and I'll see you when you come flying down onto Campbell Parade. There's no better finish line in Sydney, and no better feeling than earning that first swim at Bondi once you're done.

Ask me who Bondi's most famous residents are and I won't point to a celebrity's clifftop mansion - I'll point straight at the sand. The best-known faces around here are the Waverley Council lifeguards in blue, the men and women made famous around the world by the TV show 'Bondi Rescue'. If you've ever watched them sprint into a rip on television, you've already met the locals who define this beach.

'Bondi Rescue' first aired in 2006 on Network 10 and has since been broadcast in something like 100 countries, which means visitors turn up already knowing the flags, the tower and the routine. For a lot of people, the lifeguards ARE Bondi - and honestly, spend a summer here and you'll see why.
The lifeguards in blue

The professionals you see on the show are employed by Waverley Council and patrol Bondi every single day of the year - not just Bondi, either, but nearby Tamarama and Bronte as well. They're the ones in blue: putting out the red-and-yellow flags each morning, watching the water like hawks, running first aid and, when a rip fires up on a packed day, pulling swimmer after swimmer back to safety.

A busy summer at Bondi means thousands of rescues, and on the worst days - big swell, strong rips, a beach packed with people who don't know the water - the crew can be pulling swimmers back to safety one after another from morning to dark. It's a genuinely high-stakes job dressed up as a day at the beach, which is exactly what makes the TV show so watchable.

Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags. That patch isn't decorative - it's the stretch the lifeguards have judged safest and are actively watching. Step outside it and you're on your own with Bondi's rips, which is where the overwhelming majority of rescues happen.
Blue vs red-and-yellow: two kinds of hero

Here's a distinction worth knowing, because visitors mix it up constantly. The paid council lifeguards wear blue and work year-round. The volunteers - the surf lifesavers based at the local Surf Life Saving Clubs - wear the classic red and yellow, and you'll mostly see them patrolling on weekends and public holidays through the warmer months. Same beach, same mission, two different crews. Both are keeping an eye on you.

blocks.title: Patrol hours change with the season
blocks.text: Bondi is patrolled all year, but the exact hours shift between summer and winter (and around daylight saving). Rather than trust an out-of-date timetable, check Waverley Council's beach safety page for the current patrol times before you plan a swim - especially early morning or late afternoon.
Meeting the famous residents

You don't need a camera crew to see them at work - just come down to the beach. The lifeguard tower sits above the sand towards the southern end, and the crew are out on the flags all day. Give them room to do their job, but a friendly nod goes a long way; they're locals, and most are happy to point you to the safest spot to swim.

What I love is that for all the international fame, they've stayed exactly what they always were: people who love this beach and take its safety seriously. That's the real story behind Bondi's most famous residents - not the celebrity of the show, but the fact that the water is watched from dawn to dusk, every day of the year.

items.q: Who are Bondi's most famous residents?
items.a: The Waverley Council lifeguards, made internationally famous by the TV show 'Bondi Rescue'. They patrol Bondi (plus Tamarama and Bronte) 365 days a year and are the faces most visitors associate with the beach.

items.q: What's the difference between lifeguards and surf lifesavers at Bondi?
items.a: The lifeguards in blue are paid professionals employed by Waverley Council and work year-round. The surf lifesavers in red and yellow are volunteers from the local Surf Life Saving Clubs, typically patrolling on weekends and public holidays in the warmer months.

items.q: When did 'Bondi Rescue' start?
items.a: It first aired in 2006 on Network 10 and has run for many seasons since, screening in roughly 100 countries around the world.

items.q: Can I meet the Bondi Rescue lifeguards?
items.a: You can see them working on the beach any day of the year around the lifeguard tower towards the southern end. They're on duty, so give them space, but they're locals and usually happy to advise on where it's safe to swim.

items.q: How many rescues do Bondi lifeguards do?
items.a: Thousands over a summer season, with the busiest days - strong rips, big crowds - keeping the crew pulling swimmers out one after another. Swimming between the red-and-yellow flags is the single best way to avoid needing one.

blocks.text: So next time you spread your towel out on the sand, take a second to look up at the tower. The people watching over you are the ones the whole world tunes in to see - and they're doing it live, for free, right in front of you.

If you've ever wondered who the aerobics instructor in Eric Prydz's "Call On Me" film clip actually was - and whether you can take her class here in Bondi - here's the short answer. Her name is Deanne Berry, she's a Sydney-born professional dancer, and after that leotard-and-legwarmers routine made her one of the most recognised faces on British TV, she came home to Australia and has taught high-energy dance-fitness right here on the beach. I went looking for her story, because a local link to one of the 2000s' most talked-about music videos is far too good to keep quiet.

items.label: The video
items.value: "Call On Me" by Eric Prydz, released 2004

items.label: Bondi link
items.value: Has taught dance-fitness classes in the Bondi area

items.label: Best for
items.value: Anyone who loves moving to music - no dance experience needed

items.label: Booking
items.value: Check her current classes via her own website and social channels

blocks.text: The most talked-about aerobics video of the 2000s

You almost certainly remember it: a room full of dancers in high-cut leotards, legwarmers and sweatbands, working through a suggestive aerobics routine to Eric Prydz's thumping club track. Released in 2004 on Ministry of Sound, and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie", the song became a UK number-one hit and the video one of the most recognised - and most debated - dance clips of the decade. At the time it was about as risqué as a mainstream music video got. And the instructor front and centre? A Bondi local in the making.
Who is Deanne Berry?

As Deanne tells it, her career began in Sydney at 16, dancing and performing before touring interstate and through Asia with musicals and artists. That work eventually took her to the UK, where a tour backing Sir Cliff Richard led to a stint in London - and, during a break between concert dates, to a casting call for an eighties-inspired Ministry of Sound video. She landed the role of the instructor, and a few days later found herself in that now-infamous black thong leotard, legwarmers and not much else.

She didn't expect it to go anywhere. "I thought not too many people would see it," she told me - so jumping around and pelvic-thrusting felt harmless enough. Then the track shot to the top of the charts, the video spread around the world, and almost overnight she went from working dancer to accidental fitness guru. She took the moment and ran with it: enrolling in fitness courses, choreographing and presenting a Ministry of Sound fitness DVD that sold strongly, and later waking up Britain as a fitness presenter on breakfast television.
The Bondi dance-fitness class

Back in Australia, Deanne has channelled all of that into a dance-conditioning class - each workout themed to a different pop artist, so you sweat your way through the sounds of the likes of Rihanna, Kylie, Beyoncé and Michael Jackson while building stamina, flexibility and strength. Her pitch is simple: leave your inhibitions at the door, come with an open mind, and don't worry if you can't dance. She's had mums and daughters in the same session; the only real requirement is a love of moving to music.

blocks.title: Classes and studios change - check before you go
blocks.text: This interview dates back a few years, and dance-fitness timetables and studios move around. Rather than turn up on spec, look up Deanne Berry's current classes and locations on her own website and social channels for what's actually running now.

Fancy recreating the routine? Deanne told me she still gets asked to bring back the "Call On Me" moves at parties and events, and clearly still loves performing the track - so if you're planning an eighties-themed do, she's the person who danced the original.

items.q: Who was the aerobics instructor in the Call On Me video?
items.a: Deanne Berry, a Sydney-born professional dancer. She was cast as the instructor for Eric Prydz's 2004 "Call On Me" clip and later returned to Australia, where she has taught dance-fitness in the Bondi area.

items.q: Is the Call On Me clip really by Eric Prydz?
items.a: Yes. "Call On Me" was released by Swedish producer Eric Prydz in 2004 on Ministry of Sound and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie". It became a UK number-one hit.

items.q: Can I take Deanne Berry's class in Bondi?
items.a: She has run dance-fitness classes in the Bondi area, but timetables and studios change over time. Check her current website and social channels for what's on now rather than relying on this older interview.

items.q: Do I need dance experience to join?
items.a: No. Her classes are pitched at all levels - she's had complete beginners, and even mums and daughters, in the same session. The only thing you really need is a willingness to move to music.

items.q: Did the Call On Me video top the charts?
items.a: Yes - the track was a UK number-one hit and the video became one of the most recognised and talked-about dance clips of the 2000s.

blocks.text: It's a lovely little piece of Bondi trivia: the face of one of the era's most famous music videos quietly getting people dancing a few streets back from the sand. If the story's tempted you to try a class, do check what she's running before you go - and either way, next time that Eric Prydz track comes on, you'll know the instructor is one of our own.

Yes - you can absolutely swim at Bondi Icebergs, and it's one of my favourite things to send visitors off to do. The famous ocean pool at the southern headland of Bondi Beach isn't a members-only secret; it's a public saltwater pool where anyone can pay the entry fee ($10 for adults as at August 2026), tumble into 50 metres of Pacific Ocean, and swim laps against a backdrop that shows up on half the postcards of Sydney.

It's often called the most photographed pool in the world, and once you're standing on the deck watching waves crash over the far wall while you swim, you understand why. Here's how to actually get in, what it costs, and the quirks worth knowing before you go.

items.label: Where
items.value: 1 Notts Ave, southern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Pool
items.value: 50m seawater lap pool + shallow kids' pool

blocks.text: Can the public swim at Bondi Icebergs?

This is the question I get more than any other, and the answer is a happy yes. You don't need to be an Iceberg or know one. You walk up to the entry desk, pay for a single visit, and you're in. As at August 2026, entry is $10 for an adult, $7 for a child and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in your admission, plus towel and locker hire if you need them. Prices do get reviewed, so I'd confirm the current rate on icebergs.com.au before you set off rather than trust a figure you read online.

The pool is filled with real seawater pumped straight from the ocean, so it's bracing rather than heated - glorious in summer, character-building in winter. Entry also includes the sauna and hot showers, which brings me to my favourite cold-season ritual.

In the cooler months, do a few laps, warm up in the sauna, then get straight back in the cold pool. That hot-cold-hot cycle is the whole point of a winter swim here, and the sauna is already included in your entry - no extra charge.
Opening hours and the Thursday clean

The pool generally opens early - from 6am on weekdays and a touch later on weekends - and runs through to early evening. The one catch that trips people up: it closes on Thursdays so the whole thing can be drained, scrubbed and refilled. In summer, when the tides cooperate, it sometimes reopens on a Thursday afternoon, but there's no guarantee, so don't build your day around it.

blocks.title: Check before a Thursday visit
blocks.text: Because Thursday is cleaning day and hours shift a little between summer and winter, always check the official Icebergs pool-conditions page for the day you're going. Big swell can also close the pool for safety when waves are washing over the walls.
The lanes, the ocean gate and the 2km loop

A couple of things surprise first-timers. The lap lanes are wide - effectively double a normal lane - so the etiquette is to swim down one black line keeping left, and come back on the other line, again keeping left. Follow the locals and you won't cross anyone.

For stronger swimmers there's a small gate at the ocean end of the pool that lets you slip out into the sea. Confident open-water types do the 'point to point' - a loop out around the bay and back that works out to roughly 2km. Only attempt that if you genuinely know the conditions and your own limits; the ocean here is not the pool.
What about becoming an actual Iceberg?

Membership of the Icebergs winter swimming club is the stuff of local legend and deliberately hard-won: the tradition requires committing to winter Sunday swims across five years. It's a badge you earn in the cold, not something you buy. For a visitor, the public swim gives you the same water and the same view without the five-year vow.

items.q: Do you have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. Icebergs is a public pool. Anyone can pay a single-visit entry fee and swim - membership is only for the winter swimming club, not for using the pool.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: There's a single-visit entry fee, with reduced rates for children and families and cheaper multi-visit passes if you're staying a while. Prices change from time to time, so check the current rate on the official Icebergs pool page before you go rather than relying on an old figure.

items.q: Why is Bondi Icebergs closed on Thursdays?
items.a: Thursday is cleaning day - the pool is drained, scrubbed and refilled. In summer it sometimes reopens on Thursday afternoon if the tides allow, but it's not guaranteed.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No. It's filled with seawater pumped from the ocean, so it's cold, especially in winter. Your entry does include a sauna and hot showers to warm up afterwards.

items.q: Can I swim in the ocean from the pool?
items.a: There's a small gate at the ocean end for experienced open-water swimmers. Only do this if you're a strong swimmer who understands the day's conditions.

blocks.text: Whether you're chasing laps, a winter sauna ritual or just that one perfect photo of waves breaking over the edge, Icebergs delivers. Pay your entry, keep left in the lanes, dodge Thursdays, and you'll leave understanding exactly why this little pool on the rocks is famous the world over.

sources.label: Bondi Icebergs Club - Pool Conditions & Hours

blocks.text: If you want to swim a proper organised ocean race out of Bondi, the two I'd build a summer around are the Bondi to Bronte and the North Bondi Classic - both well-run, decades-old events that welcome anyone who can confidently cover the distance in open water. Bondi's headlands, patrolled sand and swim-club culture make it one of the best places in Sydney to pin on a cap and give it a crack, whether it's your first 1km or your fiftieth.
The two Bondi swims I'd put on your calendar
Bondi to Bronte

This is Bondi's most famous ocean swim and, for a lot of Sydneysiders, the one that matters. You start on Bondi's sand, swim out and around Mackenzies Point, then track down the coast into Bronte - a course of roughly 2 to 2.4km depending on how the organisers set the buoys on the day. Swimming around the cliffs gives you a perspective of Bondi almost no one else gets, but don't underestimate it: the middle section past the point can serve up real swell and current. It typically runs in early December - 2026 is its 25th year. Entries and the exact date go up on the official Bondi to Bronte site, so check there rather than trusting a date you read second-hand.
North Bondi Classic

Run by the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club - one of the oldest clubs in the country - the Classic is my pick for a first ocean race. It offers a 1km and a 2km option, starting and finishing on the sand in front of the club at the northern, calmer end of the beach, sheltered by Ben Buckler headland. The atmosphere is fantastic: hundreds of swimmers, families along the promenade, lifesavers everywhere. It usually runs in the back half of summer, so confirm the current date and course on the club's website before you enter.

blocks.title: These are open-water races, not pool laps
blocks.text: Conditions off Bondi can turn quickly - swell, chop and rips are all part of the deal, especially once you're past the flags and around the point. Only enter a distance you can comfortably swim in the open ocean, not just a pool. If in doubt, start with a 1km event and always follow the on-water safety crew.
How to enter and what to expect
Most Sydney ocean swims, including these, use online entry that opens weeks or months ahead and can sell out - so plan early rather than rocking up on the day. Here's how I'd approach it:

items: Enter online in advance via each event's official site; don't count on race-day entries.
Build up your open-water distance beforehand - swimming in surf and chop is very different to a still pool.
Get comfortable sighting (lifting your eyes to spot the buoys) and swimming a straight line without a lane rope.
Bring a bright cap, goggles you trust, and maybe a thin wetsuit early or late in the season.
Know the rules - some events are wetsuit-optional and have their own categories.

blocks.text: Do a few practice swims between the flags on a calm morning first, and get a feel for sighting off the headlands. If you can swim to the buoy line and back a couple of times without stopping, you're in good shape for a 1km event.
Finding the full season

Bondi's swims are part of a whole eastern-suburbs summer circuit, and exact events and dates shift from year to year, so I won't quote a calendar that might be stale by the time you read it. The best place to see what's on is oceanswims.com, which lists the NSW season with entry links, so you can line up Bondi's races alongside neighbours like Bronte and Coogee.

items.q: What's the most famous ocean swim at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim - a roughly 2 to 2.4km point-to-point from Bondi's sand around Mackenzies Point to Bronte. It usually runs in early December; check the official Bondi to Bronte site for the current date and entries.

items.q: Which Bondi ocean swim is best for beginners?
items.a: The North Bondi Classic's 1km option is a great first race - it starts and finishes at the calmer northern end of the beach, with plenty of on-water safety support.

items.q: Do I need to be a strong swimmer?
items.a: You need to confidently swim the distance in open water, which is harder than a pool because of swell, chop and current. Start with a 1km event and train in the surf beforehand.

items.q: How do I enter a Bondi ocean swim?
items.a: Enter online through each event's official website ahead of time - races can sell out and race-day entries aren't guaranteed. For the full NSW season and entry links, oceanswims.com is the best hub.

items.q: When is the ocean swim season at Bondi?
items.a: Most events run through the Sydney summer, roughly December to March, when the water is warmest. Exact dates change each year, so always confirm on the official event site before planning your trip.

blocks.text: There's nothing quite like rounding the point on a clear Bondi morning, cliffs on one side and open ocean on the other. Train sensibly, enter early, respect the conditions - and I'll see you out past the flags.
