blocks.text: If you want the honest, local answer to where to eat in Bondi, here it is: for a special occasion with an ocean view it's Icebergs, for a long boozy Italian lunch it's Totti's, for the best porchetta it's Da Orazio, for produce-driven fine dining it's Sean's, and for a Bondi breakfast institution it's bills. I've eaten my way around this beach for years, so here's what each place is actually good for - and when I'd book it.
The special-occasion pick: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Perched on the southern headland above the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool, this is the view every postcard of Bondi is trying to be. It's Maurice Terzini's flagship - polished Italian food, a serious wine list, and that sweep of turquoise water and surf through floor-to-ceiling glass. It's my go-to for anniversaries and 'my parents are visiting' lunches. It's genuinely fine dining - treat it as a splurge, book well ahead, and note the smart-casual dress code. Session times, menus and prices shift, so check the Icebergs website before you go rather than trusting an out-of-date number online.

Book for around 45 minutes before sunset in the cooler months: you get the drama of the light on the water without the peak-lunch crowd, and the walk down Notts Avenue afterwards is one of the prettiest in Sydney.
The long-lunch pick: Totti's

Totti's, inside The Royal Bondi on Bondi Road, is where I take a group when the plan is 'sit down at one, leave at four'. It's Merivale's warm, woodfired Italian - the sort of sharing menu built around that pillowy house bread, charcoal-grilled meats and fish, and negronis that arrive a little too easily. The leafy courtyard is made for a crowd - my default for birthdays. Weekends book out, so reserve ahead through the Merivale site.
The pizza-and-porchetta pick: Da Orazio

Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta on Hall Street is the one I send every visitor to. Orazio D'Elia's blistered, wood-fired Neapolitan pizza is the headline, but the move is the focaccia con porchetta - roast pork tucked into pizza bread - which is exactly as good as it sounds. It reopened at Bondi in 2022 and picked up a Chef's Hat in the Good Food Guide the following year, so it's not just a nostalgia play. It's lively, family-friendly and more relaxed (and affordable) than the fine-dining rooms.
The chef's-choice pick: Sean's

Sean's (long known as Sean's Panorama) on Campbell Parade has been a Bondi institution since 1993, and it still feels like eating in someone's home. Chef-owner Sean Moran changes the menu daily around what's good - much of it from his own Bilpin farm - so I just turn up hungry and let the kitchen decide. It's a small room with limited service days, so book directly.
The breakfast pick: bills

No honest Bondi list skips bills. Bill Granger's original sunlit dining room made ricotta hotcakes and creamy scrambled eggs famous worldwide, and a late breakfast here is a proper Bondi ritual. It's popular, so expect a weekend queue - go early, or slide in mid-morning on a weekday.

blocks.title: One honest caveat on 'rankings'
blocks.text: Any list that claims to 'objectively rank' restaurants is really just one crew's taste. Bondi's dining changes fast - venues rebrand, chefs move, hours shift. Treat this as a starting point, and always confirm opening days, menus and prices on each venue's own site before heading down.
How to choose in 30 seconds

items: Want the view and don't mind spending: Icebergs.
Big group, long lunch, Italian sharing plates: Totti's.
Casual, wood-fired, the famous porchetta: Da Orazio.
Trust-the-chef, seasonal, intimate: Sean's.
Classic Bondi breakfast: bills.

items.q: What is the best restaurant in Bondi?
items.a: There's no single winner - it depends on the occasion: Icebergs for an ocean-view splurge, Totti's for a long Italian lunch, Da Orazio for wood-fired pizza and porchetta, Sean's for chef's-choice seasonal cooking, and bills for the classic Bondi breakfast.

items.q: Do I need to book a table in Bondi?
items.a: For Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's, yes - book directly through each venue, especially on weekends and in summer. Da Orazio and bills are more walk-in friendly, but expect a wait at peak times.

items.q: Where can I get the best view while I eat?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, on the headland above the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool, has the standout view over the beach. Time a booking near sunset in the cooler months for the best of it.

items.q: Are there cheaper places to eat in Bondi?
items.a: Plenty. The fine-dining rooms are a splurge, but Da Orazio is more relaxed, and Bondi's cafés, bakeries and casual spots along Hall Street and Gould Street cover great cheap eats. Always check current prices before you go.

items.q: Is Da Orazio still open in Bondi?
items.a: Yes. Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta reopened at its Hall Street, Bondi home in 2022 and earned a Chef's Hat the following year. Check the official Da Orazio website for current opening days and hours.

blocks.text: That's my honest shortlist. Whichever you choose, do what I do - open the venue's own website first, confirm the day and time, and book if you can. Then go early enough to walk it off along the promenade afterwards. That's the real Bondi dining experience.

sources.label: Broadsheet - Da Orazio returns to its original Bondi home

blocks.text: If you're planning a Bondi trip around something special, here's the short answer: our event calendar peaks twice - high summer (January to March) for cinema-on-the-sand and festival energy, and spring (September to early December) for kites, sculpture and ocean swimming. Below is the rhythm I plan my year around - just confirm each event's exact dates on its official page before you book, because they shift every year.

blocks.title: Dates move every year
blocks.text: This is the annual pattern of Bondi's big events, not a promise of specific dates. Organisers set fresh dates each season and sometimes reschedule for weather, so check the official links below for the current year before you commit to travel.
The annual rhythm, month by month

stops.title: Flickerfest & Openair Cinema
stops.detail: Flickerfest, the Academy- and BAFTA-recognised short film festival, screens under the stars at Bondi Pavilion late in the month. Down on the promenade, Openair Cinemas runs its summer season with the surf as your soundtrack.

stops.title: Peak summer on the sand
stops.detail: Long beach days, the tail of the Openair Cinema season, and Bondi at its liveliest - the busiest, warmest stretch of the year.

stops.title: City2Surf
stops.detail: The world's largest fun run - 14km from Hyde Park in the CBD, over Heartbreak Hill, finishing at Bondi Beach. Tens of thousands of runners pour in; a brilliant morning to be a spectator.

stops.title: Festival of the Winds
stops.detail: Bondi's beloved free kite festival, presented by Waverley Council. Giant kites fill the sky above the beach alongside live music, roaming performers and kite-making for kids.

stops.title: Sculpture by the Sea
stops.detail: The free, open-air sculpture exhibition strung along the coastal walk from Bondi to Tamarama - around 100 works over roughly two kilometres of clifftop. One of my favourite fortnights of the year.

stops.title: Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim
stops.detail: The classic point-to-point ocean race down the coast, held early in the month. Whether you swim it or watch from the headland, it's a proper Sydney summer send-off.

blocks.text: The big ones, worth planning a trip around
City2Surf (August)

This is the one that turns Bondi into a finish-line party. Runners and walkers of every ability tackle the 14km from the city, and the beach fills with delighted finishers collecting their medals. Even if you're not running, come down mid-morning. Roads across the eastern suburbs close and buses reroute, so check Transport for NSW and the official City2Surf site for start waves and travel advice.
Sculpture by the Sea (October–November)

For about two and a half weeks each spring, the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk becomes a free open-air sculpture gallery. It's one of the best things Bondi does. It gets very busy on weekends and evenings, so I go on a weekday morning if I can - you get the art, the light and the ocean almost to yourself.
Festival of the Winds (September)

A gloriously simple, free community day: enormous, colourful kites over the beach, food stalls, music and workshops for kids. It's weather-dependent by nature, so check the Waverley Council listing in the lead-up.

items.label: Biggest free events
items.value: Sculpture by the Sea, Festival of the Winds

blocks.text: Whatever you're coming for, leave the car at home. Parking around Bondi is scarce and metered at the best of times, and near-impossible on event days - roads close for City2Surf and crowds swell for Sculpture by the Sea. The 333 and 380 buses, or a short walk from Bondi Junction station, are far less stressful.

You'll also see mentions of a beachside winter ice rink or one-off festivals. Some come and go year to year, so I've left out anything I can't confirm is running now. If a specific event matters to your trip, the Waverley Council 'What's On' page is the most reliable source for it.

items.q: What's the biggest event at Bondi Beach each year?
items.a: For sheer scale, City2Surf in August - the world's largest fun run finishes at Bondi Beach. For visitor draw, Sculpture by the Sea (October–November) pulls hundreds of thousands of people to the free coastal-walk exhibition.

items.q: When is Sculpture by the Sea at Bondi?
items.a: It runs for roughly two and a half weeks from mid-October into early November along the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk, and it's free. Confirm the exact dates on the official Sculpture by the Sea website before you travel.

items.q: Is there an outdoor cinema at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - Openair Cinemas runs a summer season by the beach (typically January to March), and Flickerfest screens short films at Bondi Pavilion in January. Season dates and programs are on their official sites.

items.q: Are Bondi's events free?
items.a: Many of the best are - Festival of the Winds and viewing Sculpture by the Sea both cost nothing. City2Surf, the Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim, Flickerfest and Openair Cinema are ticketed. Check each event's site for current pricing.

items.q: How do I find confirmed dates for this year?
items.a: Each event sets its own dates annually. Use the official links in this article, and cross-check the Waverley Council 'What's On' page, which lists confirmed events happening at Bondi in the current season.

blocks.text: That's the Bondi year as I live it - sun and cinema to start, kites, sculpture and one last big swim to finish. Pin the month that suits you, confirm the dates officially, and you'll catch Bondi at its best.

sources.label: Macquarie Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim

blocks.text: If you're after a genuinely local Sydney run while you're staying near Bondi, the 440 Run Club at Bronte Beach is about as good as it gets - it's free, there's no sign-up, and everyone is welcome, no matter how fast or slow you are. It meets early on Saturday mornings just a couple of kilometres down the coast from Bondi, and honestly it's one of my favourite ways to start a weekend.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bronte Beach (a short walk or drive south of Bondi)

items.label: Good for
items.value: All ages, all abilities - runners and walkers

blocks.text: What the 440 actually is

The club takes its name from the loop it's built around: a roughly 440-metre circuit at Bronte that runners tackle again and again, with a proper hill thrown in to keep you honest. The loop is short, so nobody ever gets left behind on their own - you're always looping back past the rest of the group. But don't let the distance fool you. Repeat that incline enough times in the half-dark and you'll have earned your breakfast.

It started back in 2016 as a small group of mates and has grown into a genuine Bronte institution, with a big, friendly crowd turning up week after week. The whole ethos is inclusivity: you run your pace, walk if you want to, and the faster runners loop back around to sweep up everyone else. There's no fee, no membership card and no pressure - just show up.

The exact start time shifts with the seasons (they genuinely do start in the dark), so before you set your alarm, check the club's Instagram @the_440 for that week's meet time and spot. It saves you standing on a cold beach wondering if you've got the wrong Saturday.
How to get there from Bondi

Bronte sits just south of Bondi, and getting between the two is half the fun. If you're already awake and moving, the Bondi to Bronte stretch of the famous coastal walk is the scenic route - clifftops, ocean on your right, past Tamarama on the way. It's a beautiful warm-up, though allow yourself plenty of time in the dark and watch your footing on the path.

items: On foot: the Bondi–Bronte coastal walk connects the two beaches directly (give yourself a good half hour or so, and take care on the unlit sections pre-dawn).
By bus: several routes run between Bondi and Bronte - check Transport for NSW or the Trip Planner for early-morning services, as weekend timetables are thinner.
By car: there's street parking around Bronte, but it fills fast on weekends, so arriving early genuinely helps.

blocks.title: Come as you are
blocks.text: You don't need to be a 'runner' to belong here. Plenty of people walk the loop, push a pram, or just do a lap or two and then cheer everyone else on. Bring water, wear something you can move in, and that's it.
The bit that makes it special

For me, the running is only half of it. What keeps people coming back is what happens after: the sun coming up over the water, a swim in the Bronte ocean pool to wash off the effort, and a coffee with a crowd of people who were strangers a few Saturdays ago. If you're visiting Sydney, this is a rare chance to slot straight into local life instead of watching it from the outside - and the regulars are a goldmine for tips on where to eat and what to do while you're here.

It's a community-run group rather than a formal business, so the friendliest thing you can do is turn up, say hello, and follow whatever the group's doing on the day. No one's going to hand you a race bib - you just fall in and become part of it.

items.q: Is the 440 Run Club really free?
items.a: Yes. There's no membership fee and nothing to book - it's a free, open, community running group. You simply turn up on the morning.

items.q: Do I need to be a fast or experienced runner?
items.a: Not at all. The club is built around welcoming every ability. The loop is short so no one gets stranded, and plenty of people walk it or do just a lap or two. Beginners are genuinely welcome.

items.q: What time and day does it meet?
items.a: It meets early on Saturday mornings, often before sunrise. The precise start time changes through the year, so check the club's Instagram (@the_440) for the current week's meet time before you head down.

items.q: Where exactly do I go?
items.a: It's based at Bronte Beach, just south of Bondi. The club posts the meeting spot on its social channels - that's the safest way to find the group in the pre-dawn dark.

items.q: What should I bring?
items.a: Comfortable running gear, water, and - if you fancy the tradition - swimmers for a dip in the Bronte ocean pool afterwards and a few dollars for a post-run coffee.

blocks.text: So if you find yourself in Bondi with a free Saturday and an early alarm, wander down to Bronte and jump in. It's free, it's open to everyone, and it might just be the most memorable run - and the friendliest one - of your trip.

sources.label: Why I Run: Trent Knox - Men's Health Australia

blocks.text: If you want to understand Bondi's true character, forget the postcard shots for a minute and scroll the Bondi Local Loop - the neighbourhood Facebook group where a lost cat, a badly parked Tesla and a mystery sea-creature can all become front-page news in the same afternoon. I've spent years lurking (and occasionally posting) in the Loop, so here's my affectionate, thoroughly biased ranking of the moments that went from a local mutter to genuine national headlines.

A quick disclaimer before we dive in: I'm ranking these on sheer memorability and how far the story travelled, not on how important they actually were. That, honestly, is the whole joy of the Loop - the outrage rarely matches the crime.

items.label: What it is
items.value: A community Facebook group for Bondi locals

items.label: Famous for
items.value: Turning tiny local dramas into national news

items.label: Recurring themes
items.value: Parking, rent, beach finds, price gouging

items.label: Best enjoyed with
items.value: A flat white and zero expectations

blocks.text: The categories every Loop legend falls into
After enough scrolling you start to notice the Loop runs on a handful of reliable obsessions. Nearly every viral post fits one of these buckets:

items: Parking justice - the photo-shaming of a double-parked ute, a footpath motorbike or a supermarket-carpark Tesla can run for days.
Rental-crisis horror - a sunroom, a converted laundry or a 'cosy' box advertised at an eye-watering weekly rate.
Mystery on the sand - an 'alien-like' creature, a strange wash-up, or something a beachgoer swears they've never seen before.
Price gouging - a local business allegedly charging way over the odds, from RATs in the lockdown days to a $12 juice.
Small-scale civic outrage - bins, backpackers, buses and beach etiquette.

blocks.text: My top five, counting down

stops.title: The pandemic-era RAT price gouging
stops.detail: Reports of local retailers charging absurd amounts for a single rapid antigen test. It was happening nationwide, but the Loop's collective fury put a Bondi face on it and pushed it up the news agenda.

stops.title: The great sunroom rental saga
stops.detail: A tiny Bondi sunroom listed for rent at a price that made everyone gasp. Slumlords, consider yourselves warned - the Loopers notice.

stops.title: The 'alien-like' creature on the sand
stops.detail: A baffling wash-up that had half the group naming it and the other half googling frantically. Peak Bondi.

stops.title: The endless parking wars
stops.detail: No single post - a whole genre. Nothing unites and divides the Loop like a badly parked car, and the media laps it up every time.

stops.title: The council water-quality panic
stops.detail: A speculative post about swimmers feeling unwell grew until Waverley Council was fielding real media questions. Opinion versus evidence, live.

blocks.title: A note on the 'facts'
blocks.text: Many of these stories were reported by members based on a single photo or a second-hand claim, and figures got repeated long before anyone checked them. I've kept the specifics deliberately loose here - treat the Loop as entertainment first and a news source a distant second. For anything official (water quality, beach closures, local rules), Waverley Council is the source that actually counts.

If you're new to Bondi and want the real pulse of the place, join the Loop but mute notifications. You'll get the gossip and the genuinely useful stuff - lost dogs, storm warnings, tradie recommendations - without your phone buzzing every time someone's affronted by a parked scooter.
Why we can't look away

Under the theatrics, the Loop is doing something quite lovely: it's a village square for a suburb that can feel transient. The same group that will spend 200 comments arguing about a bus seat will also rally in minutes to reunite a lost child with their parents, find a missing cat, or flag a dodgy operator preying on backpackers. The outrage and the warmth come from the same place - people who care, sometimes a little too much, about this patch of coast.
The reaction rarely matches the crime - and that, somehow, is exactly why it works.

So no, I won't pretend the Loop is high journalism. But as a running, real-time diary of Bondi's quirks, obsessions and big-heartedness, nothing else comes close. Long may the mundane and the outrageous keep colliding in our feeds.

items.q: What is the Bondi Local Loop?
items.a: It's a community Facebook group for people who live in and around Bondi. It's part noticeboard, part gossip column - locals post everything from lost pets and storm warnings to parking disputes and strange beach discoveries, and the more colourful posts often get picked up by national media.

items.q: Is the Bondi Local Loop a reliable news source?
items.a: Treat it as entertainment and community chatter rather than verified news. Plenty of viral posts start from a single photo or an unconfirmed claim. For anything official - beach safety, water quality, local rules - check Waverley Council or Surf Life Saving before you rely on it.

items.q: Why do so many Bondi stories go viral?
items.a: Bondi is a small, intensely local place with a global profile, so a tiny neighbourhood drama here carries an instantly recognisable postcode. Add a passionate group of residents who love a debate, and even a parking gripe can end up on national news.

items.q: Can visitors join the group?
items.a: It's aimed at locals, but it's a public-facing group, so newcomers and new residents are generally welcome to request to join. If you're just visiting, it's a fun window into the suburb's personality - expect strong opinions about parking.

blocks.text: If you want something a little different for New Year's Day at Bondi, this is it: a Dutch-flavoured ocean plunge known as the Nieuwjaarsduik, or “New Year's Dive.” On January 1, a crowd of orange-clad swimmers - many of them Dutch expats and friends of the Netherlands - gathers on the sand to run into the Pacific together and wash off the old year. It's part cultural ritual, part joyful excuse for a cold-ish swim, and anyone is welcome to join in.

The Nieuwjaarsduik is a genuine Dutch institution. Back home in the Netherlands, thousands plunge into the freezing North Sea every New Year's Day, traditionally pulling on a bright orange hat - orange being the national colour. Transplanted to Bondi, the ritual keeps the orange and the camaraderie but swaps the icy grey North Sea for a sunny Sydney summer, which, frankly, is a much easier sell.
How to find the plunge

This gathering is community-organised by Bondi's Dutch crowd rather than a ticketed, council-run festival, so I won't pin down an exact meeting time or a fixed spot that could be wrong by the time you read this - those details shift from year to year. In practice it forms up on the main stretch of sand, and you'll spot it a mile off: look for the cluster of orange hats and shirts near the flags. The reliable way to get the confirmed date, time and meeting point for the coming year is to check the organisers' own website and social channels before you head down.

Pack an orange hat or shirt if you can - it's the whole point, and it's how the group finds each other on a packed beach. If you forget, don't stress; nobody's turned away for wearing the wrong colour.
Swim smart on the day

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi is patrolled by Surf Life Saving lifeguards, but New Year's Day brings big crowds and plenty of tired swimmers into the water. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, keep an eye on the kids, and if the surf looks heavy, ease in slowly rather than sprinting in with the pack. A group plunge is a laugh; a rip is not.

A few things worth knowing whether or not you join the dive: Bondi Beach is a permanent alcohol-free and glass-free zone that Waverley Council enforces, New Year's Day included, so any celebrating with a drink happens up on the promenade or inside the venues, not on the sand. January is peak Sydney summer, too - the water is refreshing but the sun is fierce, and the promenade offers almost no shade.

items.label: When
items.value: New Year's Day - confirm the time with the organisers

blocks.text: Getting there

Leave the car at home if you can. Parking near the beach is scarce and metered, and New Year's road closures and clean-up can make the surrounding streets a headache. Public transport is far easier: take a train to Bondi Junction and connect to a bus down to the beach - the 333 and 380 both run to Bondi Beach. Check Transport for NSW for live times, because holiday timetables differ from an ordinary day.

Bring reef-safe sunscreen, a hat for after the swim and your own water bottle. There are public bubblers along the promenade to refill - I've watched too many visitors get fried by 11am with nothing to drink.

items.q: What is the Dutch New Year's Dive at Bondi?
items.a: It's a Bondi version of the Nieuwjaarsduik, the Dutch tradition of plunging into the sea on January 1. A crowd, many of them Dutch expats, wears orange and runs into the ocean together to start the year fresh. Anyone can join.

items.q: Do I have to be Dutch to take part?
items.a: Not at all. It's an open, welcoming swim - locals, tourists and curious passers-by are all encouraged to jump in. Wearing orange is the only real dress code, and even that's optional.

items.q: What time and where does it happen?
items.a: The meeting time and spot are set by the community organisers and can change year to year, so I won't quote a time that might be out of date. It gathers on the main beach near the flags; check the organisers' website and social channels for this year's confirmed details.

items.q: Is it free?
items.a: Yes, joining the swim itself is free. Some organisers sell commemorative orange hats to mark the occasion, but there's no ticket needed to run into the water.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol on the beach to celebrate?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach is a permanent alcohol-free and glass-free zone enforced by Waverley Council, on New Year's Day too. Save the toast for the promenade or a nearby venue.

blocks.text: That's the Dutch twist on a Bondi New Year - no fireworks, no cover charge, just a sea of orange, a bracing swim and a big shared laugh to kick off the year. Wear the hat, swim between the flags, and I'll see you in the water.

Christmas Day at Bondi Beach is exactly the Aussie summer Christmas the postcards promise - sunshine instead of snow, Santa hats over swimmers, and the sand packed with families, backpackers and homesick travellers all sharing the same patch of coast. If you're weighing up whether to come down on the 25th, my short answer is yes: it's one of my favourite days of the year here. But there are a few things I always tell people first, because a Bondi Christmas rewards anyone who turns up prepared.
What Christmas Day actually feels like here

The beach doesn't run on a schedule on Christmas Day - people drift down from mid-morning and stay until the light goes. You'll see picnics and beach barbecues (seafood and salads far more than roast turkey), pick-up volleyball games, surfers in Santa hats, and groups of travellers who've adopted each other for the day. If you're far from home and feeling it, this is the place to be - almost everyone around you is too, and Bondi's come-as-you-are spirit makes it easy to fall in with a crowd.

For a quieter version of the day, walk it off - the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk is stunning in the morning light, and the northern end of the beach near the children's pool is usually calmer than the busy middle.

blocks.title: Bondi is an alcohol-free zone
blocks.text: Bondi Beach is an alcohol-free zone under Waverley Council rules, and glass is a no-go on the sand. Police and rangers do patrol on Christmas Day. Plan for a booze-free beach day and keep the celebrating for a licensed venue or a private place afterwards - check Waverley Council for the current alcohol-free zone details.
Swim safety comes first

Bondi is patrolled every day of the year by Waverley Council's professional lifeguards, and through summer they're backed up by volunteer surf lifesavers. Wherever you swim, get in between the red and yellow flags - that's the stretch the lifeguards have judged safest and are actively watching. If there are no flags up, the message is simple: don't swim.

blocks.title: Alcohol and the ocean don't mix
blocks.text: Every Christmas the lifeguards deal with avoidable rescues, and alcohol is behind a lot of them - it slows your reactions and clouds your judgement, and even confident swimmers get caught out. If you've had a drink, stay out of the water.

The Sydney sun in late December is fierce - much stronger than a northern-hemisphere winter sun, and it catches visitors out. Slip on a shirt, slop on SPF50+ and reapply every couple of hours, grab a hat, and bring your own shade and water. An umbrella and a full bottle will save your whole afternoon.
What's open (and what to plan around)

Christmas Day is a public holiday in New South Wales, so treat the surrounding shops, cafés and venues as closed or on reduced hours unless you've confirmed otherwise. Don't count on grabbing lunch or a coffee on the strip - bring what you need with you. (Any other day of the year it's a different story: our [guide to eating and drinking in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink) covers the whole strip - but the 25th isn't the day to rely on it being open.) Public transport also runs to a holiday timetable, so check Transport for NSW before you set out.

The famous Bondi Icebergs pool and its restaurant, [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), keep their own festive-season hours, which change year to year - check the Icebergs website directly if you're hoping to swim laps or book a table over Christmas.

items: Pack in: sunscreen, hat, water, snacks or picnic food, shade, a rubbish bag.
Leave at home: alcohol and anything glass - both are prohibited on the beach.
Arrive earlier for parking and a good spot; it fills up fast on a warm 25th.
Bin your rubbish or take it with you - the clean-up after big beach days is brutal.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol on Bondi Beach on Christmas Day?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach is an alcohol-free zone under Waverley Council rules, and glass isn't allowed on the sand either. Police and rangers patrol on Christmas Day, so keep any celebrating to a licensed venue.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi on Christmas Day?
items.a: Yes, if you swim between the red and yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and only if you're sober. Bondi is patrolled year-round, but rips are real - if there are no flags, don't swim.

items.q: Will cafés and shops be open?
items.a: Assume most are closed or on reduced hours, since Christmas Day is a NSW public holiday. Bring your own food and water rather than relying on grabbing something nearby. For any other day, our [guide to eating and drinking in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink) has the current picture.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi on Christmas Day?
items.a: Public transport runs to a holiday timetable, so check Transport for NSW before you travel. If you're driving, arrive early - parking near the beach disappears fast on a warm Christmas.

items.q: What's the one thing first-timers forget?
items.a: Sun protection. The late-December Sydney sun is much stronger than a European winter sun. Bring SPF50+, a hat, shade and water, and reapply sunscreen every couple of hours.

blocks.text: That's the whole trick to a Bondi Christmas: come prepared, respect the ocean and the sun, take your rubbish with you, and let the day carry you. Local or traveller far from home, Christmas on Bondi has a way of becoming one you remember for all the right reasons.

sources.label: Waverley Council - Alcohol Free Zones and Alcohol Prohibited Areas

blocks.text: If you're planning a Christmas Day at Bondi, here's the honest local answer: it's the middle of a Sydney summer, so expect warm, bright, often humid weather rather than snow and jumpers - but our December sky is genuinely changeable, and a sunny morning can turn into an afternoon storm without much warning. Because the actual Christmas Day forecast shifts right up until the week itself, the single most useful thing I can tell you is to check the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney 7-day forecast a few days out and plan your beach time around it.
What a Bondi Christmas usually feels like

Christmas here lands in high summer, so the vibe is thongs, sunscreen and a swim rather than mulled wine by a fire. Over the long climate record, December at Observatory Hill - the nearest long-running Bureau site to Bondi - averages a daily maximum around 25°C and overnight lows near 18°C, though individual days swing well either side. Some Christmases are gloriously blue and still; others are warm, muggy and cloud-heavy with a thunderstorm rolling through late in the day. December is also one of our wetter summer months, so a shower isn't unusual.
The pattern I see most often: a bright, calm morning that clouds up as the afternoon heats up, with storm risk building later - which is why locals treat the early hours as the safe bet.

Get down to the sand before mid-morning. The light is soft, the crowds are thinner, parking is easier, and you're beating both the fiercest UV and the afternoon storm risk. By early afternoon the promenade and car parks fill fast.
How to check the real Christmas forecast

I won't pretend to know exactly what this Christmas Day holds - nobody reliably can more than about a week out, and a precise temperature quoted weeks ahead is a guess. Instead, here's how I check it myself:

items: Open the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney forecast (linked in sources) three to five days before Christmas - that's when the daily detail becomes genuinely reliable.
Look at the chance of rain and the wind, not just the top temperature. A southerly buster or an afternoon storm changes your beach plans more than a couple of degrees does.
Check the UV index and sun protection times - in a Sydney summer they routinely reach extreme, even under cloud.
On the day, check Surf Life Saving's Beachsafe or the on-beach flags for surf and hazard conditions before you swim.

blocks.title: Don't be fooled by cloud
blocks.text: Bondi's UV is punishing in December whether the sky is blue or grey - cloud doesn't stop you burning. Slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, slide on sunnies, and reapply after every swim. Overcast Christmas mornings catch visitors out every year.
Planning your Christmas Day at the beach

Whatever the forecast, a few things hold true. Always swim between the red and yellow flags - on a busy Christmas the lifesavers set them where it's safest. Bring water, pack a light rain layer if storms are showing, and remember Bondi is an alcohol-free beach, so keep the celebrating to picnic food. If the afternoon turns grey, it's no disaster - that's when I duck up to a café along Campbell Parade. Bondi is lovely in moody weather too.

items.q: What's the weather usually like at Bondi Beach on Christmas Day?
items.a: It's peak summer, so warm and often humid rather than cold. December at the nearest long-term Bureau station averages a daily maximum around 25°C and overnight lows near 18°C, but individual Christmas Days vary a lot - some are clear and hot, others cloudy with an afternoon shower. Check the BoM Sydney 7-day forecast close to the day for the real picture.

items.q: Does it rain at Bondi at Christmas?
items.a: It can. December is one of Sydney's wetter summer months, and afternoon showers or storms are fairly common even when the morning is dry. It rarely rains all day, though, so many people just plan their swim for the morning.

items.q: When is the best time to go to the beach on Christmas Day?
items.a: The morning, in my experience. It tends to be sunnier and calmer, the UV and afternoon storm risk are lower, and it's much easier to find parking and space on the sand before the midday crowds arrive.

items.q: Where can I get the official Christmas Day forecast for Bondi?
items.a: Use the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney forecast - it covers the Bondi area and becomes reliable about three to five days out. For surf and beach-hazard conditions on the day, check Surf Life Saving's Beachsafe page for Bondi or the flags and signage on the beach.

items.q: Do I still need sunscreen if it's cloudy on Christmas?
items.a: Absolutely. Bondi's summer UV reaches extreme levels and cloud doesn't block it. Apply sunscreen, wear a hat and shirt, seek shade in the middle of the day, and reapply after swimming - cloudy Christmas mornings are exactly when visitors get burnt.

blocks.text: So here's my Christmas wish for you: an easy morning swim between the flags, a shady lunch spot, and a good coffee if the clouds roll in later. Check the Bureau's forecast, pack sunscreen either way, and have a wonderful day. Happy holidays from all of us at Bondi.

sources.label: Bureau of Meteorology - Sydney (Observatory Hill) December climate statistics

blocks.text: Here's the thing every local knows: you cannot see the famous Sydney Harbour fireworks from Bondi Beach. The Bridge and Opera House sit on the far side of the city, behind the headlands, so no patch of sand will conjure them into view. But New Year's Eve in Bondi is no write-off. Want the harbour pyrotechnics? Head to high ground to the west. Want the salt-air, barefoot, party-till-sunrise version? Stay right here - here's how I'd play both.

items.label: Harbour fireworks from Bondi?
items.value: No - wrong side of the headlands

blocks.text: If you want to see the harbour fireworks

Sydney typically runs two shows on 31 December - a family display in the early evening and the main event at midnight, launched from the Harbour Bridge, the Opera House and barges across the harbour. To catch either from our side of town you want elevation - the eastern suburbs look back over the rooftops toward the city.

My first pick is Dudley Page Reserve at Dover Heights, one of the highest points in the eastern suburbs. Waverley Council runs a ticketed, family-friendly celebration up there most years, with a clear line of sight to both the early and midnight fireworks and a no-BYO-alcohol policy that keeps it civil - one of the better-value ways to see the show.

blocks.title: Book ahead - and check this year's details
blocks.text: The Dudley Page event is ticketed and sells out, and capacities, entry times and conditions change year to year - it can even be cancelled for weather or fire risk. Don't turn up on spec: confirm this year's dates, tickets and rules on the Waverley Council events page first.

Further along the coast, Nielsen Park at Vaucluse sits inside Sydney Harbour National Park and gives a more relaxed outlook toward the harbour - lovely if you'd rather picnic than party. Access and NYE arrangements change year to year, so check the official vantage-points map first - the Sydney New Year's Eve site lists which spots are free, ticketed or closed.
If you'd rather celebrate in Bondi itself

Plenty of people I know skip the fireworks scramble and spend the night in Bondi - a brilliant call. The beachfront bars, pubs and restaurants along Campbell Parade book out fast, so if you want a table with a view, reserve it weeks ahead. Walking up on the night rarely works on 31 December.

In recent seasons a New Year's Eve event has run on the sand at Bondi, often pairing a ticketed music show with a free family zone. Whether it runs - and in what form - changes year to year, so treat it as 'check before you commit' rather than a fixture.

The beach is alcohol-free and the promenade gets heaving, so don't BYO onto the sand - you'll be tipped out. Book a venue if you want a drink, get there early, and sort your ride home first: rideshare surges and taxis are gold dust after midnight.

blocks.title: And the morning after?
blocks.text: Bondi does New Year's Day beautifully - a sunrise swim, a long breakfast and a slow walk to Bronte are the perfect antidote to a big night.
Getting there and home

items: Public transport is your friend - roads, parking and clearways near every vantage point are chaos. Plan with Transport for NSW and tap on with an Opal card or contactless.
Trains and buses usually run extended timetables on NYE, but they get packed; leave earlier than feels necessary in both directions.
Bring layers, water and a charged phone - even a balmy night cools off on an exposed headland, and networks clog when everyone messages at midnight.
If you're driving near the harbour, expect to park a long walk away and build that into your timing.

items.q: Can you see the Sydney fireworks from Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - the Bridge and Opera House sit behind the headlands on the far side of the city, so the harbour fireworks aren't visible from Bondi itself. For an eastern-suburbs view you need high ground, and Dudley Page Reserve at Dover Heights is the standout.

items.q: What time are the Sydney New Year's Eve fireworks?
items.a: There are usually two displays - a family show in the early evening and the main midnight one. Exact timings are confirmed each year on the official Sydney New Year's Eve website.

items.q: Is the Dudley Page Reserve event free?
items.a: No - Waverley Council's Dudley Page Reserve celebration is ticketed and typically sells out. Details and prices vary year to year, so book through the Waverley Council events page in advance.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol on Bondi Beach on New Year's Eve?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach is an alcohol-free area, actively enforced on NYE. If you want a drink, book a licensed bar, pub or restaurant along Campbell Parade well ahead of time.

items.q: What's the best way to get home from Bondi after midnight?
items.a: Public transport on extended NYE timetables is usually your most reliable bet - rideshare surges and taxis are scarce after midnight. Plan your route with Transport for NSW before you head out.

blocks.text: So that's the insider's take: for the fireworks, go up high at Dover Heights and book early; for the atmosphere, stay in Bondi and sort your way home in advance. Either way, verify this year's specifics with the official sources above first. See you out there.

blocks.text: If you've heard that Bronte Beach is where Sydney throws its big Christmas Day beach party, you've heard right - for years Bronte has been the go-to gathering for backpackers, working travellers and locals who fancy an outdoor Christmas over a formal lunch. The grassy park behind the sand fills with picnics, cricket and Santa-hatted swimmers, and it has a reputation as one of the city's largest travellers' Christmas get-togethers. Here's what the day is like, and how to do it well - it's a brilliant day out if you turn up prepared and respectful.
Why Bronte on Christmas Day

What makes Bronte different from Bondi on the 25th is the park. A wide band of grass, shade trees and public barbecues sits right behind the beach, so instead of everyone crammed onto the sand you get a proper picnic ground overlooking the ocean. Over the years that made Bronte the natural meeting point for travellers spending Christmas far from home.
What the day actually feels like

People drift down from mid-morning and settle in for the long haul. You'll see picnic rugs and Esky lunches, backyard cricket on the grass, groups swapping stories in a dozen accents, and a steady stream of people cooling off in the ocean and the Bronte rock pool. It's relaxed rather than rowdy - closer to a giant shared picnic than a nightclub - and easy to fall in with a crowd.

blocks.title: Check the alcohol rules before you pack
blocks.text: Bronte's beach and park fall under Waverley Council's alcohol-free and alcohol-prohibited area rules, and police manage the area closely at Christmas. Restrictions and enforcement change year to year, so check Waverley Council for the current rules before you assume you can bring drinks - and leave glass at home regardless.
Swim safety and the sun

Bronte is a patrolled beach, but it's also known for a strong rip near the southern rocks, so treat the water with respect. Swim between the red and yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and if no flags are up, stay out. The calm Bronte rock pool is a good alternative if the surf is big or you've got kids. Never swim after drinking - alcohol is behind a huge share of avoidable rescues, and even strong swimmers get caught out.

The late-December Sydney sun is fierce - much stronger than a northern-hemisphere winter sun, and it catches visitors out fast. Slip on a shirt, slop on SPF50+ and reapply, grab a hat, and bring shade and plenty of water. The shady spots in Bronte Park go early, so arrive in good time if you want a tree.
Leave it better than you found it

The one blemish on Bronte's Christmas is the mess a big crowd can leave behind. Overflowing bins and litter are hard on the wildlife and on the residents who share this beach year-round, and it's easily avoided if everyone chips in:

items: Use the bins provided, and take your rubbish with you if they're full.
Bring reusable plates, cups and cutlery instead of single-use.
Pack a spare bag for your rubbish and recycling.
Respect the local wildlife and the rock platform habitats.
Follow any directions from rangers, lifeguards and police on the day.

blocks.text: Getting there

Christmas Day is a NSW public holiday, so public transport runs to a holiday timetable and nearby cafés and shops are likely closed or on reduced hours - bring your food and water. Check Transport for NSW before you set out. Bronte's parking is limited and fills early on a warm 25th, so a bus or an early arrival saves a lot of circling.

items.q: Is Bronte really Australia's biggest Christmas party?
items.a: Bronte has a long-standing reputation as one of Sydney's largest Christmas Day beach gatherings, especially among travellers, thanks to the big grassy park behind the beach. It's famous rather than officially ranked, so treat 'biggest' as reputation, not a measured fact.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol at Bronte on Christmas Day?
items.a: Bronte's beach and park fall under Waverley Council's alcohol-free and alcohol-prohibited area rules, and enforcement is tight at Christmas. The rules can change year to year, so check Waverley Council for the current details and leave glass at home either way.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bronte on Christmas Day?
items.a: Only between the red and yellow flags, and only if you're sober. Bronte is patrolled but has a strong rip near the southern rocks. If no flags are up, don't swim - the calm rock pool is a safer alternative.

items.q: Will cafés and shops nearby be open?
items.a: Assume most are closed or on reduced hours, since Christmas Day is a NSW public holiday. Bring your own picnic, water and snacks.

items.q: How do I get to Bronte on Christmas Day?
items.a: Public transport runs to a holiday timetable, so check Transport for NSW before you travel. Parking is limited and fills early, so a bus or an early arrival is easier.

blocks.text: That's the trick to a Bronte Christmas: come prepared for sun and surf, check the current rules, and take your rubbish home. Local or traveller far from home, a morning in Bronte Park has a way of becoming one you remember.

blocks.text: When Gwyneth Paltrow put Bondi on her Goop city guide, most of her picks were spot on - Icebergs for dinner, the coastal walk, Bondi Wash and Playa by Lucy Folk. As a local, I'd happily send a first-timer to every one of them. But there was one thing about the beach itself that made me put my flat white down, and it's the reason I can't fully sign off on her guide.
The Goop picks I completely agree with
Her picks skew toward the stylish, design-conscious side of Bondi, and on that front she nailed it. Here's what she flagged and why I'd back each one.

items: Icebergs Dining Room - the clifftop Italian above the famous ocean pool. It's a special-occasion spot with arguably the best view of the beach in Sydney. Book ahead and check the venue for current sittings and dress code.
The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk - the sandstone cliff path south from the beach. It's free, spectacular, and the best introduction to this stretch of coast there is.
Bondi Wash - the local, plant-based home and body brand. A genuinely nice, very Bondi thing to take home.
Playa by Lucy Folk - the jewellery designer's Bondi boutique, mixing her own pieces with hard-to-find labels.

blocks.text: Do the Bondi to Bronte walk early - I aim to be on the path by about 8am. You beat the crowds and the heat, the light on the cliffs is gorgeous, and you can reward yourself with breakfast in Bronte afterwards.

items.label: Gwyneth's Bondi picks
items.value: Icebergs, coastal walk, Bondi Wash, Playa by Lucy Folk

items.label: The disagreement
items.value: Steering dip-seekers to the pool over the ocean itself

items.label: Coastal walk
items.value: Free, clifftop path - Bondi south to Bronte

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags

blocks.text: The one we can't agree with

Here's the sticking point. For anyone whose mind is set on getting wet, the guide leans heavily on the sheltered Icebergs pool - a day pass and some laps - rather than the ocean itself, and the impression it leaves is that Bondi is a place to sunbathe more than to swim. As someone who swims here year-round, that's the bit I can't let stand.
Bondi isn't a beach you look at. It's a beach you get in.

Bondi is one of Australia's great swimming beaches. Generations of Sydneysiders learned to read the surf here, the Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club is the oldest in the world, and on any given morning you'll see everyone from nippers to eighty-year-old ocean swimmers in the water. I suspect Gwyneth simply caught a big-swell day - Bondi does get punchy surf and rips, and on those days the water is for the confident only. But that's a specific day, not the beach's character.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: The one caveat I'll happily agree with is safety. Bondi has rip currents, including the famous Backpackers' Rip near the southern end by the walk. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where the lifeguards patrol. If you're unsure, ask a lifeguard - they'd much rather answer a question than run a rescue.

And to be fair, when she skipped the surf she headed for the Icebergs pool at the southern end - a brilliant call. It lets you swim laps in salt water with the waves crashing over the edge, no rip-reading required. I just wouldn't want a single choppy afternoon to convince anyone that Bondi is only for lying on a towel.
How I'd actually spend a Gwyneth-inspired day

stops.detail: Start early along the cliff path while it's quiet, then loop back.

stops.title: A proper swim
stops.detail: Between the flags on the main beach, or laps at the Icebergs pool if the surf's up.

stops.title: Bondi Wash & Playa
stops.detail: Wander Gould and Hall Streets for the design-led shops Goop loved.

stops.title: Dinner at Icebergs
stops.detail: Book ahead; arrive for golden hour over the water.

items.q: What did Gwyneth Paltrow recommend in Bondi?
items.a: On Goop, she highlighted dinner at Icebergs Dining Room, the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk, the Bondi Wash store and Playa by Lucy Folk. As a local I'd happily recommend all four.

items.q: What was the recommendation you disagree with?
items.a: The way the guide nudges anyone wanting a dip toward the sheltered Icebergs pool rather than the ocean, leaving the impression that Bondi is more for sunbathing than swimming. Bondi is one of Australia's iconic swimming beaches; a rough big-swell day can give a misleading first impression.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach actually safe to swim at?
items.a: Yes, when you swim between the red-and-yellow flags where lifeguards patrol. Bondi does have rip currents, including the Backpackers' Rip near the southern end, so the flags matter. If in doubt, ask a lifeguard about conditions.

items.q: Where should I swim if the surf looks rough?
items.a: Head to the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool at the southern end. It's filled with sea water, sheltered from the rips, and you can swim laps while waves break over the edge. Check the Icebergs website for current public swimming times.

items.q: Is the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk free?
items.a: Yes. The clifftop path south from Bondi is free and open to the public. It's one of Sydney's best walks - go early to beat the crowds and the midday sun.

blocks.text: So: four recommendations, three enthusiastic yeses, and one gentle correction. Take Gwyneth's guide, hit the walk, browse the shops, book Icebergs - but don't you dare skip the swim. That's the whole point of Bondi.

blocks.text: New Year's Day is my favourite day to be at Bondi. While the rest of Sydney sleeps off the fireworks, the beach wakes up soft and golden, the water is clean and cool, and there's a quiet camaraderie among everyone who made it down for a swim. Here's how I'd spend it - an early dip, a slow breakfast, and a long lunch with the Pacific glittering below.

Here's what first-timers get wrong: January 1 at Bondi isn't a party on the sand. Bondi Beach is a permanent alcohol-free and glass-free zone that Waverley Council enforces, so the celebrating happens on the promenade and inside the venues, not on the beach. Once you know that, the day falls into place.
Start with the swim

My New Year's Day ritual is a morning ocean swim - nothing washes off the old year like cold salt water. For laps, the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool at the south end is the classic choice; check their site for swim hours and fees, which vary, and the pool sometimes closes for swell. If you'd rather just float, the calmer water is usually down the north end near the flags. When you climb out, [The Crabbe Hole](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-crabbe-hole) - the tiny café tucked beneath the Icebergs pool - does the best post-swim coffee on this side of the beach, if you can beat the locals to a stool.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi is patrolled by Surf Life Saving lifeguards, but rips are real and New Year's Day brings big, sometimes tired crowds into the water. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, and if the surf looks heavy, the Icebergs pool or the gentler north corner is the smarter call.
The long lunch - Bondi's real New Year tradition

The heart of New Year's Day here is a long lunch with a view. [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), over the south end since it opened in 2002, has long been the glamorous centre of Bondi's New Year and still puts on a special sitting for the day. Other clifftop and beachfront restaurants run festive lunches too - details change every year, so check each venue's own site for this year's plans.

And if Icebergs is booked out (it goes early), Bondi has plenty of other tables with the Pacific in view. [Sean's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/seans) is the north end's quietly iconic long-lunch institution, [North Bondi Fish](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-fish) sits right above the sand where the promenade curves north, and [Bondi Trattoria](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-trattoria) has watched the beach from Campbell Parade for decades. For the full sweep of tables with an ocean view, browse our guide to [Bondi's beachfront and ocean-view dining](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach) - then book whichever one calls to you, direct.

blocks.title: Book direct, and book early
blocks.text: New Year's Day menus, prices and session times at these venues change every year and sell out fast - often weeks ahead. I won't quote a price that might be stale; check each venue's website or booking page and reserve directly.

For the same southern view without the fine-dining price tag, [The Bergs Bistro](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-bergs-bistro-bondi-icebergs-club) - one flight up in the Bondi Icebergs Club, just below the famous Dining Room - is the local's-know option: honest food, the same clifftop outlook, and far easier on the New Year budget. Sign in at the door and book ahead, because it fills up too.

If a set menu isn't your speed, Bondi's cafés along Campbell Parade and Hall Street do a roaring recovery-brunch trade on January 1. [Lox Stock & Barrel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lox-stock-and-barrel) on Hall Street and [Speedos Cafe](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) up the north end are two of my go-tos for eggs and strong coffee, but there's no shortage of poached eggs a short walk from the sand - our full guide to [Bondi's best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) has the rest. Just expect a wait, and be kind to the staff.

Bring a hat, reef-safe sunscreen and your own water bottle. January is peak Sydney summer and the promenade offers almost no shade - I've watched too many visitors get fried by 11am. There are public bubblers to refill along the beach.
Getting there (leave the car at home)

Don't drive to Bondi on New Year's Day if you can avoid it. Parking is scarce and metered, and streets near the beach are often hit by New Year's road closures and clean-up. Public transport is easier: take a train to Bondi Junction, then a bus - the 333 and 380 both run to Bondi Beach. Check Transport for NSW for live timetables, as holiday services differ from a normal day.

Our [Bondi eat & drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) lists every café, restaurant, bar and bakery on the beach - 160+ venues you can filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with, so whether you're after a clifftop lunch, a recovery brunch or a quiet coffee, you can find the right table before you head down.

items.q: Can you drink alcohol on Bondi Beach on New Year's Day?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach is a permanent alcohol-free and glass-free zone enforced by Waverley Council, on New Year's Day too. The celebrating happens inside the venues and up on the promenade, not on the sand.

items.q: Is Icebergs open on New Year's Day?
items.a: Icebergs has long marked New Year's Day, these days as a relaxed sit-down lunch. Sittings, menus and prices change each year and book out early, so check its website and reserve directly. If the Dining Room is full, the more casual Bergs Bistro in the same building, or other ocean-view rooms like Sean's and North Bondi Fish, are worth a call.

items.q: What's the best time to go to Bondi on New Year's Day?
items.a: Early. A swim before roughly 10am means calmer water, easier café tables and a parking spot if you must drive. By midday the beach and cafés are packed.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi on New Year's Day?
items.a: Take public transport. Catch a train to Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus to the beach. Holiday timetables differ, so check Transport for NSW first and expect road closures near the beach.

items.q: Is it worth going to Bondi on New Year's Day?
items.a: Absolutely, if you go for the right reasons - a clean morning swim, a slow brunch and a long lunch with an ocean view. It's a calmer, more local celebration than New Year's Eve.

blocks.text: That's my New Year's Day: swim early, eat slowly, book ahead and let the beach set the pace. Leave the fireworks-night frenzy behind and you'll find the version of Bondi we locals quietly keep for ourselves. Happy new year - see you in the water.

If you only do one thing at the southern end of Bondi, make it Icebergs - the cliff-hugging ocean pool where waves crash straight over the lap lanes and swimmers plough on regardless. It's part public pool, part winter-swimming institution, part fine-dining destination, and after years living around the corner I still rate it the most photographed 50 metres of water in Australia. Here's how I'd tackle the whole complex: pool, bistro, and the famous dining room upstairs.

items.label: Where
items.value: 1 Notts Ave, southern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Closed
items.value: Thursdays for cleaning (tides permitting in summer)

items.label: Best for
items.value: Ocean swims, sunset drinks, a special-occasion lunch

blocks.text: The pool: where locals actually swim

The Bondi Baths are carved into the rocks at the beach's quiet southern corner, and the setup is simple: a full 50-metre saltwater lap pool refreshed by the ocean, plus a smaller shallow pool that's perfect for little kids. Lifeguards are on duty during opening hours, there's a sauna and hot showers, and towel and locker hire if you've turned up empty-handed. On a big swell the sea washes over the eastern wall - which is why the underwater footage from here goes viral every winter.

Admission is refreshingly cheap for something this iconic: as at August 2026 it's $10 for adults, $7 for kids and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in your admission, and multi-visit passes if you're staying a while. Prices and hours shift seasonally and the pool closes Thursdays for cleaning (in summer, when tides permit, it sometimes opens Thursdays - their words, not ours), so I always check icebergs.com.au the morning of a swim rather than trust a number read online months ago.

Go early. I love a 7am lap when the sun is coming up and the pool is nearly empty - by mid-morning in summer the deck fills with sunbathers and the lanes get busy. The pool also closes for swim-club events on some weekends, so check the club's site first.

blocks.title: Pool and dining room are different bookings
blocks.text: The pool is walk-up entry (no booking). The upstairs Dining Room and Bar is a separate business with its own reservations - you don't need to swim to eat there, but you can't wander up in your swimmers for a table.
A club born in winter

The Bondi Icebergs Swimming Club was founded in 1929 by local lifesavers who wanted to stay fit through the cold months, and winter swimming has been its heart ever since. Membership famously hinges on turning up to swim right through the Sydney winter - the stubborn, salty tradition that makes Bondi, Bondi. On opening day each season, members still toss chunks of ice into the pool to earn the name. You don't need to be a member to swim, though - the pool is open to all.
Eating and drinking: the dining room vs the bistro

There are two ways to eat here, and people mix them up constantly. Upstairs is [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), the glass-walled modern-Italian restaurant opened by restaurateur Maurice Terzini in 2002. It's a proper special-occasion room - floor-to-ceiling views down the length of the beach, a serious wine list, and prices to match - and still one of the beach's definitive [date-night tables](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach). Book ahead, dress up a little, and aim for a window table at golden hour. Menus change often, so I check idrb.com for the current offering before promising anyone a specific dish.

If you want the same view for a fraction of the price, [The Bergs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-bergs-bistro-bondi-icebergs-club) - the club's own bistro one floor down - is the local's move: relaxed, easy on the wallet, and one of the more reliably [family-friendly places to eat](/bondi-eat-and-drink/family-friendly-bondi-beach) on this stretch of beach.
More ways to eat at the southern end

You don't have to book a table to eat well at this corner. For a coffee without the swim, head to the base of the building: [The Crabbe Hole](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-crabbe-hole) is the pocket-sized café tucked into the rocks right below the pool, and I rate its takeaway coffee as some of the best-positioned in Bondi - grab one and drink it on the boulders with the swimmers churning past below. And if it's really the ocean view you're chasing rather than Icebergs itself, the whole beach is lined with it: our guide to [Bondi's beachfront and ocean-view dining](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach) rounds up every table where the water does the talking.

For the postcard photo of the pool with the whole beach curving behind it, walk up onto the start of the Bondi to Bronte coastal path. That elevated clifftop angle is the shot everyone recognises - and it's free.

items.q: Do I have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The pool is open to the public - as at August 2026, entry is $10 for adults, $7 for kids and $30 for a family pass. Membership of the Icebergs Swimming Club is a separate thing tied to winter-swimming commitments - you don't need it to swim.

items.q: How much does the Icebergs pool cost and what are the hours?
items.a: As at August 2026, entry is $10 for adults, $7 for children and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in admission. Because prices and hours change seasonally, and the pool closes Thursdays for cleaning (tides permitting in summer), check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au before you go.

items.q: Is the swimming pool the same as the famous restaurant?
items.a: No - they're separate. The Dining Room and Bar is the upmarket modern-Italian restaurant upstairs (book at idrb.com); the pool is the walk-up ocean baths below. There's also The Bergs, the casual, cheaper club bistro one floor down, if you just want lunch with the view.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs good for kids?
items.a: Yes. Alongside the 50-metre lap pool there's a smaller, shallower children's pool, and lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. The Bergs bistro is family-friendly too, though the pool gets crowded on hot summer afternoons.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: Icebergs typically closes on Thursdays for cleaning (with summer exceptions when tides permit), and occasionally for swim-club events or heavy seas. Check the official Pool Conditions page the day you visit.

blocks.title: Eating your way around the whole beach?
blocks.text: Icebergs is one unforgettable corner - but it's a big beach. For everywhere else to eat and drink, browse the full [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink): 160+ cafés, bakeries, bars and restaurants you can filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with.

That's the whole complex: swim the ocean pool, warm up in the sauna, grab a bistro lunch, then linger over a drink as the light turns gold over Bondi - which is exactly why Icebergs stays my favourite corner of the beach.

The short answer: Bondi Beach is the sand - the world-famous coastal strip you picture when someone says "Bondi" - while Bondi Junction is a busy inland shopping and transport hub about 2 kilometres uphill, with no beach in sight. They're two separate suburbs, roughly a 10–15 minute bus ride apart, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake I see visitors make when they book accommodation or plan their day.

I've lived around here long enough to have given these directions more times than I can count - usually to someone standing at Bondi Junction with a suitcase, wondering where the ocean went. So here's how the two differ and, more usefully, which one you actually want.
