blocks.text: Bondi Beach: the one you've seen on postcards

Bondi Beach is the coastal suburb about 7 kilometres east of Sydney's CBD. This is the crescent of golden sand, the Icebergs pool, the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk, Campbell Parade's cafés and the surf culture the name is famous for. It's low-rise, salty and relaxed - people come here to swim, sunbake, surf, walk the cliffs and eat with a sea view.

Crucially, Bondi Beach has no train station. You reach it by bus, car, bike or on foot. So if your reason for coming to Sydney is the beach, this is the suburb you want to be near - ideally within walking distance of Campbell Parade or Bondi Road.
Bondi Junction: the shopping and transport hub

Bondi Junction sits inland, roughly 2 kilometres up the hill from the sand and about 6–7 kilometres from the CBD. It's the urban, high-rise end of "Bondi": office towers, apartment blocks and the enormous Westfield Bondi Junction shopping centre. There is no beach here - just a genuinely excellent place to shop, and the main gateway you pass through on the way to the coast.

What makes the Junction matter to visitors is transport. It's the eastern terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs line, so trains from Central and the city terminate here, and the bus–rail interchange fans out to the beaches. In practice, most people arriving by train ride to Bondi Junction and then hop on a bus for the final leg down to the sand.

blocks.title: Getting from the Junction to the Beach
blocks.text: From the interchange above Bondi Junction station, frequent buses run down to Bondi Beach - the 333 is the fast, limited-stops service most visitors use. The ride is short, but times shift with traffic, so check live routes and departures in the Transport for NSW trip planner before you head down.
So which one do you actually want?

It comes down to why you're here. If you've come for sand, surf and the coastal walk, base yourself at Bondi Beach - waking up a two-minute stroll from the water beats a daily bus commute every time. If you're after big-brand shopping, a train connection into the city, or simply cheaper, quieter accommodation with easy transport, Bondi Junction is a smart, practical base.

items: Here for the beach, surf or coastal walk → stay at Bondi Beach.
Here for shopping, city train links or better-value stays → Bondi Junction works well.
Arriving by train → you'll pass through Bondi Junction and bus down to the beach.
Driving → the beach has limited, pricey parking; the Junction's Westfield car park is larger.

blocks.text: Double-check your booking says "Bondi Beach" and not "Bondi Junction" if the beach is your priority. I've met travellers who booked a Junction hotel expecting to open the curtains to the ocean - and got a shopping-centre view and a bus timetable instead.

items.q: How far is Bondi Junction from Bondi Beach?
items.a: About 2 kilometres - a short bus ride, a quick drive in light traffic, or a 25–30 minute downhill walk. Frequent buses, including the 333, connect the two; check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current routes and times.

items.q: Does Bondi Beach have a train station?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach has no train station. The nearest is Bondi Junction, the terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs line, and from there you take a bus down to the sand.

items.q: Can you walk from Bondi Junction to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes. It's about 2 kilometres, mostly downhill toward the water, and takes roughly 25–30 minutes. It's an easy walk down; the uphill return is a bit more of a workout, so many people bus back.

items.q: Should I stay in Bondi Beach or Bondi Junction?
items.a: Stay at Bondi Beach if the ocean and beach lifestyle are the point. Choose Bondi Junction if you want major shopping, a direct train line into the city, or more affordable, transport-friendly accommodation.

items.q: Is Bondi Junction the same as Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - they're two distinct suburbs. Bondi Beach is the coastal one with the sand and surf; Bondi Junction is an inland shopping and transport hub with no beach, about 2 kilometres away.

blocks.text: Once the map's straight in your head, the two work brilliantly together: shop and catch your train at the Junction, then ride ten minutes downhill to swim and walk the cliffs. Same name, two very different Bondis - and now you know which is which.

Ask me where to eat in Bondi and I'll give the same answer every time: the best table is one where you can smell the salt and hear the surf. From Sean Moran's dining room above North Bondi to a wood-fired pizza on Hall Street, here's my personal top ten - the places I send hungry friends to.

One honest caveat first: Bondi's food scene moves fast, and hours, menus and prices shift with the seasons. I've linked each venue's own page below - check the details there before you set your heart on a booking. Now, the good stuff.

blocks.title: Looking for more than ten?
blocks.text: This is my personal shortlist, but Bondi has well over 160 places to eat and drink. Browse the full [Bondi eat and drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) and filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with - date night, family, cheap eats - to find exactly the right table.
The special-occasion tables
1. Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Perched above the ocean pool at the south end, [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar) is the Bondi view everyone pictures - the pool below, the whole crescent of beach beyond. It's polished Italian, a genuine occasion and one of Bondi's great [date-night rooms](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach). Book ahead and dress up; if the budget's tight, come for a drink at the bar and soak up the same view.
2. Sean's

Sean Moran has cooked on this North Bondi corner since 1993, and [Sean's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/seans) is still my sentimental favourite. The menu is short, handwritten and driven by whatever's best that week, much of it from his own farm in the Blue Mountains. It feels less like a restaurant than being fed generously in someone's home.
3. North Bondi Fish

Right on Ramsgate Avenue with the sand at your feet, [North Bondi Fish](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-fish) is where I bring visitors who want seafood with a proper beach view. Oysters, whole fish, a crisp glass of white - long lunches here slide happily into the afternoon. It's my pick of Bondi's [beachfront and ocean-view tables](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).
Brunch, pizza and the everyday classics
4. bills, Bondi

Bill Granger's ricotta hotcakes and creamy scrambled eggs more or less wrote the rulebook for Sydney brunch, and the Hall Street [bills](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bills-bondi-beach) room is bright, buzzy and reliably lovely. Yes, it's popular; yes, it's worth it - and it still sits near the top of my guide to [Bondi's best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach).
5. Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta

[Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/da-orazio-pizza-porchetta) is back on Hall Street, now with the little wine bar Orazietto next door. Blistered wood-fired pizza, that legendary porchetta and a properly Italian racket of a room - my go-to for a lively group dinner.
6. Bondi Trattoria

The "Tratt" - [Bondi Trattoria](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-trattoria) - is a Campbell Parade institution: pasta, pizza and people-watching from tables that spill toward the beach. It isn't reinventing anything; it's just a warm, dependable Italian that's fed locals for decades. I love it for an unfussy weeknight spaghetti.
Cafés, casual bites and something sweet
7. Speedos Cafe

Tucked at the quiet north end, [Speedos](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) is the classic post-swim café - acai bowls, big breakfasts and a health-leaning menu, steps from the sand near Ben Buckler. Grab a table outside and watch the ocean-pool crowd stroll by. It's one of my favourites among [Bondi's best cafés and coffee](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach).
8. Porch and Parlour

Just around the corner, [Porch and Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) has done generous, produce-led breakfasts and lunches for years. It's my pick when I want somewhere calmer than the main drag but still unmistakably North Bondi.
9. Totti's Bondi

The Merivale crowd's Bondi trattoria, [Totti's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/tottis-bondi), is all about pillowy wood-fired bread and a table full of Italian sharing plates. A fun, boisterous room - best with friends and no plans for the afternoon.
10. Gelato Messina

No Bondi food day of mine ends without gelato, and [Gelato Messina](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/gelato-messina-bondi)'s Hall Street scoop shop is the reward after a long beach walk. The flavour board changes constantly, so just ask what's new - and for more sweet endings, see our guide to [Bondi's best bakeries and sweets](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach).

For beachfront tables at the popular spots - weekend brunch at bills, a sunset seat at North Bondi Fish - book a few days ahead or arrive on opening. Walk in at 12:30 on a sunny Saturday and you'll join the queue with everyone else.
Beyond the top ten

Ten is never quite enough in Bondi. When friends want something the list above doesn't cover - a cheap feed after the beach, a cold beer with a crowd, seafood without the white tablecloth - here's where I point them, with the full directory only a tap away.

items: Casual seafood: [Fish Shop](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/fish-shop) on Hall Street, or the tiny [Crabbe Hole](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-crabbe-hole) wedged beside the Icebergs pool for a coffee and a roll with the swimmers.
Cheap eats: a falafel wrap from [Sabbaba](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sabbaba-bondi-beach) never misses - the rest of my [cheap eats](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach) picks are here.

A drink with the crowd: the corner rooftop at [Hotel Ravesis](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hotel-ravesis), or a beer and a band at the [Beach Road Hotel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/beach-road-hotel) - more in our [best bars](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-bars-bondi-beach) and [Bondi pubs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) guides.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.text: Opening hours, session times and menus in Bondi change often. I've linked each venue's page in the directory - always confirm current details and book directly with the venue rather than trusting a number in any guide, including this one.

items.q: What is the most famous restaurant in Bondi Beach?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the most iconic, thanks to its perch above the ocean pool and its sweeping view across the beach. Sean's and bills are close behind as long-standing institutions.

items.q: Where's the best breakfast or brunch in Bondi?
items.a: bills on Hall Street is the classic for hotcakes and scrambled eggs. For somewhere quieter, Porch and Parlour and Speedos Cafe at the north end do generous, produce-led breakfasts near the sand. See more in our [breakfast and brunch guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach).

items.q: Do I need to book restaurants in Bondi?
items.a: For the sit-down favourites - Icebergs, Sean's, Da Orazio and Totti's - yes, especially on weekends and in summer. Cafés like Speedos and Porch and Parlour are walk-in, but expect a wait at peak brunch times.

items.q: Where can I eat with a beach view in Bondi?
items.a: North Bondi Fish sits right on the sand at Ramsgate Avenue, and Icebergs overlooks the ocean pool at the south end. Bondi Trattoria's front tables also look out to the water - our [beachfront and ocean-view dining guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach) rounds up the rest.

items.q: Is there good pizza in Bondi?
items.a: Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta on Hall Street is the local benchmark for wood-fired pizza. Bondi Trattoria and Totti's are also solid for a relaxed Italian dinner.

items.q: Are there good vegan or vegetarian options in Bondi?
items.a: Plenty - Bondi is one of Sydney's better neighbourhoods for plant-based eating, from acai and smoothie bowls to full vegan menus. Our [vegan and vegetarian guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/vegan-vegetarian-bondi-beach) has the current picks.

blocks.text: That's my ten, plus a few more for good measure - splurge-worthy views, honest neighbourhood classics and a scoop of gelato to finish. Eat from the north end to the south and you'll have tasted the real Bondi, salt air and all. When you want to go deeper, the [full eat-and-drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) has every table on the beach.

If you only have time for one stretch of Sydney coastline, make it the Eastern Suburbs beaches - Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly, Gordons Bay, Coogee and Maroubra, strung along about six kilometres of headland. I've walked this coast in every mood, and the short version I give friends is: Bondi for the buzz, Bronte for a swim with the kids, Clovelly and Gordons Bay for snorkelling, Coogee to finish with a beer. Here's how I'd actually spend the day.

items.label: How I get around
items.value: The clifftop coastal walk on foot

blocks.text: Start at Bondi - the famous one, for good reason

Bondi is the beach that ends up on the postcards, and I never tire of it - a wide sweep of pale sand with a flagged swimming area, a busy café promenade and a sea pool at each end. The Icebergs pool at the southern tip is the iconic one; swimming a few laps there with waves crashing over the wall is a rite of passage. Sessions and lane availability change seasonally, so check the Icebergs website before you go rather than trusting a timetable I might have out of date.
Bondi's parking is a headache on any warm weekend. I'll often park near Coogee or take the bus, walk north to Bondi, then stroll back - you get the whole coast twice and never circle a car park.
The walk south: Tamarama, Bronte and the sea baths

From Bondi's southern end the coastal walk begins - my favourite way to see the lot. First up is Tamarama - locals call it 'Glamarama' - a small, pretty pocket beach hemmed by cliffs. It's beautiful, but the surf can be powerful and the rips serious: swim only between the flags when it's patrolled, and if in doubt, just press on.

A little further on is Bronte, which might be the most complete beach on the coast for a family day: a patrolled surf beach, a grassy park with barbecues and shade, a kiosk row, and the Bronte Baths carved into the rocks for a sheltered swim when the shore break is dumping. It's the classic midpoint of the walk.

blocks.title: Read the beach before you swim
blocks.text: Conditions on this coast change fast - Tamarama, Bronte and Maroubra can all throw strong rips. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags at a patrolled beach, and check the daily surf report on the Beachsafe app (Surf Life Saving Australia) before you get in.
The snorkelling middle: Clovelly and Gordons Bay

This is the part visitors often miss, and I'd send you here first. Clovelly isn't a wide sandy beach at all - it's a long, narrow bay between two rock shelves, with flat concrete edges to lay a towel on and steps into calm, clear water. Because it's so sheltered it's brilliant for kids learning to snorkel, with plenty to see from little fish to the resident blue gropers. Around the headland, Gordons Bay is a quiet cobbled cove with a marked underwater nature trail for snorkellers and divers. Both sit inside the Bronte–Coogee Aquatic Reserve, so it's look-don't-touch - no fishing or collecting.
Finish at Coogee (with Maroubra as a bonus)

Coogee is where I like to end up: a friendly, family-sized beach with a Norfolk-pine promenade made for an evening walk and pubs and cafés a block back for a well-earned feed. It's also home to a cluster of ocean pools - Wylie's Baths on the southern headland, and McIver's Baths, a historic women-and-children's swimming spot. Entry fees and hours for the tidal pools change, so check locally on the day. If you've still got legs, Maroubra sits further south - a long, surf-serious beach that's less crowded, with a skate park and playground.

items.q: What's the best order to visit the Eastern Suburbs beaches?
items.a: I walk north-to-south: Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly, Gordons Bay, then Coogee, with Maroubra as an optional extra beyond. Finishing at Coogee means plenty of pubs and cafés for a late lunch or sunset drink.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: It's roughly six kilometres one way and most people take about two hours at a relaxed pace, longer with swims and coffee stops. It's a sealed clifftop path with some stairs - just bring water, sun protection and decent shoes.

items.q: Which beach is best for snorkelling?
items.a: Clovelly and Gordons Bay. Clovelly's sheltered channel is calm and easy for kids, while Gordons Bay has a marked underwater nature trail. Both sit inside the Bronte–Coogee Aquatic Reserve, so it's look-but-don't-take.

items.q: Which beaches suit young families?
items.a: Bronte and Clovelly are my picks - Bronte has a grassy park, barbecues and the sheltered Bronte Baths, and Clovelly's calm water is ideal for little swimmers. Coogee is gentle too.

items.q: Do I need to pay or book anything?
items.a: The beaches and the coastal walk are free. Some ocean pools charge a small entry fee and hours vary seasonally, so check on the day. Parking is the real cost on warm weekends - buses or an early start save the stress.

blocks.text: That's the whole coast in a day: Bondi's energy, the cliff path through Bronte's parkland, the clear water at Clovelly and Gordons Bay, and Coogee as the light goes gold. Bring a towel, sunscreen and time to spare - it's the stretch of Sydney I never tire of showing people.

sources.label: Destination NSW - Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk
Randwick City Council - Beaches and coast

blocks.text: The Bondi Farmers Market runs every Saturday morning, 9am to 1pm, in the grounds of Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade - just across the road from the sand. It's my favourite way to start a Bondi weekend: a coffee in one hand, a bag slowly filling with fruit, warm bread and flowers, and the ocean glinting nearby. If you only do one local thing on a Saturday here, make it this.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Beach Public School, Campbell Parade & Warners Ave

blocks.text: When and where to find it

You'll find the market in the schoolyard on the corner of Campbell Parade and Warners Avenue, at the northern end of Bondi Beach, across the road from the promenade. It slots perfectly into a beach morning: market first while it's cool, then the sand once you've stashed your shopping. It's open-air and runs rain or shine, so I'd never let a grey forecast put me off. That said, times can shift around public holidays, so if you're travelling a long way, check the official Bondi Farmers Market page before you set out.

blocks.title: Saturday farmers' market vs. Sunday market
blocks.text: Two different markets share the same schoolyard. Saturday is the Farmers Market - fresh food, produce and breakfast, 9am–1pm. Sunday is the general Bondi Markets, a bigger fashion, vintage and homewares affair with different hours. If you've come for fruit and veg, come on Saturday.
What you'll find at the stalls
The whole idea here is fresh and local - where possible, the people who grow or make the food are the ones selling it. On a typical Saturday you can expect a spread like this:

items: Seasonal fruit and vegetables, often picked a day or two earlier
Organically grown meat and poultry
Just-picked flowers to carry home
Artisan breads and pastries, still warm if you're early
Farmstead cheeses, homemade jams, olive oils, herbs and spices
Fresh seafood
Barista coffee, juices and hot street-food breakfasts to eat on the spot

blocks.text: It's as much a place to eat as to shop. I'll grab a coffee and something hot, do a slow loop to see what looks good that week, then double back for the produce. Buying by the season is half the fun - you learn what's actually good right now instead of what a supermarket flies in year-round. And if the warm loaves and pastries give you a taste for it, Bondi has a serious [bakery and pastry scene](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach) beyond the market too.

Come between 9 and 10am if you can. The bread and pastry stalls are fullest, the coffee queues short, and you'll beat both the late-morning crowd and the scramble for a park. Bring a tote and some cash - many stalls take card, but not all.
Where to eat and drink around the market

The market itself makes a lovely grazing breakfast, but if you'd rather settle in with a proper plate and a second coffee, the northern end of Bondi is packed with good spots a few minutes' walk away. A handful I happily send people to:

items: [Porch & Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) - a long-running North Bondi brunch favourite, just back from the sand near Warners Ave.
[North Bondi Fish](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-fish) - right on the promenade at the north end when you want something a little more special.
[Speedos Cafe](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) - a relaxed, health-leaning local café up toward the Ben Buckler point.
[Sundays Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sundays-bondi) - bright and easygoing for an unhurried all-day breakfast.
[bills Bondi Beach](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bills-bondi-beach) - the Hall Street all-day dining institution, a short stroll back from the beach.

blocks.text: For the full picture, we keep a running guide to Bondi's [best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) and its [best cafés and coffee](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) - handy for planning the sit-down part of your morning before or after a market loop.
Making a morning of it
The market pairs beautifully with everything else at this end of Bondi. Here's roughly how I'd shape an easy Saturday around it.

stops.title: Coffee and a loop
stops.detail: Arrive early, grab a coffee and walk the whole market once before you buy anything.

stops.title: Breakfast + produce
stops.detail: Eat something hot on the spot, then circle back for fruit, veg, bread and flowers.

stops.title: Across to the beach
stops.detail: Stash your bags, cross Campbell Parade and walk the promenade or dip your toes in.

stops.title: Wander north
stops.detail: Head up toward the Bondi to Bronte coastal path, or into the cafés along the northern end for a second coffee.

blocks.title: Parking is the tricky bit
blocks.text: Street parking around Campbell Parade fills fast on a fine Saturday and is metered or time-limited in most spots. If you can, walk, cycle or catch the bus in - it's far less stressful than circling for a space. Always read the signs where you do park.

blocks.title: Find your next Bondi meal
blocks.text: Loved eating your way around the market? Our [Bondi eat & drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) lists 160+ local venues - filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with to line up breakfast, coffee, seafood or dinner near the beach.
Thinking of running a stall?

The market actively welcomes local growers and makers, with priority given to the people who actually produce what they sell - that's what keeps it a farmers' market rather than a reseller row. Stall fees and application details do change, so rather than quote a number I'd send you straight to the stallholder information on the official Bondi Markets website for the current process and pricing.

items.q: What days and times is the Bondi Farmers Market open?
items.a: Every Saturday from 9am to 1pm. It's a separate market from the Sunday Bondi Markets, which run on Sundays with different hours.

items.q: Where exactly is it?
items.a: In the grounds of Bondi Beach Public School, on the corner of Campbell Parade and Warners Avenue at the northern end of Bondi Beach - directly across the road from the promenade.

items.q: Is it on if it rains?
items.a: Yes. It's an open-air market that runs rain or shine. Bring an umbrella if the forecast looks iffy, but don't assume it's cancelled - check the official page if you're unsure.

items.q: Do I need cash?
items.a: Many stalls take card, but a few are cash-only, so it's worth carrying a small amount of cash just in case.

items.q: What's the difference between the Saturday and Sunday markets?
items.a: Saturday is the Farmers Market - fresh produce, food and breakfast. Sunday is the general Bondi Markets, focused more on fashion, vintage and homewares. Come Saturday for fruit, veg and a feed.

items.q: Where's good for a proper sit-down breakfast near the market?
items.a: The northern end of Bondi is full of options a few minutes away - Porch & Parlour, North Bondi Fish, Speedos Cafe and bills Bondi Beach are all reliable. For more, browse our [best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) guide.

blocks.text: That's the market in a nutshell: fresh, friendly, and about as local as Bondi gets. Turn up early, take your time, eat well, and cross the road to the beach when your bags are full. It's a simple ritual, but it's one of the nicest things you can do here on a Saturday morning.

Here's my honest answer to the question I'm asked most about Mackenzies Bay: it's real, it's genuinely magic, and there's a good chance it isn't there right now. "Maccas", as we call it, is a tiny cove tucked between Bondi and Tamarama that only becomes a golden-sand beach in certain years - then vanishes back to bare rock, sometimes for the better part of a decade. If you catch it with sand, you've caught one of Sydney's true hidden gems.

items.label: Where
items.value: Between Bondi & Tamarama, on the coastal walk

items.label: Sandy?
items.value: Only in certain years - highly unpredictable

blocks.text: The beach that comes and goes

Most years, most of the time, Mackenzies is a rugged little rock platform you'd stroll straight past. Then, every so often, the ocean quietly rebuilds it: sand gets carried in from nearby sandbanks and piled into the cove until - seemingly overnight - there's a proper beach where there was bare stone. It's the same spot; it just changes costume. One season it's a sunbathing pocket, the next a rocky enclave good for peering into tidal pools.

Coastal scientists put it down to a recipe of waves in the right size and direction, a nearby supply of loose sand, and calm-ish conditions to let it settle. Low-pressure swells, offshore winds and stretches without big storms all help it pile up - and El Niño years, which bring less storm activity, have lined up with some of its appearances. A serious storm can strip the same sand just as fast.
How long has it been gone this time?

The bay keeps no schedule. It's often quoted as appearing "every seven years or so", but that's a rough average, not a promise. A cyclone stripped the sand in the late 1990s and it reportedly stayed bare rock until around 2007, when it returned briefly as a wide sweep of sand before winter gales carried it off within months. Because it's this fickle, I never claim it's here right now - check a recent photo or a local's Instagram before you make the trip.

blocks.title: This is not a swimming beach
blocks.text: Mackenzies isn't an official, patrolled beach - there are no lifeguards, access is over slippery rock, and the cove is known for unpredictable surges and rips. Even when the sand looks inviting, treat the water with real caution and never turn your back on it, because unexpected waves can wash right across the rocks. For a swim, walk the few minutes to patrolled Bondi or Tamarama instead.
How to find it (and when to bother)

There's no road to Maccas - the only sensible way in is on foot along the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. From the southern end of Bondi, follow the path past the Icebergs and over the headland toward Tamarama; Mackenzies is the little cove between the two, below the track. The last scramble down is over rock and can be slick, so wear proper shoes and skip it in the wet.

Even without sand, this stretch of the coastal walk is worth doing for the clifftop views alone. Go early for soft light, fewer people, and easy parking before Bondi fills up. If you're chasing the sand, a lower tide gives you the best look - a high tide can hide what little there is.

Part of the charm is the crowd, or lack of one. Because it's off the radar and unpatrolled, Maccas draws a small, easygoing group of locals rather than the crowds of Bondi - and yes, plenty of dogs. Just know that dog rules on Waverley's beaches and reserves are set and enforced by the council, so check their current signage and website before you bring the pup rather than assuming it's a free-for-all.

items.q: Is Mackenzies Bay there right now?
items.a: Impossible to promise. It's a rocky inlet most of the time and only becomes a sandy beach in certain years, sometimes vanishing for years in between. Before you go specifically for the sand, check a very recent photo or ask a local - its status can even change with the tide.

items.q: Where exactly is Mackenzies Bay?
items.a: It's the small cove between Bondi and Tamarama beaches, tucked below the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. There's no road access - you reach it on foot from the walking track.

items.q: Can you swim at Mackenzies Bay?
items.a: It's not recommended. There are no lifeguards, access is over slippery rock, and the cove is known for rips and unpredictable surges. Swim at patrolled Bondi or Tamarama instead, both only minutes away.

items.q: Why does the beach disappear?
items.a: The sand is delivered by the ocean under the right mix of swell, wind and calm conditions, then carried away again by storms. There's no fixed pattern - it's at the mercy of the weather.

items.q: Can I bring my dog?
items.a: You'll often see dogs there because the cove is unpatrolled, but dog access on Waverley's beaches and reserves is governed by council rules. Check the council's current signage and website before you go rather than assuming it's allowed.

blocks.text: That's what I love about Maccas: it refuses to be pinned down. In a city full of famous, reliable beaches, here's one that shows up on its own terms and slips away when it feels like it. Catch it with sand and it feels like a secret the ocean let you in on. Catch it as bare rock and, well - that's just an excuse to try your luck another year.

sources.label: Waverley Council Library - Mackenzies Bay, the disappearing beach
Time Out Sydney - Sydney's disappearing beach

blocks.text: Yes - Bondi absolutely gets busy. On a hot summer weekend it's one of the most crowded stretches of sand in Australia, but here's the good news: the crowds are wonderfully predictable. Once you know the rhythm of the beach, you can catch Bondi at its best and skip it at its most hectic, sometimes on the same day.

I live around here, so I've watched this beach fill and empty thousands of times. The pattern barely changes - it's driven by heat, weekends, holidays and a handful of big events. Learn those four levers and you'll always know what you're walking into.
When Bondi is at its busiest

The peak is summer, December through February, climaxing over the Christmas–New Year stretch when half of Sydney seems to head for the coast. On the hottest days the crowds are enormous - widely cited estimates put a peak day in the tens of thousands, on a beach only about a kilometre long. Weekends and public holidays run a close second, and a run of 30-degree days will pack the sand whatever the calendar says.

items.label: Beat the crowd
items.value: Arrive early or come late afternoon

blocks.text: Within a single day there's a rhythm too. Mornings are calm and the light is beautiful; the crowd builds through late morning, peaks in the early-to-mid afternoon, then eases as the sun drops. The southern end near the Icebergs pool is always most crammed - everyone wants that postcard view - while the northern end breathes a little easier.
The event days that change everything
A few times a year, big events pull huge crowds and snarl the surrounding streets - the ones to watch:

items: City2Surf - Sydney's giant fun run finishes at Bondi in winter, filling the beach and roads for a morning.
Sculpture by the Sea - the free coastal art walk between Bondi and Tamarama runs in spring and draws large weekend numbers.
Festival of the Winds - Bondi's colourful kite festival brings families down to the sand, usually in September.

blocks.title: Check dates before you come
blocks.text: Event dates shift year to year and can change at short notice. Don't rely on a date from an old blog post - confirm on the official event site or Waverley Council's events page before you plan around one.
How I dodge the crowds

You don't have to give up on Bondi just because it's popular - my whole strategy is timing. Get down early: before mid-morning on a summer day the sand is open, the water's glassy and parking is far less of a nightmare. If mornings aren't your thing, late afternoon is the other sweet spot - the day-trippers pack up, the light turns golden, and you can actually find room on the sand.

Parking is the real bottleneck on a busy day, not the beach itself. Skip the endless loop for a space and catch public transport - the train to Bondi Junction then a short bus saves you the worst of the gridlock. If you must drive, arrive early and be ready to walk a few streets back from the sand.

If you want Bondi genuinely quiet, come on a weekday outside summer. Autumn and spring mornings are a local secret - mild, uncrowded, and often with the best surf. And whatever the season, remember the crowd doesn't spread evenly: a five-minute walk north, or along the coastal path toward Tamarama, and the density drops away fast.

blocks.title: Busy also means safe
blocks.text: Big crowds mean more people in the water, which is why Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards and volunteer surf lifesavers. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags - on the busiest days that matters more than ever, because rip currents don't care how many people are around.

items.q: What is the busiest time to visit Bondi Beach?
items.a: The busiest time is a hot summer weekend or public holiday between December and February, peaking over the Christmas and New Year period. Within a day, the crowd is heaviest through the early-to-mid afternoon.

items.q: When is Bondi Beach least crowded?
items.a: Weekday mornings and the cooler months (autumn and spring) are the quietest. An early start or a late-afternoon visit will always beat the worst of the crowds, even in summer.

items.q: How many people visit Bondi on a busy day?
items.a: Estimates commonly put a peak summer day in the tens of thousands - a huge number for a beach only about a kilometre long. Exact figures vary by source and conditions.

items.q: Is it hard to park at Bondi Beach?
items.a: On busy days, yes - parking is the real challenge, not space on the sand. Public transport (train to Bondi Junction, then a bus) is usually the least stressful way in. If you drive, come early.

items.q: Which end of Bondi Beach is less crowded?
items.a: The southern end near the Icebergs pool is always the most packed. Head toward the northern end, or onto the coastal walk, for more room.

blocks.text: So does Bondi get busy? Undeniably. But busy is part of what makes it Bondi - the buzz, the sense that the whole city has come down for a swim. Time your visit well and you get both worlds: that famous atmosphere when you want it, and a quiet golden morning when you don't.

Here's the honest answer I give every visitor who asks: you can legally fly a drone in the Bondi area, but almost certainly not the way you're imagining - hovering low over the sand, the surf break or the Icebergs pool full of swimmers. On a normal Bondi day the beach is a crowd, and Australia's drone rules don't allow flying over people, so the classic "buzz the beach" shot is off the table. The good news: with a bit of planning you can still get jaw-dropping aerial photos and stay on the right side of the law.
What Australia's drone rules actually say
Drones are governed nationally by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). If you fly recreationally, these core rules apply at Bondi just as they do everywhere else:

items: Stay at or below 120 metres (400 ft) above ground level.
Keep the drone at least 30 metres away from other people - and never fly directly over anyone.
Don't fly over crowds, gatherings, sporting events or a busy beach.
Fly only one drone at a time, in daylight, and always within your visual line of sight.
Don't fly near where emergency operations (like a surf rescue) are underway.
Keep well clear of controlled airspace and away from helicopters and other aircraft.

blocks.title: Check before you launch
blocks.text: To know whether the airspace above you is open, use a CASA-verified drone safety app (the "Can I fly there?" tools). It shows restricted zones and airport buffers in real time - which matters in Sydney, where airspace changes quickly.
The Bondi problem: it's almost always a crowd

The biggest thing that trips people up isn't the height limit - it's people. A patrolled, populated beach counts as a populous area, so the 30-metre rule and the no-flying-over-people rule make a full beach on a sunny Saturday a no-go for casual flying. Bondi also sits under busy Sydney airspace with helicopters passing along the coast, which is why keeping clear of aircraft and staying in line of sight isn't optional.
Where you take off and land matters too

On top of CASA's air rules there's a second layer people forget: the ground. The beach, promenade and surrounding parks are Waverley Council land, and councils can restrict or prohibit launching, landing and operating drones from their reserves - often with on-site signage. So even when the airspace looks clear, you may still not be permitted to take off from the sand or the park.

blocks.title: Obey the signs and the council
blocks.text: Before you fly, read any on-site signage and check Waverley Council's current position on drones on council land. Anything commercial - paid photography, film or media - will generally need a council permit and, depending on the job, CASA accreditation. When in doubt, ask the council first.
Whales, wildlife and your neighbours' privacy

From roughly May to November the humpbacks migrate past Bondi, and it's tempting to chase them with a drone. Don't. NSW has strict approach distances for marine mammals, and a drone diving in on a whale is both illegal and a fast track to serious social-media backlash from locals. Keep your distance, check the current NSW National Parks marine mammal rules, and give sunbathers the same courtesy: no one wants a camera over their towel.

My move for a clean Bondi aerial: get down for a weekday sunrise before the beach fills up, launch from a quiet, open spot away from people, and shoot out over the empty water toward the headland rather than back over the sand. Early light on the pool and the curve of the bay does the work for you.

items.q: Can I legally fly a drone over Bondi Beach?
items.a: Not when the beach is populated, which is most of the time. CASA rules ban flying over people and require you to stay 30 m from them, so hovering over a busy beach isn't allowed. You can fly in the wider area if you keep clear of people, stay under 120 m and in line of sight, and check that both the airspace and the council land you use permit it.

items.q: Do I need a licence to fly a drone for fun at Bondi?
items.a: For purely recreational flying within CASA's standard rules you generally don't need a licence, but you must follow all the operating conditions. Anything commercial - paid photos, film or media - usually needs a Waverley Council permit and, depending on the job, CASA accreditation.

items.q: Can I film the whales migrating past Bondi with my drone?
items.a: No. NSW sets minimum approach distances for whales and other marine mammals, and flying close to them is against the rules. Watch from the clifftops instead and check the current NSW National Parks guidance first.

items.q: How do I get a great Bondi aerial shot without breaking the rules?
items.a: Go at a quiet time like a weekday sunrise, launch from open ground away from people, stay under 120 m and in sight, and shoot out over open water rather than the sand or crowd. Check airspace with a CASA-verified app and obey on-site signage first.

blocks.text: Bondi from the air really is something special - the pool, the sweep of the bay, the light at dawn. Earn it the responsible way: right time, right place, clear of people and wildlife, and a quick check of the rules before you launch. Nail the shot and tag @visitbondibeach and #visitbondibeach so we can all admire it.

blocks.text: If you hear a wall of drums rolling up off North Bondi on a Sunday afternoon, don't go looking for a festival - that's Bondi Sunset Music, a free, come-as-you-are drum circle that gathers on the grassy knoll at the northern end of the beach and plays until the sun drops into the sea. It's my favourite unscripted thing in Bondi all week - no ticket, no instrument, and not the faintest idea of how to keep a beat required.

It started the way the best local things do: by accident. A couple of musicians drumming solo up on the knoll one gold-lit evening decided to play together instead, came back the next Sunday, and kept going as more people joined. Now it's a rolling circle of djembes, congas, samba surdos and whatever anyone thinks to bring, with dancers barefoot in the grass and a crowd that swells as the sun drops lower.

items.label: What
items.value: Bondi Sunset Music - free community drum circle

items.label: Where
items.value: The grassy knoll, northern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Cost
items.value: Free - bring an instrument or just come to listen

blocks.text: Where and when to find them

They set up on the grassy hill above the northern end of the promenade, near North Bondi, where the lawn looks down over the sand. It's the natural amphitheatre of the beach - you'll hear them before you see them. Sessions run on Sunday afternoons through to sunset, but this is a weather-and-vibe thing rather than a fixed timetable: rain or a big southerly can move or cancel it, and I've seen them shift down onto the sand between the ramps when the knoll's busy.

blocks.title: Times shift with the season and sky
blocks.text: Because start and finish track the sunset, the hours drift across the year and a wet forecast can call it off. Check the Bondi Sunset Music Facebook or Instagram page before you head down - that's where they post any change.
What it's actually like

Warm. That's the word I keep coming back to. There's a loose structure to keep everyone roughly in rhythm, but no audition and no gatekeeping - kids get handed shakers, first-timers get shown a simple pattern, and dancers just find space in the middle. It runs as a deliberately sober, alcohol- and drug-free gathering, which is a big part of why it works for all ages. Grandparents, toddlers, backpackers and Bondi lifers all end up in the same circle.
The idea is simple: reconnect with yourself and each other through rhythm, bare feet in the grass, and a beach sunset. No looking cool required.

Drum circles are one of humanity's oldest social rituals, and this is less a performance you watch than a thing you join. On a good Sunday you'll see a proper little community: regulars who've made friends here, visitors who wandered up by chance, and onlookers spread across the grass with the ocean glowing behind the drummers.
How to join in (and be a good guest)

items: Anyone can play - bring a djembe, a shaker, a tambourine, or empty hands and dancing feet.
Come a bit before sunset so you can find the circle, settle in and catch the light at its best.
Bring a picnic rug, water and warm layer - the knoll cools off fast once the sun's gone.
Follow the group's lead on volume and breaks; they keep sets to a few hours out of respect for neighbours.
Kids are genuinely welcome - there are usually spare instruments to hand around.

blocks.text: Pair it with an early swim or the Bondi to Bronte walk, then drift up to the knoll for the drums as the day winds down. A takeaway feed and a spot on the grass is about as good as a free Sunday in Sydney gets.

items.q: Where exactly is the Bondi Sunday drum circle?
items.a: On the grassy knoll at the northern end of Bondi Beach - the lawn on the hill above the promenade near North Bondi. When it's crowded they sometimes move down onto the sand near the northern ramps.

items.q: What time do the drummers play?
items.a: Sunday afternoons through to sunset, so the exact hours shift with the season. It's weather dependent - check the Bondi Sunset Music Facebook or Instagram page before heading down, as rain or a strong southerly can cancel or relocate a session.

items.q: Do I need to bring an instrument or pay anything?
items.a: No on both counts. It's completely free, and you're just as welcome to listen, dance, or watch the sunset as to play. If you have a hand drum or shaker, bring it - but there are usually spare instruments floating around.

items.q: Is it family and kid friendly?
items.a: Very. It's a deliberately sober, alcohol- and drug-free gathering for all ages, and the group actively hands instruments to kids to get them involved.

items.q: Can I join in even if I've never drummed before?
items.a: Absolutely - that's the whole point. There's a simple structure to keep everyone in rhythm, and regulars are happy to show newcomers an easy pattern. No experience needed.

blocks.text: So if you're in Bondi on a Sunday as the afternoon softens, follow the drums up to the knoll. Sit on the grass, or grab a shaker and join in. It's free, it's unpretentious, and one of the truest bits of Bondi you'll find all week.

If you want the best chance at a jaw-dropping sunrise at Bondi Beach, chase a morning that's partly cloudy after an overnight change - a sky with scattered high cloud for the light to set on fire, and clean air behind a passing front. That's the combination I've watched turn the whole eastern horizon pink and gold more times than a clear sky ever has. Bondi faces due east across the Pacific, so the sun climbs straight out of the water in front of you; the only variable that really changes the show is the weather.
The weather conditions that make Bondi glow

A completely clear sky gives you a clean, fiery orb lifting out of the ocean - beautiful, but the colour is often over in minutes. A completely overcast sky usually means a flat grey lid and no show at all. The magic lives in between.

items: Partly cloudy with high or mid-level cloud - the clouds catch the light before the sun even breaches the horizon, and the colour can last 20-30 minutes.
A gap on the eastern horizon under a cloudy sky - if the deck of cloud stops short of the sea, the first rays fire up under it from below. These are often the most dramatic mornings of all.
The morning after an overnight storm or southerly change - the air is scrubbed clean and clear, so the colours read more saturated.
Low humidity - crisp autumn and spring mornings tend to deliver cleaner light than muggy summer ones.

blocks.text: Don't write off a cloudy forecast. The mornings I've cancelled on turned out spectacular as often as not - a break in the cloud right on the horizon is unpredictable and produces the best light. If in doubt, get up and go; the walk is worth it either way.

blocks.title: Coffee comes later
blocks.text: Most Campbell Parade cafes open after first light, not before it. Bring a thermos, or plan to reward yourself once the beachfront wakes up - you'll be down there a good while before anything's serving.
When to set your alarm

Sunrise time swings by well over an hour across the year, so the season completely changes your alarm. Around the December solstice the sun is up not long after 5:40am; around the June solstice it's closer to 7am. Because those times drift day to day, I always check the exact time for the morning I'm going rather than guessing.

items.label: Aspect
items.value: Faces due east - sun rises over the ocean

items.label: Best light
items.value: The 20-40 min around sunrise (civil twilight into golden hour)

items.label: Check first
items.value: Exact sunrise time + cloud forecast the night before

blocks.text: Aim to be in position around half an hour before the listed sunrise time. The pre-dawn glow during civil twilight is frequently better than the moment the sun actually clears the horizon, and you don't want to be still walking down when it happens.
Where I stand

For a sunrise directly over the water, the southern end near the Bondi Icebergs and the start of the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk is my favourite - you get the ocean pool, the headland and the sun all in one frame. The northern headland and the promenade itself work beautifully too. Wherever you settle, give yourself room to reframe as the sun climbs; it moves faster than you expect.

Check the swell and tide as well as the light. A bigger swell exploding against the Icebergs pool at dawn is a photo in itself, and a low tide opens up wet-sand reflections along the main beach that double the colour in the sky.

items.q: What's the best weather for a Bondi sunrise?
items.a: Partly cloudy - enough high or mid-level cloud for the light to catch, ideally with a gap on the eastern horizon so the first rays fire up under the cloud. Clear skies give a short, clean sunrise; fully overcast skies usually give nothing. The morning after an overnight change is often the clearest and most colourful.

items.q: What time is sunrise at Bondi Beach?
items.a: It ranges from roughly 5:40am around the December solstice to about 7am around the June solstice, and shifts a little every day. Check the exact time for your date on a source like timeanddate.com or the Bureau of Meteorology before you go.

items.q: What time should I arrive?
items.a: About 30 minutes before the listed sunrise. The pre-dawn twilight glow is often the best colour of the whole morning, so you want to be in position and settled before the sun actually breaks the horizon.

items.q: Does Bondi Beach face the sunrise?
items.a: Yes. Bondi faces due east across the Pacific Ocean, so the sun rises straight out of the water in front of the beach - which is exactly why it's a sunrise beach rather than a sunset one.

blocks.text: So the honest answer to "what's the perfect condition?" is: a bit of cloud, clean air, and a horizon that isn't sealed shut. Read the forecast the night before, set the alarm for half an hour before sunrise, and go. Even the mornings that don't ignite are quiet, salty and worth being awake for - and the ones that do will stop you in your tracks.

For a few weeks every spring, my favourite stretch of coastline becomes the world's most beautiful gallery. Sculpture by the Sea lines the Bondi to Tamarama clifftop with more than 100 works, set against the ocean, free to walk, and utterly unlike a gallery with a roof. I've done it most years and it still stops me in my tracks.

items.label: Distance
items.value: About 2 km along the Bondi to Tamarama coastal walk (check the official site)

items.label: When
items.value: Spring, roughly late October (dates vary - check the official site)

blocks.text: It started in 1997, when founder David Handley - a former commercial lawyer inspired by a sculpture park he'd seen in Bohemia - staged a single-day show of 64 works along this same path. It drew around 25,000 people on a shoestring budget, and the idea has never changed: put ambitious work by Australian and international artists against the sea and let the ocean do half the job. It's now billed as the world's largest free-to-the-public sculpture exhibition.
The walk itself

It's roughly 2 kilometres one way, from the Icebergs pool at the southern end of Bondi around to Tamarama. As a plain stroll that's about 25 minutes, but you won't stroll - you'll stop constantly, so give yourself two to three hours. Works are scattered across the sand, perched on the cliffs, and clustered through Marks Park on Mackenzies Point, the grassy headland roughly halfway along with uninterrupted views north and south. Part of the joy is watching the light and tide reshape each piece as you go.
The path is sealed but narrow in places, with steps and a few steep pinches, so wear proper shoes rather than thongs. A few practical notes before you set off:

items: It's an active clifftop - stay behind the barriers and keep kids and dogs close near the edges.
Toilets are at Bondi and Tamarama beaches, with little in between, so go before you start.
The Bondi end has plenty of food and coffee; Tamarama has far fewer options, so carry water and a snack.
Most sculptures are for sale, and many are works you genuinely can't see anywhere else.

blocks.text: Getting there

Public transport is the smart call - parking around Tamarama fills fast during the festival. Take a train to Bondi Junction, then a bus down to the beach, and pick up the path at the southern headland by the Icebergs. To walk against the main flow of the crowd, start instead at the quieter Tamarama end. Confirm current bus routes and any road closures on Transport for NSW or the event's own getting-there page.

Come at sunrise on a weekday. The path is emptiest in the first hour after dawn, the light is soft and gold, and you'll have the headline sculptures almost to yourself before the tour groups arrive. Weekday mornings beat weekends by a mile.

blocks.title: Confirm this year's dates before you plan
blocks.text: The exhibition runs each spring, usually across late October into early November, but the exact dates, opening hours and any ticketed extras (early-access or twilight tours) change year to year and can shift with the weather. Check the official Sculpture by the Sea site before you set a day.

items.q: Is Sculpture by the Sea free?
items.a: Yes - walking the exhibition is free and open to the public. Donations are warmly welcomed, and there are sometimes optional paid extras such as guided or early-access tours you can book through the official site.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: The route is about 2 kilometres between Bondi and Tamarama - around 25 minutes as a plain walk, but with 100-plus sculptures to stop for, most people spend two to three hours end to end.

items.q: Is the walk suitable for kids and prams?
items.a: Families do it every year and children love the scale of the works, but steps and steep, narrow sections make prams hard going - a carrier is easier for little ones. Keep everyone close to the barriers near the cliff edges.

blocks.text: The best sculpture here is never just the object - it's the object, the cliff and the sea, all at once.

blocks.text: If you only do one walk while you're in Bondi, make it this one. The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk is a short, cliff-hugging stretch - roughly 2.5km one way - that most people knock over in 45 minutes to an hour, and it's the single best way I know to understand why we live here. You'll pass three beaches, an ocean pool or two, sandstone headlands and more ocean than your camera can hold. It's free, open year-round, and you don't need to be a hiker to do it.

items.label: Time
items.value: 45 min–1 hr at a gentle pace

blocks.text: The route, from my front door to Bronte

The walk kicks off at the southern end of Bondi Beach. Head up Notts Avenue past Bondi Icebergs and you'll find the paved path curling around the cliff - from there it's almost impossible to get lost, because the ocean is on one side the whole way.

First you round Mackenzies Point, the rocky headland with the best wide-angle view back over Bondi - the postcard shot everyone stops for. Every few years, when the sand shifts just right, a fleeting little beach appears at Mackenzies Bay; never guaranteed, but a treat when it shows up.

Next comes Tamarama, affectionately known as 'Glamarama' - a tiny cove tucked between the cliffs. Then it's a short stroll through Bronte Park, under the Norfolk pines, down to Bronte Beach. Bronte feels smaller and more local than Bondi, with an ocean-fed pool at the southern end and cafés across the road made for a post-walk breakfast.

stops.title: Bondi (Notts Ave)
stops.detail: Grab a coffee, take the stairs down to the path past Icebergs.

stops.title: Mackenzies Point
stops.detail: The classic look-back-over-Bondi viewpoint. Whale-watching in season.

stops.title: Tamarama Beach
stops.detail: Small, steep and scenic. A good spot to catch your breath.

stops.title: Bronte Beach & Baths
stops.detail: Finish with a swim in the ocean pool and breakfast across the road.

blocks.text: When to go (and how to beat the crowds)

My honest answer: early. Sunrise over the Pacific from Mackenzies Point is worth setting an alarm for, and before about 8am the path is quiet and the light soft and golden. Late afternoon is the runner-up, and weekday mornings are calmer than weekends, when the path fills with joggers, prams and tour groups.

Between roughly May and November you've got a decent chance of spotting humpback whales migrating offshore - scan the horizon from the headlands for a spout or a breach. And in spring, the walk hosts a big free outdoor sculpture exhibition (more below).

blocks.title: Sculpture by the Sea
blocks.text: Each spring the Bondi to Tamarama stretch hosts Sculpture by the Sea - a free open-air exhibition of artworks along the cliffs. Dates shift each year, so check sculpturebythesea.com for this year's exact dates and expect big crowds while it's on.

Do the walk in reverse - Bronte to Bondi - and you'll finish at Bondi with its [bigger choice of cafés](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) and afternoon swims, facing the better views the whole way. Same path, half the crowds coming at you.
What to bring, and swimming along the way

There's very little shade on the cliffs, so treat this as proper sun exposure even in cooler months. Trainers or sturdy sandals are plenty, and there are public toilets and water fountains at both Bondi and Bronte.

items: Sunscreen, hat and water - the path is exposed and there's little shade
Swimmers and a towel if you fancy a dip at Tamarama, Bronte or the ocean pools
Comfortable shoes - sealed path, but with stairs and a few climbs
A camera or phone for Mackenzies Point and the Icebergs pool shot
Cash or card for a café stop at the Bronte end

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: If you swim, only do it at a patrolled beach between the red-and-yellow flags, and check conditions first - this coast has strong rips and the ocean pools can be closed or hazardous in big swell. When in doubt, stay out and enjoy the view instead.

Keen to keep going? Bronte is only the halfway mark of the famous Bondi to Coogee walk, which continues past Waverley Cemetery, Clovelly and Gordons Bay. But even if you turn around at Bronte, you'll have seen the best of it.

items.q: How long does the Bondi to Bronte walk take?
items.a: Most people take about 45 minutes to an hour one way at a relaxed pace over roughly 2.5km. Allow longer if you stop for photos, a swim or a coffee along the way.

items.q: Is the Bondi to Bronte walk easy?
items.a: Yes - it's a sealed, well-marked path suitable for most fitness levels, with some stairs and gentle climbs rather than steep hiking. Ordinary walking shoes are fine, though the stairs mean it isn't fully pram or wheelchair accessible.

items.q: Where does the walk start?
items.a: At the southern end of Bondi Beach. Head up Notts Avenue past Bondi Icebergs to pick up the coastal path. You can walk it either way.

items.q: Can I swim along the way?
items.a: Yes. You'll pass Tamarama and Bronte beaches plus the Bronte ocean pool, plus Bondi Icebergs at the start. Only swim at patrolled beaches between the flags and check conditions, as this coast has strong rips.

items.q: When is the best time to do the walk?
items.a: Early morning for sunrise and quiet paths, or late afternoon for golden light. Weekdays are calmer than weekends. Aim for whale-watching season (roughly May–November) or catch Sculpture by the Sea in spring.

items.q: How do I get back from Bronte to Bondi?
items.a: Either walk back the same way - it's only 2.5km, and the views run in reverse - or catch a bus from Bronte up to Bondi Junction and then the 333 or 380 back down to Bondi Beach. Use the Transport for NSW trip planner for today's times. Plenty of people deliberately walk one way and bus back.

blocks.text: That's the walk in a nutshell - short enough to do before breakfast, beautiful enough to do again the next morning. Lace up, and I'll see you at the Bronte pool.

Here's the short answer people are really after: no, El Niño does not flip a switch and make Bondi's water cold. In an El Niño year the ocean off Sydney can run a touch cooler or drier at the surface, but the day-to-day temperature you feel when you wade in is driven far more by the East Australian Current, the wind and local upwelling than by whatever the Pacific is doing thousands of kilometres away. I've swum here through El Niño summers that were beautifully warm and La Niña ones that turned suddenly icy, so I always tell visitors to check the actual water temperature the week they arrive rather than trusting a headline.
What El Niño actually is

El Niño is one phase of a natural climate cycle called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). During an El Niño, the trade winds that normally blow warm surface water westward across the Pacific weaken, and that warm water pools instead in the central and eastern Pacific, off South America. For eastern Australia, the Bureau of Meteorology links El Niño with warmer, drier conditions on land and a higher chance of below-average rainfall - which is why it grabs headlines here.
That's the land story. The ocean story right at Bondi is more local and more interesting, and it's where the 'chilly' reputation really comes from.
Why Bondi's water can turn surprisingly cold

The single biggest control on our sea temperature is the East Australian Current - the warm river of tropical water (the one made famous by Finding Nemo) that CSIRO tracks flowing south down the coast. When a warm eddy sits offshore, Bondi feels balmy. When that current meanders away, the water cools.

The other culprit is upwelling. On a run of hot summer days, strong north-easterly winds can push the warm surface layer offshore, and cold water from deeper down rises to replace it. That's when you get the classic Bondi surprise: a warm morning that turns breathtakingly colder by afternoon. It has nothing to do with El Niño - it's wind and local ocean physics - but it's the effect swimmers most often remember.
