blocks.text: Let me be upfront: I write this from a towel on Bondi Beach, so I'm about as impartial as a magpie in spring. But if you've ever argued Sydney versus Melbourne over a schooner, here's my honest answer - Sydney wins, and the case starts with the sand between my toes. Melbourne has its charms (I'll give them the coffee and the trams), yet nothing there wakes you up like a Sydney morning, with the harbour, the headlands and half a dozen surf beaches all a short ride away.
It always comes back to the water

This is the whole argument in one sentence: Sydney has genuine ocean beaches inside the city, and Melbourne doesn't. I can finish a workday and be swimming between the flags at Bondi within the hour. Manly, Coogee, Bronte, Tamarama - a string of them, each with its own personality, all reachable on a bus, ferry or a good pair of legs. Melbourne's bay beaches are pleasant, but they're not a Pacific swell rolling in under a headland.

Then there's the harbour. I still catch the ferry sometimes just for the joy of it, watching the Opera House and the Bridge slide past like a postcard. The Opera House is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and no amount of laneway street art quite competes with that skyline at golden hour.
My 25 (cheerfully partisan) reasons

items: Ocean beaches you can reach on public transport.
The Sydney Opera House, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Sydney Harbour Bridge - climb it or just gawp at it.
The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk, free and world-class.
Bondi Icebergs and its ocean pool carved into the rocks.
Surf culture that's part of everyday life, not a novelty.
Generally warmer, sunnier days for beach weather (check the Bureau of Meteorology for the season).
Ferries that double as the best-value harbour cruise going.
The Bondi Rescue lifeguards keeping the flags honest.
Winter whale-watching straight off the headlands.
The Blue Mountains a short drive west for a nature reset.
Royal National Park - one of the world's oldest - on the doorstep.
Coastal cliff walks with a new sea view around every bend.
Ocean pools dotted right along the eastern beaches.
Harbourside picnics with a skyline most cities would kill for.
Sunrise swims before the crowds arrive.
Fish and chips eaten with sand on your feet.
The eastern suburbs' laid-back, sun-first pace of life.
World-famous New Year's Eve fireworks over the harbour.
Markets like Bondi's weekend stalls a block from the sand.
Sea breezes that take the sting out of a hot afternoon.
Headland lookouts made for whale and dolphin spotting.
Snorkelling and diving at Gordons Bay and Clovelly.
A café scene that holds its own (yes, even against Melbourne).
And the simple, daily luxury of a beach at the end of the street.

blocks.text: If you're settling the debate with a visiting Melburnian, don't argue - just walk them from Bondi to Bronte at sunrise. By the second cove, with the swimmers doing laps in the ocean pool below, the case tends to make itself.

blocks.title: In fairness to Melbourne
blocks.text: I'll concede the coffee, the laneways, the live music and the sport. This is a love letter to Sydney, not a hit piece - Melbourne's a great weekend, just one without a surf beach at the end of the tram line.
The everyday, not just the postcard

What really tips it for me isn't the big-ticket stuff - it's the ordinary Tuesday. A dawn dip before work, a coastal walk with a takeaway coffee, a swim between the flags on a lunch break. Sydney folds the outdoors into daily life, and that's the quiet reason locals here are so smug about it.

So is Sydney objectively better than Melbourne? Of course not - it's a matter of taste, and half the fun is the arguing. But if your idea of a good life includes salt water, headlands and sun on your back, I know which side of the Hume Highway I'm staying on.

items.q: Is Sydney really better than Melbourne?
items.a: It's a friendly, unwinnable rivalry - but if you love ocean beaches, harbour views and an outdoor lifestyle, Sydney is hard to beat. Melbourne counters with coffee, laneways, live music and sport. This guide is happily biased toward the beach.

items.q: What's the one thing Sydney has that Melbourne doesn't?
items.a: Genuine surf beaches inside the city. Bondi, Manly, Bronte and Coogee are all part of everyday Sydney life, reachable by public transport - something Melbourne's calmer bay beaches can't quite replicate.

items.q: Does Sydney have better weather than Melbourne?
items.a: Sydney is generally warmer and sunnier, which suits its beach-first lifestyle, while Melbourne is famous for changeable 'four seasons in a day' weather. For exact averages by month, check the Bureau of Meteorology's climate statistics.

items.q: Is Bondi the best of Sydney's beaches?
items.a: It's the most famous, and my home patch, but part of Sydney's magic is choice. I love Bronte for families, Tamarama for a smaller cove, and the Bondi to Bronte walk to see several beaches in one go.

items.q: How do I settle the Sydney vs Melbourne debate with a friend?
items.a: Skip the argument and take them for a sunrise walk from Bondi to Bronte, then a swim. It's the most persuasive rebuttal I know.

blocks.text: If you want to live in Bondi Beach, the fastest and cheapest way in is almost always a room in a share house - and the best places to find one are Flatmates.com.au, Flatmate Finders and the local Bondi share-house Facebook groups. I've moved around the eastern suburbs more times than I'd like to admit, and rooms here go quickly. A little strategy is the difference between a sunny room near the sand and refreshing listings for a month.

items.label: Move fast
items.value: Good rooms are often gone within days

blocks.text: Where I actually look
There's no single magic website, so I cast a wide net and check a few every day. Each has a different crowd, and good rooms rarely sit around long.

items: Flatmates.com.au - the biggest share-accommodation site in Australia. Filter by suburb, budget, room type and move-in date, and message people directly. Start here.
Flatmate Finders - a long-running Sydney share-house specialist with a strong eastern-suburbs presence and plenty of Bondi Beach listings.
Bondi share-house Facebook groups - busy, local and fast-moving, with new posts most days. Good for a feel of the vibe before you commit.
Domain and realestate.com.au - mostly whole-property rentals, but useful if you want to grab a place with friends and split it yourselves.
Gumtree and university noticeboards - still turn up rooms, especially around the start of semester.

blocks.text: Don't underestimate word of mouth. Bondi is smaller than it looks, and plenty of rooms never get advertised - they're filled by a friend of a housemate. Tell people you're looking: ask at your gym, your café, your work. Some of the best houses I've lived in came from a passing conversation, not a listing.
How to actually land the room

Bondi is competitive, so treat the search like a mini job hunt. When a room looks right, reply within the hour with a short, warm, specific message - who you are, what you do, when you can move in, and why that particular house appeals. A generic "is this still available?" gets lost in a sea of identical ones.

items: Have your basics ready: references, proof of income or savings, and a couple of friendly lines about yourself.
Always view in person (or on a live video call) before paying anything.
Ask the boring-but-important questions up front: what's included in the rent, how bills are split, how the bond is held, and whether you'll be on the lease or subletting.
Trust the vibe - you're choosing housemates as much as a room. A cheap room with the wrong people is no bargain.

blocks.text: Rooms move faster in spring and early summer, and again around February with the university intake. If you can, start looking two to three weeks before you need to move - and be ready to say yes quickly when the right one appears.

blocks.title: Watch for rental scams
blocks.text: Never pay a deposit or bond before you've seen the place and met the people, no matter how good the photos or how urgent the story. If someone can't meet, refuses a viewing, or pushes for money by transfer straight away, walk away. In NSW your bond should be lodged through Rental Bonds Online, not paid into a stranger's personal account - see NSW Fair Trading for how renting and bonds are meant to work.
What it costs

Bondi Beach is one of Sydney's pricier postcodes, and share-room rents move with the market and the season, so I won't quote a figure that'll be stale next month. For a current sense of what a room costs, scan the live listings on Flatmates.com.au and Flatmate Finders and check whole-property medians on Domain. As a rule of thumb, the closer to the sand and the more you want your own bathroom, the more you'll pay; a room a few streets back, or in North Bondi or Bondi Junction, stretches the budget further.

items.q: What's the best website to find a housemate in Bondi Beach?
items.a: Start with Flatmates.com.au, the largest share-accommodation platform in Australia, and Flatmate Finders, a long-running Sydney specialist with lots of Bondi listings. Pair those with the local Bondi share-house Facebook groups for the fastest-moving rooms.

items.q: How much does a room in a Bondi share house cost?
items.a: It varies by proximity to the beach, room size and the season, and prices change often - so check current listings on Flatmates.com.au or Flatmate Finders rather than a fixed figure. Rooms a few streets back, or in North Bondi and Bondi Junction, tend to be cheaper.

items.q: How quickly do share rooms in Bondi get taken?
items.a: Fast - good rooms are often gone within days, especially in spring, early summer and around the February university intake. Reply to listings within the hour and have your references and details ready to go.

items.q: How do I avoid rental scams when looking for a share house?
items.a: Always view the place and meet the housemates before paying anything, and never transfer a bond into a personal account. In NSW, bonds are lodged through Rental Bonds Online - if someone dodges a viewing or rushes you for money, treat it as a red flag.

blocks.text: Finding a place in Bondi takes some hustle, but it's absolutely doable - there's nothing like walking home from a morning swim to a house full of people who love this coast as much as you do. Cast a wide net, move quickly, choose your housemates as carefully as your room, and you'll be into beach life before you know it.

blocks.text: Can you go metal detecting at Bondi Beach? In short, yes - swinging a detector across the open sand is a hobby plenty of locals quietly enjoy, and you don't need a special licence to do it on a public NSW beach. But a few sensible rules and courtesies keep it legal and the lifeguards onside, so before you start digging, here's how to do it properly.

items.label: Licence needed?
items.value: No licence for public-beach detecting in NSW

items.label: Best time
items.value: Early morning, at or near low tide

items.label: Off-limits
items.value: National parks, dunes, heritage & Aboriginal sites

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Leave no holes, leave no trace

blocks.text: The rules: what's actually allowed

In New South Wales you generally don't need a permit or fossicking licence to metal detect on a public beach, and the wet sand below the high-tide line is Crown land. What complicates it is that beaches sit under local council control, and the rules genuinely vary. Bondi is managed by Waverley Council, so they are the final word on whether, when and where detecting is permitted here - I'd check their current guidance or call them before a first outing.

blocks.title: Where you must never detect
blocks.text: Metal detecting is strictly prohibited in national parks and NPWS-managed reserves, including the coastal reserves and dune systems near the Bondi to Coogee walk. Disturbing an Aboriginal object or a heritage item is an offence under NSW law, whether or not you knew it was there. Stick to the open recreational sand and stay clear of dunes, vegetation and any signed or fenced-off area.
When and where to search

Timing is everything. My favourite window is early morning at or just after low tide, before the crowds arrive and while the receding water has freshly exposed the lower beach. The day after a busy weekend or a public holiday is prime - that's when the most rings, coins and sunglasses have slipped off warm fingers into the sand. A southerly change or a decent swell that reshapes the beach can also uncover things buried for weeks.

items: Low tide - check Bureau of Meteorology tide times before you leave so you catch the water at its furthest out.
The 'towel line' - the band of dry sand where sunbathers sit is where most modern drops happen.
The wet sand and shallows - heavier items like rings sink and migrate down the beach face.
Early or late - fewer people means you're not swinging a detector past someone's picnic.

blocks.text: Fill every hole you dig, straight away. A sand scoop lets you sift and backfill in one motion, and a neat beach is the biggest reason councils keep tolerating detectorists. One person leaving craters near the flags is how a whole hobby gets banned.
Gear that suits a saltwater beach
Bondi is a saltwater, mineralised-sand environment, so the kit matters more than at an inland park. You don't need the priciest machine on the shelf, just one built for the beach.

items: A detector rated for saltwater use - pulse-induction or a VLF unit with good ground balance handles wet sand without falsing.
A long-handled sand scoop with drainage holes so you can sift and backfill fast.
A pinpointer to zero in on the target once you've dug.
Headphones to hear faint signals over the wind and surf.
Sun protection and water - you'll be out in the open for hours.

blocks.text: What people actually find (and what to do with it)

Realistically, most of what comes up at a beach as busy as Bondi is modern: coins, bottle caps, keys, the odd pair of sunglasses, and - the prize every detectorist hopes for - lost rings and jewellery. If you find something of obvious value like a ring, the decent thing (and the legal expectation) is to try to reunite it with its owner. Handing found property in to NSW Police is the proper route, and some detectorists make a point of reuniting lost jewellery with its owner. If you ever turn up something that looks genuinely old or culturally significant, stop, don't remove it, and report it to Heritage NSW.

items.q: Do I need a permit or licence to metal detect at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No specific licence is required to detect on a public NSW beach. Because beaches are council-controlled and rules vary, check Waverley Council's current guidance before your first outing at Bondi.

items.q: When is the best time to metal detect at Bondi?
items.a: Early morning at or near low tide, ideally the day after a busy summer weekend or public holiday. Check Bureau of Meteorology tide times first.

items.q: Where am I not allowed to detect?
items.a: Steer clear of national parks and NPWS reserves, dune systems, vegetated areas and any heritage or Aboriginal cultural sites - detecting there is prohibited and disturbing protected objects is an offence.

items.q: What should I do if I find a valuable ring or piece of jewellery?
items.a: Try to reunite it with its owner. Handing found property in to NSW Police is the proper channel, and gives the person who lost it a real chance of getting it back.

blocks.text: Metal detecting at Bondi is a lovely, low-cost way to slow down and read the beach - you start noticing the tides, the wind, where the crowds sit. Do it early, do it tidily, respect the rules and the reserves, and you'll be welcome to keep swinging for years. And who knows - the next signal might just be somebody's wedding ring waiting to go home.

blocks.text: Short answer: no - Bondi Junction and Bondi Beach are not the same place, and I promise you're not the first person to get them muddled. They sit in the same corner of Sydney's Eastern Suburbs and share the "Bondi" name, but one is a busy shopping and transport hub set back from the coast, and the other is the golden stretch of sand you've seen a thousand times on a postcard. If you've booked a hotel at one expecting the other, this is the article I wish you'd read first.

items.label: Getting between
items.value: Bus (333 or 380) or a 30-ish min walk

blocks.text: So what's the actual difference?

Bondi Junction is where the trains stop. It's the terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line, so if you catch a train from the city, this is as far as the rail takes you - the beach itself has no train station. Around the station you'll find Westfield Bondi Junction, one of Sydney's biggest shopping centres, plus office towers, cinemas, restaurants and a genuinely enormous bus interchange. It's urban, fast-paced and, frankly, a bit removed from the ocean. You can't see the water from here.

Bondi Beach is the coastline - about a kilometre of sand curving along the Pacific, backed by Campbell Parade with its cafés, surf shops, the Bondi Pavilion and the famous Icebergs pool at the southern end. This is where people swim, surf, sunbake and start the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. The vibe is salt-air and swimwear, not shopping bags and escalators.

blocks.title: Check which "Bondi" your accommodation is in
blocks.text: Plenty of hotels advertise "Bondi" but are actually up in Bondi Junction, a couple of kilometres from the sand. That's not necessarily a bad thing - the Junction is well connected and often cheaper - but if you booked picturing a beach out the window, confirm the address before you arrive.
How far apart are they, and how do I get between them?

They're only about 2.5 kilometres apart, so hopping between the two is easy. The most common way is a short bus ride: routes like the 333 and 380 run between Bondi Junction interchange and Bondi Beach along Campbell Parade, and they come frequently.

items: By bus: catch the 333 or 380 from Bondi Junction interchange down to the beach - a short hop of well under 15 minutes in normal traffic.
By train + bus: ride the T4 line to Bondi Junction, then transfer to a beach-bound bus upstairs at the interchange.
On foot: it's roughly a 25–35 minute walk, mostly downhill on the way to the beach (and a decent uphill workout coming back).
By car or taxi: a few minutes' drive, though beach parking is limited and pricey in summer.

blocks.text: Tap on and off with a contactless card or your phone - you don't need a separate Opal card for the bus. Transferring between train and bus within about an hour can earn an Opal transfer discount rather than two full fares, but check the current fare rules and live times on the Transport for NSW website before you head out.
Which one should I actually stay in or visit?

It depends what you're after. If your holiday is about morning swims and sunset walks, stay near Bondi Beach and Campbell Parade. If you want big-brand shopping, easy train access to the rest of Sydney and often better value, Bondi Junction makes a smart base - you're one quick bus from the beach anyway, which is why plenty of locals happily live there for the best of both.
Think of Bondi Junction as the front door and Bondi Beach as the backyard - same house, very different rooms.

items.q: Is there a train to Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. The train line ends at Bondi Junction - the beach itself has no railway station. From Bondi Junction you finish the trip on a bus (333 or 380) or on foot. Check current times on the Transport for NSW trip planner.

items.q: How far is Bondi Junction from Bondi Beach?
items.a: About 2.5 kilometres. It's a short bus ride, a few minutes by car, or roughly a 25–35 minute walk - downhill heading to the beach and uphill on the way back.

items.q: Can you see the beach from Bondi Junction?
items.a: No. Bondi Junction is set back inland and surrounded by shops and offices, so there's no ocean view. You'll need to head down to Campbell Parade to actually see the water.

items.q: Why are they both called Bondi?
items.a: They're neighbouring suburbs in the same coastal pocket of Sydney's Eastern Suburbs, both taking the "Bondi" name. The Junction grew up around the transport interchange and shops, while Bondi Beach is the seaside end of the same area.

items.q: Is it cheaper to stay in Bondi Junction?
items.a: Often, yes. Accommodation in the Junction can be better value than beachfront stays, and you're still only a short bus ride from the sand - which is why many visitors happily base themselves there.

blocks.text: So next time someone tells you they're "staying in Bondi," it's worth asking which one they mean. Get the two straight and you'll navigate this corner of Sydney like a local - shopping and trains at the Junction, sand and surf down at the beach, and a quick, easy bus tying the two together.

sources.label: Transport for NSW - trip planner & timetables

blocks.text: Yes - anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool. Despite the famous "Club" name over the door, you do not need to be a member, book ahead, or know a local. You just walk down the ramp at the southern end of Bondi Beach, pay the entry fee at the kiosk, and you're in the most photographed pool in Australia. I've sent countless first-time visitors down there, and the only thing that surprises them is how easy it is.

There's one thing worth clearing up, because it trips people up constantly. The Icebergs Swimming Club - the winter-swimming institution that gave the place its name - is separate from the public pool. Membership is about competing in the winter races, not getting a swim. The pool itself is open to everyone, and that's the bit almost everyone comes for.

items.label: Public access
items.value: Yes - no membership or booking needed

items.label: Where
items.value: Southern end of Bondi Beach (Notts Ave)

items.label: Lifeguards
items.value: On patrol during opening hours, year-round

blocks.text: How public access actually works

Entry is first-come, first-served - there's no online ticket or reservation system for the pool itself. You rock up, pay at the entrance, and swim. It's a saltwater pool cut into the rocks, so waves wash over the edge and top it up with fresh ocean water. That's why it feels so alive next to a chlorinated lap pool - and why I tell people to respect the conditions on a big-swell day.

Entry is refreshingly cheap for something this famous: as at August 2026 it's $10 for an adult, $7 for a child and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in your admission - plus towel and locker hire if you need them. Pool prices creep up over time, so check the current rates on the official [Icebergs pool page](https://icebergs.com.au/pool-conditions/) before you go. There are also multi-visit passes if you plan to swim often.

blocks.title: The pool closes on Thursdays
blocks.text: Icebergs closes the pool most Thursdays for cleaning. In the warmer months, when the tides allow, they sometimes keep it open on Thursdays - but never bank on it. If a Thursday swim is the whole plan, check icebergs.com.au that morning first.
What to expect when you get there

There are two pools: the 50-metre lap pool everyone photographs, and a smaller, shallower children's pool beside it - handy if you've got little ones and want the same view without the depth. Lifeguards patrol during opening hours, and there are changing rooms, showers and lockers on site. Above the pool sits the Icebergs Dining Room and a café-bar, but you don't need either to use the pool - they're a separate visit.

Go early. I aim for the 7–8am window on a weekday: the light on the water is unreal, the lap lanes are calm, and you'll get the classic empty-pool photo before the tour groups arrive. By mid-morning on a summer weekend it's a much busier scene.
A note on rough days

Because the pool is fed by the ocean, a strong swell sends water crashing over the southern wall - dramatic to watch, but powerful if you're near the edge. On big-surf days the lifeguards may restrict swimming or close the pool altogether. If the sea looks angry and you're not a confident swimmer, keep to the shallow end or come back when it's settled.
Opening hours

The pool keeps long days, opening early in the morning and running through to the evening, every day except the Thursday cleaning closure. The exact opening and closing times shift with the seasons, the tides and the swell, so rather than quote a timetable that might be stale by the time you read this, I glance at the official [pool-conditions page](https://icebergs.com.au/pool-conditions/) the day before I go.

items.q: Do you have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The public pool is open to everyone - you just pay the entry fee at the kiosk and swim. Membership of the Icebergs Swimming Club is a separate thing, tied to the winter-swimming races, and isn't needed for a normal swim.

items.q: Do I need to book in advance?
items.a: No booking is required. Entry to the pool is first-come, first-served - turn up, pay at the entrance and go in.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: As at August 2026, single-visit entry is $10 for adults, $7 for children and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in admission; towel and locker hire cost extra. Prices change, so check icebergs.com.au before you visit.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: It closes most Thursdays for cleaning. In summer, when the tides permit, it may stay open on Thursdays. It can also close temporarily during big swells or swimming races, so check the pool-conditions page if you're unsure.

items.q: Is the pool suitable for children?
items.a: Yes - there's a separate shallow children's pool next to the main 50-metre lap pool, and lifeguards are on patrol during opening hours. On rough-surf days, keep kids well away from the ocean-facing edge.

blocks.text: So the short answer stands: yes, the public can absolutely swim at Bondi Icebergs. Pick a calmer day, get there early, avoid Thursdays, and you'll see in about thirty seconds why this rectangle of ocean has drawn swimmers for the better part of a century.

If you want my honest local's shortlist for the best ice cream at Bondi, it's this: Gelato Messina on Hall Street for the showstopper flavours, Anita Gelato on Campbell Parade for sheer variety, and Mapo just up the hill for the purist, natural-ingredient gelato I keep coming back to. Add a self-serve tub from Yo-Chi or an açaí bowl for the beach, and you've covered every mood a hot Bondi afternoon can throw at you.

I've walked this stretch more times than I can count, usually with a scoop melting faster than I can eat it. So rather than list every freezer in the postcode, here's where I actually send friends when they visit - and how to time it so you're not queuing behind the entire beach.
The gelato I actually queue for
Gelato Messina, Hall Street

Messina is the one visitors have usually heard of, and it earns the hype. The Bondi shop sits just off Campbell Parade on Hall Street, and alongside the signature line-up there's a rotating set of weekly specials that range from genuinely clever to gloriously silly. My move is to order one safe scoop (their salted caramel white chocolate is a classic for a reason) and one wildcard special. Flavours change constantly, so check the counter - or the Messina site - for what's on this week.
Anita Gelato, Campbell Parade

Anita is right on the beachfront, which makes it dangerously convenient. The draw here is the sheer wall of flavours - well over a hundred spanning gelato, sorbet and yogurt, including vegan and sugar-free options - so it's my pick when I'm with a group who can never agree. Ask for a taste before you commit; the staff are used to it, and it saves you from flavour regret.
Mapo

Mapo is my quiet favourite. It's the artisanal end of the spectrum - natural ingredients, authentic Italian technique, and no stabilisers in the cream, which is why the texture tastes so clean. Look for the Italian benchmarks like fior di latte, Sicilian pistachio and single-origin chocolate. It's less of a spectacle than Messina and less of a menu than Anita, but if you care about the gelato itself, this is where I'd point you first.

Skip the after-dinner rush. The queues at Messina and Anita balloon from about 7pm on warm evenings. Go late afternoon straight off the sand instead - shorter lines, softer light, and you can eat it on the grass at the north end overlooking the water.
Lighter and beach-friendly alternatives

Not every hot day calls for a double scoop. When I want something lighter, Yo-Chi is the self-serve frozen yogurt spot where you build your own tub and pay by weight - great with kids, since everyone assembles their own and no one complains. And if you've just come off the sand and want something that feels almost virtuous, an açaí bowl is the Bondi classic - you'll find a few good spots around Campbell Parade and Hall Street. Take it down to the promenade and you've got the perfect post-swim refuel.

blocks.title: Opening hours shift with the seasons
blocks.text: Bondi's dessert shops stretch their hours over summer and pull them back in winter, and specials rotate weekly. I've deliberately not baked exact times or prices into this guide - check each venue's own website or Instagram for current hours before you make a special trip.

items.q: What's the best ice cream in Bondi?
items.a: For gelato, my top three are Gelato Messina on Hall Street for standout signature and weekly-special flavours, Anita Gelato on Campbell Parade for the biggest variety (including vegan and sugar-free), and Mapo for natural, purist gelato. Which is 'best' honestly depends on whether you want spectacle, choice, or craft.

items.q: Where can I get vegan or dairy-free ice cream in Bondi?
items.a: Anita Gelato carries a wide range of sorbets and vegan options among its very large flavour list, and most Bondi gelato shops keep a few dairy-free sorbets alongside the dairy gelato. Açaí bowls are also naturally dairy-free. Ask at the counter, as the specific line-up changes.

items.q: Is there frozen yogurt in Bondi?
items.a: Yes - Yo-Chi offers self-serve frozen yogurt where you fill your own tub with soft-serve and toppings and pay by weight. It's a good lighter, customisable option, especially with kids.

items.q: When's the best time to go for ice cream in Bondi?
items.a: Late afternoon, straight off the beach. The big queues at Messina and Anita build in the evening, particularly after dinner on warm nights, so you'll wait far less if you go before the crowds arrive.

items.q: How much does gelato cost in Bondi?
items.a: Prices vary by shop, scoop size and season, so I'd rather not quote a figure that goes stale - check the venue's own menu. Expect Bondi beachfront pricing, and note that açaí bowls and build-your-own frozen yogurt are charged differently (often by weight or by bowl size).

blocks.text: That's my real-world loop: a scoop of something clever at Messina, a group graze at Anita, a quiet cone at Mapo, and an açaí bowl for the walk home. Whatever the weather's doing, Bondi's frozen-treat scene has you covered - just save room, and don't let it melt before you reach the sand.

blocks.text: Is the Bondi Hum real or a hoax? After years of fielding this over coffee on the promenade, here's my honest answer: it's real in the sense that people genuinely hear it - it isn't invented for attention - but nobody has ever pinned down a confirmed external source, and the latest science points inward, at our own hearing, rather than out to sea. So: not a hoax, but not the tidy villain everyone hopes to catch either.

items.label: Who hears it
items.value: A small minority in affected areas

blocks.text: So what exactly is the Bondi Hum?

People who hear it describe a steady, monotonous drone - a distant idling truck, a far-off fan, a low-flying plane that never arrives. It's low-frequency and relentless, and here's the strange part: the person next to you often can't hear a thing. It's loudest indoors and after dark, once the clamour of the suburb dies down and nothing masks it.
For most of us it's a curiosity. For the unlucky few, it's miserable - disturbed sleep, headaches, a sense of pressure, and the frustration of a problem no one else can hear and no meter has caught.
Part of a worldwide mystery

The thing I always tell people: Bondi isn't special here. "The Hum" is a global phenomenon reported for decades - famously in Bristol, England, from the mid-1970s, then in the 1990s in Taos, New Mexico and Kokomo, Indiana, each with its own name and baffled residents. The reports are remarkably consistent: a low rumble, usually put in the 30–80 Hz range, worse at night, audible to only a small slice of the local population.

If you think you're hearing it, try a simple test: step well away from any building and see whether it fades. A real external source usually changes as you move; a hum that follows you everywhere, even out in the open, is a strong hint it's your own hearing rather than the neighbourhood.
Real or hoax? Where the science actually sits

Here's where it gets interesting. A 2026 study led by Professor Markus Drexl at Norway's NTNU tested people who hear the Hum and found that, for most, the likeliest explanation is low-frequency tinnitus - a sound generated within the auditory system itself, even though it feels utterly external. Of 28 participants, only two showed better-than-average low-frequency hearing, and the inner-ear emissions you'd expect from unusually sensitive ears simply weren't there. Most of the time, in other words, the hum may be coming from inside the listener, not the coastline.

That said, the researchers were careful - and so am I. They didn't rule external sources out, and standard tests can miss extremely narrow sensitivities. Some hums genuinely are machinery, traced over the years to industrial or infrastructure noise. So the honest verdict is split: not a hoax; often a real quirk of hearing; occasionally a real external source that simply hasn't been found.

blocks.title: If it's affecting your health
blocks.text: A hum that's wrecking your sleep or causing headaches is worth taking seriously. See a GP or an audiologist - low-frequency tinnitus is a recognised, manageable condition, and ruling it in or out beats chasing a phantom machine. If you're convinced it's an external source, the NSW EPA handles noise complaints.
What locals and authorities have made of it

Over the years, eastern-suburbs residents have raised low-frequency noise with local authorities, and the usual suspects - traffic, sewerage infrastructure, industrial plant - have been floated and largely dismissed without a smoking gun. The NSW Environment Protection Authority investigates persistent noise complaints across Sydney, and its noise pages are the best place to check what's currently on its radar. For the Bondi Hum itself, no conclusive cause has ever been confirmed.

items.q: Is the Bondi Hum a hoax?
items.a: No. People genuinely perceive it - it isn't made up. What's unproven is the cause. There's no confirmed external source, and recent research suggests it may, for many, be low-frequency tinnitus generated within the ear itself.

items.q: Why can only some people hear the Bondi Hum?
items.a: That's the defining feature of 'the Hum' everywhere: only a small minority report it. If it were loud environmental noise, most people nearby would notice - part of why an internal, hearing-based explanation is taken seriously.

items.q: Has the cause of the Bondi Hum ever been found?
items.a: No. Suggested sources like traffic, sewerage plant and industrial equipment have been considered and not confirmed. As with the Taos and Bristol hums, no definitive external cause has been established for Bondi.

items.q: What should I do if I can hear it?
items.a: Try moving well away from any building to see if it fades. If it persists and affects your sleep or wellbeing, see a GP or audiologist about low-frequency tinnitus. If you believe it's genuinely an outside source, the NSW EPA handles noise investigations.

blocks.text: So, real or hoax? Neither label quite fits - which is why the Bondi Hum endures in local folklore. It sits in the genuinely unexplained middle: a real experience with a stubbornly elusive cause. Next time someone swears they hear a droning out over the water on a still night, don't dismiss them. They might be one of the few - and if you are too, you're in good company, from Taos to Bristol.

If you're travelling to Bondi with kids, my honest answer to "where are the best playgrounds?" is that you're spoilt - the two I send every family to are the playground right on the sand at North Bondi and the rocket-ship playground at Waverley Park in Bondi Junction. Between those two, plus a couple of quieter local favourites, you can fill a whole weekend without the kids ever getting bored. Here's how I'd actually plan it.
North Bondi Playground - play with an ocean view

This is the one I send first-timers to: a compact playground tucked into the leafy corner of Biddigal Reserve at the northern end of Bondi Beach, up on the grass off Ramsgate Avenue. The draw here isn't the size of the kit - it's small and geared to younger kids - it's that you can let the little ones play while the surf rolls in behind you. We come with buckets and towels so it doubles as a beach day: playground for a while, then straight down onto the sand.

It sits at the calmer north end, close to the North Bondi kiosks and the start of the coastal walk, so a coffee is never far away. Metered street parking on Ramsgate Avenue is the closest and fills fast on sunny weekends, which is my single biggest tip for this spot.
Come before 9am on a summer weekend. You'll get a shady spot, an easy park on Ramsgate Avenue, and the playground to yourselves for an hour before the beach crowds arrive.
Waverley Park - the famous rocket ship

If it's blowing a southerly or the kids need more room than the beach allows, we head inland to Waverley Park in Bondi Junction. The centrepiece is a multi-storey rocket ship - a modern rebuild of the beloved 1960s original - surrounded by a jungle gym, swings, musical play and water-play features for hot days. It's a genuine all-ages, all-abilities playground, and crucially for parents of runners, it's fully fenced.

There's a kiosk inside the park for coffee and snacks, public toilets nearby, and huge open lawns for a picnic or a kick of the footy. It's roughly a ten-minute walk from Bondi Junction station and minutes from Westfield, so it's the easy pick if you're arriving by train or want everything in one place.

blocks.title: Check before a special trip
blocks.text: Kiosk hours, water-play operation and occasional maintenance closures change with the seasons. If you're travelling specially for a particular feature, check the current details on the Waverley Council park page first.
Quieter local favourites

When we want to dodge the crowds, there are smaller neighbourhood playgrounds worth knowing. Tamarama has a compact, grassy playground a short stroll from its little beach - lovely and low-key for toddlers, with the ocean breeze right there. Bronte Park, one bay further south, pairs a playground with big shady lawns, a saltwater pool and the famous Bronte kiosk, and it's the easiest of the three beaches for parking and picnics.

items: Tamarama Beach - small, grassy playground steps from a sheltered beach; great for younger kids.
Bronte Park - playground plus lawns, the Bronte Baths and a much-loved kiosk; a solid rainy-plan B and picnic spot.
North Bondi - the ocean-view classic when you want beach and play in one hit.

blocks.text: String them together along the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk: start at North Bondi, then drive or stroll to Tamarama and Bronte. It turns "which playground?" into a proper half-day out.

items.q: Which Bondi playground is best if we want beach and play together?
items.a: North Bondi, in Biddigal Reserve at the northern end of the beach. It's up on the grass off Ramsgate Avenue, so kids can play and then head straight down for a swim or a paddle.

items.q: Are any of the playgrounds fully fenced?
items.a: Waverley Park in Bondi Junction is fully fenced, which is the reason we recommend it for families with toddlers who like to bolt. The beachfront playgrounds are open, so keep little ones within reach.

items.q: Is there anywhere to get coffee and use a toilet?
items.a: Yes. Waverley Park has a kiosk and public toilets inside the park. North Bondi and Bronte both have kiosks and public amenities close to the playgrounds.

items.q: What's the best playground on a very hot or very windy day?
items.a: Waverley Park. It sits back from the coast so it's more sheltered from the sea breeze, it has shade and water play, and being fully fenced it's the most relaxed option for parents.

items.q: Do the playgrounds cost anything?
items.a: No - all of these are free public playgrounds managed by Waverley Council. Your only likely cost is metered parking near the beaches or a coffee from the kiosk.

blocks.text: That's my local shortlist: North Bondi for the view, Waverley Park for the works, and Tamarama or Bronte when you want it quieter. Pack water, hats and a picnic rug, aim for an early start, and you've got a Bondi family day that keeps everyone happy - kids and parents alike.

blocks.text: The 2024 TCS Sydney Marathon ran on Sunday 15 September 2024, starting near North Sydney Oval and finishing at the Sydney Opera House forecourt - and here in Bondi we watched with more than the usual interest, because this was the race that clinched Sydney's place as the seventh Abbott World Marathon Major. I've cheered friends across that finish line, so here's my local's guide to the day and how you'd tackle it from this side of town.
Why the 2024 edition mattered

For years the Sydney Marathon was our city's best-kept running secret. The 2024 event was its final candidacy assessment for the Abbott World Marathon Majors - the elite club that includes Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York and Tokyo. It passed, with a record field crossing the line, and in November 2024 Sydney was officially confirmed as the seventh Major, the first ever in the southern hemisphere. If you ran it in 2024, you were part of that history.

items.label: Start
items.value: Miller Street, North Sydney (near North Sydney Oval)

items.label: Milestone
items.value: Confirmed as 7th Abbott World Marathon Major

blocks.text: The course, and why it's a stunner

This is one of the most scenic marathon routes I know. Runners leave North Sydney and cross the Sydney Harbour Bridge in the first few kilometres - closed to traffic, which almost never happens - with the harbour opening up on both sides. From there the course rolls through The Rocks and Circular Quay, out along the water past Pyrmont, and through the green calm of Centennial Park before the run home to the Opera House. It's a genuine highlight reel of Sydney, and that Bridge crossing at dawn is the moment everyone remembers.

items: Sydney Harbour Bridge - the early, iconic crossing with harbour views
The Rocks & Circular Quay - historic laneways and big early crowds
Pyrmont waterfront - a calmer, breezy stretch beside the water
Centennial Park - leafy green respite before the final push
Sydney Opera House - the finish, with the sails as your backdrop

blocks.text: Course details, start times and entries change every year. For the next edition, don't rely on last year's numbers - check the official TCS Sydney Marathon site for the current date, route map and registration before you plan anything.
Doing it from Bondi - spectating and getting there

Bondi isn't on the marathon course, but it's an easy base, and race morning is early. The start is over on the north side of the harbour, and public transport is the only sensible way in - roads around the Bridge, the CBD and the finish close for hours. From the eastern beaches I'd catch a bus toward the city and connect to a train, and I always check the Transport for NSW trip planner the night before, because event-day timetables shift.

blocks.title: Plan for road closures
blocks.text: On race morning, large parts of North Sydney, the Harbour Bridge, the CBD and the Opera House precinct close to traffic from the early hours. Leave the car at home, allow extra time, and treat the official event and Transport for NSW pages as the source of truth for closures and replacement services.

If you're spectating, Circular Quay and the Opera House forecourt are the spots I'd aim for - the early-race energy near the Quay, or the raw emotion of the finish by the sails. Get there early and bring layers for a cool September morning. When the medals are handed out, you've the perfect excuse to head back east and let the runners recover with a flat white and a swim at Bondi.

items.q: When was the 2024 Sydney Marathon held?
items.a: The 2024 TCS Sydney Marathon took place on Sunday 15 September 2024, starting near North Sydney Oval and finishing at the Sydney Opera House forecourt. Future editions have moved to late August - check the official site for the current year's date.

items.q: Is the Sydney Marathon a World Marathon Major?
items.a: Yes. The 2024 race was its final successful candidacy assessment, and in November 2024 Sydney was confirmed as the seventh Abbott World Marathon Major, joining Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York and Tokyo - the first Major in the southern hemisphere.

items.q: Does the marathon route go through Bondi?
items.a: No - the course runs across the Harbour Bridge and through the city, The Rocks, Pyrmont and Centennial Park before finishing at the Opera House. Bondi still makes a great base, and a post-race swim is the ideal reward.

items.q: What's the best way to get to the start and finish?
items.a: Public transport, without question. The Bridge, CBD and Opera House precinct close to traffic for hours on race morning. From Bondi, take a bus toward the city and connect to a train, and check the Transport for NSW trip planner for event-day services and closures.

items.q: How do I enter the next Sydney Marathon?
items.a: Entries, distances and prices are set each year by the organisers. Head to the official TCS Sydney Marathon website for current registration details rather than relying on past information.

blocks.text: Whether you ran it, cheered it, or watched the Bridge crossing on the news, the 2024 Sydney Marathon was a landmark day - it turned a much-loved local race into a global one, and gave everyone from North Sydney to Bondi a reason to feel proud.

sources.label: Abbott World Marathon Majors - Sydney becomes seventh Major

blocks.text: If you're staying in Bondi and running (or cheering at) the Sydney Marathon, the simplest way to reach the start line is public transport: bus from Bondi Beach up to Bondi Junction, then the train through the city and over to the North Shore. Race morning brings big road closures around the Harbour Bridge and the CBD, so leave the car behind - this is one day where the train genuinely is faster than driving.

The TCS Sydney Marathon is now an Abbott World Marathon Major, so tens of thousands of runners and supporters funnel toward the same corner of the harbour on one morning. A little planning from Bondi is the difference between a calm warm-up and a stressful scramble.

items.label: From Bondi
items.value: Bus to Bondi Junction, then train

items.label: Get around
items.value: Opal card / contactless tap on & off

blocks.text: Getting to the start line in North Sydney

The marathon starts in North Sydney, on the northern side of the Harbour Bridge, and the course crosses the bridge before finishing at the Opera House. From Bondi the cleanest route is a two-leg public-transport trip.
Step 1 - Bus up to Bondi Junction

Get from the beach to Bondi Junction interchange. The 333 (limited-stop) and 380 both run this corridor along Bondi Road and Campbell Parade, and on a clear early morning the hop up the hill is quick. Bondi Junction is where the buses meet the train line - that's your connection point.
Step 2 - Train through the city to the North Shore

At Bondi Junction, jump on a T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra line train to Central or Town Hall, then change to a T1 North Shore line service running north across the bridge to North Sydney station. From there it's a short walk to the start precinct, following the crowds and marshals.

blocks.title: Timetables change for the event
blocks.text: Transport for NSW usually adds extra early services on race morning, and closures can alter normal routes. I won't quote a fixed departure time because it shifts year to year - plug your start wave into the trip planner the week of the race and build in a buffer.

Set up your Opal or contactless card the night before and check the balance. Tap on and off with the same card each leg - the last thing you want on a cold Bondi morning is to be fumbling at a top-up machine while your wave is called.
Getting back to Bondi after the finish

The finish is at the Sydney Opera House forecourt, and Circular Quay station and the ferry wharves are a short, gentle walk away once you've collected your medal and found your people. To get home, reverse the journey: a T4 train from Circular Quay or Town Hall toward Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus down to the beach.

blocks.title: Expect crowds on the way home
blocks.text: Everyone finishes in roughly the same window, so Circular Quay and the trains get busy. If your legs allow, walk to a quieter station or let the peak ease over a coffee first.
Race-morning tips from a local

items: Leave earlier than feels necessary - road closures and crowds slow everything down, and you can't sprint to a start wave the way you can a normal train.
Don't drive toward the bridge or CBD; closures are extensive and parking near the start is a headache. Public transport is the plan.
Screenshot the official course and closure maps before you set off, in case mobile coverage is patchy in the crush.
If friends are spectating, agree a meeting point at the finish beforehand; phone signal near the Opera House can be jammed with everyone messaging at once.

items.q: Where does the Sydney Marathon start and finish?
items.a: The marathon starts in North Sydney on the northern side of the Harbour Bridge and finishes at the Sydney Opera House forecourt. The course crosses the Harbour Bridge, so road closures on race morning are significant.

items.q: What's the best way to get from Bondi Beach to the start line?
items.a: Take the 333 or 380 bus from Bondi Beach to Bondi Junction, then a T4 train into the city, changing to a T1 North Shore line service to North Sydney station. Public transport beats driving because of the closures.

items.q: Should I drive to the marathon from Bondi?
items.a: No. Widespread road closures around the bridge and CBD make driving slow and parking scarce on race morning. Public transport is genuinely the faster and less stressful option.

items.q: How do I get back to Bondi after finishing at the Opera House?
items.a: Walk to Circular Quay, catch a T4 train toward Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus down to Bondi Beach. Expect crowds, so allow extra time or let the post-race peak ease first.

items.q: How early should I leave Bondi on race day?
items.a: Earlier than you think. Check your start-wave time and route in the Transport for NSW trip planner the week of the race, then add a buffer for crowds and the walk to the start line.

blocks.text: For anything that changes year to year - the date, your start-wave time, the full road-closure map and any event transport - check the official TCS Sydney Marathon site and the Transport for NSW trip planner before race day. Get those right and the trip in from Bondi is the easy part. See you on the other side of the bridge.

If you're after the best vegetarian and vegan food in Bondi Beach, my short answer is this: start at [Funky Pies](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/funky-pies) for a fully vegan pie, graze your way through [Sabbaba](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sabbaba-bondi-beach)'s falafel and salads, and finish with a [Gelato Messina](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/gelato-messina-bondi) sorbet on Hall Street. Bondi has quietly become one of Sydney's easiest suburbs to eat plant-based in, and after years of wandering these streets between swims, these are the spots I actually send friends to. If you'd rather see the whole field at a glance, we keep a running directory of Bondi's [best vegan and vegetarian spots](/bondi-eat-and-drink/vegan-vegetarian-bondi-beach).
Where I go for fully vegan food

Funky Pies, tucked away on Glenayr Avenue a short walk back from the sand, is the one I rate most highly for a proper hot meal. The whole menu is vegan - handmade, chunky pies and pastries, with the classics done properly rather than as an afterthought. It's a small shop with a cult following, so it's not somewhere you sit down for a long lunch; it's grab-a-pie-and-eat-it-on-the-grass energy, which is exactly what you want after a morning in the water. Check their site for current hours before you make a special trip.

For a lighter plant-based option, [Fishbowl](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/fishbowl) does a build-your-own poke-style bowl that's easy to keep fully vegan - tofu, brown rice, plenty of veg and a light dressing. It's a reliable, fast, post-beach lunch, and their online menu lists what's in each bowl if you have allergen questions.

Bondi's most beloved sweet spot is genuinely plant-based-friendly: at Gelato Messina on Hall Street the sorbets are dairy-free, and the chocolate sorbet in particular is so rich most people can't believe it's vegan. Check the vegan flavours list on the Messina site, since specials rotate weekly.
The best vegetarian-friendly eats

Sabbaba is my go-to for a cheap, generous veggie feed. It's a Middle Eastern street-food spot, and the vegetarians and vegans are genuinely looked after here - falafel pita stuffed with salad, hummus and tahini, plus dips, dolmades, chips and salads you can mix and match. It's fast, it's filling, and it's the kind of meal that suits a sandy, salty afternoon when you don't want to sit still for long. If a cheap, no-fuss feed is what you're chasing, it sits near the top of our roundup of Bondi's [best cheap eats](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach).

For brunch, the beachfront cafés along the promenade all carry solid vegetarian options these days - think smashed avo, grain bowls, veg-forward toasts and, at many, a vegan pancake or two. Menus and daily specials change constantly, so rather than promise you a specific dish, I'd say scan the board when you arrive and ask the staff what's vegan that day. In my experience they're used to the question and happy to help. If you want the full line-up before you set out, we've mapped Bondi's [best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) spots separately.
Bowls, açaí and sweeter plant-based treats

Bondi runs on smoothie bowls and açaí, and most of it is easy to keep plant-based. [OAKBERRY Açaí](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/oakberry-acai-bondi-beach) builds bowls on a naturally dairy-free açaí base - just swap the honey and choose your toppings - and [Cali Press](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cali-press) is my pick for cold-pressed juices, smoothies and a veg-forward menu when I want something lighter than a pie. Both are the kind of quick, colourful refuel that suits a between-swims kind of day.

And if the queue at Messina is out the door, you're not stuck for something sweet. [Anita Gelato](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/anita-gelato-bondi) and [Rivareno Gelato](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/rivareno-gelato-bondi-beach) both scoop sorbets alongside their gelato, and [Yo-Chi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/yo-chi-bondi-beach) does self-serve frozen yoghurt where you assemble your own cup, sorbet options included. Ask which flavours are dairy-free on the day, since specials rotate everywhere. For the full sweet-tooth trail, see our guide to Bondi's [best bakeries and sweets](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach).
Fine dining with real vegetable dishes

[Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), perched above the ocean pool, is best known for seafood, but it builds genuine, seasonal vegetable dishes into its menu too. It's a special-occasion place with a changing menu, so if you're vegetarian or vegan, phone ahead and mention it when you book so the kitchen can look after you properly. It's also one of a handful of [ocean-view dining rooms](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach) in Bondi worth the splurge.

blocks.title: Menus move fast
blocks.text: Bondi's food scene turns over quickly - cafés change hands, hours shift with the seasons, and dishes rotate. I've pointed you at each venue's official channel rather than quoting prices or opening times that could be out of date by the time you visit. Always check the venue's own site or socials before heading out.

blocks.title: Find your own plant-based Bondi
blocks.text: These are my personal picks, but they're only a slice of what's here. Our [vegan and vegetarian directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink/vegan-vegetarian-bondi-beach) lists every plant-based-friendly spot in the suburb, and you can open the full [Bondi eat-and-drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink) to filter all 160+ venues by cuisine, area, price or who you're with.
How to plan a plant-based day in Bondi

items: Morning: coffee and a vegetarian brunch at a promenade café, or an açaí bowl from OAKBERRY, before it gets busy.
Midday: a swim, then a fully vegan pie from Funky Pies or a tofu bowl from Fishbowl.
Afternoon: a falafel and salad plate from Sabbaba to refuel.
Evening: a dairy-free sorbet from Gelato Messina, or book ahead for a seasonal vegetable menu at Icebergs.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach good for vegans?
items.a: Yes - it's one of the easier Sydney beach suburbs to eat vegan in. Funky Pies is entirely vegan, Fishbowl bowls can be built fully plant-based, Sabbaba has strong vegan options, and Gelato Messina's sorbets are dairy-free. Browsing our [vegan and vegetarian directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink/vegan-vegetarian-bondi-beach) is a good way to see everything that's nearby.

items.q: Where's the best fully vegan restaurant in Bondi?
items.a: For a hot, sit-down-style meal, Funky Pies on Glenayr Avenue is my top pick - the entire menu is vegan and the pies are handmade. Check their website for current opening hours before you go.

items.q: Can I get good vegetarian food at Bondi's fine-dining restaurants?
items.a: Yes. Icebergs Dining Room and Bar includes seasonal vegetable dishes on its menu. Because those menus change, phone ahead and flag that you're vegetarian or vegan when you book.

items.q: Is there vegan dessert in Bondi?
items.a: Gelato Messina on Hall Street is the classic choice - its sorbets are dairy-free, and the chocolate sorbet is a standout. Anita Gelato, Rivareno and Yo-Chi all offer plant-based options too. The flavours rotate, so check the current list in-store.

items.q: How do I know a café's options are actually vegan?
items.a: Ask. Bondi kitchens are very used to the question, daily specials change often, and staff can tell you what's plant-based that day - which is far more reliable than any menu photo online.

blocks.text: That's the loop I'd walk on a plant-based day here - a veggie brunch, a swim, something hearty and vegan for lunch, and a sorbet to finish. Bondi rewards eating the way it rewards everything else: slowly, with sand on your feet.

Yes - Bondi Beach is safe to swim as long as you stay between the red and yellow flags during patrol hours. Lifeguards patrol year-round and place the flags on the safest sand for the day's conditions. The main hazard is rip currents, which is exactly why the flags matter.

That single habit - swimming between the flags - is the difference between a relaxed dip and a scary afternoon, because those flags are placed by the lifeguards on the safest patch of sand for the conditions that day, and it's the stretch they watch most closely. I've swum here in every season, and the ocean is genuinely welcoming most days. But Bondi is a real surf beach, not a swimming pool, so a little know-how goes a long way.

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Swim between the red & yellow flags

items.label: Calmest water
items.value: Bondi Icebergs / Ross Jones rock pools

blocks.text: The flags are the whole game

If you remember one thing, make it this: swim between the flags. The red and yellow flags mark the supervised zone where the lifeguards have judged conditions to be least hazardous, and it's the area under constant watch. Outside that zone you might be swimming over a rip, a sudden drop-off, or a spot no one is scanning. The flags also move through the day as the surf shifts, so glance up and check where they are before you wade in, not just when you arrive.

Bondi is patrolled year-round by Waverley Council's professional lifeguards - the same crew you've seen on Bondi Rescue - backed by volunteer surf lifesavers on weekends and holidays. Patrol hours change with the season, and are longer in summer than winter, so if you want the exact times for the day you're visiting, check Waverley Council's beach safety page rather than trusting a number that drifts through the year.

blocks.title: Don't swim outside patrol hours
blocks.text: Early-morning and after-dark swims outside the flagged, patrolled window mean no one is watching if something goes wrong. If you love a dawn or dusk dip, the Icebergs pool or the rock pools at each end are a far safer bet than the open surf.
Rip currents: the real risk, and how to beat one

The genuine danger at Bondi isn't sharks or jellyfish - it's rip currents. A rip is a strong, narrow channel of water flowing back out to sea, and it can carry a swimmer away from shore faster than they can swim. Bondi has a notorious one at the southern end near the rocks, long nicknamed the "Backpackers' Rip" because visitors who don't know the beach tend to wander in there, straight into trouble.

You can often spot a rip if you know what to look for: a darker, calmer-looking gap in the breaking waves, a rippled channel of water sitting between areas of white surf, or foam and sand streaming out past the break. That deceptively calm patch is usually the rip - not the easy option it looks like.
If you're ever caught in one, the advice from Surf Life Saving is simple and it saves lives:

items: Don't panic and don't try to swim straight back against the current - you'll only exhaust yourself.
Stay calm and float. A rip pulls you out, but it won't pull you under.
Raise one arm and call out for help - the lifeguards are watching the flagged zone and will come.
If you're a confident swimmer, swim parallel to the beach, towards the breaking waves, until you're out of the channel, then head in.

blocks.text: Before you get in, take thirty seconds on the promenade to actually read the water. Find the flags, then look for that darker, wave-free gap that marks a rip - and put a good stretch of sand between it and where you swim. Reading the beach first is the most local thing you can do.
Calmer options and knowing your limits

Some days the surf is big and dumping, and there's no shame in staying out of it. The northern end of the beach is generally the gentler half, and when the ocean looks too rough I head for the seawater pools instead: the famous Bondi Icebergs pool at the south end, or the free Ross Jones Memorial rock pool tucked below it. They give you the salt water and the view with none of the rip risk, which makes them brilliant for kids and less-confident swimmers. For current session times and entry fees, check the Icebergs website directly, as those do change.

blocks.caption: Where to swim at Bondi, from calmest to most exposed
rows: Kids, a free calm dip at the south end
Families, gentler surf on most days
Lower, but still swim between the flags

blocks.text: The rest is common sense that locals live by: never swim alone, don't swim straight after drinking, keep a constant eye on children in or near the water, and if you're at all unsure, ask a lifeguard - they would genuinely rather you ask than get into difficulty. Slip on a rashie or sunscreen too; the Australian sun is fierce even when the water is cool.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes, provided you swim between the red and yellow flags during patrol hours. That flagged zone is chosen by lifeguards as the safest area for the day's conditions and is watched constantly. The main hazard is rip currents, which is exactly why the flags matter so much.

items.q: Are there lifeguards at Bondi Beach all year?
items.a: Yes. Bondi is patrolled year-round by Waverley Council's professional lifeguards, with volunteer surf lifesavers on weekends and public holidays. Patrol hours are longer in summer than winter - check Waverley Council's beach safety page for the current day's times.

items.q: What should I do if I get caught in a rip current?
items.a: Don't panic and don't fight it. Stay calm, float, raise an arm and call for help so the lifeguards can reach you. If you're a strong swimmer, swim parallel to the beach towards the breaking waves until you're clear of the channel, then head back in.

items.q: Are sharks or jellyfish a danger at Bondi?
items.a: Serious encounters are very rare. Bondi is a busy, heavily patrolled urban beach, and by far the bigger real-world risk to swimmers is rip currents, not marine life. You may occasionally get a minor jellyfish sting - lifeguards can help with first aid.

items.q: Where is the calmest place to swim at Bondi?
items.a: The northern end of the beach is usually gentler than the south. For the calmest water, the Bondi Icebergs seawater pool and the free Ross Jones rock pool below it offer a controlled swim with no rip risk - ideal for children and nervous swimmers.

items.q: How cold is the water - do I need a wetsuit?
items.a: The sea peaks at about 23-24°C in February and bottoms out around 17-18°C in August-September. Most visitors swim comfortably in just swimwear from December to April; locals tend to pull on springsuits or wetsuits from May to October. See our [month-by-month temperatures](/bondi-blog/2024/8/28/average-sea-temperatures-at-bondi-beach-month-by-month-guide) guide for the detail.

blocks.text: So, is it safe to swim at Bondi? Absolutely - it's one of my favourite swims in Sydney. Just respect the ocean the way locals do: read the water, stay between the flags, and never be shy about waving down a lifeguard. Do that, and Bondi gives you one of the best swims of your life.

If you want Sydney's best hidden beaches, skip the postcard names and hunt the little coves tucked behind headlands, national parks and quiet harbour streets. I live on the eastern beaches and spend half my weekends chasing exactly these - the sheltered swims, the boat-only bays, the sand most visitors walk past. Here's my honest local shortlist of 20, with the ones I'd send you to first.

A quick word before you pack the towel: "hidden" usually means unpatrolled. Most of these have no lifeguards, no flags and sometimes no easy exit. Swim within your limits, check conditions first, and treat the calm harbour beaches as the safer bet if you've got kids.
My favourite hidden beaches around the harbour

The harbour hides Sydney's most magical little beaches - glassy water, ridiculous backdrops. Milk Beach, off the Hermitage Foreshore Walk in Vaucluse, frames the Opera House and Harbour Bridge across the water; it's my go-to for a late-afternoon swim and a picnic. Nearby, Parsley Bay in Vaucluse is a gentle, netted cove with a suspension bridge and grass for the kids, and Camp Cove near Watsons Bay is a calm, golden crescent a short walk from the ferry crowds.

Over on the lower north shore, Chinamans Beach in Mosman is a wide, quiet stretch that's brilliant for paddleboarding, and Store Beach near Manly is the real secret - inside Sydney Harbour National Park, reachable only by kayak or boat, with a protected penguin colony ashore, so landing is restricted at times to keep the birds safe.

For the harbour coves, aim for a rising-to-high tide - several shrink to almost nothing at low water. Go early on summer weekends too: parking around Vaucluse and Mosman fills fast, so take the ferry or a bus.
Where I go to snorkel

Two spots earn their reputation. Shelly Beach at Manly sits inside the Cabbage Tree Bay Aquatic Reserve - a no-take reserve since 2002 - so the marine life is genuinely abundant; on a calm day you'll spot wrasse, gropers and sometimes a resident turtle. Closer to home, Gordon's Bay between Clovelly and Coogee has an underwater nature trail and clear, sheltered water - perfect for a first snorkel.

blocks.title: These beaches are mostly unpatrolled
blocks.text: Bushwalk and boat-only beaches have no lifeguards and can have strong currents, sudden swell and slippery rock scrambles. Check the surf forecast and any national-park access notes first. If it looks sketchy, the calm harbour beaches are the safer choice.
The full 20 - and how to reach them
Beyond my favourites, here's the rest, grouped by effort. The bush-and-boat ones reward a walk or a paddle.

items: Easy harbour coves: Milk Beach, Parsley Bay, Camp Cove, Kutti Beach, Queens Beach, Redleaf (Murray Rose Pool), Chinamans Beach, Fairlight
Snorkelling favourites: Shelly Beach (Manly), Gordon's Bay, Little Congwong (La Perouse)
Reached by bushwalk: Reef Beach, Castle Rock and Collins Flat (Manly area), Resolute Beach (Ku-ring-gai Chase), Little Bay
Boat or kayak only: Store Beach, Washaway Beach
Tide-and-timing gems: Mackenzies Beach (between Bondi and Tamarama), Balmoral's quiet Rocky Point end

blocks.text: Mackenzies Beach, the closest to us, is less a beach than a strip of sand that surfaces between Bondi and Tamarama when the tide and swell cooperate - a happy surprise on the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk, not a whole-day plan.

For national-park beaches like Resolute and the Manly bushwalk coves, wear proper shoes, carry water, and check the relevant NSW National Parks page for track closures or seasonal alerts - trails do close after storms.

items.q: What is the most hidden beach in Sydney?
items.a: Store Beach near Manly is hard to beat - inside Sydney Harbour National Park, reachable only by kayak or boat, with a protected penguin colony ashore. Washaway Beach nearby is similarly cut off, reached only on foot or by boat.

items.q: Which hidden beaches are best for families?
items.a: Stick to the calm harbour beaches. Parsley Bay in Vaucluse has a netted swimming area and grassy picnic space, and Redleaf (the Murray Rose Pool) in Double Bay has a floating pontoon and gentle water - far safer for little swimmers than the ocean coves.

items.q: Are these hidden beaches patrolled by lifeguards?
items.a: Mostly no. Unlike Bondi or Manly, most of these coves are unpatrolled, with no flags and sometimes strong currents or rock-scramble access. Check conditions on Surf Life Saving's BeachSafe and swim within your limits.

items.q: Where's the best hidden snorkelling near Sydney?
items.a: Shelly Beach at Manly, inside the Cabbage Tree Bay Aquatic Reserve, is the standout - a no-take reserve packed with fish. Gordon's Bay between Clovelly and Coogee is a calmer alternative with its own underwater nature trail.

items.q: Do I need to pay to visit any of these?
items.a: The beaches are free; access is the catch. National-park beaches like Resolute in Ku-ring-gai Chase may involve a vehicle-entry fee if you drive in, and boat-only spots like Store Beach mean hiring a kayak or a tour. Check the relevant NSW National Parks page for current fees.

blocks.text: That's my map to Sydney's quiet corners. Start with Milk Beach or Camp Cove for the view, Shelly Beach for the fish, and save Store Beach for the day you feel like earning it. Tread lightly, check conditions, and leave each cove as gorgeous as you found it.

blocks.text: Want the honest answer to what's worth your time in Sydney? The harbour icons deserve the hype, but my best days are spent on the coast, in the water and in the corners of the city most guidebooks skip. I live a few streets back from Bondi, and this is the list I hand friends flying in - sorted the way a local thinks, not how a brochure sells.
The harbour icons I'd never talk you out of

Some things are famous for a reason. Climbing the Sydney Harbour Bridge and touring the Sydney Opera House are both worth doing once, and a public ferry gives you the same skyline as a pricey cruise. My rule: do the icons early, then slow down.

items: Climb the Sydney Harbour Bridge, or just walk the free pedestrian path across it
Tour the Sydney Opera House or catch an evening performance
Ride a public ferry to Manly and back for the best-value harbour cruise in town
Wander the Royal Botanic Garden and Mrs Macquarie's Chair for the classic Opera House-and-Bridge shot
Explore historic The Rocks and its weekend markets
Catch the ferry to Cockatoo Island / Wareamah, a UNESCO-listed convict and shipbuilding site

blocks.text: Tap on with an Opal or contactless card and ferries become public transport, not a tour - the Circular Quay to Manly run costs an ordinary fare and delivers the same postcard. Opal fares are capped daily; check Transport for NSW for current caps and plan a harbour day around one.
Beaches, ocean pools and the coast walk

This is where I spend most weekends. The Bondi to Coogee coastal walk is the headline act - around six kilometres of clifftop path linking Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee, roughly two hours at an easy pace with coffee and swim stops on the way.

items: Swim between the flags at Bondi, then cool off in the Bondi Baths
Snorkel the underwater nature trail at Gordons Bay
Do a lap of the sea pool at McIver's Ladies Baths in Coogee (women and children only)
Cross the harbour to gentle, family-friendly Balmoral Beach in Mosman
Walk from Manly to Shelly Beach for calm-water snorkelling
Surf the local, low-key breaks at Maroubra
Picnic at quiet Milk Beach for a skyline-and-yachts view most visitors never find

blocks.title: Some spots are for looking, not chancing
blocks.text: The Figure Eight Pools in the Royal National Park are stunning but genuinely dangerous at the wrong tide - people have been swept off the rock shelf by rogue waves. Go only on a low, calm tide, check the official National Parks safety and tide guidance first, and never turn your back on the ocean.
Green escapes and the wilder edges

You don't have to go far to swap sand for bushland. The Blue Mountains are an easy train day trip for the Three Sisters and waterfall walks, and closer in there are pockets of calm hidden in plain sight.

items: Take the train to Katoomba for the Three Sisters and Blue Mountains walking tracks
Find Wendy's Secret Garden in Lavender Bay, a free harbourside labyrinth of greenery
Stroll Barangaroo Reserve, replanted entirely with native species
Meet native wildlife at Taronga Zoo, reached by its own ferry
Kayak the sheltered inlets of Middle Harbour
Scan the horizon from the Bondi cliffs for whales in season (roughly May to November), often for free

blocks.text: Culture, markets and rainy-day plans

When the weather turns, and in Sydney it can turn fast, I lean on the city's galleries and markets. The Art Gallery of NSW and the Museum of Contemporary Art in The Rocks are both free for general entry, the weekend Bondi Markets are the best browse in the east, and in winter Vivid Sydney lights the harbour after dark. Always check each venue's site for current hours and dates.

items.q: What's the one thing I shouldn't miss in Sydney?
items.a: If I had to pick one, it's the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk - six kilometres of clifftop path with beaches, ocean pools and cafes the whole way, and it's free. It's the side of Sydney locals actually love.

items.q: How many days do I need to see Sydney properly?
items.a: Three to four full days cover the harbour icons, the eastern beaches and a Blue Mountains day trip without rushing. A week lets you slow down and find quieter spots like Milk Beach and Shelly.

items.q: Do I need a car to get around?
items.a: No. An Opal or contactless card covers trains, buses and ferries, and most of this list is reachable. A car mainly helps for the Royal National Park.

items.q: When is whale-watching season in Sydney?
items.a: Humpbacks migrate along the coast roughly from May to November. On a clear day you can often spot them for free from the Bondi clifftops - bring binoculars and some patience.

items.q: Which of these activities are free?
items.a: Plenty: the coastal walks, ocean swims, Wendy's Secret Garden, Barangaroo Reserve, the pedestrian walk across the Harbour Bridge, cliff-top whale watching, and general entry at the Art Gallery of NSW and MCA.

blocks.text: The trick to Sydney isn't ticking every box - it's picking a handful, doing them unhurried, and leaving room to find your own favourite. Start with the coast walk and a ferry; the rest follows.
