blocks.text: Who can swim at the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool? Everyone. That's the honest, one-word answer, and it surprises people every time. The "Club" sign over the door makes visitors assume it's members-only, or that you need to book, or know someone. You don't. You walk down to the southern end of Bondi Beach, pay at the kiosk, and swim in the most photographed pool in the country.

The confusion comes from two separate things that share a name. One is the Icebergs Swimming Club, the winter-swimming institution that's been going for the better part of a century. The other is the ocean pool itself, a public facility open to anyone who pays to get in. You do not need to be a member to swim - membership is about competing in the winter races, not earning a spot in the water.

items.label: Who can swim
items.value: Anyone - no membership or booking needed

items.label: Where
items.value: Southern end of Bondi Beach, Notts Avenue

items.label: The pools
items.value: 50m lap pool plus a separate shallow children's pool

items.label: Usually closed
items.value: Thursdays for cleaning - check before you go

blocks.text: Families and beginners

This is a great spot for kids and nervous swimmers. Alongside the deep 50-metre lap pool there's a smaller, shallower children's pool with the same headland view, so little ones can paddle safely while you keep an eye on them. Because the water sits inside walls cut into the rock, it's calmer and more predictable than the open surf a few metres away. On rough days, though, keep children well clear of the ocean-facing edge.
Lap swimmers and fitness folk

If you're here to train, the main pool is a full 50 metres, which is why you'll spot serious swimmers grinding out lengths at dawn. It's divided into lanes, so there's room for everyone from the once-a-week breaststroker to the squad swimmer. Swimming a saltwater 50 with the Pacific crashing over the far wall is why regulars keep coming back.
The winter swimming club is a separate thing

Here's the part people most often get wrong. Becoming a full member of the winter swimming club means committing to swim through the cold months over a number of seasons - a real endurance tradition, which is how the club earned its name. The precise requirements change over time, so rather than repeat a number that might be out of date, I'd point you at the official [Bondi Icebergs Club site](https://icebergs.com.au/) for the current rules. None of it affects your ability to swim: membership is for the races, not for entry to the pool.

blocks.title: The pool usually closes on Thursdays
blocks.text: Icebergs typically closes the pool on Thursdays for cleaning (in summer, when tides permit, it sometimes opens Thursdays - their words, not ours), and it can also close during big swells or club races. If a specific day is the whole plan, check the official pool-conditions page that morning first.
Fees and opening hours

Entry is cheap for something this famous: as at August 2026 it's $10 for an adult, $7 for a child and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in your admission; towel and locker hire cost a little extra. Pool prices creep up over time, so check icebergs.com.au before you go. The pool keeps long days, but exact times shift with the season, tides and swell, so I check the official [Icebergs pool page](https://icebergs.com.au/pool-conditions/) the day before I visit.
Go early. I aim for the 7 to 8am window on a weekday - the light is unreal, the lanes are calm, and you'll get the classic empty-pool photo before the tour groups arrive.
A word on rough-swell days

Because the pool is topped up by the ocean, a strong swell sends water surging over the southern wall - spectacular to watch and genuinely powerful near the edge. On big-surf days the lifeguards may restrict swimming or close the pool. If the sea looks angry and you're not a confident swimmer, keep to the shallow end or come back when it has settled.

items.q: Do you have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The ocean pool is open to everyone - pay the entry fee at the kiosk and swim. Club membership is separate, tied to the winter-swimming races, and isn't needed for a normal swim.

items.q: Do I need to book in advance?
items.a: No. Entry is first-come, first-served - turn up, pay at the entrance and go in. There's no reservation system for the pool.

items.q: Can children swim there?
items.a: Yes. There's a separate shallow children's pool beside the main 50-metre pool, and lifeguards patrol during opening hours. On rough-surf days, keep kids away from the ocean-facing edge.

items.q: How much does it cost?
items.a: As at August 2026, single-visit entry is $10 for adults, $7 for children and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in admission; towel and locker hire cost extra. Prices change, so check icebergs.com.au before you visit.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: It usually closes Thursdays for cleaning (in summer, when tides permit, it sometimes opens Thursdays - their words, not ours), and can close during big swells or club races. Check the official pool-conditions page if you're planning around a particular day.

blocks.text: So the short answer holds: anyone can swim at Bondi Icebergs. Lap-counting regular, family with toddlers, or visitor chasing that one perfect photo - the pool is yours for the price of entry. Pick a calmer day, get there early, dodge the Thursday cleaning, and you'll see why this rectangle of ocean has drawn swimmers for generations.

Every school holidays I get the same question from friends visiting with kids: what actually keeps them happy in Bondi all day? The short answer is that you barely need a plan - a learn-to-surf lesson in the morning, a splash at a rock pool, and a walk along the cliffs with a play stop built in will fill a day easily. Here's how I'd string it together, plus the rainy-day backups I lean on when the weather turns.

items.label: Getting here
items.value: Bus/train to Bondi Junction, then bus

blocks.text: Get them in the water

Bondi's south end, near the Icebergs, is where the waves are gentlest and the surf schools set up. Let's Go Surfing runs kids' lessons and school-holiday programs with qualified instructors and soft foam boards, so even a nervous first-timer usually stands up before the session's out. Check their site for current age brackets, session times and prices - these change with the seasons, so I won't quote a figure here.

Whatever you do, swim between the red and yellow flags. Bondi has strong rips, and the flagged zone is the patrolled area the lifeguards are actively watching. If you're unsure about conditions, ask a lifeguard - they'd far rather you asked.

blocks.title: Flags first, always
blocks.text: Bondi's rips can pull strongly even on calm-looking days. Keep kids between the red-and-yellow flags and within arm's reach in the shallows. Check the current beach-safety status with Surf Life Saving before you go in.
Playgrounds, pools and the coastal walk
When little legs need a break from the sand, there's plenty within a short stroll or drive:

items: Bondi to Bronte coastal walk - a scenic clifftop path of roughly two and a half kilometres, with rock pools and beaches to peer into along the way. Bronte's playground and grassy park at the far end make a perfect turnaround-and-picnic point.

Bondi Icebergs ocean pool - the famous seawater pool at the south end has a shallow children's pool alongside the main one. Session times and entry fees vary, so check the Icebergs website before you set out.

Wild Play Garden, Centennial Park - a short drive away, this nature playground has a water-play area, a treehouse, bamboo forest and dry creek bed. Bring a change of clothes; someone always ends up soaked.

blocks.text: Do the coastal walk early - before about 9am in summer - while it's cool and quiet, then reward everyone with breakfast back at the beach. Push a pram? The Bondi-to-Bronte path has steps and narrow sections, so a carrier is easier with toddlers.
Council programs and rainy-day backups

Waverley Council runs a genuinely good school-holiday program each break - think art and craft workshops, sport clinics, science and STEM sessions, and activities based at Bondi Pavilion, the library and the Margaret Whitlam Recreation Centre. It's the first thing I'd check when you know your dates: the timetable and bookings go up ahead of each holiday period on the council's events page, and popular sessions fill fast.

For a wet day, the restored Bondi Pavilion is a lovely place to duck into for creative workshops and exhibitions, and Westfield Bondi Junction - a short bus ride away - has a cinema that usually screens kids' films through the holidays. Both are easy, low-stress fallbacks when the forecast lets you down.

stops.title: Coastal walk
stops.detail: Bondi to Bronte before the heat, with rock-pool spotting along the way.

stops.title: Beach & surf
stops.detail: Learn-to-surf lesson or a swim between the flags at the south end.

stops.title: Picnic & playground
stops.detail: Lunch and a run-around at a nearby park to burn off the last of the energy.

stops.title: Workshop or pool
stops.detail: A council holiday session, the Icebergs pool, or the cinema if it's raining.

items.q: What's the best free activity in Bondi with kids?
items.a: The beach itself and the Bondi-to-Bronte coastal walk cost nothing, and Bronte's playground at the far end is a great free finish. Bring water, hats and sunscreen - Sydney sun is fierce even in the cooler months.

items.q: Where can young kids surf safely in Bondi?
items.a: The gentler waves are at the southern end near the Icebergs, where the surf schools operate. Let's Go Surfing runs kids' lessons and holiday programs; check their site for current ages, times and prices.

items.q: What can we do in Bondi with kids when it rains?
items.a: Head to Bondi Pavilion for workshops and exhibitions, catch a kids' film at the cinema in nearby Bondi Junction, or book an indoor session from Waverley Council's school-holiday program.

items.q: How do I find out what's on these particular school holidays?
items.a: Check the Waverley Council events page ahead of your dates. Their school-holiday timetable lists workshops, sport clinics and creative sessions, and popular ones sell out early, so book as soon as it's published.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach safe for children to swim?
items.a: It can be, as long as you swim between the red-and-yellow flags in the patrolled area and keep young children within arm's reach. Bondi has rips, so always check conditions and ask a lifeguard if you're unsure.

blocks.text: That's the beauty of Bondi with kids - you can throw the schedule out and still have a brilliant day. Sun, saltwater, a play in the park and an ice cream on the promenade is a holiday all on its own.

sources.label: Let's Go Surfing - Bondi families & kids

blocks.text: People ask me this more than you'd think, usually with one eyebrow raised: are there snakes in Bondi? I always give the same answer - only one, and his name is Blake.

If you've wandered down Blair Street lately, you might have spotted a curious creature slithering along the footpath. Don't panic - this isn't the sort of snake that sends you running. He's the friendliest serpent in Sydney: Blake the Blair Street Snake, a community art project made entirely of painted rocks.

It starts with a single boulder - Blake's cheerful head, painted minty green with pink and black patches, perched beside a hand-lettered sign that reads: "I'm Blake the Blair St Snake. Add a painted rock to see how long I can get :)"

From there, a colourful line of rocks winds down the stone wall like scales on a giant, happy reptile. Some are splashed in pastels, others flecked with stars or faces, and a few were clearly painted by very small and very enthusiastic hands. Every week Blake stretches a little further as locals and passers-by add to him.
Why I love stumbling across Blake

In a world of "Do Not Touch" signs and endless screens, here's a simple invitation to join in. No permissions, no forms - just grab a rock, grab some paint, and make your mark. I've watched joggers pause mid-stride to admire him before carrying on toward the beach, and I've never once seen someone walk past without smiling.

Each rock tells a tiny story: maybe painted on a rainy afternoon, maybe made at a weekend craft session, maybe left by a visitor who wanted to be part of something local. To me, Blake is like Bondi's community diary - only instead of words, it's written in colour. Bondi's famous for its shimmering water and perfect surf, but this quirky reptile has become just as iconic in his own way.

If you're bringing kids, paint a rock at home the night before and let it dry - then it's ready to add to Blake's tail on the day. A weatherproof outdoor paint or a coat of clear sealer helps your rock survive Bondi's sun and salt air.

items.q: Are there actually dangerous snakes at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi is a busy urban beach, so you're extremely unlikely to encounter a wild snake on the sand or promenade. The only "snake" locals talk about is Blake, the painted-rock art trail on Blair Street.

items.q: Where exactly is Blake the Blair Street Snake?
items.a: Along the stone wall on Blair Street in Bondi. Look for the minty-green painted boulder with the sign inviting you to add a rock - the trail of rocks grows from there.

items.q: Can I add my own rock?
items.a: Yes - that's the whole idea. Paint a rock, bring it down to Blair Street, and add it to the end of Blake's body to help him grow a little longer.

blocks.text: So next time you're wandering Blair Street, keep an eye out. Bring a rock, add your touch, and help Blake slither a little further. Because yes - there is a snake in Bondi. Just one. And he's the kind that makes everyone smile.

Every spring my favourite stretch of coastline quietly turns into the world's largest free outdoor gallery, and 2025 is no different: Sculpture by the Sea returns to the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk, with around 100 works by Australian and international artists set against the cliffs, the swell and that impossibly blue horizon. Entry is free, the sculptures sit right along the public path, and you don't need a ticket to wander in - just good shoes and a bit of patience with the crowds.

I've walked this exhibition more times than I can count, and it never gets old. One minute you're reading the swell, the next you round a headland and meet a giant steel form or a mirrored orb perched on the rocks. Below is what I'd want a first-timer to know before setting off.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Beach to Tamarama coastal walk

blocks.title: Confirm this year's dates first
blocks.text: The exhibition runs for roughly three weeks and the exact dates shift each year - for 2025 they fell in the second half of October through early November. Before you plan your day, check sculpturebythesea.com for the confirmed dates, opening details and the official map.
Where it is and how the walk works

The exhibition threads along the clifftop path from the southern end of Bondi Beach, past Mackenzies Bay, over Marks Park headland and down into Tamarama. It's roughly two kilometres one way, and it's the same public coastal walk you can do any day of the year - the sculptures are simply installed along it for the duration of the show.

The sculptures themselves are outdoors and visible throughout the day, but the extras - kiosks, the indoor 'Sculpture Inside' display, the artist book and app support - keep their own set hours. If you want to see those, aim to arrive within the staffed daytime window rather than at first light. The official site lists the current times.

Start from the Tamarama end rather than Bondi. Everyone pours in from the big beach, so walking against the flow gives you cleaner sightlines, easier photos, and a well-earned coffee or swim at Bondi when you finish.
Beating the crowds (and the parking)

This is one of the busiest events on Sydney's calendar - hundreds of thousands of people pass through across the run - so timing matters more than anything else. Weekday mornings are far calmer than weekends, and early or late in the day gives you the soft, golden light that makes the sculptures sing against the sea.

items: Go on a weekday if you can, and early - the middle of a sunny weekend is the busiest it gets.
Skip the car. Street parking around Bondi and Tamarama is scarce and heavily restricted during the event; public transport to Bondi is far less stressful.
Wear proper walking shoes - the path has steps, slopes and uneven sandstone.
Bring sun protection, water and a hat. There's very little shade along the cliffs.
Give yourself two to three hours if you want to actually read the works, not just march past them.

blocks.title: Stay on the path
blocks.text: The coastal walk runs along genuine clifftops with unfenced drops in places, and it gets shoulder-to-shoulder busy. Keep children close, don't climb on the sculptures, and take extra care near the edges when you stop for photos.
Why it's worth the effort

What began decades ago as a modest, volunteer-run, one-day show has grown into the largest free outdoor sculpture exhibition in the world, and a fixture of the Sydney spring calendar. For me the magic is in the pairing: ambitious contemporary art and one of the most beautiful walks in Sydney, with the works changing character as the light and tide shift around them. You could see it in twenty minutes; I'd argue it deserves an afternoon.

items.q: Is Sculpture by the Sea at Bondi free?
items.a: Yes. It's free to walk the exhibition along the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal path. There's no ticket to see the outdoor sculptures - some optional extras and indoor components may have their own arrangements, listed on the official site.

items.q: When is Sculpture by the Sea 2025?
items.a: The 2025 Bondi exhibition ran for around three weeks from the second half of October into early November. Dates change every year, so confirm the current year's dates on sculpturebythesea.com before you go.

items.q: Where does the walk start and finish?
items.a: It follows the coastal walk between the southern end of Bondi Beach and Tamarama Beach - about two kilometres one way. You can start from either end; I prefer beginning at Tamarama to avoid the heaviest crowds.

items.q: What's the best time to visit to avoid crowds?
items.a: Weekday mornings, or early and late in the day. Sunny weekends are by far the busiest, and the softer morning and evening light is also much kinder for photos.

items.q: Can I drive and park nearby?
items.a: I wouldn't. Parking around Bondi and Tamarama is limited and tightly restricted during the event. Public transport to Bondi is much easier - check Transport for NSW for current routes and timetables.

blocks.text: Whichever end you start from, take your time. Sculpture by the Sea is one of those rare events where the setting is as much a part of the show as the art - and it's right here on our doorstep, for free. I'll see you on the cliffs.

sources.label: Sculpture by the Sea - Bondi 2025 exhibition

blocks.text: When the shooting began at Bondi on the evening of 14 December 2025, the people trained to run toward the water ran toward the danger instead. As gunfire tore through a Hanukkah gathering at Archer Park, our lifeguards and volunteer surf lifesavers - the same faces you see on the sand every summer - became the first responders on one of the darkest nights this community has ever known. This is what I understand about how they answered.

blocks.title: A note before you read
blocks.text: This piece is about a real and deeply painful event. I've written it to honour the people who helped, and I've kept to facts confirmed by news reporting and Surf Life Saving. For the official record, the memorial details, and ways to support the families, please follow the linked sources.

items.label: The gathering
items.value: A public Hanukkah celebration, around 1,000 people

items.label: First responders
items.value: On- and off-duty lifeguards & surf lifesavers

blocks.text: Why the lifeguards were even there

People forget that Bondi's surf clubs sit right on top of the action. North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club and the Bondi clubhouse are metres from where families had gathered for the festival. So when the attack unfolded over roughly six terrible minutes, there wasn't time to wait for anyone else - the lifesavers were already the closest trained hands on the scene, and they moved.

These are volunteers and council-employed professionals whose whole discipline is running toward trouble on a beach: rips, spinal injuries, cardiac arrests in the shallows. That training - the muscle memory of triage, of staying calm while everyone else can't - is exactly what met the moment. As reporting later made clear, many of them were off duty and simply came running.
What they actually did

The details that have been confirmed are hard to read and, I think, important to hold onto. Lifesavers pulled people away from the gunfire to cover. They turned surfboards into makeshift stretchers to carry the wounded. They ran through their entire supply of bandages giving first aid in the minutes before police and paramedics could reach everyone. The North Bondi clubhouse, a building most of us only associate with nippers and Saturday-morning swims, was used to shelter roughly 250 people while the surf sheds nearby became casualty stations.

One image travelled around the world: lifeguard Jackson Doolan running barefoot along the road from a neighbouring beach, a defibrillator in his hands, sprinting toward Bondi rather than away from it. To me that single photograph captures the whole night - ordinary beach people doing an extraordinary, selfless thing.
Some of our team chose to respond while shots were still being fired. - the Bondi lifeguards, in their own words

If you visit the North Bondi and Bondi surf clubhouses this summer, take a quiet moment. These aren't just kiosks and change rooms - on that night they were shelter and sanctuary. A respectful nod to the volunteers on patrol goes a long way.
How Bondi has remembered

In the days afterward, lifesaving crews up and down the New South Wales coast stood together on the sand and fell silent for the victims. A National Day of Mourning followed on 22 January 2026, when the country paused for a minute's silence at 7:01pm and flags flew at half-mast. Across the beaches, red and yellow flags flew for people who never made it home - and for the rescuers who carried the weight of what they'd seen.
Grief here has been quiet and communal rather than showy. That feels very Bondi to me: no fanfare, just people showing up for one another, the same way the lifesavers showed up when it counted most.
How you can help

The most useful thing any of us can do is support the organisations that keep these volunteers equipped and the families supported. If you'd like to give, go directly to the official Surf Life Saving channels rather than any link forwarded to you - that's the safest way to make sure it reaches the right place.

items: Donate through the Surf Life Saving Foundation (slsfoundation.com.au) - check for the current, verified appeal before giving.
Support Surf Life Saving NSW (surflifesaving.com.au), which coordinates the clubs and crews along our coast.
If you swim at Bondi, always swim between the red-and-yellow flags - it's the simplest way to honour what these lifesavers do every single day.

items.q: What happened at Bondi Beach on 14 December 2025?
items.a: An attack was carried out at a Hanukkah gathering at Archer Park beside Bondi Beach, where around 1,000 people had assembled. Gunmen opened fire over roughly six minutes. For the confirmed facts, casualty figures and the investigation, see the linked news and Wikipedia sources.

items.q: Were the Bondi lifeguards really the first to respond?
items.a: Yes. Because the surf clubs sit right beside where the crowd had gathered, on- and off-duty lifeguards and volunteer surf lifesavers were among the first trained responders, giving first aid, sheltering people and carrying the wounded before other emergency services could reach everyone.

items.q: Who was the lifeguard photographed running with a defibrillator?
items.a: Lifeguard Jackson Doolan was widely photographed running barefoot toward Bondi from a neighbouring beach carrying a defibrillator to help the victims. The image became one of the most shared from that night.

items.q: How can I support the Bondi lifesavers and the victims' families?
items.a: Give through official Surf Life Saving channels - the Surf Life Saving Foundation (slsfoundation.com.au) and Surf Life Saving NSW (surflifesaving.com.au). Always confirm you're on the verified official appeal before donating, and be wary of links forwarded through social media.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach safe to visit now?
items.a: Bondi remains one of Sydney's most-loved and closely watched beaches, patrolled daily in season by professional lifeguards and volunteer surf lifesavers. As always, swim between the red-and-yellow flags and follow their directions.

blocks.text: I don't have neat words for a night like that one. What I do have is enormous pride in the people who wear the red and yellow on this stretch of sand. They train for the surf, but when the worst came ashore, they ran toward it anyway - and that is the inside story of the Bondi lifeguards who ran toward danger.

blocks.text: Yes - after more than a decade of quiet sand on the 31st of December, Waverley Council formally backed the return of a major New Year's Eve festival to Bondi Beach. In March 2025 councillors supported a motion to bring a proper NYE event back to our shoreline for the first time since the old Shore Thing parties wrapped up in 2014, and by spring the shape of it was public. I've watched this story closely from the promenade, so here's what was actually approved, what was planned, and where things landed.

items.label: Behind it
items.value: Cr Michelle Stephenson & Mayor Will Nemesh

blocks.text: How the festival came back

For anyone who was around in the late '90s and 2000s, Bondi on New Year's Eve used to mean one thing: Shore Thing, the beachfront dance festival that pulled big-name acts down to the sand. It ran until 2014, then disappeared amid concerns about crowds and behaviour, and for years our end-of-year nights went weirdly quiet for such a famous beach.

That changed at a Council meeting in March 2025. A motion led by Bondi Ward Councillor Michelle Stephenson and Mayor Will Nemesh - to bring a New Year's Eve beach event back to Bondi - won the room. The pitch wasn't just nostalgia; it was about giving locals and visitors a reason to gather again, and putting Bondi back on the global NYE map alongside the Harbour.
The idea was simple: give Bondi its New Year's Eve back - a night on the sand that belongs to the community as much as the crowds.
What was planned for New Year's Eve 2025

By September 2025 the format was announced. Council appointed Sydney promoter Fuzzy - the same crew behind long-running Sydney dance events - to produce it, and the night was built in two halves so there'd be something for everyone.

items: elrow Bondi Beach XXL - a ticketed music festival on the sand, reported at around a 15,000-person capacity, headlined by the wildly colourful elrow brand.
Locals Lawn - a free family zone near the Pavilion with roaming entertainment, food trucks and an early fireworks display, so families could celebrate without a ticket.
A run-of-night across Bondi Beach and Bondi Pavilion, reported from early evening through to just after midnight.

blocks.text: The smartest move for any big Bondi event is to leave the car at home. Parking near the beach is brutal on a normal summer day, let alone New Year's Eve - take the train to Bondi Junction and the bus down, or walk in, and check Transport for NSW for extra late-night services before you set out.
So did it actually happen?

Here's the honest part, and why I'd always tell you to check before planning a night around it. The inaugural December 2025 edition was ultimately cancelled - the decision made in consultation with Waverley Council out of care for the community following a tragedy in Sydney. Ticket holders were contacted directly about refunds: the right call in the moment, even if it stung for everyone hoping to see the beach light up again.

blocks.title: Always confirm the current year's plans
blocks.text: A New Year's Eve beach festival is exactly the kind of event that can change year to year - approved, reshaped, or paused. Before you build a trip around it, check Waverley Council's events pages and the official festival/promoter site for the latest on dates, tickets and the free family zone.

What hasn't changed is Council's appetite for bringing a proper New Year's Eve celebration back to Bondi. The approval and the framework are there, and the ambition - a signature beach event locals and visitors can share - is very much alive. My hunch is we'll see it return in some form; I'll just always point you at the official source for the year you're visiting.

items.q: Is there a New Year's Eve festival at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council approved the return of a major NYE beach festival in March 2025 after more than a decade without one. A ticketed festival (elrow Bondi Beach XXL) plus a free family zone called Locals Lawn were planned for 31 December 2025, though that inaugural edition was ultimately cancelled. Check Council's events page for the current year's plans before you go.

items.q: Who is behind the revived Bondi NYE festival?
items.a: The revival was championed at Council by Bondi Ward Councillor Michelle Stephenson and Mayor Will Nemesh, and Sydney promoter Fuzzy was appointed to produce the event.

items.q: Was there a free part of the event?
items.a: Yes - the plan included Locals Lawn, a free family zone near Bondi Pavilion with roaming entertainment, food trucks and an early fireworks display, sitting alongside the ticketed elrow festival on the sand.

items.q: When did Bondi last have a big New Year's Eve festival?
items.a: The last major recurring NYE event on Bondi Beach was Shore Thing, which ran through the 2000s and ended in 2014. The 2025 approval was the first serious move to bring a large-scale festival back since then.

blocks.text: For me, the takeaway is hopeful: the door is open again. Bondi's New Year's Eve story isn't finished - it's being rewritten. Check the official listings each December, and one of these years I fully expect to be down on the sand with you, counting in the new year where it belongs.

blocks.text: The honest answer is that there is no single best time to visit Bondi Beach - it depends entirely on the Bondi you're after. If you want warm water, packed sand and long lit-up evenings, come in summer (December to February). If you'd rather have the coastal walk mostly to yourself, mild sunny days and whales offshore, I'd send you in autumn or winter. After years of watching the beach shift with the seasons, here's how I'd time your trip.
Summer (December to February): peak Bondi

This is Bondi at full volume - warm days generally in the mid-to-high 20s°C, the ocean at its most swimmable, and the sand busy from mid-morning. It's my pick if you love a crackling atmosphere: everyone's out, the promenade hums until late, and the water is genuinely inviting. The trade-off is crowds. Christmas Day and New Year draw huge numbers, and on a hot January weekend the good spots vanish early.

In summer I get down by 8–9am, claim a patch between the red-and-yellow flags, and I'm swimming before the car parks fill. By midday parking near the beach is a lost cause - take the bus, or park up the hill and walk down.

blocks.title: Always swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi has rip currents, and they catch strong swimmers too. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and check current conditions with Surf Life Saving before you go in.
Autumn (March to May): my quiet favourite

Autumn is Bondi's best-kept secret. The summer heat eases into mild, settled days, the ocean still holds plenty of its summer warmth well into April, and the crowds thin out noticeably. This is when I do the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk without dodging anyone, linger over a long breakfast, and actually get a table. If you want warm-enough beach weather without the peak-season scrum, this is your window.
Winter (June to August): whales, waves and space

Winter days at Bondi are cooler and the beach empties out, which is exactly why some of us love it. Swimming is bracing (the Icebergs pool crowd will tell you that's the point), but the surf often gets bigger and cleaner, and the light on a crisp morning is beautiful. The headline act is whale watching: humpbacks migrate along the NSW coast roughly May to November, and from the elevated coastal path or Ben Buckler headland you can often spot them without a boat.

Bring binoculars and walk up to the northern headland (Ben Buckler) on a clear winter morning. Look for the puff of a blow or a splash on the horizon, then wait - where there's one whale there's usually another.
Spring (September to November): the sweet spot

Spring is where the balance tips just right - warming days, water climbing back toward swimmable, and crowds that haven't yet hit summer levels. It's also the strongest stretch for events. September brings Festival of the Winds, Waverley Council's free family kite-flying day on the sand, and in October–November the coastal walk between Bondi and Tamarama becomes the open-air gallery of Sculpture by the Sea, the world's largest free outdoor sculpture exhibition.

blocks.title: Event dates move each year
blocks.text: Festival of the Winds and Sculpture by the Sea run on dates that shift annually, and sometimes change format. Before you build a trip around one, confirm the current dates on the Waverley Council and Sculpture by the Sea websites listed in my sources.
So when should you actually come?

If forced to choose, I'd point most first-timers at late spring or early autumn: you get warm, swimmable days and Bondi's easy outdoor energy, but without summer's shoulder-to-shoulder sand. Come in summer for maximum buzz and warmest water, and in winter if you want dramatic surf, whales and a beach that feels like it's yours.

items.q: What is the best month to visit Bondi Beach?
items.a: For the best balance of warm, swimmable weather and manageable crowds, I'd pick March (early autumn) or late October–November (spring). January is warmest and liveliest but by far the busiest, while June–August is quiet and best for whales and surf rather than swimming.

items.q: When is Bondi Beach least crowded?
items.a: Winter (June to August) is the quietest, followed by autumn weekdays. If you want space on the sand and the coastal walk without a warm-weather trade-off you can't accept, autumn is the sweet spot.

items.q: Can you swim at Bondi in winter?
items.a: Yes - plenty of locals do, and the beach is patrolled. The water is cold, so most winter swimmers keep it short or use the Icebergs ocean pool. Always swim between the flags and check conditions with Surf Life Saving first.

items.q: When can you see whales from Bondi?
items.a: Humpback whales migrate along the NSW coast roughly from May to November, with strong sightings through the winter months. You can often see them from the coastal walk or Ben Buckler headland - no boat required, just clear conditions and a bit of patience.

items.q: What are the big events at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Spring is the busiest for events: Festival of the Winds (a free kite-flying day) in September, and Sculpture by the Sea along the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk in October–November. Dates change each year, so check the official sites before planning around them.

blocks.text: If you only have one day at Bondi, spend the morning swimming between the flags at the south end, walk the cliff path toward Tamarama before lunch, and save sunset for the grassy hill above the Icebergs pool - that single loop hits the famous stuff and the quiet corners both. I've wandered this coast for years, so here's my honest, local-first guide: the must-see spots that earn the hype, the hidden gems most visitors walk straight past, and the practical bits that make the day.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Beach, eastern suburbs of Sydney, NSW

items.label: Getting here
items.value: Train to Bondi Junction, then the 333/380 bus

items.label: Patrols
items.value: Lifeguards year-round; swim between the red-and-yellow flags

items.label: Best for
items.value: Swimming, the coastal walk, cafés and people-watching

blocks.text: The must-see spots

Start where Bondi shows off. The southern end, near the Bondi Icebergs, is where the postcard photos happen - the ocean pool sits right on the rocks and the waves wash straight into it at high tide. Icebergs is a working swimming club with a public pool anyone can swim in, but session times and entry change with the seasons, so check the Icebergs website before you build your morning around it.

From there, the Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk is the one thing I'd never let a first-timer skip. It runs roughly 6 km along the cliff tops, linking Bondi to Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee, with sea views the whole way. You don't have to do all of it - even the first stretch to Bronte is worth it, with ocean pools and cafés to stop at. Wear proper shoes, bring water, and go early in summer.

Back at the beach, the Bondi Pavilion is the grand old building on the promenade - a community and cultural hub with event spaces since its restoration. Wander the promenade for the famous graffiti wall, grab a coffee, and just watch Bondi be Bondi.
Hidden gems the crowds miss

Most visitors cluster in the middle of the beach and never move; the locals I know drift to the ends. North Bondi is calmer, with the free ocean pools (the "kiddie pools") tucked into the rocks - lovely for families and gentler swimming when the surf's up, and my pick for a quiet coffee away from the Campbell Parade bustle.
The Sunday Bondi Markets at Bondi Beach Public School - vintage, jewellery, art and food, and a genuine slice of the local creative scene. Check the Bondi Markets site for current days and hours.
The laneways and walls behind Campbell Parade, where Bondi's ever-changing street art lives - no two visits look the same.
Hall Street and the streets just back from the sand, where the café and food scene is far better value than the beachfront strip.
Ben Buckler, the rocky headland at the far north end, for wide clifftop views and a whale-watching chance in the winter migration months.
Come on a weekday if you can. Bondi on a summer Saturday is a different animal - parking is brutal and the sand fills fast. Midweek mornings you get the same beach with half the people.
Getting here and staying safe

There's no train to the sand itself. Take a train to Bondi Junction, then a short bus (the 333 or 380) down to Campbell Parade - check Transport for NSW for live timetables and to tap on with an Opal or contactless card. Parking near the beach is limited and metered, so I only drive here off-peak.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi has real rip currents. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where lifeguards are watching. If you're caught in a rip, don't fight it - stay calm, raise an arm for help, and float or swim parallel to the beach until you're free.

Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards year-round, backed by volunteer surf lifesavers in the busy months, but conditions change quickly - if in doubt, ask a lifeguard where it's safest to swim that day.

items.q: What are the absolute must-sees at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi Icebergs ocean pool at the south end, the Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk, the Bondi Pavilion and promenade, and a swim between the flags on the main beach. If you add one hidden gem, make it quieter North Bondi.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach from the Sydney CBD?
items.a: Take a train to Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus down to Bondi Beach. Use an Opal card or contactless payment and check Transport for NSW for current timetables. There's no train that goes all the way to the sand.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: It's roughly 6 km one way along the cliff tops, typically taking a couple of hours at a relaxed pace with stops. You can do just the first section to Tamarama and Bronte if you're short on time.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach safe for swimming?
items.a: Yes, when you swim between the red-and-yellow flags where lifeguards patrol. Bondi is patrolled year-round, but it does have rip currents, so avoid unpatrolled areas and always check conditions before you go in.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Bondi to avoid crowds?
items.a: Weekday mornings, especially outside the peak summer weekends. You get the same beach and cafés with far fewer people and much easier parking.

blocks.text: That's my Bondi - famous for a reason, but far richer once you step past the middle of the beach. Do the walk, find the quiet ends, eat a street back from the sand, and respect the ocean, and you'll leave with the real version, not just the postcard.

sources.label: Sydney.com - Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk

blocks.text: If you're picturing Christmas Day at Bronte as one enormous, boozy beach party, I have to gently update you: that Bronte is gone. After years of the so-called 'Backpackers' Christmas' drawing huge crowds, Waverley Council brought in a firm set of rules for December 25, 2025 - an alcohol ban, a glass ban and a heavy police presence - and the message landed. The big drinking crowd largely stayed away or drifted to Coogee, and Bronte had a calm, family-friendly day by the sea. So here's my honest local guide to a Bronte Christmas now, and how to have a lovely one.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bronte Beach & Bronte Park, Eastern Suburbs

blocks.text: What changed - and why it matters for your day

For years, Christmas at Bronte meant thousands of travellers, eskies of drinks and, by late afternoon, a fair amount of mess and antisocial behaviour that local residents were tired of. In the lead-up to Christmas 2025, Waverley Council rolled out an enforcement plan: alcohol prohibited, glass containers banned, extra police and security with checkpoints, and tighter parking and transport controls.

The council's follow-up said Bronte was spared its usual chaos as the party crowd thinned right out. For you that's simple, and rather nice: turn up expecting a quiet, sunny, sober Christmas by the water, and that's exactly what's on offer.

blocks.title: Leave the drinks at home
blocks.text: Bronte is an alcohol-free zone and this is actively enforced on Christmas Day. Rangers and police can confiscate alcohol, and glass isn't allowed either. Bring your festive spread - just make the drinks non-alcoholic and pack everything in cans, cartons or plastic.
How I'd plan a Bronte Christmas

Bronte is compact - a golden crescent of sand tucked between headlands, with a big grassy park behind it, a famous ocean pool at the southern end and a gentler 'Bogey Hole' rock pool that kids adore. It fills up on a hot Christmas, so timing and a bit of prep help.

stops.title: Arrive early
stops.detail: Get in before the midday heat to claim a shaded patch of park or a spot on the sand. Parking is very limited on Christmas Day, so public transport or a walk from Bondi Junction is your friend.

stops.title: Swim between the flags
stops.detail: Lifeguards patrol Bronte and the surf can have a serious rip. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags. For calmer water, the Bronte Baths ocean pool and the Bogey Hole are hard to beat.

stops.title: Picnic in the park
stops.detail: Bronte Park has free electric barbecues, picnic shelters and a playground. On Christmas Day the BBQs get busy fast, so have a no-cook picnic as a backup.

stops.title: Pack it out
stops.detail: Take every scrap of rubbish with you. Keeping Bronte clean is a big part of why the day stays welcome - bins overflow quickly, so a spare bag in your kit is gold.

blocks.text: The classic Aussie Christmas move here is cold prawns, a couple of salads, stone fruit and plenty of water - no cooking, no fuss. Freeze a few water bottles the night before: they keep the esky cold and give you icy drinking water by lunchtime.
What to bring

items: Sun protection - hats, sunglasses, high-SPF sunscreen and a beach umbrella or shade tent
Towels, swimmers and a rashie; water shoes if you're exploring the rock pools
A no-glass, no-alcohol picnic and lots of drinking water
A rubbish bag (carry your waste out) and a small first-aid kit
Cash isn't essential, but a card for the nearby Bronte cafés if any are open

items.q: Is there still a big Christmas party at Bronte Beach?
items.a: Not the way there used to be. After Waverley Council's 2025 crackdown - an alcohol ban, glass ban and stronger police presence - the large drinking crowd stayed away and many headed to Coogee instead. Bronte is now a quiet, family-friendly beach day on Christmas rather than a party.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol at Bronte on Christmas Day?
items.a: No. Bronte is an alcohol-free zone and it's actively enforced on Christmas Day, with alcohol and glass liable to be confiscated. Bring non-alcoholic drinks in cans or plastic.

items.q: Can I have a barbecue at Bronte Park?
items.a: Bronte Park has free public electric barbecues, but they're in high demand on Christmas Day and rules can change - check the Waverley Council Bronte Park page for current facilities and any event-day restrictions, and have a no-cook picnic as backup.

items.q: How do I get to Bronte and where do I park?
items.a: Parking near Bronte is very limited, especially on Christmas Day, so public transport or ride-share is smarter - check Transport for NSW for current timetables, as holiday services differ from a normal day. Many locals walk the coastal path from Bondi.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bronte on Christmas Day?
items.a: Bronte is patrolled by lifeguards, but the surf can be powerful with strong rips. Always swim between the flags. For calmer water, use the Bronte Baths ocean pool or the shallow Bogey Hole rock pool at the southern end.

blocks.text: So no, Christmas at Bronte isn't the wild backpacker blowout it once was - and I think it's better for it. Arrive early, keep it alcohol-free, swim between the flags, spread a picnic in the park and take your rubbish home. That's a genuinely lovely Sydney Christmas.

blocks.text: If you turned up at the Icebergs pool in early April 2025 and found the gates locked, here's what happened: an enormous overnight swell smashed into the pool on the night of 1 April, tearing through glass fencing and railings and forcing the club to close the ocean pool for repairs, with a reopening flagged for 18 April. It was one of the rare times in living memory that Bondi's most famous pool has shut its gates completely.

I've watched the Icebergs take a battering from big southerly swells more winters than I can count, but this one was different. The pool sits right on the rocks at the southern end of the beach, deliberately built so the surf washes over it - that's the magic of swimming there. This time, though, the sea won.
What actually happened

A deep low off the coast lined up with a king tide, and together they drove a swell that reached far higher than the pool deck. Waves surged over the terrace, shattered a long run of glass fencing near the change rooms, buckled steel railings and punched up into the lifeguard tower above the water. General manager Bob Tate, quoted in the news coverage at the time, said he'd never seen anything like it.

blocks.title: This was a one-off event
blocks.text: This article documents a specific storm from April 2025. The pool has long since been repaired and reopened - this page is here for history and context, not a current closure notice.

items.label: What
items.value: Storm damage to Bondi Icebergs ocean pool

items.label: Cause
items.value: Large coastal swell coinciding with a king tide

blocks.text: Why the Icebergs is so exposed

People are often surprised that a near-century-old pool sits where the ocean can reach it like this, but that exposure is the point. The Bondi Icebergs Club has been swimming here since 1929, and the pool was carved into the rock platform precisely so the Pacific spills straight into it. On a calm day it's one of the most photographed pools in the country; on a wild day, the same walls that make it beautiful take the full force of the swell.

Closures are genuinely rare. The club shuts the pool whenever the surf is dangerous, but a full multi-week closure for structural repairs happens once in a couple of decades, not once a season - which is what made this event newsworthy well beyond Bondi.

Even in normal conditions, check the swell before you plan an Icebergs swim. When there's a big southerly running, the club often closes the pool for safety and the water turns churny and cold. A calmer, smaller-swell morning gives you the glassy, turquoise pool everyone comes for.

blocks.title: Session times change - always check first
blocks.text: Opening hours, lap-swim sessions, public access and closure days at the Icebergs shift with maintenance, weather and club events. Don't rely on a number in an old blog post - check the official Icebergs website before you go.
Can I still swim there?

Yes. The April 2025 damage was repaired and the pool returned to normal operation, so on any ordinary day you can pay the entry fee and swim in the same iconic pool. Just remember it's a working club pool, not a council facility - it closes on certain days for cleaning and lap squads, and always when the surf is unsafe. For current prices and session times, go straight to the official Icebergs site rather than trusting cached figures online.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs still closed?
items.a: No. The closure covered in this article was a specific event from April 2025, after a large overnight swell damaged the pool. It was repaired and reopened, and operates normally today. For live opening hours and any short-term closures, check the official Icebergs website.

items.q: What caused the Icebergs pool to close in April 2025?
items.a: A powerful coastal swell overnight on 1 April 2025, coinciding with a very high tide, washed over the pool deck and damaged glass fencing, railings and parts of the club building. The club closed the pool for repairs, with reopening flagged for 18 April.

items.q: How often does the Icebergs pool close?
items.a: Short safety closures during big surf are fairly common - the pool sits on the rocks where the ocean washes in. But a full multi-week closure for structural repairs, like the one in April 2025, is very rare and happens only once in many years.

items.q: Can visitors swim in the Bondi Icebergs pool?
items.a: Yes. It's open to the public on most days ($10 adult, $7 child, $30 family, sauna included, as at August 2026), though it's a private club pool that closes on certain days for maintenance and squad training, and whenever the surf is dangerous. Check icebergs.com.au for the current schedule and prices.

items.q: How old is the Bondi Icebergs pool?
items.a: The Bondi Icebergs Club was founded in 1929, so the ocean pool and its winter-swimming tradition go back close to a century - which is part of why the storm damage drew so much attention.

blocks.text: The fact that the Icebergs keeps taking hits like this and keeps coming back is exactly why locals love it. It's not a sanitised resort pool tucked safely inland - it's a piece of Bondi that lives and breathes with the ocean, storms and all. Come for a swim on a clear morning and you'll understand why we're so protective of it.

blocks.text: If you only remember one thing before visiting Bondi Beach, make it this: always swim between the red and yellow flags. Beyond that, a smooth day comes down to timing your arrival, leaving the car at home, and knowing which end suits you. Here's what I'd tell a friend before a first visit.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Beach, Waverley, ~7km east of the Sydney CBD

items.label: Swim zone
items.value: Between the red & yellow flags only

items.label: Easiest transport
items.value: Train to Bondi Junction, then a bus

items.label: Cost to enjoy
items.value: The beach and coastal walk are free

blocks.text: 1. Swim between the flags

Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards (the Bondi Rescue crew) and volunteer surf lifesavers, and it can throw up strong rips, so the flags matter. Lifeguards move them to the safest water each day, and swimming inside them is the best thing you can do for your safety. The northern end near Ben Buckler is gentler and more family-friendly; the southern end towards Icebergs pulls the bigger swell and the surfers. Unsure? Ask a lifeguard.

blocks.title: Rips are the real risk, not sharks
blocks.text: Rip currents are the main hazard at Bondi. If you're caught in one, don't fight it - stay calm, raise an arm for help, and float until it eases or a lifesaver reaches you.
2. Getting here is easiest without a car

Parking around Bondi is metered, time-limited and brutal on a sunny weekend. The stress-free route is public transport: a train to Bondi Junction, then a bus to the beach. The 333 runs between the city and North Bondi, with the 380 on the same corridor, and you tap on and off with an Opal or contactless bank card. For live timetables, check the Transport for NSW trip planner.

Coming from the CBD, the train-to-Bondi-Junction-then-bus combo usually beats a direct bus for reliability, especially in summer when Bondi Road clogs up. Tap the same card the whole way and the transfer is handled automatically.
3. Come early

Bondi rewards early risers. A sunrise swim, a quiet promenade and a café table are all easier before the mid-morning crowd rolls in - and if you must drive, early is your only realistic shot at a park. Summer weekends and public holidays are busiest; a weekday morning feels like a calmer beach.
4. The Bondi to Coogee coastal walk is unmissable

If you do one thing beyond the sand, walk the roughly 6km Bondi to Coogee coastal path. It hugs the cliffs past Tamarama, Bronte and Clovelly, with the clifftop Waverley Cemetery and ocean pools along the way. It's free and spectacular, with cafés and swimming spots to break it up. Wear proper shoes and bring water.
5. Bondi Icebergs - check times first

That famous ocean pool jutting into the surf at the southern end is Bondi Icebergs, the club pool established in 1929. Non-members can swim for an entry fee, and [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar) upstairs pairs a proper meal with one of Sydney's best views. Session times, cleaning-day closures and prices change, so check the Icebergs website first.
6. Sun, shade and etiquette

Australian sun is no joke - the UV here burns faster than you'd believe, so bring a hat, a rashie and high-SPF sunscreen, and reapply. Natural shade on the sand is limited, so claim a spot early or bring your own. A few unwritten local rules go a long way, too:

items: Give surfers and boardriders room - the flagged zone keeps everyone apart for a reason.
Take your rubbish with you; the bins fill fast on busy days.
Dogs aren't permitted on Bondi Beach itself - check Waverley Council for dog-friendly areas nearby.
Keep music low and share the promenade with runners and prams.

blocks.text: 7. Markets, festivals and a buzzing food scene

Bondi is far more than sand. The Bondi Markets run on Sundays at the local public school, and each spring the clifftop fills with Sculpture by the Sea, the free exhibition along the Bondi to Tamarama stretch. Hall Street and the beachfront brim with cafés and gelato - if you'd rather plan your eating properly, our full guide to [where to eat and drink in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink) has the current line-up. Market and festival dates shift year to year, so check the official event pages first.
8. There's more to do than just the beach

Even if the surf's flat or the weather turns, Bondi holds up: the coastal walk, the ocean pools, the cafés, and the boutiques around Gould and Hall Streets. Come for a swim, but leave time to linger - that's when the place gets under your skin.

items.q: What's the best way to get to Bondi Beach from the city?
items.a: Take a train to Bondi Junction, then a bus to the beach - the 333 and 380 run this corridor. It's usually faster and less stressful than driving. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for live times.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes, as long as you swim between the red and yellow flags, where the lifeguards patrol. Rip currents are the main hazard, so check the daily conditions and ask a lifeguard if you're unsure.

items.q: Which end of Bondi is best for families?
items.a: The northern end near Ben Buckler is generally calmer and more sheltered, so it's friendlier for kids and less confident swimmers. The southern end gets the bigger surf.

items.q: Do I need to pay to enjoy Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - the beach, the promenade and the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk are free. You only pay for extras like the Icebergs pool, parking, food and tours.

blocks.text: Ask me where to drink in Bondi and I'll answer before you finish: start beachfront for a sundowner, then wander inland as the night warms up. After years living just back from the sand, these are the ten bars I actually send friends to - ocean-view balconies, heritage pubs, cosy locals' corners and one or two that run late.

items.label: Best for views
items.value: Icebergs, North Bondi RSL, Hotel Ravesis

items.label: Getting here
items.value: Bus to Bondi Beach, or the 333 from the city

blocks.text: My beachfront big-hitters
1. Hotel Ravesis

You can't miss the flamingo-pink corner where Hall Street meets Campbell Parade. [Ravesis](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hotel-ravesis) is my pick for the whole spectrum in one building - a schooner or a rosé on the terrace early, then upstairs as the DJs get going and it tips into the small hours. Grab a front-terrace spot for the wide view.
2. Icebergs (the Bondi Bar balcony)

For the postcard, nothing beats the balcony bar at [Icebergs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), above the famous ocean pool at the south end. It's dress-up-a-little and priced for the view, but a negroni at golden hour is a genuinely Sydney moment. It books out - reserve ahead through the Icebergs site, and if you want more tables with that same ocean outlook, see our guide to [beachfront and ocean-view dining](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).
3. North Bondi RSL

My tip for the best-value view in Bondi: the [North Bondi RSL](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-rsl) at the north end. Sign in as a guest, head to the wrap-around glass balcony and you get the same knockout beach outlook for far less. Check the RSL's own site for sign-in and hours first.

Bondi faces east, so the sun sets behind you over the rooftops, not the sea. The magic is the glow on the water and the headlands - have a drink in hand about half an hour before sunset and watch the beach turn gold.
Pints, cocktails and cosy corners
4. Hotel Bondi

The grand heritage pub right on Campbell Parade, [Hotel Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hotel-bondi) has watched over the beachfront for the better part of a century. A quick note for anyone chasing a beer I used to send people out for: Bondi's much-loved microbrewery, Curly Lewis, has sadly closed since I first wrote this list - so a beachfront pub like this is now my easy pick for a cold one near the sand. Grab a spot in the front bar, catch the sport, and you're a minute from the promenade.
5. El Topo

[El Topo](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/el-topo-mexican) is a snug, low-lit spot for agave and cocktails just back from the beach - mezcal, tequila and a margarita list that rewards a bit of adventurousness. It's tight and loud in the best way, and my go-to for kicking a night into gear; there are proper Mexican plates too, so an early stop can easily turn into dinner.
6. Beach Road Hotel

A couple of streets back on Beach Road, [Beach Road Hotel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/beach-road-hotel) is the reliable all-rounder - cold schooners, pub classics, live sport, and DJs and bands upstairs on weekends. It's where a lot of Bondi nights quietly end up, and one of [Bondi's best pubs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) if you fancy a proper crawl.
The rest of my ten
These four round out the list - a different mood for each night.

items: [Beach Bar at Promenade](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/beach-bar-at-promenade-bondi-beach) - beachfront spritzes and people-watching right on Campbell Parade, and a happy stand-in for a feet-in-the-sand summer session now that the Pavilion's Bucket List has closed.
[Neighbourhood](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/neighbourhood-bondi) (Curlewis Street) - a lively little local back from the sand, good for a natural wine with the after-beach crowd.
[The Shop & Wine Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-shop-and-wine-bar) (Curlewis Street) - café by day, snug wine bar by night; my pick for a quiet drink and a cheese plate.
[The Stuffed Beaver](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-stuffed-beaver) (Bondi Road) - an unpretentious, good-fun bar for burgers, mezcal and a night that doesn't take itself too seriously.

blocks.title: Summer weekends fill fast
blocks.text: From December through February the beachfront venues can hit capacity by mid-afternoon on a hot day. If a table matters - especially at Icebergs or for a big group - book ahead through the venue's own site and confirm current hours.
Grab a bite between rounds

A good crawl runs longer if you line your stomach. Most of these bars do food, but half the fun of Bondi is ducking out between rounds - a taco, a wood-fired slice, a banh mi or a late-night burger are all within a block or two of the sand. Our [cheap eats in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach) guide has the best quick bites, or if you'd rather build the night around a proper sit-down, browse our [date-night restaurants](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach).
How I'd string them together

stops.detail: Best-value beach view while the light is still high.

stops.title: Beach Bar at Promenade
stops.detail: Down to the sand for a spritz as the beach turns gold.

stops.title: Hotel Bondi or El Topo
stops.detail: Shift gears - a cold pint or a mezcal margarita.

stops.title: Hotel Ravesis or Beach Road
stops.detail: Finish where the DJs are for a late one.

blocks.title: Beyond the bars
blocks.text: Chasing something specific - a rooftop spritz, a natural-wine list, a long lunch with a view? Our full [Bondi eat-and-drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) covers 160+ venues you can filter by cuisine, area, price and who you're with. If you just want the drinking spots, jump to our hand-picked [best bars in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-bars-bondi-beach).

items.q: Which Bondi bar has the best beach view?
items.a: The balcony bar at Icebergs, above the ocean pool, wins for the postcard shot. For the same outlook at a much lower price, head to North Bondi RSL's upstairs balcony. Ravesis' front terrace pairs the view with a livelier crowd.

items.q: Where can I drink late in Bondi?
items.a: Hotel Ravesis and the Beach Road Hotel reliably keep going into the night on weekends, with DJs upstairs. Closing times vary by season, so check each venue's own site for current hours.

items.q: Is there craft beer brewed in Bondi?
items.a: Not any more, sadly - Curly Lewis Brewing Co., Bondi's own microbrewery, has closed, so there's no beer brewed in the postcode right now. For a good tap list your best bets are the beachfront and back-street pubs like Hotel Bondi and the Beach Road Hotel. Our [best pubs in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) guide has the full line-up.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach for a night out?
items.a: The easiest route from the city is the 333 or 380 bus, or the train to Bondi Junction and a beach-bound bus. Check Transport for NSW for timetables and plan your way home before the last service.

items.q: Do I need to book ahead?
items.a: For most pubs and casual bars you can just turn up. For Icebergs, or larger groups on summer weekends, book directly through the venue's site.

blocks.text: That's my ten - enough range for any kind of Bondi night, from a quiet wine after the beach to a full sunset-to-late crawl. Hours and prices move with the seasons, so treat this as the shortlist and confirm details on each venue's own site.

Everyone comes to Bondi for the golden crescent of sand and the surf - and honestly, on a good day that's reason enough. But after years of living a short walk from the promenade, I've learned that the beach is really just the front door. Beyond the sand and surf, Bondi hides a whole side of itself: dancing in the dark, ice skating with the ocean at your back, ancient stories carved into the cliffs, and coffee-worthy views from a floatplane. Here are nine of my favourite only-in-Bondi experiences to try when you're ready to look past the shoreline.
1–3: Dance, skate and dip

The heritage-listed Bondi Pavilion and the beach around it are the beating heart of the area's off-sand life, and that's where I'd start. On select evenings, a short walk away in North Bondi, No Lights No Lycra takes over a hall for a pitch-black, no-instructor, no-judgment dance floor where you move however you like to 80s, 90s and 00s tunes. It's cathartic, a little silly, and one of the friendliest rooms in Sydney. Check the No Lights No Lycra site for the current venue, session night and entry fee before you rock up.

Come mid-winter, the park beside the Pavilion transforms for Bondi Festival, whose signature open-air ice rink lets you skate with the beach just metres away - genuinely one of the more surreal things you can do in Australia. The festival runs for a couple of weeks in July; see the Bondi Festival website for this year's dates, rink sessions and ticket prices.

And if you want the most old-school Bondi experience of all, brave a winter dip at the Bondi Icebergs ocean pool, carved into the rocks at the beach's southern end. The Icebergs Club has run winter swimming here since 1929. Anyone can pay to swim the public pool (weather and cleaning schedule permitting) - check the Icebergs website for current opening hours and pool fees, as they close periodically for maintenance.

The Icebergs pool is at its most photogenic when a big swell sends spray over the sea wall - but that's also when it's most likely to be closed for safety. If a dip is the whole reason you're visiting, check the pool's status online that morning rather than turning up on spec.
4–6: Art, culture and a walk to remember

Every spring, the clifftop path from the southern end of Bondi to Tamarama becomes the world's largest free outdoor sculpture show, Sculpture by the Sea. For a few weeks across October and November, more than a hundred large-scale works line the coastal walk against a backdrop of sea cliffs and crashing surf. It's free to wander any time of day; check the official site for the current year's dates and the best times to avoid the crowds.

For something far older than any of it, I always point people to a Bondi Aboriginal Walking Tour with Walangari Karntawarra, an Aboriginal elder, artist and musician. He shares Dreaming stories, points out ancient rock carvings along the headland, and talks through the bush foods and deep history of this coast. It completely changes how you see the place. Check the tour's website for the current schedule and to book directly.

Third in this trio is a slower pleasure: the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk itself. Even without the sculptures, this cliff-hugging path past Tamarama and Mackenzies Bay is, to me, the single best free thing to do in the whole area. Go early, take your time, and swim at Bronte's little bogey hole at the end.
7–9: On the water, under it, and above it

items: Stand-up paddleboard yoga - flowing through poses on a board in the sheltered southern corner of the bay, usually at sunrise or sunset. Balance is optional; the odd splash is guaranteed.

A freediving taster - learning breath-hold and finning basics before slipping beneath the surface on a single breath, no tanks required. Several qualified operators run beginner sessions in and around Sydney's east.

A scenic seaplane flight - Sydney Seaplanes departs nearby Rose Bay and arcs over Bondi's famous curve and the harbour. It's the splurge of the list, but the aerial view of that beach is unforgettable.

blocks.title: Book the seasonal and specialist ones ahead
blocks.text: The ice rink, sculpture walk, cultural tours, SUP yoga, freediving and seaplane flights all run on their own schedules and sell out - especially in peak summer and school holidays. Reserve online before you travel rather than hoping for a walk-up spot.

None of these ask you to give up the sand - think of them as the extra chapters. Dance in the dark on Monday, walk the sculptures in spring, swim the Icebergs in winter, and if the budget stretches, see the whole coast from a floatplane. Do a couple and you'll leave with a version of Bondi most day-trippers never meet.

items.q: What is there to do in Bondi besides swimming and surfing?
items.a: Plenty - No Lights No Lycra dance nights at the Pavilion, the winter ice rink, a dip at the Icebergs pool, Sculpture by the Sea, an Aboriginal walking tour, the Bondi to Bronte walk, SUP yoga, a freediving taster and a seaplane flight.

items.q: When is Sculpture by the Sea at Bondi?
items.a: It runs along the Bondi to Tamarama clifftop walk for a few weeks across October and November each year, and it's free. Check the official site for this year's exact dates.

items.q: Can I skate at the Bondi ice rink?
items.a: Yes - the open-air rink beside the Pavilion is part of Bondi Festival, which runs a couple of weeks in July. Sessions and prices are on the Bondi Festival website; book ahead.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool open to the public in winter?
items.a: Generally yes - visitors can pay to swim, though it closes periodically for cleaning and during big swells. Check the Icebergs website for current hours and pool status.

items.q: Where do seaplane flights over Bondi leave from?
items.a: Sydney Seaplanes departs Rose Bay on Sydney Harbour, a short trip from Bondi. See their website for routes and pricing.

blocks.text: Bondi's dining goes well beyond fish and chips on the sand. There's cliff-top Italian, produce-driven fine dining that's been going since the early '90s, beachfront seafood and a new wave of share-plate spots on Hall Street. Below is the shortlist I'd steer a visitor towards - grouped by the kind of night you're after, with what each place is known for and who it suits. I write as a local curator rather than claiming to have dined at each one this month, so book ahead for the big ones and check current details before you go.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Restaurants change - menus, chefs and hours shift, and the best tables book out. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm opening days and book ahead on the venue's own channels before a special trip.
Best for a special occasion
Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Icebergs is the Bondi bucket-list dinner - a glamorous, glass-walled Italian dining room on the southern cliff, looking straight down over the Icebergs pool and the ocean. Overseen by hospitality figure Maurice Terzini, it's polished coastal Italian with one of the best views of any restaurant in Sydney. Best for: a celebration, a long lunch, or impressing visitors - book well ahead, and it's at the premium end. You can pair it with a look at the [Icebergs pool and where to swim](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) below.
Sean's (formerly Sean's Panorama)

A genuine Bondi institution: chef Sean Moran has run this small, produce-led restaurant on Campbell Parade since 1993 (now simply "Sean's"). The short, hand-written menu changes with what's good, much of it from the chef's own farm. It's understated and beloved rather than flashy. Best for: a considered, ingredient-first dinner or weekend lunch - a small room, so booking is wise.
Beachfront seafood
North Bondi Fish

About as beachfront as dining gets - right on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end, with the sand almost at the door. The menu is easy-going seafood: sashimi, calamari, tacos, and fish and chips, plus cocktails. Best for: a relaxed lunch or early dinner with a view, and a solid choice with kids in tow.
Fish Shop

A casual, nautical-themed seafood spot a short walk back from the beach - the more laid-back, everyday alternative to a big seafood night out. Best for: an unfussy seafood feed without a special-occasion price tag.
Italian & share plates
Totti's Bondi

Totti's, behind The Royal on Bondi Road, is the crowd-pleasing Italian everyone seems to end up at - famous for its pillowy wood-fired bread and generous, family-style plates in a sunny, convivial room. Best for: a group, a birthday, or a long boozy lunch - it's popular, so book ahead.
Newer and something different
LULU

One of the newer names worth knowing, LULU is a funky Pan-Asian bar and kitchen on Hall Street built around share plates - think Vietnamese-style prawn banh mi, Korean fried chicken and fresh sashimi, with drinks to match. Best for: a livelier, share-and-graze dinner away from the beachfront. (As a newer venue, check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
What's changed recently

A couple of things to note for 2026. Hall Street has picked up newer, more casual share-plate venues like LULU, which are worth a look alongside the classics. Sean's Panorama now trades simply as "Sean's" - same chef, same Campbell Parade address, so don't be thrown by the shorter name. And the refurbished Bondi Pavilion has reopened on the beachfront with its food and drink line-up reshuffled since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting older guides.
What to know before you go

items: Book ahead for the big ones: Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's fill up, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings.
Timing: sunset tables with a view (Icebergs, North Bondi Fish) are the most sought-after - reserve early or aim for lunch.
Price: Icebergs and Sean's sit at the premium end; North Bondi Fish, Fish Shop and LULU are more mid-range.
Getting there: it's an easy night out on foot or by bus - see [getting to Bondi](/getting-to-bondi) if you're coming from the city.
Make a day of it: line up a swim or the coastal walk first - see [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

blocks.text: Which Bondi restaurant is right for you?

items: Special occasion with a view: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar.
Ingredient-led, understated dinner: Sean's (Campbell Parade).
Beachfront seafood: North Bondi Fish.
Casual, everyday seafood: Fish Shop.
Group Italian / long lunch: Totti's Bondi.
Livelier newer share plates: LULU (Hall Street).

items.q: What is the best restaurant in Bondi?
items.a: For a special-occasion dinner with a view, Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the classic pick. For understated, produce-driven cooking, Sean's on Campbell Parade has been a favourite since 1993.

items.q: Where can I eat right on Bondi Beach?
items.a: North Bondi Fish is the most beachfront option, on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end. Icebergs sits above the pool on the southern cliff with the best elevated view.

items.q: Which Bondi restaurant has the best view?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, looking over the Icebergs pool and the ocean, is hard to beat; North Bondi Fish gets you closest to the sand.

items.q: Are there any newer restaurants in Bondi?
items.a: Yes - Hall Street has picked up newer share-plate spots such as LULU, a Pan-Asian bar and kitchen. Note that Sean's Panorama now trades simply as "Sean's".

items.q: Do I need to book a Bondi restaurant?
items.a: For Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's, yes - book ahead, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings. Casual spots like Fish Shop and North Bondi Fish are more forgiving.

blocks.text: Whether it's a big night at Icebergs or fish and chips on the sand, Bondi eats well. For cafés and coffee, see my [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink); for the rest of your visit, [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi) and [what's on](/whats-on); and if you're still choosing a base, [where to stay in Bondi](/stay).
