blocks.text: The honest answer to "where do I park at Bondi?" is this: yes, there's free, unrestricted parking, but it's in the residential streets north of Blair Street - about a 5–7 minute walk from the sand - and on a sunny weekend you need to be in it before roughly 9am. Everything closer is paid or time-limited. Here's every option, and what each one is actually good for.

items.label: Free option
items.value: Residential streets north of Blair St

items.label: Closest paid
items.value: Queen Elizabeth Drive car park (~500 bays)

blocks.text: The free streets north of Blair Street

My go-to on a busy day is the residential grid north of Blair Street - the streets climbing away from the water. Get far enough back from the beach and you'll find bays that are genuinely free and untimed, with no meters. The trade-off is the walk and the timing: on weekdays the bays tend to hold until residents come home in the late afternoon; on a sunny weekend they fill from mid-morning, which is exactly why arriving early matters. One thing I won't do is hand you a fixed list of "free streets" - Waverley keeps expanding its permit zones and the rules change block by block, so read the sign at the bay you actually pick rather than trusting any list. What's unrestricted one street can be permit-only the next.

The closer you get to the water, the more those free bays give way to Waverley Council Resident Parking Scheme zones - a free-looking bay near the beach can quietly be permit-only. My rule is simple: keep heading north until the restriction signs drop off, then park. The blocks behind the southern end are my quiet secret too - everyone aims for the middle of the beach, so the south end often has room when the north is chaos.

Read the closest sign every single time, even if the car in front of you is parked there. Time limits, permit zones and no-stopping lines change street by street in Bondi, and inspectors patrol hard on weekends. Blocking a driveway is one of the costliest tickets you can collect - never worth it for a five-minute dash.
Paid parking, closest to furthest
When I've got beach gear, kids, or it's just too hot to walk, I pay. Roughly in order of how close they sit to the sand:

items: Queen Elizabeth Drive car park - Waverley Council's own metered car park running right behind the beach, with around 500 bays. It's the closest and most convenient, and the first to fill on a nice day, so treat it as an early-morning play.

Campbell Parade meters - the paid on-street bays opposite the beach. Handy for a quick visit, but time-limited and the priciest per hour, so they suit a coffee-and-a-swim rather than a full beach day.
The Notts Avenue / Icebergs (south) end - metered street parking down toward the pool. Limited and sought-after, but a lovely spot to land if you time it right.
Side streets a block or two back - often overlooked once the beachfront meters are full; check the posted rate and time limit at the sign before you leave the car.

blocks.text: The council's beach meters are pay-by-plate - there's no paper ticket. Enter your number plate at the machine, or (far easier) pay from your phone through the PayStay app; the meters also take the NSW Park'nPay app. They run 7am to 7pm seven days a week and switch off after 7pm, so an evening swim is one of the few times the beachfront comes free. On rates I won't bake a dollar figure into this page: Waverley reviews meter prices and charges more for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets further back, so check the current rate on the council's parking page and budget a daily total before you go.

blocks.title: Staying all day, often?
blocks.text: A Waverley Council beach parking permit lets you park for unlimited time in the metered bays on Queen Elizabeth Drive and Park Drive without feeding the meter. Anyone can apply, but residents, ratepayers, local teachers and active Surf Life Saving members get a lower rate - if you're a Bondi regular it can pay for itself. Eligibility and fees are set by the council, so check the current terms on the beach parking permit page.
Accessible parking and the busy-day plan

There are designated accessible bays around the beachfront, including near Queen Elizabeth Drive and the Bondi Pavilion, and a valid Mobility Parking Scheme permit gives concessions on time limits in metered and timed bays. Exact bay locations and any current works can change, so confirm on the council's parking page or with the Pavilion before relying on a specific spot.

And on a perfect summer Saturday? Don't fight it. Drive to Bondi Junction, park there, and jump on the 333 - the "Bondi Link", Sydney's busiest bus route, which runs 24 hours and connects Circular Quay to North Bondi via the Junction. On a hot weekend that short ride down Bondi Road genuinely beats doing laps for a beachfront bay. Tap on with an Opal card or contactless, and check Transport for NSW for live times.

items.q: Is there free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - the residential streets north of Blair Street, heading away from the water, have free, unrestricted bays about a 5–7 minute walk from the sand. Watch for permit-only and timed zones closer to the beach, and get in before about 9am on sunny weekends.

items.q: What's the closest car park to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council's Queen Elizabeth Drive car park, a metered car park of around 500 bays right behind the beach. It's the first to fill on a nice day, so arrive early or have a backup ready.

items.q: What hours do the Bondi meters run, and how do I pay?
items.a: The beachfront meters operate 7am to 7pm, seven days a week, and switch off after 7pm. They're pay-by-plate - enter your number plate at the machine, or pay from your phone using the PayStay or NSW Park'nPay app. Rates are set by the council and are higher for beach-adjacent bays in summer, so check the current figure on Waverley's parking page.

items.q: When should I arrive to actually find a spot?
items.a: Before about 9am, or after 7pm once the meters switch off, on busy weekends and holidays. The 9am–3pm window is the hardest; if you're arriving then, plan on a paid meter, the South Bondi streets, or the Bondi Junction park-and-ride.

blocks.text: I've talked more friends and visitors through a [Totti's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/tottis-bondi) reservation than I can count, so let me save you the midnight stress. The surest table is booked online through Merivale the moment your date opens - but if you've left it late, same-day walk-ins are genuinely welcome and cancellations reappear online all the time. Here's exactly how I'd go about it.

items.label: Where
items.value: At the back of The Royal, 283 Bondi Road (corner of Denham Street), Bondi

items.label: The room
items.value: A 185-seat restaurant and courtyard; the woodfired bread is non-negotiable

blocks.text: How I'd book it

Reservations run through Merivale's own system on the Totti's venue page - that's the one platform to use. Tables release a set window ahead of time, and that window shifts, so don't trust a fixed number you read on a blog. Open the booking calendar, scroll to the furthest bookable date, and work backwards from there.

items: Jump on the booking page the day your date first opens - lunch and prime dinner slots go fast.
Have your details ready (name, phone, card if requested) so you're not fumbling as tables vanish.
Bend on timing where you can: an early lunch or later dinner beats the 7pm-Saturday scramble, midweek beats the weekend, and a table of two or three slots in where a table of eight won't.

blocks.text: Keep a tab open on the booking page even after you've missed your ideal night. Totti's spills into that big open courtyard, so when Bondi's weather turns, last-minute cancellations pop back online - I once grabbed a Saturday table on the Thursday before, just by refreshing at the right moment.

blocks.title: Larger groups and special occasions
blocks.text: Big tables, birthdays and set-menu events work differently from a standard booking, and Totti's has a private dining room too. For anything beyond a regular table, call the venue on +61 2 9114 7371 or use the enquiry form on the private dining page rather than the online booking.

No booking? Don't write off a spontaneous visit. A limited number of walk-in tables are held back each day, and your odds are best if you turn up early rather than at peak, keep the group small, and are happy to perch wherever they can seat you - a weekday afternoon is your friend. Failing that, a quick phone call the morning of can turn up a cancellation the website hasn't caught yet.
If Totti's is fully booked

If your date's a wash and nothing's opening up, you're not stuck - this stretch of Bondi is thick with Italian and special-occasion tables. For wood-fired pizza a short stroll north, [Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/da-orazio-pizza-porchetta) is my go-to; for a long, leisurely Italian lunch with a sliver of ocean, [Bondi Trattoria](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-trattoria) has held down Campbell Parade for years. If it's the occasion you're chasing rather than Totti's specifically, [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar) brings the same handmade-pasta-with-a-view drama (book that one just as far ahead), while [Lola's Italian & Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lolas-italian-and-bar) is the easier walk-up when you haven't planned a thing. For the full spread, browse our roundup of [Bondi's best date-night restaurants](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach) and [the best restaurants in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-restaurants-bondi-beach).

A bit of history for context: [The Royal](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-royal-bondi) has anchored this corner of Bondi Road since 1902, and Merivale opened Totti's at the back of the pub in December 2018 with chefs Mike Eggert and Khan Danis. That pedigree is exactly why the room stays busy - and why a little planning pays off. Order the bread.

blocks.title: Hungry for more of Bondi?
blocks.text: Totti's is one table in a very deep field. Browse all 160+ Bondi eateries in our full [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink) - filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're dining with to find your next booking.

items.q: How do I book a table at Totti's Bondi?
items.a: Through Merivale's online booking system on the Totti's venue page (merivale.com/venues/tottis), or by phone on +61 2 9114 7371. Booking online is the most reliable route for a standard table.

items.q: How far in advance do bookings open?
items.a: Tables release a set window ahead of your date, and that window can change over time. Rather than trusting a fixed number, open the booking calendar, scroll to the furthest date you can select, and book the moment your date first appears.

items.q: Does Totti's Bondi take walk-ins?
items.a: Yes - a limited number of same-day walk-in tables are held back. Arrive early rather than at peak, keep the group small, and you'll give yourself the best shot.

items.q: Where exactly is Totti's Bondi?
items.a: At the back of [The Royal](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-royal-bondi) at 283 Bondi Road, on the corner of Denham Street, a short walk up from the beach. Check the official Merivale page for current opening hours before you go, as they change seasonally.

items.q: Where else can I eat if Totti's is booked out?
items.a: Bondi has strong Italian and special-occasion alternatives nearby - [Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/da-orazio-pizza-porchetta), [Bondi Trattoria](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-trattoria), [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar) and [Lola's Italian & Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lolas-italian-and-bar) among them. See our [best date-night restaurants](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach) guide for more.

blocks.text: Bondi packs one of Sydney's best café scenes into a few walkable streets behind the beach - beachfront brunch rooms, serious coffee windows, and a run of newer openings worth knowing about in 2026. Below is the shortlist I'd hand a visitor: what each place is known for, roughly where it is, and who it suits. I write these as a local curator rather than claiming to have eaten at every one this week, so treat the details as a well-researched starting point and check current hours before a special trip. For the full, filterable picture - every café and coffee window we've mapped around the beach - there's our [complete Bondi cafés and coffee guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach).

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Bondi's café scene moves fast - hours, menus and even owners change. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm anything time-sensitive on the venue's own channels before you go.
Best beachfront cafés for brunch
Speedos Café - North Bondi

[Speedos](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) sits up at the quieter North Bondi end (Ramsgate Avenue) with some of the best ocean views of any café on the beach. It's the classic post-swim spot - health-leaning brunch, bowls, pancakes and juices, with window benches looking straight out to the water. Best for: a relaxed, view-first breakfast at the north end.
Chapter One - Campbell Parade

Right on Campbell Parade opposite the sand, [Chapter One](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/chapter-one-caf-and-wine-room) is a café-meets-wine-bar that's been going since 2012, pouring Allpress coffee alongside an all-day menu. It's an easy, central choice if you want to be directly across from the beach - one of a handful of genuine [beachfront and ocean-view spots](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach) around the sand. Best for: an all-rounder in the middle of the action.
bills - Hall Street

The Sydney institution founded by Bill Granger has been on Hall Street (number 79) since 2014, and [bills](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bills-bondi-beach) is still open and busy. Come for the dishes that made it famous - ricotta hotcakes and sweetcorn fritters - in a light, airy room. Best for: a benchmark Bondi brunch and a bit of Sydney food history.
Best for specialty coffee
Harry's Bondi - Wairoa Avenue

[Harry's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/harrys-bondi) has been caffeinating Bondi since 1997 and is my pick if coffee is the point. It grew from a hole-in-the-wall into a full café, with batch brew, espresso and cold drip plus a following for its matcha and specialty lattes. Best for: coffee-first locals and a quick, quality cup.
Sonoma - bakery coffee

[Sonoma](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sonoma-bakery-cafe-bondi) is the well-known Sydney sourdough bakery with a Bondi outpost - a reliable stop for a proper coffee and a pastry or bakery-driven breakfast without the full brunch sit-down. If it's the pastry cabinet you're chasing, it sits alongside Bondi's other [bakeries and sweet spots](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach). Best for: a quick, high-quality grab-and-go.
Gertrude & Alice - Hall Street

Genuinely one of a kind: [Gertrude & Alice](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/gertrude-and-alice-cafe-bookstore) is a second-hand bookshop and café on Hall Street where you can settle in with Campos coffee, a Middle Eastern-leaning breakfast and a stack of books. It's the antidote to Bondi's see-and-be-seen rooms. Best for: a slow, quiet morning and something different.
Strong all-rounders just back from the sand
Blackwood - Glenayr Avenue

An Eastern Suburbs brunch staple a couple of streets back, [Blackwood](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/blackwood-bondi) is known for a seasonal menu that blends Mediterranean and Asian influences - ricotta pancakes, chilli scrambled eggs - with carefully made coffee. It's one of my go-tos when I want a considered sit-down away from the crowds; for more in that vein, see our [best breakfast and brunch guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach). Best for: a considered brunch away from the beachfront crush.
Porch and Parlour - North Bondi

A long-running North Bondi favourite (Ramsgate Avenue), [Porch & Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) is built around local produce, with its well-known pea pancakes and a reliably buzzy weekend. It's also one of the better-known dog-friendly spots. Best for: a neighbourhood brunch with the dog in tow.
Newer and more unusual spots
Cafe Bondi - North Bondi (new)

One of the more recent openings, [Cafe Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cafe-bondi) is on Campbell Parade at the North Bondi end and opens early for coffee, sunshine and an easy all-day menu. Best for: an early start at the quieter north end. (As a newer venue, double-check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
Up South - Bondi Road

Further up Bondi Road, [Up South](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/up-south-bondi) made its name on playful matcha creations and a rotating treats cabinet - the spot for a strawberry or pistachio matcha and a photo. Best for: matcha fans and a sweet mid-morning stop.
Lox, Stock & Barrel - bagels & deli

A Bondi take on a Jewish deli, [Lox, Stock & Barrel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lox-stock-and-barrel) is known for artisan bagels and generous, deli-influenced brunch plates. Best for: a bagel-led breakfast or an easy weekday lunch.
Makaveli & Pocket - café by day, bar by night

From the same team, [Makaveli](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/makaveli) (Glenayr Avenue) and [Pocket](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/pocket-bondi) (Campbell Parade) both work the café-to-cocktail-bar angle - pastries, loaded sourdough and coffee in the morning, share plates and drinks later. If it's the evening end that appeals, they also turn up in our [best Bondi bars](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-bars-bondi-beach) roundup. Best for: a laid-back start that can roll into the afternoon.
A few more coffee windows worth knowing
Coffee is half the reason people love a Bondi morning, so beyond the rooms above here are a few more cups worth a short detour - handy when the beach-view spots are full.
Jacks North Bondi - Brighton Boulevard

An absolute North Bondi institution: the coffee window at the top of Brighton Boulevard that locals knew for years as Bru is now [Jacks](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bru-coffee-bondi), run by Jack Murat, who grows his own single-origin coffee up in Far North Queensland and pours it beachside here. It's the spot for the ritual every North Bondi swimmer knows - grab a flat white straight out of the water and dry off in the sun with a hot cup in hand, down on the grass or the sand. Little seating, mornings only, always humming. Best for: drying out with a coffee after a dip at the north end.
% Arabica - Bondi Beach

The Bondi outpost of the global specialty-coffee brand [% Arabica](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/arabica-bondi) trades on pared-back design and carefully sourced beans - a small destination if you take your coffee seriously. Best for: a considered espresso or matcha and a bit of coffee-world pedigree.
Will & Co - HQ tasting bar

Sydney roaster [Will & Co](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/will-and-co-hq-tasting-bar) runs an HQ tasting bar in Bondi - the spot to drink a local roaster's coffee close to the source. Best for: coffee drinkers who want to taste the roast.

A few more to keep in your back pocket: [Cortado](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cortado-bondi-cafe) for an unfussy espresso away from the queues, the all-day [Bennett St Dairy](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bennett-st-dairy) a couple of streets back, and [Cali Press](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cali-press) if you'd rather a cold-pressed juice or açai bowl than a coffee.
What's changed recently

Two things worth flagging for 2026. First, there's genuine new blood at the north end - Cafe Bondi being the clearest recent opening. Second, the former Hall Street all-day spot Bondi Hall has closed, so ignore older lists that still feature it. The refurbished Bondi Pavilion has also reopened with food and drink operators on the beachfront; those line-ups have shifted since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting an older guide.
What to know before you go

items: Timing: arrive close to opening or after about 2pm to dodge the worst queues; weekend mornings are the busiest.
Booking: most Bondi cafés are walk-in, though a few take reservations for larger groups - check ahead if there are more than four of you.
Dogs: several are dog-friendly, with Porch and Parlour the best-known; outdoor tables are your friend.
Reusables: bring a keep-cup - some cafés knock a little off for it.
Make a morning of it: pair a café with the Saturday [Bondi Farmers Market](/whats-on/markets), or a swim first - see [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach).

blocks.text: Which Bondi café is right for you?

items: Best ocean view: Speedos Café (North Bondi).
Best coffee: Harry's Bondi (serving since 1997).
Most iconic brunch: bills (Hall Street).
Something different: Gertrude & Alice (bookshop café, Hall Street).
Newest: Cafe Bondi (North Bondi).
Best with a dog: Porch and Parlour (North Bondi).

items.q: What is the best café in Bondi?
items.a: It depends what you want. For a beachfront brunch with a view I'd point you to Speedos Café or Chapter One; for the best coffee, Harry's Bondi; and for an iconic Sydney breakfast, bills on Hall Street.

items.q: Which Bondi café has the best view?
items.a: Speedos Café at North Bondi and Chapter One on Campbell Parade both look straight out over the beach - the two I'd choose for a view-first breakfast.

items.q: Where is the best coffee in Bondi?
items.a: Harry's Bondi has been a coffee benchmark since 1997. Sonoma is a reliable bakery-coffee stop, Gertrude & Alice pours Campos in a bookshop setting, and for a serious cup it's worth seeking out % Arabica or roaster Will & Co.

items.q: Are there any new cafés in Bondi?
items.a: Cafe Bondi at the North Bondi end is one of the clearer recent openings. Note that the older Hall Street spot Bondi Hall has closed, so skip it on out-of-date lists.

items.q: Do I need to book a Bondi café?
items.a: Most are walk-in. Expect queues on weekend mornings, so arrive early or after about 2pm, and check ahead only if you're a larger group.

items.q: Are there dog-friendly cafés in Bondi?
items.a: Yes - Porch and Parlour in North Bondi is the best-known dog-friendly option, and many cafés welcome dogs at their outdoor tables.

blocks.title: Looking for more than ten?
blocks.text: This is my hand-picked shortlist, but it's a fraction of what's on the beach. Browse every café, restaurant, bar and bakery in [our full Bondi eat & drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) - 160+ venues you can filter by cuisine, area, price and who you're with, from a quick coffee to a long lunch by the water.

However you play it, Bondi rewards a bit of café-hopping - a coffee at the north end, a swim, then brunch on Campbell Parade. For more on eating and drinking around the beach, see my [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink); for the rest of a day here, [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi); and for markets and events, [what's on in Bondi](/whats-on).

blocks.text: Every year I get asked the same thing the moment the mornings turn crisp: when is whale season at Bondi? The short answer is roughly May to November - and the best part is you don't need a boat. Some of the finest whale watching in Sydney happens for free, right from the headlands either side of the beach. This is my local guide to when the humpbacks pass, where I stand to watch them, and how to give yourself the best chance of a breach.
When whales pass Bondi

Sydney's whale-watching season runs from around mid-May to early November as tens of thousands of humpbacks migrate along the NSW coast. It splits into two acts. On the northbound leg - roughly May to July - the whales head to warmer breeding waters and travel with real purpose, so June and July are wonderful for sheer numbers. On the southbound return - around September to November - mothers bring their new calves back toward Antarctic feeding grounds, often hugging the coastline and moving slower, which for my money makes the most tender sightings of the year.

I always aim for the first couple of hours after sunrise on a clear, calm day. The light is behind you, the sea is glassier so spouts and breaches stand out, and the crowds haven't arrived. A gentle offshore wind and low swell make an enormous difference.
The best land-based spots near Bondi
You genuinely don't need to pay for a cruise to see whales here. These are the free vantage points I return to, all within a short walk of the beach:

items: Ben Buckler Point (North Bondi) - Bondi's most easterly headland and my first choice. It sits high above the water at the end of Ramsgate Avenue, with an open outlook over the Pacific where locals gather with binoculars all season.
Mackenzies Point - the small headland between Bondi and Tamarama, with a wide southern view that's ideal for scanning.
Waverley Cemetery clifftop - a dramatic, unobstructed stretch of the coastal walk perched right above the ocean.
The Bondi to Bronte (and on to Coogee) coastal walk - not one spot but a whole string of them; I walk slowly and stop wherever I see others looking out to sea.

blocks.title: Mind the edge
blocks.text: These clifftops are stunning but the rock is uneven and the drops are real. Stay behind fences and well back from wet or crumbling edges, keep an eye on children, and never turn your back on the ocean to line up a photo. No whale is worth a slip.
Cruises from nearby Sydney

No whale-watching cruises leave from Bondi Beach itself - the boats depart from Sydney Harbour, mostly Circular Quay and Darling Harbour, and head out through the Heads to the migration route. If you'd rather get close, a half-day tour is a lovely way to do it. For current departure times, durations and prices, which change every season, check the operators' own websites - Destination NSW's Sydney.com whale-watching page is a good starting point.
How to actually spot one
The trick is learning what to look for. Whales usually give themselves away before you see the animal itself:
A blow - a puff of white mist hanging above the water is often the very first sign.
A breach - the full-body leap and enormous splash that everyone hopes for.
A tail or pectoral fin slapping the surface, and dark backs rolling as they travel.

Scan the horizon slowly and let your eyes settle rather than darting about; binoculars help enormously. Give it time - sightings come in waves, and the people who see the most are the ones who stayed longest. If the sea is rough and grey, spotting is hard, so I'll happily come back another morning rather than strain for nothing.

items.q: When is the best time for whale watching at Bondi?
items.a: The season runs roughly May to November. June and July bring the biggest northbound numbers, while September to November is best for mothers with calves travelling close to shore. Early morning on a calm, clear day is ideal.

items.q: Can you see whales from Bondi Beach for free?
items.a: Yes - that's the beauty of it. Head to a headland like Ben Buckler Point at North Bondi, Mackenzies Point, or anywhere along the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. No ticket required, just bring binoculars and a bit of patience.

items.q: What kind of whales pass Bondi?
items.a: The vast majority are humpback whales, with occasional southern right whales, and tens of thousands migrate along the NSW coast each season.

items.q: Do whale-watching cruises leave from Bondi?
items.a: No cruises depart from Bondi Beach itself. Boats leave from Sydney Harbour - mainly Circular Quay and Darling Harbour - and head out through the Heads. Check the operator's website for current times and prices.

items.q: What should I bring for land-based whale watching?
items.a: Binoculars, warm layers and a windproof jacket (headlands are exposed and cool in winter), sun protection, and patience. A thermos never hurts.

blocks.text: There's something I never tire of: standing on Ben Buckler with the wind off the water, waiting - and then that first white blow appears and the whole headland goes quiet. Pick a calm morning between May and November, wrap up warm, and give yourself an hour. Bondi will do the rest.

blocks.text: Yes - kids can absolutely swim at Bondi Icebergs, and it's one of my favourite spots to bring young families in Bondi. Alongside the famous 50-metre ocean pool you've seen on a thousand postcards, there's a separate, shallower children's pool, and lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. It's a public pool, not a members-only club, so you and the little ones can buy a day pass and jump straight in.

That said, this is real ocean swimming, not a heated leisure centre. The water is pumped straight in from the surf, so it's bracingly cold in winter and lively when a big swell is running. Below I'll walk you through the kids' pool, safety, costs and the practical tips I share with visiting families.
The children's pool: a gentler place to start

The reason I happily recommend Icebergs for families is the separate kids' pool that sits beside the main lap pool. It's smaller and shallower, which keeps little swimmers out of the deep water and away from the serious lap-swimmers ploughing up and down the 50-metre pool. For a first taste of ocean swimming it's ideal - the salty, sun-on-the-water Bondi experience without the deep end, literally.

Because both pools are fed by the sea, the kids' pool is unheated and its temperature shifts with the ocean through the year. On a warm summer morning it's glorious; in winter it's genuinely chilly, so I always pack extra layers for afterwards.

blocks.title: Watch the swell and the wall
blocks.text: On big-surf days waves can wash right over the pool's ocean edge, and the pool sits below the promenade with steps down. Keep young kids close, hold hands on wet edges, and if the sea looks wild, the flagged lifeguard-patrolled area on Bondi Beach itself may be the safer call.
Safety and supervision

Lifeguards are on duty at the pool during opening hours, which is a big part of why I trust it with families. But lifeguards are a backstop, not a babysitter - the water is real ocean, cold enough to take a small body's breath away, so active adult supervision is the golden rule.

items: Stay within arm's reach of young or non-swimming children the whole time.
Ease kids in slowly - cold saltwater is a shock after a warm beach.
Mind the slippery pool edges and the steps down from the promenade.
Check the day's conditions before you commit little ones to the water.

blocks.text: Go early on a summer weekday if you can. The pool is calmest, the deck is quiet, and you'll have space to help a nervous swimmer find their feet before the crowds and the lap-swimming regulars arrive.
Costs, hours and what to bring

Entry is by day pass and it's an affordable outing for a family. Prices and hours change with the season, so treat everything below as a rough guide and confirm the current figures on the official Icebergs pool page before you go.

items.label: Entry
items.value: Day passes for adults, children and families; multi-visit passes too. Check current rates on the official pool page

items.label: Hours
items.value: Early morning to evening most days - confirm the day's hours on the official page

items.label: Cleaning day
items.value: Closed one weekday each week (traditionally Thursday); double-check before you go

items.label: Water
items.value: Unheated, ocean-fed saltwater that tracks the sea temperature

blocks.text: The one that catches people out is the weekly cleaning closure - I've watched families arrive with towels and toddlers only to find the gates shut, so check the pool page the day before. Towel and locker hire are usually available for a small charge if you travel light.

For a family swim I'd pack: warm layers and a spare towel each (that ocean chill lingers), rashies and sunscreen for the exposed deck, water and snacks, and thongs for the walk down. The deck offers little shade and the glare off the water is fierce.
Frequently asked questions

items.q: Can toddlers and young children swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes. There's a separate, shallower children's pool beside the main lap pool that suits young and less-confident swimmers, but it's unheated ocean water, so keep toddlers within arm's reach and supervise them closely at all times.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No. Both the main pool and the kids' pool are filled with seawater straight from the ocean, so the temperature changes with the sea - pleasant in summer and very cold in winter. Pack warm layers for afterwards.

items.q: How much does it cost for a family to swim?
items.a: Entry is by day pass, with separate adult, child and family rates and cheaper multi-visit passes available. Prices change from time to time, so check the official Icebergs pool page for current rates before you visit.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: The pool closes one weekday each week for cleaning (traditionally Thursday - though in summer, when tides permit, it sometimes opens Thursdays; their words, not ours), and it can also close during rough surf or maintenance, so always check the day's pool conditions before setting out.

items.q: Are there lifeguards on duty?
items.a: Yes - lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. They're there for emergencies, but parents and carers remain responsible for actively supervising their own children in and around the water.

blocks.text: Bottom line: Icebergs is a wonderful introduction to ocean swimming for kids, as long as you go in clear-eyed about cold water and changing conditions. Pick a calm summer morning, bring the layers, keep the little ones close, and you'll have one of those salty Bondi mornings the whole family remembers.

blocks.text: A rainy day at Bondi is not a write-off - it's just a different Bondi, and honestly one of my favourites. When the surf turns grey and the sand empties out, you can duck into the Pavilion for free art, catch a film up at Bondi Junction, swim in the rain at the Icebergs pool, or walk the coast under a moody sky with a takeaway coffee. Here's how I spend a wet day around the beach, with the tricks that keep it fun rather than soggy.
Stay dry at the Bondi Pavilion

The Pavilion is the first place I send anyone caught in a downpour. Sitting right on the promenade after its heritage restoration, it's the cultural heart of the beach - an art gallery, a theatre, and music and pottery studios with rotating exhibitions. The gallery is free and there's almost always something on. Because the programme changes constantly, I never quote specific shows or times - check the Pavilion's What's On calendar on the day.
Pair the Pavilion with a long coffee. The beachfront cafés with big front windows are made for watching rain sweep across the sand - all the drama, none of the wet.
Rainy-day activities beyond the sand
If you'd rather keep moving, Bondi and the streets just behind it have plenty under cover:
Catch a film at Bondi Junction - the cinemas inside Westfield are a short bus or train hop away, with heated seats and the latest releases. Check session times online before you head up.

Swim in the rain at the Bondi Icebergs pool. The ocean-fed saltwater pool stays open in most weather - there's nothing like doing laps while rain dimples the surface and waves crash over the edge. It closes for cleaning and big surf, so confirm hours first.
Browse the boutiques and surf shops along Gould Street and Hall Street, then warm up in a café - retail therapy is the classic Bondi wet-weather move.
Go bigger at Westfield Bondi Junction - hundreds of shops and food courts, all indoors and dry.

blocks.title: Check before you commit
blocks.text: Opening hours, session times and pool closures all shift with weather and season. For anything time-sensitive, check the venue's own website or socials the same day rather than relying on yesterday's info.
Embrace the weather: the coast in the rain

Some of my most memorable Bondi mornings have been the drizzly ones. Light rain turns the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk cinematic - dark cliffs, churning surf, empty paths and dramatic skies. Pull on a jacket, grab a coffee, and go slowly. Use judgement, though: the clifftop path gets slippery and gusty in a storm, and the rock platforms near the water are dangerous when the swell is up.

blocks.title: Big swell and slick rocks
blocks.text: Rain often arrives with heavy surf. Never venture onto exposed rock shelves or ocean pools during large swell, and keep well back from the edge on the coastal walk. If lifeguards have flagged dangerous conditions, believe them.

Pack smart: a packable rain jacket, a waterproof phone pouch and a small towel beat a bulky umbrella that fights the sea breeze. Most indoor spots are only a few minutes apart, so you can hop between them without getting soaked.
Getting around when it's wet

Parking near the beach is tight at the best of times and worse in the rain, so I skip the car. Trains run to Bondi Junction, and from the interchange frequent buses (333 and 380 among them) drop you right at the beach. Tap on with an Opal or contactless card, and check the Transport for NSW trip planner for live times.

items.q: What is there to do in Bondi when it rains?
items.a: Plenty. Visit the free Bondi Pavilion gallery, catch a film at Westfield Bondi Junction, swim at the ocean-fed Icebergs pool, browse the Gould and Hall Street shops, or walk a moody stretch of the Bondi to Coogee path with a coffee.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool open in the rain?
items.a: Usually, yes - it's an outdoor saltwater pool, so rain alone doesn't close it. It does close for cleaning and can shut in big surf, so confirm the day's hours on the Icebergs website first.

items.q: Is the Bondi Pavilion free to visit?
items.a: The Pavilion's art gallery is free and open to the public, and many events are free too. Because the programme changes often, check the What's On calendar for current exhibitions and workshops.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach without a car on a rainy day?
items.a: Take a train to Bondi Junction, then a bus (333 or 380) down to the beach - quicker and far less stressful than hunting for beachside parking. Use the Transport for NSW trip planner for live departures.

items.q: Is the Bondi to Coogee walk safe in the rain?
items.a: In light rain it's a beautiful, atmospheric walk - just wear grippy shoes and take it steady, as the path gets slippery. Avoid it in storms or big swell, and never step onto exposed rock shelves when the surf is up.

blocks.text: So don't let a grey forecast change your plans. Some of Bondi's best moments happen when the sun clocks off - just swap the towel for a raincoat and lean in.

sources.label: What's on at Bondi Pavilion - Waverley Council

blocks.text: Yes - anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs pool. It's a public ocean pool, open seven days, and you don't need to be a club member to jump in. It's the one you've seen a thousand times: two turquoise pools cut into the rocks at the southern end of Bondi, waves crashing straight over the edge, with the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk starting on the path right beside it. I swim here often, so here are the questions I actually get asked - answered straight. Where a price or session time is the sort of thing that changes, I'll send you to the official page rather than risk something stale.

items.label: Pools
items.value: 50 m lap pool + smaller, shallower second pool

blocks.title: Check the tide before you cross town
blocks.text: Entry can be affected by tides, swimming races and event days, and the pool occasionally closes to public swimmers at short notice. If you've travelled for it, a quick look at the official Pool Conditions page saves a wasted trip.

items.q: Can anyone swim at Bondi Icebergs, or do I need to be a member?
items.a: Anyone can swim. The pool has public entry seven days a week - you just pay at the kiosk and walk down. Club membership is a separate thing entirely and isn't needed for a casual dip.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim?
items.a: As at August 2026, entry is $10 for adults, $7 for children and $30 for a family pass, with the sauna included in admission - plus cheaper multi-visit passes for regulars. Because prices change, check icebergs.com.au for the current figures before you go.

items.q: What are the opening hours?
items.a: It opens early - dawn most days - and runs into the early evening, seven days a week, though it's usually closed Thursdays for cleaning (in summer, when tides permit, Thursdays often stay open). Times shift with the season, races and the surf, so I check the official pool status the morning I'm heading down.

items.q: How big is the pool?
items.a: There are two: a 50-metre lap pool that faces the ocean and takes the full force of the waves, and a smaller, more sheltered 25-metre pool tucked behind it. Both are ocean-fed.

items.q: Is the pool heated?
items.a: No. Both pools are unheated and topped up with sea water, so the temperature tracks the ocean - glorious in late summer, seriously bracing come winter. On a big swell, waves break clean over the sea wall and wash through the lanes, which is exactly the drama people come for.

items.q: Is it good for young kids?
items.a: The sheltered 25-metre pool behind the main lap pool is calmer and better for little swimmers, and lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. That said, this is the ocean: when it's pumping, the seaward lanes get lively, so keep children in the sheltered pool on big days.

items.q: Is there a sauna?
items.a: There is, and it's included with your pool admission - a proper reward after a cold lap. It's a shared space with time-capped sessions, so don't plan to linger, and bring your own towel. Freezing dip, warm sauna, repeat: my favourite winter ritual.

items.q: Can I eat and drink there without swimming?
items.a: Yes. Upstairs is the members' club - a relaxed bistro and bar with one of the best views in Sydney, open to visitors as a guest (bring photo ID). Higher still is Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, the fine-dining restaurant that books out well ahead. You can enjoy either without going near the water.

items.q: How do I join the Icebergs Winter Swimming Club?
items.a: It's a serious commitment, not a walk-up membership. The club's famous 'Rule 15B' historically required swimming three Sundays out of four for five years to earn lifetime membership. For the current induction and qualifying process, contact the club directly through icebergs.com.au.

blocks.text: Go at dawn. Soft light, calm lap lanes, and the postcard shot with waves over the wall and almost nobody in it. Towel and locker hire are on-site for a small fee, but it's easier to pack your own.

A little history for the swim: the club was founded in 1929 by a band of local life savers who wanted to keep fit through winter, and it still bills itself as the only licensed winter swimming club in the world. Women were admitted as members in 1995, and the premises you see today reopened after a major redevelopment in 2002. Pack a towel, check the tide, and I'll see you in the slow lane.

If you've only got one day in Sydney and you want it to count, come to Bondi. The short version I give every visitor: train to Bondi Junction, bus down to the sand, come in the shoulder seasons if you can, and walk at least the first stretch of the coastal path. Below is everything else - how to get here, when to come, and what to actually do.

items.label: From the CBD
items.value: Train to Bondi Junction, then a short bus

items.label: Best months
items.value: Spring & autumn for walking; summer for swimming

items.label: Cost to enjoy it
items.value: The beach and coastal walk are free

blocks.text: How to get to Bondi Beach

Bondi isn't on the train line itself, which trips up a lot of first-timers. The easiest route is a train to Bondi Junction (the end of the T4 line), then a bus down the hill. The 333 and 380 both run to Campbell Parade, right on the sand - the 333 is the express and my usual pick.

items: From Sydney Airport: train to Bondi Junction, then a bus.
From the CBD: T4 train to Bondi Junction, then the 333 bus.
Driving: parking near the beach is metered and hotly contested - I'd only drive midweek.
Rideshare and taxi: simplest with luggage or kids, though weekend traffic can crawl.

blocks.text: No paper ticket needed - just tap a contactless bank card or your phone on the Opal reader, on the train and again on the bus. Fares cap daily and on Sundays, with a discounted train-to-bus transfer. Check current fares on the Transport for NSW site.
The best time to visit
Bondi is a year-round beach, but it changes a lot with the seasons - and the busiest days aren't always the best. Here's how I think about it:

items: Summer (Dec–Feb): warm water and a real buzz, but the biggest crowds - come early or midweek.
Autumn (Mar–May): my quiet favourite - water still warm, gorgeous light, empty promenade.
Winter (Jun–Aug): cool and crisp. Fewer swimmers, but the coastal walk is glorious and it's prime whale-watching season.
Spring (Sep–Nov): mild, bright and the run-up to Sculpture by the Sea along the cliffs.

blocks.title: Time your trip with Sculpture by the Sea
blocks.text: Each spring the Bondi to Tamarama clifftop turns into a free open-air sculpture exhibition - one of my favourite times to be here. It usually runs for a few weeks from late October into early November, but the dates move each year, so check the official Sculpture by the Sea site before planning around it. Go on a weekday morning to beat the crush.
My favourite things to do
You could fill a weekend here easily, but if I had to rank the essentials, here's the order I'd do them in.

stops.title: Walk the Bondi to Coogee coastal path
stops.detail: The signature Sydney walk - roughly 6 km of clifftop track past Tamarama, Bronte and Waverley Cemetery. Even the first stretch is worth it.

stops.title: Swim at the Icebergs ocean pool
stops.detail: The iconic sea pool carved into the rocks at the southern end. Session times and prices vary - check the Icebergs website first.

stops.title: Learn to surf or swim the flags
stops.detail: Bondi's beach breaks are forgiving for beginners, and surf schools run lessons with boards and wetsuits included.

stops.title: Coffee and Campbell Parade
stops.detail: Bondi's café scene is world-class. Grab a flat white, then browse the weekend Bondi Markets.

stops.title: Bondi Pavilion and the sunset
stops.detail: Wander the restored heritage Pavilion, then watch the light go pink over the sand from the grass.

blocks.text: Walk it north-to-south, Bondi to Coogee, so the best headland views open up ahead of you - and you finish at Coogee, where a swim and a beer wait before the bus back.

blocks.title: Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags
blocks.text: Bondi has strong rips and the surf changes fast. The flagged zone is the patrolled area the lifeguards are watching - swim there, not the quieter-looking edges, which is often exactly where the rips run. If you're caught in one, don't fight it: raise an arm and float.

items.q: How do I get from Sydney city to Bondi Beach without a car?
items.a: Train to Bondi Junction, then a bus - the 333 or 380 both run to Campbell Parade. Tap on and off with an Opal or contactless card; from the CBD it's usually under an hour.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - this catches many visitors out. The nearest is Bondi Junction, roughly 3 km uphill; finish by bus, rideshare or a steep walk.

items.q: What's the best time of year to visit Bondi?
items.a: December to February is warmest for swimming. For walking, photos and fewer crowds I love autumn and spring; winter is quiet and great for whale watching.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: About 6 km one way, roughly two hours at a relaxed pace with stops. It's well signposted and free, passing Tamarama, Bronte and Clovelly.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach free to visit?
items.a: Yes - the beach, promenade and coastal walk all cost nothing. You'll only pay for extras like the Icebergs pool, surf lessons, parking or food and drink.

blocks.text: That's the local's shortlist. Bondi rewards an early start and a slow afternoon more than a packed schedule - pick two or three, leave time for a swim and a long coffee, and you'll see why the rest of us never leave.

blocks.text: When the rain rolls in off the Tasman and the flags come down at Bondi, I don't head home - I move the day indoors. So what is there to do in Bondi Beach on a rainy day? Plenty. Between the Pavilion's galleries, a long lunch above the pool, café-hopping and the undercover world of Bondi Junction, a wet day here is often one of my favourites. Here are the seven I keep coming back to.
1. Bondi Pavilion - art, theatre and pottery under one roof

The restored Bondi Pavilion is the first place I send anyone caught in a downpour. Right on the promenade, this heritage building reopened in 2022 after a major restoration and now holds an art gallery, a theatre, music studios, a pottery studio and the Bondi Story Room. Programming rotates constantly, so check the Waverley Council Pavilion page for what's on - and the galleries are free to wander.
Grab a window seat upstairs between showers - you get the whole sweep of the beach and the surf turning moody and grey, a better view than any blue-sky day.
2. A long lunch at Icebergs, dry above a churning sea

There's no better place to watch a storm than the dining room and bar at [Icebergs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar), on the top level of 1 Notts Avenue above the famous ocean pool. It's a celebrated Italian restaurant with floor-to-ceiling views, and on a wild day the waves crashing over the pool below are pure theatre. Check idrb.com for current menus, prices and reservations.
3. Café-hopping through North Bondi

Rain is the perfect excuse to slow down over coffee, and Bondi's café scene is genuinely world-class - if you want to plan a proper crawl, our full guide to [Bondi's best cafés and coffee](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) maps out where to go. I'll linger over eggs and a flat white at [Porch & Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) on Ramsgate Avenue, or grab a corner at [Speedos Café](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) up the North Bondi end and watch the wet promenade go by.

blocks.title: Cafés get cosy-busy when it rains
blocks.text: Everyone has the same idea on a wet Sunday, so the popular spots fill fast mid-morning. Go early, or wait out the peak under the Pavilion arches.
4. A wellness reset - massage, sauna or a yoga class

A grey day is tailor-made for self-care. Bondi is full of day spas, massage studios and yoga schools where you can book a treatment or drop into a class while the rain empties the streets. Rather than name prices that change, find a studio near your accommodation and book directly.
5. Read, borrow or just shelter at Waverley Library

One of Bondi's best rainy-day secrets is free: Waverley Library at the Ron Lander Centre in Bondi Junction. It's a lovely public library with quiet reading nooks, a big children's section, newspapers and free Wi-Fi - a no-pressure spot for families or anyone who wants to dry off with a book. Check the Waverley Council library page for current opening hours, which vary on weekends.
6. Lose an afternoon in a bookshop-café at Gertrude & Alice

When I want to disappear from the weather entirely, I head to [Gertrude & Alice](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/gertrude-and-alice-cafe-bookstore) on Hall Street - a much-loved Bondi bookshop-café stacked floor to ceiling with new and secondhand books, with communal tables, good coffee and cake. Pull something off the shelf, order a chai and settle in. Check gertrudeandalice.com.au for opening hours and events.

blocks.title: Planning on the Bondi Junction cinema?
blocks.text: Event Cinemas Bondi Junction is closed while Westfield's Level 6 entertainment precinct is rebuilt, with a reopening flagged for later in 2026 - check the Event Cinemas page before counting on a film there.
7. Retail therapy, all undercover

When you just want to stay bone dry for hours, Westfield Bondi Junction is the answer - hundreds of shops, food courts and cafés under one roof with the transport interchange right there. It's a short bus ride from the sand on the 333 or 380, so you can duck out the moment the sky clears.
The 333 and 380 buses link Bondi Beach straight to the Bondi Junction interchange, so you can chain the library, the shops and a long lunch into one dry afternoon.

items.q: What is there to do in Bondi Beach when it rains?
items.a: The Bondi Pavilion galleries and theatre, a long lunch at Icebergs, café-hopping through North Bondi, a spa or yoga session, Waverley Library, a browse at Gertrude & Alice, and undercover shopping at Westfield.

items.q: Is there anything free to do in Bondi on a rainy day?
items.a: Yes - wandering the Bondi Pavilion's art gallery and public spaces is free, and Waverley Library in Bondi Junction is a free place to read, use the Wi-Fi or entertain the kids.

items.q: What can families do with kids in Bondi when it's wet?
items.a: Waverley Library has a big children's section and quiet corners, and the Bondi Pavilion often runs family workshops and has the interactive Bondi Story Room.

items.q: Do I need to book anything in advance?
items.a: For a table at Icebergs or a spa treatment, yes - book through their websites and confirm prices there. The Pavilion, library and Gertrude & Alice are all walk-in.

blocks.text: So don't write off a rainy day in Bondi. Some of my best afternoons started with the flags coming down - a gallery, a long lunch and a good book. Rain or shine, this corner of Sydney always has somewhere dry to be.

Everyone who visits Bondi finds the beach, the surf and the crowds on Campbell Parade - but the Bondi I love is the one just off the main drag. Here are ten hidden-ish gems I send friends to first: quiet headland lookouts, a free gallery, a Saturday market, a sauna most people walk straight past, and a few pockets of calm the day-trippers never find.

items.label: My tip
items.value: Go early - Bondi belongs to the locals before 9am

items.label: Getting here
items.value: 333/380 bus or a short walk from Bondi Junction

blocks.text: The headland, the views and the wild edges
1. Ben Buckler headland and its lookouts

At the beach's northern tip, the Ben Buckler headland strings together little lookouts - Ray O'Keefe Reserve and Sam Fiszman Park among them - staring down the length of Bondi. It's my favourite sunrise spot: rugged, usually empty and free. Follow the footpath up from North Bondi towards the point.
2. Tamarama, the beach next door

Walk south on the coastal path about ten minutes and you drop into Tamarama - 'Glamarama' to locals - a tiny, dramatic cove between the cliffs, a fraction of Bondi's size and crowd. The surf can be punchy, so read the flags and swim between them.
3. Public art along the coastal walk

Everyone knows Sculpture by the Sea, the free open-air show that lines the Bondi-to-Tamarama walk each spring (dates shift year to year - check the official site). Fewer notice the art that stays: near Marks Park is 'Rise', the permanent Bondi Memorial to victims of gay-hate violence.
Walk the coast south-to-north in the late afternoon: the light's behind you, Bondi opens up as you round the last headland, and you finish right where the good coffee is.
Culture, shopping and a proper market
4. Bondi Pavilion

The Pavilion reopened after a major multi-year restoration, yet most beach-goers still treat it as somewhere to change and grab an ice cream. Go inside: a free art gallery, the Bondi Story Room on local history, a theatre and a pottery studio. Hours vary by space, so check the Waverley Council page first.
5. Gould Street's independent boutiques

One block back from the sand, Gould Street is where locals actually shop - small Australian labels and independent design stores instead of chain-store sameness. An easy, low-pressure browse away from the promenade crush.
6. Bondi Wash flagship

Also on Gould Street, the Bondi Wash flagship is worth a detour even if you buy nothing. Founded by a local, it builds its home and body products around native Australian botanicals, with fresh natives dotted about so you can smell the plants behind each scent.
7. The Saturday Farmers Market

Every Saturday morning the grounds of Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade fill with a farmers market - produce, bread, cheese, flowers and coffee. It runs from around 9am, but confirm current times on the official listing, then cross the road to the sand.
Calm, water and a warm-up
8. The Icebergs sauna

You've seen the Icebergs ocean pool in a thousand photos, but here's what visitors miss: your pool admission also covers the sauna and hot showers on the deck. After a cold swim it's blissful. Fees, hours and closures change (Thursdays are often maintenance days), so check the Icebergs Club site.
9. North Bondi's early-morning café scene

The northern end has a gentler rhythm than the tourist strip. Get there before 9am on a weekday and you'll find the real Bondi - surfers checking the sets, dog-walkers, people reading over a coffee. Speedos and the North Bondi cafés shine in that quiet window.
10. A green escape at Waverley Community Garden

When I need a break from salt and sunscreen I head up to the Waverley Community Garden at Clementson Park, near Bondi Junction - plots, native borders and shade most visitors never realise is there. It's a Council-run community space, so treat it gently.

blocks.title: A note on the 'secret' Bondi
blocks.text: Half of what makes these spots special is that locals use them daily. Take your rubbish, keep the noise down at the lookouts early, and swim between the flags - the friendlier you are, the more the neighbourhood opens up.

items.q: What's the best hidden gem in Bondi that's actually free?
items.a: The Ben Buckler headland lookouts at the northern end - free, uncrowded and the best sunrise view over the beach. The Bondi Pavilion's art gallery and Story Room are free too, and perfect if the weather turns.

items.q: Is there a sauna at Bondi Icebergs, and can the public use it?
items.a: Yes - a sauna and hot showers on the pool deck come with public pool admission. Fees, hours and maintenance closures change, so check the official Icebergs Club site before you go.

items.q: When is the Bondi Farmers Market on?
items.a: Saturday mornings at Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade, typically from around 9am. Confirm current times on the official listing, as they can change.

items.q: Where can I go in Bondi to escape the crowds?
items.a: Head for the edges: Tamarama just south along the coastal walk, North Bondi early in the morning, and the Ben Buckler lookouts, usually near-empty at sunrise.

blocks.text: That's my short list, but Bondi keeps handing out new favourites the longer you slow down. Step one street back, beat the crowds, and you'll find a suburb far more than its famous sand.

Let me be honest up front: Bondi doesn't hide a menu of secret dishes you can unlock with a password. What people mean by “off-menu” here is quieter and far more useful than that - it's the daily blackboard specials, the customisations the kitchen will happily make, and the simple “what would you order today?” question that gets you the best thing in the room. If you've read a listicle promising a specific secret toastie or a hidden smoothie at a named café, take it with a pinch of salt: those things come and go with the produce and the roster, and the only reliable way to find them is to ask on the day. Here's how I actually do it around the beach.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Menus, specials and opening hours around Bondi change constantly, and none of the “off-menu” requests below are guaranteed on any given day. I last checked this in August 2026 - confirm anything time-sensitive on each venue's own site or socials before you build a trip around it.
What “off-menu” really means around the beach

The closest thing Bondi has to a genuine secret menu is the blackboard. [Sean's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/seans), up on Campbell Parade in North Bondi, has run a daily-changing board for more than thirty years, driven by whatever owner Sean Moran has pulled from the farm and the market that morning. There's no fixed hidden dish to request - just today's board, so ask what's best right now rather than chase something you read about last spring. Plenty of Bondi kitchens work the same way on a smaller scale, running a special or two that never makes the printed menu.

The other kind of “off-menu” is customisation. Most of Bondi's [cafés and juice bars](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) will happily tweak a smoothie, build a bowl to your liking or adjust a coffee, and the staff nearly always have a personal go-to that isn't written on the board. That “what do you order?” recommendation is the real insider order - it's honest, it's current, and it costs you nothing but a friendly question.
How to actually ask

items: Lead with the day: “What's good today?” beats naming a dish you half-remember from an article.
Ask for the staff pick: “What would you order?” gets you the best current thing, on or off the menu.
Be specific about a craving, not a recipe: “something smoky” or “extra spicy” gives the kitchen room to say yes.
Go off-peak: a quiet midweek morning is when staff have time to make something special.
Accept a no gracefully - it depends on the produce and how busy the kitchen is.

blocks.text: A few spots where asking pays off

For a beachfront breakfast, [Porch & Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) and [Speedos Cafe](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) - near neighbours around Ramsgate Avenue in North Bondi - both bake and prep a lot in-house and run seasonal specials, so it's always worth asking what came out of the kitchen that morning rather than defaulting to the menu. They're two of my favourites in our [best breakfast & brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) roundup, and I'd still check each venue's own site or Instagram for current hours and specials before heading down.

For [dinner and a drink](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach), [Totti's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/tottis-bondi) on Bondi Road is built around a share menu and wood-fired bread, and a good bar team there will happily build something to your taste if you tell them the mood you're in. It's popular and often booked out, so reserve through Merivale rather than banking on a walk-in.

The customisation trick really comes into its own at Bondi's juice bars and health kitchens, where the printed combos are a starting point rather than a limit. Places like [Cali Press](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cali-press), [RND (Raw Next Door)](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/rnd-bondi) and [The Health Emporium](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-health-emporium) are built around bowls, smoothies and cold-pressed juices, and the staff will usually swap an ingredient, dial the sweetness down or build something to whatever you're after if you just ask - which is exactly the kind of quiet “off-menu” order that never needs a secret handshake.

The best off-menu intel isn't a secret order - it's rapport and timing. Become a familiar face, go when it's quiet, and be nice to the person making your food. That's how locals end up with the good stuff, not by reciting a code word.

blocks.title: Line up your shortlist first
blocks.text: The easiest way to have a good “what's good today?” conversation is to walk in already knowing the room. Our [Bondi eat & drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) lists every venue around the beach - 160+ of them - and lets you filter by cuisine, area, price and who you're with, so you can pick the blackboard kitchens and juice bars worth asking at before you go.

items.q: Does Bondi have a secret menu?
items.a: Not in the password-and-hidden-dish sense. What people call “off-menu” here is really daily blackboard specials and customisations the kitchen will make on request - so ask what's good on the day rather than chase a specific secret item.

items.q: How do I order off-menu without being awkward?
items.a: Keep it friendly and open-ended: “What would you order today?” or “Anything off the menu you'd recommend?” Describe a craving rather than a set recipe, and take a no in good humour.

items.q: Which Bondi places are best for daily specials?
items.a: Blackboard-driven kitchens like [Sean's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/seans) on Campbell Parade change their offering with the produce, and many beachfront cafés run in-house specials. Check each venue's own site or socials for current details, since these change constantly, or browse the full [Bondi eat & drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink).

items.q: Are off-menu items always available?
items.a: No - that's the point. They depend on the day's produce, how busy the kitchen is and who's on shift, so treat any “secret” order as a maybe, not a guarantee.

items.q: Can I customise smoothies or coffee in Bondi?
items.a: Usually, yes. Most Bondi juice bars and cafés will tweak a smoothie or build something to your taste, and staff often have a favourite that isn't on the board - just ask for their go-to. Our [best cafés & coffee](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) guide is a good place to start.

blocks.text: Off-menu eating in Bondi is less about secret codes and more about curiosity and good manners: ask what's fresh, ask what the staff love, and be easy to say yes to. For more on where to eat around the sand, see my [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink), and for the rest of a day here, [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

If you want to watch English football in Bondi, your two most reliable bets are [The Royal Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-royal-bondi) and the [Beach Road Hotel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/beach-road-hotel) - both proper pubs with big screens, cold taps and a crowd that cares. I've watched more late-night Premier League here than I'd like to admit, so here's my honest local rundown, plus the thing that catches every visitor out: the kickoff times.

blocks.title: The rights have changed - this matters in 2025/26
blocks.text: Optus Sport shut down in August 2025. The Premier League and the Emirates FA Cup are now shown in Australia by Stan Sport, with a handful of marquee matches also free-to-air on the Nine Network. So when you ask a venue "are you showing the football?", you're really asking whether they've got the Stan Sport (or Nine) feed on that night. Always confirm the specific fixture before you head down.
The two pubs I'd actually send you to
The Royal Bondi

Up on Bondi Road, The Royal is the closest thing Bondi has to a dedicated footy local - a Merivale pub with a classic front bar, plenty of screens and a live-sport schedule they publish online - so you can check whether your team's game is going up before you leave the house. It gets loud and good-natured on a big matchday, which is half the fun. See their live-sport page (linked in my sources) for what's on.
Beach Road Hotel

A couple of blocks back from the sand, the Beach Road Hotel is the big, buzzy option - multiple bars over multiple levels, so there's usually room even when something major is on. It leans party-pub later in the night, which suits those late European kickoffs. Check their socials or ring ahead to confirm your match is being screened, since which games go where can vary week to week.

items.label: Broadcaster (AU)
items.value: Stan Sport; select games free-to-air on Nine

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Confirm the exact fixture before you go

blocks.text: Mind the time difference - this is the real catch

Here's what nobody tells visitors: Sydney is roughly nine to ten hours ahead of the UK, so English football rarely lands at a civilised hour here. A Saturday 3pm kickoff in England is around midnight in Bondi, and early kickoffs can mean the small hours. Only the biggest late-window games fall at a friendly Bondi evening time - so I check the local kickoff first, then check the venue is open and putting that game on.

For the truly antisocial kickoffs, ask the pub directly whether they're opening early or staying open late for that fixture - some will, some won't, depending on the match. A quick call or DM the day before saves a wasted 2am trek across Bondi.
Other pubs and clubs worth a call

If The Royal and Beach Road can't put your game on - or you just want a plan B in a different pocket of Bondi - these are the places I'd ring next. They all keep screens on for live sport, though you'll still want to confirm they've got your exact fixture (and that they're open for that kickoff time) before you head over.

items: [Hotel Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hotel-bondi) - the grand old pub right on Campbell Parade, with several bars and a big public-bar crowd; handy if you're already down by the beach.

[North Bondi RSL](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-rsl) - a community club up the north end with screens, cheap pots and one of the best ocean views you'll ever watch a match in front of. Sign in on arrival.
[Hotel Ravesis](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hotel-ravesis) - the corner pub at the north end of the promenade; a smaller, more relaxed room if the bigger pubs are packed.
[Bondi Bowlo](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-bowlo-bondi-bowling-club) - the bowling club on Bondi Road, laid-back and good value, an easy walk from The Royal.
[Bondi Beach Public Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-beach-public-bar) - a casual Campbell Parade spot for a pint and a screen when you don't want a full-scale party pub.

blocks.text: For the full picture - opening hours, which pubs do food, and where each one sits - it's worth a look through our guide to the [best pubs in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) and the wider [best bars in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-bars-bondi-beach).
Prefer to watch it from your Bondi apartment?

If you're staying nearby and the kickoff is brutal, streaming from the couch is a perfectly good shout. In Australia the Premier League lives on Stan Sport, so a subscription plus decent WiFi is all you need. Grab a few things from the bottle shop on the way home and you've got your own Bondi viewing party - without the 3am walk back up the hill.

blocks.title: A note on the other spots you'll see listed
blocks.text: Older guides point at various beachfront bars and clubs. Plenty of Bondi venues will put a big game on if you ask early enough, but few commit the way a sports-focused pub does. If watching your team is the whole point of the night, start with The Royal or Beach Road and treat everywhere else as a bonus.

blocks.title: Sorting dinner before (or after) the match?
blocks.text: Late kickoffs mean you'll often be eating around the football. Our full Bondi eat-and-drink directory lets you browse 160+ local venues and filter by cuisine, area, price and who you're with - from a quick pre-match feed to somewhere still serving at midnight. Start with the [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink), or go straight to the [best pubs in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) if you want food and the game under one roof.

items.q: Where's the best place to watch the Premier League in Bondi?
items.a: For a reliable big-screen atmosphere, I'd point you to The Royal Bondi on Bondi Road or the Beach Road Hotel. Both are proper pubs that regularly show live football - confirm your fixture is going on before you head down. If they can't screen your game, North Bondi RSL, Hotel Bondi and the other spots in our [best pubs in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) guide are worth a call.

items.q: How do I watch English football in Australia now that Optus Sport has closed?
items.a: From August 2025 the Premier League and FA Cup are shown in Australia by Stan Sport, with select matches also free-to-air on the Nine Network. Optus Sport has shut down, so pubs will be running the Stan Sport or Nine feed.

items.q: What time do Premier League games kick off in Bondi?
items.a: Sydney is around nine to ten hours ahead of the UK, so most matches fall late at night or in the early morning here. A UK Saturday 3pm kickoff is roughly midnight in Bondi. Always check the local kickoff time and whether your venue is open for it.

items.q: Do I need to book or call ahead?
items.a: You don't usually need a booking, but I'd always call or message ahead for anything other than a marquee fixture. Which games go on which screens varies, and some pubs only open early or stay late for bigger matches.

items.q: Can I watch the football at my Bondi accommodation instead?
items.a: Yes - with a Stan Sport subscription and reliable WiFi you can stream every Premier League match from your apartment, which is often the sanest option for a 2am kickoff.

blocks.text: That's my playbook: pick The Royal or Beach Road, confirm the exact game and the local kickoff time, and remember the rights now sit with Stan Sport rather than Optus. Do that and you'll be shoulder-to-shoulder with fellow supporters when the whistle blows - or on the couch with the surf just down the road. Up the football.

blocks.text: First run in September 1971 and now billed as the largest event of its kind in the world, the City2Surf sends a tide of runners from the CBD out to Bondi every August. Whether it's your first or you're chasing a personal best, a bit of preparation goes a long way. Here are the ten things I'd tell any mate before they line up.
1. Know the course

It's 14 km from the CBD to Bondi. The opening kilometres are fast and net downhill, then near halfway you hit Heartbreak Hill - a roughly 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse along New South Head Road. Knowing exactly where the hill sits lets you save something for it instead of blowing up early.
2. Enter early and pick the right wave

Entries open earlier in the year and sell out - the 2026 event was gone well before race day. Register the moment entries open, and choose a start wave that matches your realistic finish time so you're not weaving through slower runners or holding up faster ones.
3. Train for the hill

Heartbreak Hill is what everyone remembers. Add hill repeats once a week in the lead-up so your legs and your head both know what a sustained climb feels like. It's the single best thing you can do for your time.
4. Build up gradually

Increase your weekly distance slowly rather than cramming. One longer run, some faster efforts and easy recovery jogs beats a couple of heroic long runs. Consistency is what carries you to 14 km comfortably.
5. Sort hydration and fuelling

Hydrate across the days before, not just on the morning. Have a light, familiar breakfast a couple of hours out. Whatever gels or drinks you plan to use, practise with them in training first - race day is no time for surprises.
6. Wear what you've tested - and sunscreen
Well-broken-in shoes, light moisture-wicking clothing, nothing brand new. And even in August, put on sweat-resistant sunscreen before the start; the sun really shows up by the time you reach Bondi.
7. Plan your transport

Roads close and the nearest stations fill early. Give yourself a solid hour of buffer to reach the start, find gear check, queue for the loo and warm up. Public transport beats driving every single time on race day.
8. Check the weather

Early-August Sydney swings from cool and grey to surprisingly warm. Check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast the night before and dress for it - a cheap throwaway layer you can ditch at the start line is a good friend on a cold morning.
9. Pace it in thirds

Start conservatively, run the hill on effort rather than staring at your watch, and use the long downhills to recover without over-striding. Break the run into thirds and reassess at each. Negative-splitting the City2Surf feels a lot better than fading.
10. Recover and celebrate

Keep walking for a few minutes past the line rather than stopping dead, grab water and a snack, and agree a meeting spot with your crew in advance - signal gets patchy in the finish-line crowd. Then reward yourself: brunch, a swim, or a dip at the Icebergs pool. You've earned it.
The Bondi finish is on Queen Elizabeth Drive, right above the sand. Tell your crew to wait north end, near the pavilion - it's calmer than the main chute and far easier to actually find each other.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and how hilly is it?
items.a: 14 km, and hillier than first-timers expect. The main climb is Heartbreak Hill, a roughly 2 km ascent from Rose Bay to Vaucluse along New South Head Road near halfway, with a few shorter rises after it.

items.q: Do City2Surf entries sell out?
items.a: Yes - it's the world's biggest fun run and sells out ahead of race day, so enter early through city2surf.com.au and pick a start wave matching your expected finish time.

items.q: What should I avoid on race day?
items.a: Don't wear or eat anything you haven't tested in training, don't go out too fast down the early hill, and don't skip sunscreen - the Sydney sun is strong by the Bondi finish.
