NSW Planning Portal - Short-term rental accommodation

blocks.text: If you've ever walked to the far north end of Bondi and wondered who on earth 'Ben Buckler' was, here's the honest answer: nobody knows for certain. The rocky headland guarding the northern tip of the beach has carried the name since at least 1831, but its origin is a genuine local mystery - a tangle of convicts, bushrangers and half-remembered words that historians still argue over. Let me walk you through the theories, and the one hard fact we can actually pin down.

items.label: What
items.value: Rocky headland at the north end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Also known for
items.value: The 'Big Rock', Ben Buckler Point lookout

blocks.text: The one fact we can prove

Most of Ben Buckler's story is guesswork, but there's a single documented anchor point. The earliest recorded use of the name comes from an 1831 land grant to Richard Hurd at North Bondi, which describes the boundary as running '…to a point called Ben Buckler.' So by 1831 the name was already in common enough use that a surveyor could drop it into a legal document without explanation. That tells us the name is older than the paperwork - it was already stuck. Everything before that date is where the fun begins.
The theories - take your pick
Waverley Council's own local-history researchers have gathered several competing explanations, and I love that they've never tried to force a tidy conclusion. Here are the main contenders.
The convict

The most colourful theory says the headland is named after a convict called Benjamin Buckler - sometimes recorded as Ben Buckley - who lived locally among the Aboriginal people around 1810. According to a fellow convict named James Ives, Buckler met a grim end right here: he was standing on a rock shelf near the point when it gave way beneath him. If that's true, the man didn't just lend his name to the headland - the headland took his life.
The bushranger

A close cousin of that story swaps the convict for a bushranger, also named Ben Buckley, who supposedly holed up in a cave in the rocks at the northern end of the beach. Whether Buckler the convict and Buckley the bushranger were the same half-remembered man, two different people, or one story that split in the retelling, I genuinely can't tell you - and neither, I suspect, could anyone in 1831.
An Aboriginal word

Obed West (1807–1891), one of the great early chroniclers of the Sydney coast, offered a very different idea: that 'Ben Buckler' is an English corruption of an Aboriginal word for the place. Given how many Sydney place names were mangled from the languages of the Eora people, this one has always felt plausible to me - though the original word, frustratingly, seems lost.
The Scottish island

The most unexpected theory claims the name is a corruption of 'Benbecula', an island in the Outer Hebrides off the west coast of Scotland, supposedly bestowed by Governor Macquarie. Say 'Benbecula' out loud a few times and you can just about hear 'Ben Buckler' emerge - but I'd file this one firmly under 'charming but unproven.'

Walk out to Ben Buckler Point at the northern tip for one of the best free views on the whole coast - the full sweep of Bondi to the south, and whales passing offshore during the winter migration (roughly May to November). It's a short, flat stroll past the North Bondi surf club and it's quietly one of my favourite spots to end a beach day.
While you're up there: the Big Rock

Ben Buckler hides another curiosity - an enormous boulder in the rocks below the point, marked with a brass plaque. The popular story is that a ferocious storm in July 1912 tore the 235-tonne rock loose and flung it up the shore. It's a cracking tale, cast in metal on the plaque - but I'll be straight with you: geographers have argued for years that the rock may have been there long before 1912. For the properly researched version, David Booth's paper 'Bondi's Big Rock' is the place to go rather than trusting the plaque.

blocks.title: History with an asterisk
blocks.text: None of the name theories is settled, and even the Big Rock's date is disputed. Treat every version here - including the plaque - as a story worth enjoying rather than a fact to memorise. That uncertainty is part of what makes Ben Buckler such a good local mystery.

items.q: Where is Ben Buckler?
items.a: It's the rocky headland at the northern end of Bondi Beach, in the suburb of North Bondi within Waverley Council. Ben Buckler Point is an easy, flat walk past the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club.

items.q: How did Ben Buckler get its name?
items.a: Honestly, no one knows for sure. The leading theories are that it's named after a convict (Benjamin Buckler / Ben Buckley) who died on the rocks around 1810, after a bushranger who lived in a cave nearby, after a corrupted Aboriginal word recorded by Obed West, or even after the Scottish island of Benbecula. The name was already in use by an 1831 land grant.

items.q: Is there really a giant rock at Ben Buckler?
items.a: Yes - a large boulder with a brass plaque sits in the rocks below the point. The plaque credits a 1912 storm with washing it ashore, though some researchers argue the rock predates that storm. Either way it's an easy detour on your walk out to the headland.

items.q: Is Ben Buckler worth visiting?
items.a: Absolutely, and it's free. The lookout gives you the full length of Bondi Beach, a great vantage for winter whale-watching, and a bit of quiet away from the busy south end. Bring water and decent shoes for the rock platform.

blocks.text: So next time you're standing at the north end of Bondi with the surf pounding the rocks below, remember you're on one of the few corners of the beach whose very name is an unsolved puzzle. Convict, bushranger, lost Aboriginal word or misheard Scottish island - take your pick. I rather like that we'll probably never know.

sources.label: Ben Buckler, New South Wales - Wikipedia
Booth, Douglas (2016) 'Bondi's Big Rock', Geographical Research 54(4)

blocks.text: If you want to fall asleep to the sound of the surf and walk to the sand in your thongs, stay right in the beach village between Campbell Parade and Hall Street - the heart of Bondi and where I send first-timers. But the honest answer to "where should I stay in Bondi?" depends on your budget and how close to the water you need to be, so here's how I'd choose, from a beachfront splurge to a bed in a buzzing hostel.
Right on the beach: hotels and apartment-hotels

For the classic Bondi arrival - bags down, swimmers on, feet in the sand within minutes - nothing beats staying inside the beach village. QT Bondi sits on Beach Road above the retail arcade, a short stroll from the promenade, and it's the polished, design-led option if you want a proper hotel by the water. A minute back from the sand on Hall Street, Adina Apartment Hotel Bondi Beach gives you self-contained studios and apartments with kitchens and laundries - my go-to for families or anyone staying more than a couple of nights, since cooking a few meals genuinely saves money.

Rates in the beach village swing hard with the season, so I won't quote a number that'll be wrong by the time you read this - check each hotel's own site for live pricing, and expect summer, school holidays and long weekends to be dearest.

The gap between a room "with ocean views" and one facing the street can be significant. If you'll be out at the beach all day anyway, book the cheaper aspect and spend the saving on breakfast at a Hall Street café.
Boutique stays and guesthouses

If you'd rather something smaller and more characterful, Bondi has a handful of boutique places and small guesthouses tucked into the streets behind the beach - designed rooms and a neighbourhood feel rather than a lobby-and-lifts experience. They come and go and vary wildly, so read recent reviews and confirm what's included (parking in particular is tight and often paid) before you commit.
Backpackers and budget beds

Bondi has a long, genuine backpacker culture, and the hostels are clustered right on Campbell Parade opposite the sand. Wake Up! Bondi Beach is the big, social, well-run choice - dorms and private rooms, and the kind of place where solo travellers actually meet people. For a bed this close to the water the Campbell Parade hostels are unbeatable value; just book early over summer - the good-value dorms sell out first.

blocks.title: Bondi Beach vs Bondi Junction
blocks.text: Bondi Junction sits a few kilometres inland - a different place from the beach. It's a major transport interchange (train plus buses), so it's handy and often cheaper for a bed, but you'll ride a bus or train to reach the sand. If waking up near the water matters, book in the beach village.
How I'd choose

items: Want to walk to the surf in seconds and don't mind paying - a beachfront hotel or apartment-hotel.
Travelling as a family or staying a week - a self-contained apartment with a kitchen and laundry.
After character over polish - a boutique hotel or guesthouse in the back streets.
On a budget or travelling solo - a Campbell Parade hostel.
Chasing the lowest price and happy to commute - Bondi Junction, then the bus in.

blocks.text: Whatever you pick, book well ahead for December through February and any long weekend - Bondi fills up and the closer-to-the-sand rooms go first. Getting here without a car is easy: plan trains and the frequent Bondi buses on the Transport for NSW trip planner and skip Bondi's notoriously scarce parking.

items.q: Where is the best area to stay in Bondi Beach?
items.a: For the full Bondi experience, stay in the beach village between Campbell Parade and Hall Street - you can walk to the sand, the cafés and the coastal walk. Bondi Junction, a few kilometres inland, is cheaper and a transport hub but isn't at the beach.

items.q: How much does accommodation in Bondi cost?
items.a: It varies a lot by season and how close to the water you are, so I won't quote a figure that dates quickly. Hostels are cheapest, apartment-hotels and boutique stays sit in the middle, and beachfront hotels are the top end. Check each property's own website for live rates.

items.q: Is Bondi good for families?
items.a: Yes. A self-contained apartment with a kitchen and laundry - such as an apartment-hotel on Hall Street - makes family stays far easier and cheaper than eating out every meal, and you're still walking distance from the patrolled beach.

items.q: Do I need a car to stay in Bondi?
items.a: No - you're better off without one. Parking is scarce and often paid, while trains to Bondi Junction and frequent buses to the beach make getting around easy. Plan trips on the Transport for NSW trip planner.

items.q: How far ahead should I book?
items.a: For summer (December to February), school holidays and long weekends, book as far ahead as you can - the best-value and closest-to-the-beach rooms sell out first. Outside peak times you have far more flexibility.

blocks.text: Staying in Bondi is really about the walk to the water - pick the closest bed your budget allows and let the beach be the first thing you see each morning.

If you want my honest shortlist, the three backpacker hostels I send budget travellers to in Bondi are Wake Up! Bondi Beach, Bondi Beach Backpackers and Little Drifter Bondi (formerly The Village Bondi Beach) - all within a few minutes' walk of the sand, each with its own personality. Here's how I'd pick between them, plus the local know-how that saves you money and hassle.

Bondi is easily Sydney's most popular base for backpackers, and it's not hard to see why: a world-famous beach on your doorstep, the coastal walk a few steps away, and cafés and pubs on every corner. The catch: the good beds fill fast, so picking the right hostel and booking early matters more here than almost anywhere in Sydney.
My top three Bondi hostels
Wake Up! Bondi Beach - best for the view and the buzz

Sitting right on Campbell Parade opposite the beach (110 Campbell Parade), Wake Up! is the one I point people to when they want that wake-up-and-see-the-ocean moment. It's the polished, sociable option: a rooftop overlooking the sand, an on-site bar and restaurant, free surfboard hire, and a full activity calendar - group workouts, yoga, sauna and ice-bath sessions and beach BBQs. Dorms run from small 3-bed rooms up to 8-bed, plus private twins and doubles. If you like your hostel busy and social, it's my first pick.
Bondi Beach Backpackers - best for a homely, laid-back vibe

Tucked on Hall Street (35a Hall Street), Bondi's main pedestrian drag, Bondi Beach Backpackers has long had a reputation for a warmer, more community feel than the big party places. You're a two-minute stroll from the beach, surrounded by the cafés, bakeries and cheap eats that make Hall Street so easy to live on. It's my pick if you'd rather meet people over a shared kitchen than a rooftop DJ set.
Little Drifter Bondi (formerly The Village) - best for a quieter, sunny base

A short walk back from the water on Lamrock Avenue, Little Drifter Bondi - which longtime visitors know as The Village - trades absolute beachfront for a calmer stay, with a sunny courtyard made for slow mornings. Travellers who aren't chasing a party scene love it: close enough to everything, far enough from the noise to actually sleep.

blocks.title: On prices
blocks.text: Hostel rates swing hard by season, day of week and how far ahead you book - a summer Saturday dorm can cost several times a quiet winter weekday. Rather than quote a figure that'll be wrong by the time you read this, check live prices for your exact dates on each hostel's site or a booking platform.
How to choose - and how to book smart
Here's the quick call I'd make in your shoes:

items: Want the view, the rooftop and a built-in social scene? Wake Up! Bondi Beach.
Want a homely, community feel a step off the beach? Bondi Beach Backpackers.
Want somewhere calmer and sunnier to unwind? Little Drifter Bondi (formerly The Village).

blocks.text: The single best money move is booking early. Bondi's good hostels sell out weeks ahead in summer, and for Christmas or New Year - peak everything - booking six to twelve months out is not overkill. Flex into spring or autumn for better rooms and friendlier rates in the same sunshine.
Getting there and getting around

You don't need a car - parking in Bondi is painful and expensive. From the city or Bondi Junction, the 333 and 380 buses run down Campbell Parade to within a couple of minutes of all three hostels. For live times and the cheapest route, plug your start point into the Transport for NSW trip planner.

items.q: Which Bondi hostel is best for solo travellers who want to meet people?
items.a: Wake Up! Bondi Beach, for the most social atmosphere - rooftop, bar and a packed activity calendar. Bondi Beach Backpackers is the friendlier, community-feel alternative if you'd rather meet people over the kitchen table.

items.q: How far in advance should I book a hostel in Bondi?
items.a: Weeks ahead for most of the year, and six to twelve months ahead for the December–January peak and especially New Year, when beds are scarce and prices spike.

items.q: How much does a hostel in Bondi cost per night?
items.a: It varies too much by season, day and lead time to quote reliably. Check live prices for your exact dates on each hostel's own website or a booking platform rather than trusting a single 'average'.

items.q: Do I need a car to stay in Bondi?
items.a: No - and I'd advise against one. Parking is scarce and pricey, the 333 and 380 buses run past all three hostels, and everything you need is within walking distance.

items.q: Are these hostels close to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - all three sit within roughly a five-minute walk of the sand. Wake Up! is directly opposite on Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach Backpackers a couple of minutes away on Hall Street, and Little Drifter Bondi a short walk back on Lamrock Avenue.

blocks.text: Whichever you choose, you're landing in one of Sydney's best budget bases - beach, coastal walk, cheap eats and a ready-made crowd of travellers in one small, sunny corner. Book early, pack light, and I'll see you on the sand.

My honest, lived-in answer to where to have the best breakfast in Bondi right now: [bills](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bills-bondi-beach) on Hall Street for the ricotta hotcakes everyone talks about, [Porch and Parlour](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/porch-and-parlour) up the north end for a table near the sand, and [Lox Stock & Barrel](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lox-stock-and-barrel) when I'm craving a proper bagel. Those three cover most moods - but Bondi's breakfast runs deep, so let me walk you through how I actually eat my way through a morning here.

I've lived and eaten around this beach for years, and breakfast is genuinely the meal Bondi does best. Cafés open early, the coffee is taken very seriously, and half the joy is the walk between them with salt still in your hair. If you want the wider field, we keep a full guide to [Bondi's best breakfast and brunch](/bondi-eat-and-drink/breakfast-brunch-bondi-beach) and a separate one for [the best cafés and coffee](/bondi-eat-and-drink/best-cafes-bondi-beach) - but here's where I actually go.
My go-to breakfast spots
bills, Hall Street

bills is the one visitors ask me about by name, and for once the hype holds up. Bill Granger's ricotta hotcakes with banana and honeycomb butter are a genuine Sydney institution, and the sweetcorn fritters and creamy scrambled eggs are just as good. It's bright, buzzy and unmistakably Bondi. It's popular, so expect a wait on weekends - check the bills site for current hours before you head down.
Porch and Parlour, North Bondi

If I'm choosing on vibe alone, Porch and Parlour wins. It sits up at the quieter north end near the surf club, all greenery and easy light, and the menu leans fresh and vegetable-forward - think generous breakfast bowls, plant-leaning plates and very good coffee. It's my pick for a slow, unhurried morning after a swim.
Lox Stock & Barrel, Glenayr Avenue

For something heartier, Lox Stock & Barrel does European deli-style breakfasts and bagels with the fish and meat cured in-house. The lox bagel is the obvious order, but the shakshuka-style plates and the egg dishes are what keep me coming back on a cold morning.
Gertrude & Alice, Hall Street

And when I want breakfast to turn into a two-hour affair, it's [Gertrude & Alice](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/gertrude-and-alice-cafe-bookstore) - a much-loved second-hand bookshop and café where you eat surrounded by towering shelves. Grab a coffee, a plate and a book you didn't plan to buy. It's the least beachy spot on this list and all the more charming for it.

The Bondi breakfast secret isn't a café - it's timing. On weekends the queues at the famous spots start building around 9am. If you rock up by 7.30 or 8, you'll walk straight in, get the best light for photos and have the promenade almost to yourself. Sleep in and you're queuing.

blocks.title: Menus and hours change
blocks.text: Bondi cafés tweak menus, prices and opening times constantly. I've kept this guide to places I trust rather than quoting numbers that go stale, so check each venue's own site or socials for current menus and hours before you set out.
A few more, depending on the morning
The four above are my defaults, but I send people all over the beach depending on what they're after. Here's the shortlist I reach for when the mood's a bit different.
For a table near the water

Up the north end, [Speedos Cafe](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/speedos-cafe) is the local institution for eggs and a swim, and [North Bondi Fish](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-fish) does a more polished sit-down morning right by the sand. My sentimental favourite is [The Crabbe Hole](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-crabbe-hole), the tiny coffee window tucked beneath the Icebergs pool at the south end - barely any seats, but the view is the whole point. For the full run of tables with water in front of them, that's our [beachfront and ocean-view guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).
For the coffee first, food second

When the coffee is the actual mission, I point people at [% Arabica](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/arabica-bondi) on the promenade and [Will & Co](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/will-and-co-hq-tasting-bar) for a properly dialled-in cup. Both do a pastry or a light bite, but you're going for what's in the cup.
For something lighter or plant-based

For açai bowls, smoothies and the green-juice end of things, [Cali Press](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/cali-press) is the reliable one, and Porch and Parlour (above) covers vegetable-forward brunch just as well. If that's your morning, our [vegan and vegetarian guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/vegan-vegetarian-bondi-beach) has the rest.
For a bakery breakfast on the move

Some mornings breakfast is just a good pastry and a coffee eaten on a bench facing the water. [Sonoma](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sonoma-bakery-cafe-bondi) is my go-to for sourdough and baked goods, and there's a whole city of them in our [bakeries and sweets guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach).
How to plan a proper Bondi breakfast morning
My favourite way to do it is to make breakfast the centrepiece of the whole morning rather than a quick refuel. Here's the loop I'd send a friend on.

stops.title: Sunrise swim or walk
stops.detail: Start at the beach before the crowds - a dawn dip or a stroll along the promenade earns your breakfast.

stops.title: Coffee and a table
stops.detail: Beat the weekend queue at bills or Porch and Parlour while it's still calm.

stops.title: The Bondi to Bronte walk
stops.detail: Work it off on the coastal path - one of the great free things to do in Sydney.

stops.title: Second coffee
stops.detail: Because this is Bondi, and one is never really enough.

items.q: What is the most famous breakfast in Bondi?
items.a: bills on Hall Street, for the ricotta hotcakes with banana and honeycomb butter - a Sydney classic that draws visitors from all over. The sweetcorn fritters and scrambled eggs are just as loved.

items.q: Where's the best breakfast with a beach view in Bondi?
items.a: Porch and Parlour at the north end sits close to the sand and surf club with lovely light. For a table right by the water, Speedos Cafe and North Bondi Fish are up the north end, and The Crabbe Hole is the tiny coffee window under the Icebergs pool at the south end. Our beachfront and ocean-view guide rounds up the rest.

items.q: Do I need to book breakfast in Bondi?
items.a: Most breakfast cafés run on walk-ins rather than bookings, so the real trick is timing. Arrive before 8am on weekends and you'll skip the queues at the popular spots; turn up mid-morning on a weekend and you may be in for a wait.

items.q: Where can I get a good bagel in Bondi?
items.a: Lox Stock & Barrel on Glenayr Avenue is the go-to - a European-style deli baking bread daily and curing its own fish and meat. The lox bagel is the signature order.

items.q: Is breakfast in Bondi expensive?
items.a: Bondi café prices sit at the higher end of Sydney, as you'd expect for a beachside suburb, but you'll find everything from a quick takeaway coffee and pastry to a full sit-down feast. Check each venue's current menu for prices before you go.

blocks.text: That's the honest local rundown. Bondi doesn't really do a bad breakfast - but do it early, take your time, and let the walk between coffees be part of the experience. See you out there.

blocks.title: Looking for more than breakfast?
blocks.text: This is my personal shortlist, not the whole map. Our [Bondi eat and drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) has every café, restaurant and bar in the neighbourhood - 160+ venues you can filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with, whether you're after brunch now or dinner later.

If you're after the best activities for kids at Bondi Beach, here's the short answer from someone who does this most weekends: head to the northern end and build your day around the sheltered children's pool, the fenced playground and the patrolled flags. That trio keeps toddlers through to tweens happy and it's all free. Everything below is how I string those together into an easy family day.

items.label: Calmest swim
items.value: North Bondi Children's Pool, at the north end

items.label: Playground
items.value: Bondi Park, fully fenced and behind the sand

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Only swim between the red & yellow flags

blocks.text: Swim and splash at the calm northern end

The most useful thing I can tell any parent is to point your day at the north end of the beach. The North Bondi Children's Pool is a shallow, rock-sheltered wading pool tucked right at the top of the sand, protected from the open surf, so little ones can paddle while you sit close by. Bring buckets and spades, because the sand beside it is soft and gentle.

If your kids want the real ocean, the north end is usually where the surf is smallest, but the rule never changes: only swim between the red and yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and ask them about the day's conditions first. Flag positions shift with the surf, so check them each visit.

blocks.title: Flags first, always
blocks.text: Bondi is patrolled but it still has rips. Keep young children between the flags and within arm's reach, and ask a lifeguard where's safest that day. Surf Life Saving's advice if you're caught in a rip: stay calm, raise an arm and float.
Playground, park and pram-friendly strolls

When everyone needs a break from the water, the fully fenced playground in Bondi Park is my go-to. It sits on the grass just behind the beach, with picnic and barbecue areas alongside, so a packed lunch and a run-around buy you a proper rest. Because it's enclosed, you're not chasing anyone toward the road.

items: Bondi Park playground - fenced, with grass, picnic and BBQ spots right behind the beach.
The beachfront promenade - flat, pram-friendly and lined with grass, ideal for a gentle stroll or a scooter.
The skate ramps and the painted sea wall at the south end - great for older kids to watch or have a go.

The first clifftop stretch of the coastal walk, as far as the Marks Park headland - pushable with a sturdy pram, then turn around: beyond it the path to Bronte has flights of steps, so take a carrier if you want the full walk.

blocks.text: Bronte, one bay south, is my secret weapon with small children: a shallow, sheltered natural rock pool (the 'Bogey Hole') and a grassy park with its own playground behind the sand, calmer than Bondi on a busy weekend.
Markets, surfing and watching the action

Beyond the sand, the Bondi Markets are a fun morning with kids weaving between stalls of food, crafts and vintage finds. They run on set days at Bondi Beach Public School rather than daily, so check the current schedule on the official markets page first. The historic Bondi Icebergs, perched over the ocean pool at the south end, is another easy stop; the pool is for members and paying visitors, but kids love watching swimmers brave the waves crashing over the edge from the promenade above.

Bondi is also a brilliant place for a first surf. Let's Go Surfing at the north end runs kids' and family lessons with gear included, plus school-holiday programs, though age minimums and times vary, so check and book ahead. And if nobody's in the mood to get wet, parking on the grass to watch the surfers go by is a lovely way to spend an afternoon here.

items.q: Where's the safest place to swim at Bondi with young kids?
items.a: The northern end. The North Bondi Children's Pool is a shallow, sheltered wading area away from the surf, and the open-water swimming is calmest up that end too. Always keep kids between the red and yellow flags and ask a lifeguard about conditions on the day.

items.q: Is there a playground at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - there's a fully fenced playground in Bondi Park just behind the beach, with picnic and barbecue areas alongside. It suits toddlers through to primary-aged kids and it's free to use.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach pram- and stroller-friendly?
items.a: Yes. The beachfront promenade is flat and continuous and Bondi Park behind it is grassy and level. The sand itself is hard going with a pram, but the promenade, playground and cafés are all easy to reach without one.

items.q: When are the Bondi Markets on?
items.a: The markets run on set days at Bondi Beach Public School rather than every day. Days and hours can change, so check the official Bondi Markets page for the current schedule before you go.

items.q: Can kids learn to surf at Bondi?
items.a: Yes. Local schools such as Let's Go Surfing run kids' and family lessons with gear included, including school-holiday programs for younger children. Age minimums vary by lesson type, so check the school's current programs and book ahead.

blocks.text: That's the rhythm I'd aim for with kids in tow: a splash at the children's pool, a play in the fenced park, a promenade stroll, maybe a first wave, and an ice cream to finish. Keep to the north end, watch the flags, and Bondi is one of my favourite family days in Sydney.

blocks.text: If you just want the shortlist: my picks for the best restaurants in Bondi Beach are [Icebergs Dining Room and Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar) for a special occasion with a view, [Sean's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/seans) for understated produce-driven cooking, [North Bondi Fish](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-fish) for beachfront seafood, and [Totti's](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/tottis-bondi) for a long Italian lunch. Below I break those down by the kind of meal you're after. I write as a local curator rather than claiming to have eaten at every one this week, so book the big names ahead and confirm days and hours on each venue's own site before a special trip.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Restaurants change - menus, chefs and trading days shift, and the best tables book out early. I last reviewed this in August 2026; for current hours, prices and bookings, always check the venue's own channels before you go rather than trusting any number in an older guide.
Best for a special occasion
Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Icebergs is the Bondi bucket-list dinner - a glamorous, glass-walled Italian dining room on the southern cliff, looking straight down over the Icebergs pool and the ocean. It's polished coastal Italian with one of the best outlooks in Sydney. Best for a celebration or impressing visitors; it sits at the premium end, so book well ahead. For more restaurants in this vein, see our round-up of the [best date-night restaurants in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach). You can pair it with a look at the [Icebergs pool and where to swim](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach).
Sean's

A genuine Bondi institution: chef Sean Moran has run this small, produce-led restaurant on Campbell Parade since 1993 (these days simply "Sean's", formerly Sean's Panorama). The short, hand-written menu changes with what's good, much of it from the chef's own farm. It's understated and beloved rather than flashy - best for a considered, ingredient-first dinner or weekend lunch. It's a small room, so booking is wise.
Beachfront seafood
North Bondi Fish

About as beachfront as dining gets - on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end, with the sand almost at the door. The menu is easy-going seafood: sashimi, calamari, tacos, and fish and chips, plus cocktails. Best for a relaxed lunch or early dinner with a view, and a solid choice with kids in tow - it's a natural fit for our [family-friendly places to eat](/bondi-eat-and-drink/family-friendly-bondi-beach). For every table near the water, see our guide to [beachfront and ocean-view dining in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).
Bondi Trattoria

A long-running, unfussy Italian on Campbell Parade looking across to the beach - [Bondi Trattoria](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-trattoria) does pasta, pizza and a casual all-day menu that suits a spontaneous meal. Best for an easy, mid-range dinner opposite the sand rather than special-occasion prices.
Italian & share plates
Totti's Bondi

Totti's, behind [The Royal](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-royal-bondi) on Bondi Road, is the crowd-pleasing Italian everyone seems to end up at - famous for its pillowy wood-fired bread and generous, family-style plates in a sunny, convivial room. Start with the bread and build the meal around it. Best for a group, a birthday, or a long boozy lunch; it's popular, so book ahead.
LULU

One of the newer names worth knowing, [LULU](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/lulu-bondi) is a Pan-Asian bar and kitchen on Hall Street built around share plates - think Korean fried chicken, fresh sashimi and drinks to match. Best for a livelier, share-and-graze dinner away from the beachfront. As a newer venue, check its trading days before you rely on it.
A few more worth booking

The shortlist above covers the classics, but Bondi's dining has broadened a lot - these are the other tables I'd happily send you to, spanning Greek, char-grill, pizza and ramen. As with the big names, confirm days and hours on each venue's own site before a special trip.

items: [Hurricane's Grill & Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/hurricanes-grill-bar-bondi-beach) - a long-time favourite for char-grilled ribs and steaks, up on Campbell Parade with beach views. Best for a hungry group.
[Kazzi Beach Greek](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/kazzi-beach-greek-bondi) - a big, buzzy modern-Greek room for share plates, seafood and a lively night out.
[Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/da-orazio-pizza-porchetta) - wood-fired pizza and porchetta in North Bondi; a reliable, easygoing Italian.
[Chaco Ramen](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/chaco-ramen-bondi) - proper ramen and Japanese small plates when you want something warming and casual.
[bills Bondi Beach](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bills-bondi-beach) - the all-day icon known for its ricotta hotcakes; as good for a long breakfast as an easy dinner.

blocks.text: What to know before you go

items: Book ahead for the big ones: Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's fill up, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings.
Timing: sunset tables with a view (Icebergs, North Bondi Fish) are the most sought-after - reserve early or aim for lunch.

Price: Icebergs and Sean's sit at the premium end; North Bondi Fish, Bondi Trattoria and LULU are more mid-range - and if you're counting pennies, our guide to the [best cheap eats in Bondi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach) covers the under-the-radar bargains.
Getting there: it's an easy night out on foot or by bus - see [getting to Bondi](/getting-to-bondi) if you're coming from the city.
Make a day of it: line up a swim or the coastal walk first - see [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

blocks.text: Which Bondi restaurant is right for you?

items: Special occasion with a view: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar.
Ingredient-led, understated dinner: Sean's (Campbell Parade).
Beachfront seafood: North Bondi Fish.
Easy mid-range Italian opposite the beach: Bondi Trattoria.
Group Italian / long lunch: Totti's Bondi.
Livelier newer share plates: LULU (Hall Street).

items.q: What is the best restaurant in Bondi Beach?
items.a: For a special-occasion dinner with a view, Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the classic pick. For understated, produce-driven cooking, Sean's on Campbell Parade has been a favourite since 1993.

items.q: Where can I eat right on Bondi Beach?
items.a: North Bondi Fish is the most beachfront option, on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end. Icebergs sits above the pool on the southern cliff with the best elevated view. For the full set, see our guide to [beachfront and ocean-view dining](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).

items.q: Which Bondi restaurant has the best view?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, looking over the Icebergs pool and the ocean, is hard to beat; North Bondi Fish gets you closest to the sand.

items.q: Do I need to book a Bondi restaurant?
items.a: For Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's, yes - book ahead, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings. Casual spots like Bondi Trattoria and North Bondi Fish are more forgiving. Confirm current hours on each venue's own site.

blocks.text: If you want my honest local answer, the best time to visit Bondi Beach is autumn - roughly March to early May - when the ocean is still holding onto its summer warmth, the sun is out, and the elbow-to-elbow summer crowds have thinned to something civilised. That said, there's no genuinely bad time to come; Bondi just wears each season differently, and the right one really depends on whether you're here to swim, to walk, or to eat your way along the promenade.

items.label: Lifeguards
items.value: On patrol at Bondi every day of the year

blocks.text: Season by season, the way a local sees it
Summer (December–February): peak Bondi

This is Bondi at full volume - warm water, long daylight, packed sand and heaving bars. It's genuinely brilliant if you love the buzz, but be realistic: December to February brings the biggest crowds, the worst parking, and the hottest, most humid afternoons. Come early in the day, and don't expect a quiet stretch of sand to yourself. If you're chasing the classic postcard Bondi, this is it, just with a few thousand friends.
Autumn (March–May): my personal favourite

Autumn is Bondi's sweet spot. The ocean stays pleasantly swimmable well into April because the water lags behind the air and holds summer's warmth, so you get lovely swims without the summer squeeze. Mornings are crisp, afternoons are mild, and the coastal walk to Bronte is a joy without the heat haze. Cafés and restaurants are easier to get into, and the whole place feels like it exhales.
Winter (June–August): quiet, moody and underrated

Winter Bondi surprises people. Sydney's winters are mild by most standards - bright, clear days are common - so it's perfect for long coastal walks, whale-watching from the cliffs, unhurried brunches and browsing the shops and markets without a scrum. The water is cold and swimming is really for the hardy (or the wetsuited), but if your Bondi is more about atmosphere than swimsuits, winter is a beautiful, cheap, uncrowded secret.
Spring (September–November): the reawakening

Spring warms up steadily and the beach comes back to life. The water is still on the cool side early on and warms through November, but the days are long and the mood is optimistic. It's also when Sculpture by the Sea takes over the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk - check the official dates before you plan around it.

Whatever season you pick, come at the edges of the day. A sunrise swim or an early-morning walk gives you the best light, the calmest water and a near-empty promenade - even in the middle of summer. By 10am on a hot weekend, the good parking and the good coffee are both long gone.

blocks.title: Always swim between the flags
blocks.text: Professional lifeguards patrol Bondi year-round, and the red-and-yellow flags mark the safest, monitored swimming zone. Bondi's rips are real, so swim between the flags whatever the season - and if there are no flags, it's a sign the water isn't being patrolled there right then.
So when should YOU come?

items: For swimming and warm water with fewer people: late summer into autumn (Feb–April).
For the full, buzzing beach-party Bondi: December–February - just arrive early.
For quiet walks, whales and cheaper stays: winter (June–August).
For events and long, bright days: spring, around Sculpture by the Sea and the lead-up to summer.

items.q: What is the overall best time to visit Bondi Beach?
items.a: For most people, autumn (March to early May) is the sweet spot - the ocean is still warm enough to swim, the weather is mild and sunny, and the summer crowds have eased. If you specifically want the lively, packed-beach experience, come in summer (December–February) instead.

items.q: When is Bondi Beach the least crowded?
items.a: Winter, roughly June to August, is by far the quietest. You'll have room to walk, no trouble getting a table, and often cheaper accommodation - just don't expect warm swimming without a wetsuit.

items.q: When is the water warmest at Bondi?
items.a: Sea temperatures peak in late summer and early autumn, around February and March, because the ocean warms up more slowly than the air. Winter is the coldest, so many swimmers switch to a wetsuit then.

items.q: Is it worth visiting Bondi in winter?
items.a: Absolutely, if you're after atmosphere rather than sunbathing. Sydney winters are mild and often clear, making it ideal for the coastal walk, whale-watching, brunch and shopping without the summer crush.

items.q: When should I avoid Bondi if I dislike crowds?
items.a: Summer weekends, public holidays and the December–January holiday period are the busiest and hardest for parking. Come on a weekday, or shift your trip to autumn or spring, and it's a completely different, calmer beach.

blocks.text: My take after years of watching Bondi through every season: pick autumn if you can, keep summer for when you want the noise and the party, and don't write off winter - some of my favourite Bondi mornings have been cold, clear and gloriously empty. Whenever you come, start early, swim between the flags, and let the beach set the pace.

Bondi's wine scene has quietly grown up. For years it was schooners at the pub or a cocktail with a view, but these days we've got proper little neighbourhood rooms, lo-fi natural lists and cafe-to-wine-bar hybrids where you drink where you ate breakfast. Here's the short version, then the detail: for **natural wine**, go to [The Shop & Wine Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-shop-and-wine-bar) or [Neighbourhood](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/neighbourhood-bondi); for a **glass at sunset** head to the sand at [Beach Bar at Promenade](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/beach-bar-at-promenade-bondi-beach) or the glamour of [Icebergs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/icebergs-dining-room-and-bar); for **cafe-by-day, wine-by-night** it's [Chapter One](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/chapter-one-caf-and-wine-room); and for a lazy **aperitivo**, [Ciao Bella](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/ciao-bella-bondi).

I've organised this the way we actually decide where to go - by what kind of night it is, not alphabetically. Everything below is open and trading as of this update; I've left the closed places out on purpose.
For a glass at sunset (with a view)

Nothing beats a cold glass with the sand in front of you and the light going gold over the water. **Beach Bar at Promenade** sits right on the beachfront strip and is my default for a casual sundowner - it's the drinks side of the larger [Promenade Bondi Beach](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/promenade-bondi-beach) complex, so you can graze while you drink and roll straight from beach to bar stool. It's relaxed rather than fancy, which is exactly what you want with sandy feet.

If you want to dress it up, **Icebergs** is the postcard: perched above the ocean pool at the south end, glossy Italian glamour, and a wine list to match the setting. It's a special-occasion spot and priced like one, so I save it for birthdays and out-of-town guests I want to show off to - but there's nowhere in Bondi that says "look at where we live" quite like a glass on that terrace.
Beachfront tables move fast at golden hour, especially November to February. Aim for a table an hour before sunset, or perch at the bar - the view is the same and you'll actually get a seat.
For the natural-wine geeks

If you want skin-contact, low-intervention and small family growers, Bondi delivers. **The Shop & Wine Bar** on Curlewis Street is the old faithful - a genuine Bondi original that runs as a day cafe and morphs into a twilight wine bar, with a list leaning firmly into natural, lo-fi and biodynamic bottles from small Australian makers. It's a snug, low-key room; go with one or two people, order a few of their famous sandwiches or snacks, and let the staff steer you to something weird and good.

**Neighbourhood** is the other one to know - a cosy, brick-and-timber corner room a short walk back from the beach that leans into an interesting, well-chosen wine list alongside its cocktails and easy plates. It handles a small group better than most of the tiny rooms, so it's my pick when there are four or five of us who all want something different in the glass.
Cafe by day, wine by night

This is Bondi's signature move, and **Chapter One Café & Wine Room** does it beautifully. Down the southern end of Campbell Parade, it's been a neighbourhood favourite since 2011 - flat whites and brunch bowls in the morning, then an intimate little wine room after dark with a curated pour list. It's low-lit and unhurried in the evening, which makes it a sleeper date spot as much as a wine bar. The Shop (above) plays the same day-to-night trick if Chapter One is full.
For an aperitivo or a group

Sometimes you don't want a serious wine list - you want a spritz, some snacks and a bit of noise. **Ciao Bella** does an Italian aperitivo run on weekend afternoons (they've done Friday and Saturday aperitivo sessions with a DJ), which is a lovely way to ease into an evening with a group. Think spritzes and glass pours over shared plates rather than a natural-wine deep dive - perfect for birthdays and pre-dinner crowds who want the buzz without the ceremony.

items: **Natural wine:** [The Shop & Wine Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-shop-and-wine-bar), Neighbourhood
**A view / sunset:** Beach Bar at Promenade, Icebergs
**Date night:** Chapter One, Icebergs - see more in our [date-night guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach)

**Cafe-by-day-wine-by-night:** Chapter One, The Shop

blocks.text: Two honest caveats. First, opening hours and aperitivo sessions shift with the season here - always check the venue's own page or socials before you set out, especially in winter. Second, Bondi turns over fast: a couple of past wine spots (Bondi Hall, Chloe's) have closed, so if you've seen an old "best of" list, cross-check before you walk there. Everything on this page is current.

items.q: Where's the best natural wine in Bondi?
items.a: Start at [The Shop & Wine Bar](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/the-shop-and-wine-bar) on Curlewis Street, which leans natural, lo-fi and biodynamic, then try Neighbourhood for a broader, well-chosen list. Both are small, so go early or midweek.

items.q: Which Bondi wine bar has the best view?
items.a: For a casual glass on the sand it's Beach Bar at Promenade; for glossy, dressed-up ocean glamour it's Icebergs above the pool. See more waterfront options in our [beachfront dining guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/waterfront-dining-bondi-beach).

items.q: What's a good Bondi wine bar for a date?
items.a: Chapter One Café & Wine Room is intimate and low-lit after dark, and Icebergs is the special-occasion splurge. Our [date-night collection](/bondi-eat-and-drink/date-night-bondi-beach) has more.

items.q: Do I need to book?
items.a: The small rooms (The Shop, Chapter One, Neighbourhood) fill up on weekends and don't always take bookings - check each venue's own page or Instagram for current policy and hours before you go. Conservative beats a locked door.

blocks.text: Yes, you can eat well in Bondi without blowing your budget - the trick is knowing where locals actually go, which is rarely the beachfront spot with the sea-view markup. My cheap-eats shortlist runs on takeaway falafel, a good burrito, a bakery lunch, and one club bistro that quietly punches above its price. Here's how I fill up here for very little - and if you want the full picture, we keep a running list of [Bondi's best cheap eats](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach) in our restaurant directory.
My go-to cheap eats

For a proper feed under the price of a fancy coffee-and-toast, I head straight up Hall Street. This little strip a block back from the sand is where Bondi's budget food really lives, away from the priciest Campbell Parade real estate.

items: [Sabbaba](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sabbaba-bondi-beach) on Hall Street - a Middle Eastern hole-in-the-wall doing loaded falafel and shawarma pita wraps that genuinely fill you up. It's my default when I want a lot of food for a little money.

[Guzman y Gomez](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/guzman-y-gomez-bondi-beach) - burritos, tacos and burrito bowls a short walk from the sand, and about the most reliable cheap Mexican fill-up in Bondi. The value's the same all day, which makes it an easy call whatever time hunger hits.

[North Bondi RSL](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/north-bondi-rsl) Bistro - sign in as a guest and you get honest, well-priced pub-style meals with an ocean view most restaurants would charge a fortune for. Check their site for current bistro hours before you go.

A bakery lunch - grab a pie, sausage roll or filled roll from one of the [local bakeries](/bondi-eat-and-drink/bakeries-sweets-bondi-beach) and eat it on the grass above the beach. Cheap, fast and very Australian.

blocks.text: The cheapest 'restaurant' in Bondi is the seawall. Assemble a picnic from the supermarket or a bakery, grab a spot on the grassy hill above the promenade, and you've got the best dining view on the beach for the price of a loaf and some dips. There are free public barbecues in the parks nearby too - bring your own snags.
A few more budget favourites

Once you've done the Hall Street classics, these are the other spots I lean on when I want to eat cheaply but well. Most are takeaway-first, which keeps the bill (and the wait) down, and they cover the cravings the falafel-and-taco crowd doesn't.

items: [Bondi Banh Mi](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/bondi-banh-mi) - crunchy Vietnamese rolls packed with pork, pâté and pickled veg. Pound for pound one of the best-value sandwiches near the beach.
[Fishbowl](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/fishbowl) - build-your-own poke bowls that feel a lot healthier than the price suggests; my go-to when I've overdone the pastries.
[Oporto](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/oporto-bondi-beach) - Portuguese-style flame-grilled chicken burgers and wraps, an Aussie beachside staple that won't dent the budget.

[Sushi Train](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sushi-train-bondi-beach) - plates off the belt let you eat to exactly the size of your appetite and your wallet, which is why it's such an easy family option.
[Funky Pies](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/funky-pies) - a proper pie for lunch, including generous vegan versions, if the bakery queue's out the door.

blocks.text: How to keep the bill down
Beyond picking the right venue, a few small habits save a surprising amount over a Bondi weekend. This is roughly how I do it when I'm watching the spend.

items: Go one street back. Prices drop noticeably the moment you leave the Campbell Parade beachfront for Hall Street, Gould Street or Curlewis Street.
Eat takeaway, sit outside. Skipping table service and the sit-down surcharge is the single biggest saving, and Bondi has endless free spots to sit with a view.
Make lunch your big meal. Many kitchens run better-value lunch portions and midday deals than they do at dinner.
Refill your own bottle. There are free public drinking fountains and bottle-refill taps around the promenade and parks, so you're not buying water all day.

Look for weeknight specials. Local [pubs](/bondi-eat-and-drink/pubs-bondi-beach) and taquerias often run cheap-taco or discount-pizza nights midweek - always worth checking the venue's own page for what's on right now.

blocks.title: Prices change - check before you go
blocks.text: Menus, deals and opening hours in Bondi shift with the seasons and the crowds, so I've kept exact prices out of this guide on purpose. For the current cost of a wrap, a burrito or a bistro lunch, check the venue's own website or menu before you head down - that's always the most reliable source.

blocks.title: Hungry for more options?
blocks.text: This is my personal shortlist, but it's a small slice of what's down here. Browse all 160+ Bondi eateries in our [Eat & Drink directory](/bondi-eat-and-drink) - filter by cuisine, area, price or who you're with - or jump straight to the full [cheap eats collection](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach) to see every budget-friendly spot on the map.

items.label: Cheapest area
items.value: Hall Street & the streets one block back from the sand

items.label: Best free 'venue'
items.value: The grassy hill above the promenade - BYO picnic

items.label: Guest entry
items.value: North Bondi RSL welcomes visitors - sign in at the door

items.label: Biggest saving
items.value: Takeaway + eat outside, not table service

blocks.text: Is Bondi expensive to eat in?

It can be - the headline beachfront restaurants are priced for the postcode and the view. But Bondi is also a real, lived-in suburb, and the everyday food that locals rely on is refreshingly affordable if you know where to point yourself. Stick to the takeaway strips, treat the beach itself as your dining room, and you'll eat like a local for a fraction of what the tourist-facing menus suggest.

items.q: Where are the cheapest places to eat in Bondi?
items.a: Head one block back from the beach to Hall Street and the surrounding streets. That's where the budget takeaway spots cluster - [falafel and shawarma](/bondi-eat-and-drink/venues/sabbaba-bondi-beach), Mexican, banh mi, bakeries and pizza - well away from the priciest beachfront tables. You'll find the whole lot in our [cheap eats guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink/cheap-eats-bondi-beach).

items.q: Can visitors eat at North Bondi RSL?
items.a: Yes. Non-members are welcome to sign in as a guest at the door, and the bistro serves well-priced meals with an ocean view. Check their website for current opening hours and the latest menu.

items.q: Is there anywhere free to eat near Bondi Beach?
items.a: Eating itself isn't free, but the setting can be. There are free public barbecues in the parks near the beach and plenty of grassy spots above the promenade, so a supermarket or bakery picnic costs next to nothing and comes with the best view in town.

items.q: What's the best cheap meal to try in Bondi?
items.a: A loaded falafel or shawarma pita from a Hall Street takeaway is hard to beat for value - filling, fast and genuinely good. Follow it with a walk along the sand and you've had a proper Bondi day out for very little.

blocks.text: That's my honest cheap-eats map of Bondi: takeaway from the streets behind the sand, a picnic on the seawall when the weather's good, and a friendly club bistro for a sit-down feed with a view. Do it this way and Bondi turns out to be a lot kinder on the wallet than its glossy reputation suggests.

If you want the single best value in Bondi, here it is: the Bondi Golf & Diggers Club is a public 9-hole course laid out along the sandstone clifftops at North Bondi, open to anyone who turns up - you don't need to be a member, and for most of the week you don't even need a booking. I've sent plenty of visitors up who came for the golf and left talking about the view - because few places forgive a wayward tee shot the instant you see the whole sweep of coast.

items.label: Booking
items.value: Mostly walk-in - no tee time needed

blocks.text: Why I send people up here

This isn't a manicured championship layout, and that's exactly the charm. It's an old-style links course on the headland above the beach, with the sky, cliffs and ocean breeze all part of the challenge. The wind genuinely moves the ball and the greens keep you humble - but what you're really paying for is the setting, with Bondi Beach, the coastline and the city skyline around you the entire round.

Because it's a short 9-hole course, it suits people who'd never normally book a full round: families, beginners, and anyone who wants a local hour or two that isn't sitting on the sand. Play a quick loop and you're back on Campbell Parade in time for lunch.

Play late in the afternoon. The light on the cliffs in the last hour before sundown is the best it gets, the heat has dropped off, and you'll finish as the coast turns gold. Bring a windbreaker whatever the forecast - it's always breezier up on the headland than down on the beach.
How to actually play a round

The club runs a refreshingly simple format for social players: for much of the week you arrive, join the queue and tee off - no advance reservation required. The exceptions are member competition times (typically weekend mornings) and the occasional event day when the course closes to social play, City2Surf Sunday being the classic example. The golden rule: check before you commit to a specific time.

items: Turn up at the clubhouse on Military Road, North Bondi.
Confirm current social-play hours and green fees on the day - these change, so check the official website first.
Ask at the clubhouse about club and buggy hire rather than assuming; availability varies.
Weekend mornings are competition time, so aim for after the comp field has cleared, or a weekday, for the easiest walk-on.

blocks.title: Check the current rates and hours
blocks.text: Green fees, social-play windows and hire options change, and I won't quote a price that might be out of date. For today's fees and times - and to confirm the course is open to visitors on your chosen day - check the Bondi Golf & Diggers Club website or call the clubhouse.
The hidden gem within the hidden gem

Here's the part most visitors miss. On the sea side of the course, out on the flat headland rock, sits a panel of Aboriginal rock engravings cut by the Eora people - a site known as Murriverie, near Ben Buckler. The largest is a huge shark beside a human-like figure, and the engravings are thought to be around 2,000 years old. It's a genuinely significant cultural site, not a tourist reconstruction.

blocks.title: Treat the engravings with respect
blocks.text: This is a protected, culturally important site. Look, don't touch - never walk on the carved rock or trace the grooves. Keep to the edges and give it the respect a 2,000-year-old artwork deserves.

You can reach the headland on foot even without playing, but stay aware of the course - a golf ball at speed is nothing to wander into. The North Bondi end of the beach and the start of the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk are a short stroll away, so it's easy to fold the golf, the engravings and the coast into one good morning.

items.q: Can anyone play Bondi Golf Course, or do you need to be a member?
items.a: Anyone can play - it's a public course. For most of the week you can simply turn up and join the queue without a booking. The main exceptions are member competition times and big event days, so check the club's website before you go.

items.q: How many holes is it, and how long does a round take?
items.a: It's a compact 9-hole clifftop course, so a round is far quicker than a full 18 - ideal if you only have an hour or two. Exact pars and hole details are listed on the club's official website.

items.q: Do I need to book a tee time?
items.a: Usually no. The club runs a walk-in social format for much of the week - arrive, join the queue and play. Booking mainly matters around weekend competitions, so confirm current arrangements with the clubhouse.

items.q: Are the Aboriginal rock engravings really on the golf course?
items.a: Yes. On the sea side of the headland there's a significant panel of Eora rock engravings, including a large shark figure, thought to be around 2,000 years old. It's a protected cultural site, so look but never touch.

blocks.text: So that's my pitch: come for a cheap, scenic round of golf, and leave having stood beside one of Sydney's oldest artworks. Few visitors put those two together - which is exactly why the Bondi Golf Course earns its "hidden gem" reputation with me.

sources.label: Dictionary of Sydney - Bondi rock carvings

blocks.text: Yes - there are lockers at Bondi Beach, inside the Bondi Pavilion in the middle of the beachfront, open 6am-10pm daily. A small locker is $6 for 4 hours ($10 all day) and a large one is $9 for 4 hours ($15 all day), verified August 2026. If the lockers are full or you'd rather not bother, the rule is simple: bring only what you can afford to lose, and use the strategies below.

items.label: Lockers
items.value: Inside Bondi Pavilion, middle of the beach

items.label: Small locker (50 x 15 x 47 cm)
items.value: $6/4hrs, $10 all day - fits phone, wallet, keys

items.label: Large locker (50 x 45 x 47 cm)
items.value: $9/4hrs, $15 all day - fits a daypack + towel

items.label: Suitcases
items.value: Won't fit - store luggage before you come

items.label: My rule of thumb
items.value: Bank card + phone only; leave the rest at your accommodation

blocks.text: The lockers: inside the Bondi Pavilion

The only proper lockers at Bondi Beach live inside the Bondi Pavilion - the big Mediterranean-style building set back from the sand, right in the middle of the beach. They sit alongside the public change rooms and showers on the ground floor, and they're available 6am-10pm daily, which comfortably covers a dawn swim through to a sunset one. As at August 2026, a small locker (50 x 15 x 47 cm) costs $6 for four hours or $10 for the whole day, and a large one (50 x 45 x 47 cm) is $9 for four hours or $15 all day. Prices do drift, so if you're reading this well after I wrote it, double-check on the Pavilion's own site.

Size-wise, be realistic. The small locker is a tall slim slot - perfect for a phone, wallet, keys, sunglasses and not much more. The large one swallows a daypack and a towel with room to spare. What neither will reliably take is a suitcase: a standard carry-on stands around 55 cm tall, and the lockers just aren't built for it. I've watched more than one traveller wheel a bag across the sand and discover this the hard way.

blocks.title: Don't bring your suitcase to the beach
blocks.text: There is no left-luggage office at Bondi Beach, and the Pavilion lockers won't fit a suitcase. If you're between check-ins or on a layover, sort your luggage out before you come - your accommodation, a storage service in the city, or the airport. More on your options below.
No locker? The solo swimmer's playbook
On a hot Saturday the lockers can be spoken for, and honestly, most locals never use them anyway. Here's what actually works, ranked in the order I'd do it.

items: **Wear your valuables into the water.** A waterproof pouch on a lanyard or waist strap takes your card, phone and a key with you through the surf. It's the only method where nothing is ever unattended, which is why it's first. The surf and beach shops along Campbell Parade generally stock them if you didn't pack one.

**The one-person-stays-dry rotation.** In a group, take turns: one person minds the towels while the others swim, then swap. Oldest trick on the beach and still the most reliable - it costs nothing and someone gets to hold the coffee.

**Bury-it-in-the-towel is not a strategy.** I have to be straight with you: opportunistic theft of unattended bags does happen at Bondi, like at any famous beach. It's not rampant and it's rarely dramatic - I've written honestly about [how common theft really is](/bondi-blog/2025/1/5/are-there-thieves-or-pickpockets-at-bondi-beach) - but a phone tucked under a corner of towel fools precisely nobody who's looking.

**Go minimal in the first place.** Bondi is tap-to-pay everywhere - cafés, the buses, the gelato window - so a single bank card and your phone covers the whole day. Leave the passport, the spare cards and the cash pile at your accommodation, and suddenly there's nothing on the sand worth worrying about.

blocks.text: Swimming with your phone

The waterproof pouch deserves its own word, because it's genuinely the best few dollars you'll spend at Bondi. The good ones are a clear soft-plastic sleeve with a roll-top or double-clip seal and a neck lanyard - your phone stays usable through the plastic, so you can even grab a photo out past the break. Seal it, give it a squeeze test before your phone goes in, and keep it under your rashie rather than swinging free in the waves.

If you didn't bring one, you won't have to go far: the surf and beach shops along Campbell Parade, the strip that runs behind the beach, generally have them by the register in summer. I'd sort it before you hit the sand rather than after you've already staked out your spot.
Luggage and layovers: the honest answer

I'll say it plainly because nobody official does: Bondi Beach has no left-luggage office, and the Pavilion lockers are too small for suitcases. If you've checked out of your hotel at 10am and your flight is at 9pm, the beach itself cannot solve your luggage problem - you have to solve it before you get on the bus.

Your realistic options, in order of convenience: ask your accommodation to hold your bags after checkout - most hotels and plenty of hostels will, often free for the day. Failing that, use a staffed luggage-storage service in the city before you head out; they cluster around Central and Circular Quay, which is handy because the 333 bus to Bondi leaves from Circular Quay anyway. And if you're on a genuine layover, storage at Sydney Airport means you ride out and back carrying nothing but a towel and a pouch - which, frankly, is the ideal way to arrive at Bondi regardless.

The lifeguards cannot watch your stuff - they're watching the water, and they'll tell you the same. And remember the red-and-yellow flags move during the day as conditions shift, so the spot you swam out from isn't always the spot you'll swim back to. After each swim, re-check your line of sight to your towel before you head back out.

items.q: Are there lockers at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - inside the Bondi Pavilion, the large building in the middle of the beachfront, alongside the public change rooms and showers. They're available 6am-10pm daily.

items.q: How much do the Bondi Beach lockers cost?
items.a: As at August 2026: a small locker (50 x 15 x 47 cm) is $6 for 4 hours or $10 all day; a large locker (50 x 45 x 47 cm) is $9 for 4 hours or $15 all day. Check the Bondi Pavilion website for current prices.

items.q: Can I leave my bag on the sand while I swim?
items.a: You can, but an unattended bag is the one thing that does occasionally go missing at Bondi. Either have someone in your group stay with it, keep valuables on your body in a waterproof pouch, or use a Pavilion locker. Hiding things under a towel is not a plan.

items.q: Where do I store a suitcase near Bondi Beach?
items.a: Not at the beach - there's no left-luggage office and the Pavilion lockers won't fit a suitcase. Leave it with your accommodation, use a staffed storage service in the city (they cluster near Central and Circular Quay) before you come out, or use airport storage if you're on a layover.

items.q: Is theft common at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - Bondi is a busy, well-patrolled beach and serious crime is rare. What does happen is opportunistic taking of unattended valuables left on the sand, which the simple habits above almost entirely prevent.

blocks.text: So there's your system: card and phone in a pouch that swims with you, anything bigger in a Pavilion locker, and the suitcase dealt with before you ever see the sand. Once your gear's sorted, the Pavilion also covers [toilets, showers and change rooms](/bondi-blog/bondi-beach-toilets-showers-change-rooms) so you can rinse off and change before heading home - and if you're still sketching out the rest of your day, my [first-timer guide](/start-here) is the place to start.

sources.label: NSW Police - keeping valuables safe at the beach

blocks.text: If you want to catch Bondi at its most alive, time your visit around one of its big annual events - the standouts are the Festival of the Winds kite spectacular in spring, Sculpture by the Sea along the coastal walk, the July Bondi Festival with its ice rink, the summer Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim, and the City2Surf finish in August. Each one turns an already-lovely beach into a proper occasion. Here's my local's calendar for planning around them.

items.label: Free crowd favourites
items.value: Festival of the Winds, Sculpture by the Sea

items.label: Ticketed
items.value: Bondi Festival, ocean swims, open-air cinema

items.label: Getting there
items.value: Train to Bondi Junction, then bus 333/380

blocks.text: Spring: the beach's showcase season

Spring is when I tell friends to come. The Festival of the Winds - Waverley Council's free kite festival - usually lands in September and fills the sky above the sand with giant kites, live music and multicultural food stalls. It's the most joyful, family-friendly day on the Bondi calendar, and it costs nothing to turn up.

Then, straddling spring into early summer, comes Sculpture by the Sea. Over a hundred works are dotted along the free Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk for a few weeks, usually across October and November. It's the world's largest free-to-the-public outdoor sculpture exhibition, and wandering it at golden hour with the ocean behind each piece is one of my favourite things to do all year.

blocks.title: Dates shift every year
blocks.text: Annual events shift season to season. I've given reliable months here, but always confirm this year's exact dates on the official organiser's page before you lock in travel.
Winter: Bondi Festival and the City2Surf

Don't write off winter. Each July the Bondi Festival takes over Bondi Pavilion and the park around it with music, comedy, theatre and family shows. Festival favourites have included an ice rink right by the beach and a Ferris wheel over the sand, with tickets ranging from free events to modestly priced shows - check the official program for what's on and prices this year.

August brings the City2Surf, the 14-kilometre run from the Sydney CBD that finishes right here at Bondi Beach. Even if you're not running, the finish-line atmosphere on a crisp winter Sunday - tens of thousands of people cresting the final hill toward the sand - is worth planning a morning around.
Summer: ocean swims and cinema under the stars

The warmer months are for the water. The Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim is the classic - a roughly 2.2km open-water swim between the two beaches. It's genuinely challenging surf swimming, so if you're entering rather than spectating, confirm the date, course direction and safety notes on the official site, all of which change year to year.

On summer evenings, an open-air cinema sets up near Bondi Pavilion, screening films from dusk with food and a licensed bar. Seasons and line-ups vary, so book ahead through the official Openair Cinemas page.

For the big free events - Festival of the Winds, Sculpture by the Sea and the City2Surf finish - leave the car at home. Roads close and parking vanishes. Take the train to Bondi Junction and hop on the 333 or 380 bus down to Campbell Parade, or walk the last stretch.
Every weekend: the Bondi markets

You don't have to build a trip around a single festival. Two markets run at Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade most weekends year-round: the Bondi Farmers Market on Saturday mornings (fresh produce and food) and the larger Bondi Markets on Sundays (fashion, vintage and homewares). They're my reliable fallback when there's no headline event on - check current times on the official page, then grab a coffee and walk it off along the promenade.

items.q: What is the biggest annual event at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Festival of the Winds is Bondi's biggest free community event - a spring kite festival run by Waverley Council, usually in September. For a marquee ticketed program, the July Bondi Festival at Bondi Pavilion is the other heavyweight. Confirm this year's dates on each organiser's site.

items.q: When is the best time of year to visit Bondi for events?
items.a: Spring (September to November) is my pick - you get the Festival of the Winds and Sculpture by the Sea, both free, with milder crowds than peak summer. Summer brings ocean swims and open-air cinema, and winter has the Bondi Festival and City2Surf finish.

items.q: Are Bondi's main events free?
items.a: Some are. Festival of the Winds and Sculpture by the Sea are free to attend. Others - the Bondi Festival shows, the Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim entry, and the open-air cinema - are ticketed. Check the official pages for current prices, as they change each year.

items.q: Is there anything on at Bondi if I miss the festivals?
items.a: Yes - the weekend markets run year-round at Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade: a farmers' market on Saturdays and the bigger general Bondi Markets on Sundays. Times can vary with public holidays, so double-check before you go.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach for a big event?
items.a: Public transport is easiest: take a train to Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus down to the beach. On event days expect road closures and busy buses, so allow extra time.

blocks.text: That's the year in a nutshell: kites and sculptures in spring, festival lights and fun-runners in winter, ocean swims and cinema in summer, and markets any weekend in between. Pick your season, check the official dates, and come see why Bondi is never just a beach.
Come for the swim or the sculptures - you'll leave having seen the whole neighbourhood turn out to play.
