Macquarie Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim (official)

blocks.text: If you're after the short version: the best all-round playground right on the sand is the fenced Bondi Park playground beside the Pavilion, while the grandest day out is Waverley Park in Bondi Junction with its rocket ship and inclusive equipment. I've pushed a pram around every one of these with a coffee in hand, so here's my honest local's guide to which Bondi playground suits which kid - and where you'll actually find shade and toilets.
Right on the beach: Bondi Park playground

This is the one most visitors mean when they say "the Bondi playground". It sits in Bondi Park between Campbell Parade and the sand, a stone's throw from the Pavilion, and it's fully fenced with double gates at each entrance - which, if you've ever chased a bolting toddler toward a busy road, you'll appreciate enormously. There's a good spread of equipment across soft-fall, sand and grass: swings, slides, climbing frames, spring toys and a little musical corner.

The combination unit closest to Campbell Parade was upgraded by Waverley Council with more inclusive play in mind, so it works for a broader range of kids and abilities. My tip: the shade here is patchy, so come early or late in summer, and remember the closest toilets (including an accessible one) are a short walk away by the Pavilion rather than in the playground itself.

Do the beach first, playground second. Rinse the sand off at the promenade showers, then let the kids burn off their last bit of energy at the playground before you walk back up to Campbell Parade for the bus - it saves a lot of sandy-car misery.
Worth the short trip: Waverley Park

When my family wants a proper morning out rather than a quick swing-and-slide, we head up the hill to Waverley Park on Paul Street in Bondi Junction. It's fully fenced and genuinely one of the best playgrounds in the Eastern Suburbs - the centrepiece rocket ship and launch tower are the stuff of local legend, and there's water play, spinners, climbing, a dedicated toddler zone and a lot of open grass for a picnic.

blocks.title: A standout for accessibility
blocks.text: Waverley Park was designed with access and inclusion front of mind, with equipment like an inclusive multi-bay swing set (including a carer swing and an accessible swing) and step-free paths. It's the one I'd point families with a wheelchair user or sensory needs toward first - see Waverley Council's access and inclusion notes for the detail.
The best views, and the ones for older kids

Up at the northern end, tucked into leafy Biddigal Reserve, the North Bondi playground is small but special. It's perched high with some of the best beach and sunset views in Bondi, and it's dotted with bespoke play sculptures - a sea dragon, turtle, fish and octopus among them. It's a lovely one to pair with a barbecue on the grassy knoll.

Right next door is the Bondi Beach Skate Park at the northern end of the beach, with its bowl and open street area - brilliant for skaters, scooters and BMX, and honestly just a great free show to watch even if your kids aren't riding. It's not a fenced toddler space, so keep the little ones close.

Further south along the coastal walk toward Tamarama, Marks Park has a modest sand-based playground with big shady trees, seating and a toilet block nearby. It's not a destination playground, but as a mid-walk breather with headland whale-watching views in winter, it's hard to beat.

items: Toddlers & pre-schoolers: Bondi Park playground (fenced) or the toddler zone at Waverley Park.
Big kids wanting variety: Waverley Park, or North Bondi at Biddigal Reserve.
Tweens & teens: Bondi Beach Skate Park at the north end.
A picnic with a view: Biddigal Reserve or Marks Park.

items.q: Is the Bondi Beach playground fenced?
items.a: Yes - the main Bondi Park playground beside the Pavilion is fully fenced, with two gates at each entrance to stop little ones wandering toward Campbell Parade. Waverley Park in Bondi Junction is fully fenced too. The North Bondi playground and skate park are not enclosed.

items.q: Where are the nearest toilets to the Bondi Beach playground?
items.a: The closest public toilets, including an accessible toilet, are by the Bondi Pavilion, a short walk from the playground rather than inside it. Waverley Park and Marks Park each have toilets nearby as well.

items.q: Which Bondi playground is best for kids with a disability?
items.a: Waverley Park in Bondi Junction was designed with access and inclusion in mind, including inclusive swings and step-free paths. The upgraded unit at the Bondi Park playground also added inclusive play features. Check Waverley Council for the current detail.

items.q: Do the playgrounds cost anything?
items.a: No. Every playground here is free, council-run public space. You'll only pay for parking, food or a coffee if you choose to.

items.q: Which playground has the best views?
items.a: The North Bondi playground at Biddigal Reserve, up on the northern headland, has the best outlook over the beach and is a favourite of mine at sunset.

blocks.text: That's the lot - five very different spots, all free, all a short hop from the sand. Pack sunscreen, a hat and a picnic, mind the shade, and you've got a full day of play sorted.

sources.label: Waverley Council - Access & inclusion at Waverley Park Playground
Waverley Council - Major projects: parks & playgrounds

blocks.text: Here's the 15-second version: no alcohol (Bondi Beach and Bondi Park are an enforced alcohol-free zone), no glass, no smoking or vaping, no dogs on the sand or promenade at any time, and no drones without approval. BBQs are fine - but only on the free electric ones in the park, never on the sand, and never charcoal or open flame. Topless sunbathing is tolerated; full nudity isn't legal here. And the beach itself never "closes" - you can walk it at 3am - but only ever swim when the lifeguards are on and the flags are up.

items.label: Glass
items.value: Banned on the beach and in the park

items.label: Dogs
items.value: Never on the beach or promenade

items.label: Fires & charcoal
items.value: Banned - free electric BBQs in the park only

blocks.text: Drinking and glass: the rule everyone tests

This is the one visitors ask me about most, usually while holding a bottle of something nice. The answer is a flat no: Bondi Beach and Bondi Park are an alcohol-free zone, and it's actually enforced - this isn't one of those signs nobody reads. Council rangers and police patrol, they will tip your drinks out, and fines happen. The glass ban is separate and just as firm, and honestly it's the one I care about most as a local - nobody wants to find the bottom of a broken bottle with a bare foot. If you want a sunset drink, do what we do: the licensed venues along [Campbell Parade and around the beach](/bondi-eat-and-drink) exist precisely for this, most of them with a better view than your picnic rug anyway.

Picnics themselves are completely welcome, to be clear - the grass in Bondi Park fills up with them every weekend. Just keep it dry and keep it out of glass. Cans and plastic for your soft drinks, and you'll never have a problem.
Smoking and vaping

Bondi is a smoke-free beach, and has been for years - it was one of the earliest in Australia to go that way, and locals are genuinely protective of it. Don't expect a vape to be treated any differently to a cigarette; treat the ban as covering both and you'll match how it's applied on the ground. If you need to know exactly where the smoke-free area starts and ends, Waverley Council publishes the boundaries - but the simple version is: not on the sand, not on the promenade, and read the room in the park.
Dogs: I'm sorry, but no

This one breaks hearts daily, and I get it - Bondi is one of the most dog-mad suburbs in Sydney, and the cafés are full of them. But dogs are not allowed on Bondi Beach or the promenade at any time. Not early morning, not off-season, not "just for a quick photo". Rangers patrol for this specifically because so many people chance it. Waverley does have on-leash and off-leash areas elsewhere in the area - check the council's current dog map for where your dog is genuinely welcome, because those rules shift by park and by time of day and I'd rather point you at the source than guess.

The "everyone does it" myth is exactly that - a myth. I've watched rangers work the beach on an ordinary Tuesday, and alcohol and dogs are the two things they fine for most visibly. The people you see getting away with it are the ones who haven't been walked past yet.
BBQs, picnics and fires

Good news first: there are four free electric BBQ stations in Bondi Park, the grassy strip behind the beach, and they're open until dusk. They're first-come, first-served and genuinely well used - I've written a whole [local's guide to the free BBQ spots](/bondi-blog/2025/1/20/locals-guide-to-free-bbq-spots-at-bondi-bronte-tamarama) if a cook-up is the plan. The hard line is fuel: no charcoal, no solid fuel, no open fires, anywhere - not in the park and absolutely not on the sand. A bonfire on the beach might be the postcard fantasy, but at Bondi it's a fast way to meet a ranger.

items: Free electric BBQs: four stations in Bondi Park, open until dusk
Charcoal, solid fuel and open fires: banned everywhere, beach and park
Picnics on the grass or sand: welcome - just no glass and no booze
Big group or an event? That crosses into council permit territory - ask Waverley first

blocks.text: Drones and filming

Short answer: don't fly a drone at Bondi without permission. Recreational drone flight over the beach needs Waverley Council approval on top of CASA's standard rules - and a summer crowd of thousands is close to the worst-case scenario for those rules anyway. If you're serious, start with [CASA's Know Your Drone rules](https://www.casa.gov.au/knowyourdrone) and then talk to the council; if you're casual, leave it in the bag and buy a postcard. The same permit logic applies to commercial photography and film shoots - Bondi hosts them constantly, but the ones you see have paperwork.
Swimwear, topless and nudity

Bondi is about as relaxed as a city beach gets. Wear whatever you're comfortable in - budgie smugglers, burkinis, full wetsuit in January, nobody blinks. Topless sunbathing is broadly tolerated here and has been for decades; you'll see it, especially down the quieter stretches, and it isn't an issue. Full nudity is a different story: Bondi is not a designated nude beach, so it's not legal here. Sydney does have legal clothing-optional beaches - Bondi just isn't one of them, whatever a 1970s guidebook may have told you. If you’re wondering about a dress code more broadly: the beach itself has none worth naming, but venues expect a shirt and footwear.
Night: can you be on the beach after dark?

Yes - and this surprises people. Bondi Beach has no gates and no curfew; it's open 24 hours, and a moonlight walk along the sand is genuinely one of my favourite things about living here. The [333 bus even runs all night](/getting-to-bondi), roughly every 20 minutes, so you can get here and away at any hour. Being on the beach at night is legal and lovely. Swimming at night is neither smart nor safe - and that distinction matters enough that I'll give it its own box.

blocks.title: Never swim at night
blocks.text: The beach is open 24/7, but the lifeguards aren't. Outside patrol hours there are no flags, no one watching, and rips you cannot see in the dark - Bondi's rips are serious even in daylight. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags during patrol hours, full stop. In an emergency, call 000.

As for sleeping on the beach overnight: the sand not having a gate doesn't make it a campsite. Camping and sleeping in public reserves is regulated by the council, rangers do move people on, and between the sprinklers, the 5am swimmers and the seagulls you wouldn't enjoy it anyway. If you're stuck for a bed, [there are hostels and hotels at every budget](/stay) a few minutes' walk away.
Fishing, weddings, metal detecting and everything else

There's a long tail of "can I...?" questions - fishing off the rocks, a wedding ceremony on the sand, metal detecting, fitness bootcamps, busking, horses. I'm not going to bluff specifics I haven't verified, so here's the honest structure of it: anything organised, commercial or equipment-heavy generally falls under Waverley Council's permit system, and anything involving fishing sits under state rules as well as council ones. The pattern at Bondi is rarely "banned outright" - it's "allowed with the right permission, in the right place". [Waverley Council](https://www.waverley.nsw.gov.au/recreation/beaches_and_coast/beach_safety) is the authority for all of it, and a quick email to them before you plan a beach wedding will save you an expensive surprise on the day.

blocks.caption: Bondi Beach rules at a glance
rows: Patrolled year-round; the flags move during the day - swim between them
Beach and park are an enforced alcohol-free zone
Glass-free zone - bring cans and plastic instead
Smoke-free beach; treat vapes the same as cigarettes
Never on the beach or promenade; council maps show where dogs can go
Four free stations in Bondi Park, open until dusk
No open fires anywhere - park or sand
Broadly tolerated; full nudity is not legal - Bondi isn't a nude beach
Being on the beach at night
No gates, no curfew - but never swim outside patrol hours
Waverley Council approval plus CASA rules
Waverley Council's permit system covers organised and commercial use
State fishing rules plus council rules apply - confirm before you cast

items.q: Can you drink alcohol at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach and Bondi Park are an alcohol-free zone and it's enforced - rangers and police patrol, confiscate drinks and issue fines. The licensed bars and restaurants along Campbell Parade are the legal (and frankly more comfortable) option for a drink with a beach view.

items.q: Are dogs allowed at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - dogs aren't allowed on the beach or the promenade at any time, and rangers do fine for it. Waverley Council has on-leash and off-leash areas elsewhere in the area; check their current dog rules for where your dog is welcome.

items.q: Can I fly a drone at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Not without permission. Recreational drone flight over Bondi needs Waverley Council approval on top of CASA's standard drone rules, and a crowded beach is a hard place to fly legally under those rules anyway. Practical answer: don't, unless you've done the paperwork.

items.q: Is Bondi a nude beach?
items.a: No. Topless sunbathing is broadly tolerated at Bondi and has been for decades, but full nudity isn't legal here - Bondi is not a designated clothing-optional beach.

items.q: Can you smoke or vape at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No - Bondi is a smoke-free beach, and in practice vaping is treated the same as smoking. Waverley Council publishes the exact smoke-free boundaries if you need them, but the safe assumption is: not on the sand, not on the promenade.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach open at night?
items.a: Yes - the beach has no gates or curfew, it's open 24 hours, and the 333 bus runs all night. But there are no lifeguards after patrol hours, so never swim at night. Walk the sand, enjoy the moon, stay out of the water.

items.q: Is there a dress code at Bondi Beach?
items.a: On the sand, no - any swimwear is normal, from budgie smugglers to full coverage, and topless sunbathing is broadly tolerated (full nudity is not legal at Bondi). The unwritten dress code kicks in when you leave the beach: put a shirt and footwear on for cafés, shops and the bus - the “no shirt, no shoes, no service” convention is real here.

blocks.text: So that's the rulebook - and honestly, none of it is there to spoil your day. It's why the sand is clean, the water's watched and the whole place still works with a few million visitors a year. Once you've got the official rules down, there's a second, unwritten layer that locals care about just as much - I've covered that in my [Bondi Beach etiquette guide](/bondi-blog/bondi-beach-etiquette-guide). Still curious about the odder questions - is the beach man-made, can you sleep on it overnight? [I've answered those too](/bondi-blog/is-bondi-beach-man-made-and-other-questions). And when you're ready to put it all into practice, here's [how to get to Bondi](/getting-to-bondi) without the parking headache.

blocks.text: Short version: yes, you can surf at Bondi, and it's one of the friendliest beaches in Sydney to learn on - just stay well clear of the red-and-yellow swimming flags, keep beginners to the gentler northern half, and leave the punchier, rip-prone southern corner to those who know what they're doing. I've surfed here for years; below is what I'd tell a mate asking where to start.

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Never surf between the red-and-yellow flags

blocks.text: Where to surf if you're a beginner

Bondi is a roughly one-kilometre crescent, and it doesn't surf the same all the way along. The northern end tends to be more sheltered and forgiving - the sandbank is gentler and catches less swell, exactly what you want while learning to pop up. That's where I'd send anyone on a soft-top for their first sessions.

The one rule you must never break: don't surf near, and definitely not between, the red-and-yellow flags. That's a patrolled swimming-only zone - turning up on a board there is dangerous for swimmers and a fast way to get a direct word from the lifeguards. Set up to the side, and you'll be welcome.

blocks.title: The flags are for swimmers, not surfers
blocks.text: Soft learner boards are usually fine on the sandflats away from the flags; hard fibreglass boards belong at the southern breaks. When unsure, ask a lifeguard - the flag position changes daily.
Bondi's breaks for experienced surfers

Once you've got your bearings, the more interesting waves are at the southern end - the break locals call 'Backpackers', named for the hostels up the hill. It picks up more swell, breaks bigger and faster, and sits right beside Bondi's most notorious rip.

That rip, the 'Backpackers' Express', runs out along the southern rocks and is behind many rescues there each summer. For a confident surfer it can be a handy paddle-out channel - but know it's there, respect the rocks, and never rely on it unless you're a strong swimmer.

Check the sandbanks before you commit. After a big swell the banks shift, and last week's beautiful wave can become a shapeless closeout. Two minutes watching from the promenade - where the sets peak, which way the water moves - saves a frustrating session.
When to surf, and reading the conditions

Bondi surfs year-round. Summer waves are smaller and more forgiving, which suits beginners, but the beach is packed and shared with swimmers. Many locals prefer the cooler months, when the crowds thin and the swell is more consistent - bring a decent wetsuit. Early mornings are cleanest, before the sea breeze chops it up.

Rather than trust any fixed 'best time', check the forecast the morning you go. I look at the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney coast swell and wind forecast, and Surf Life Saving's Beachsafe page, which flags current hazards and whether the beach is patrolled.
Lessons, board hire and staying safe

If it's your first time, book a lesson - it's the fastest way to get standing up, and a good instructor teaches you to read rips and pick a safe spot as much as catch waves. Bondi's long-established, licensed surf school, Let's Go Surfing, runs beginner lessons and hires soft boards and wetsuits from the southern end of the promenade. Check their website for current times and prices.

items: Start on a soft-top - stable, and far kinder if the board hits you or anyone else.
Always surf near other people, ideally within sight of the lifeguard tower.
Caught in a rip? Don't fight it. Stay calm, hang onto your board, raise an arm to signal for help, and let it carry you out until it releases.
Wear a rash vest and reef-safe sunscreen - the Australian sun burns fast, even on grey days.

blocks.text: Beyond Bondi

If Bondi's crowded or the bank isn't working, the neighbouring beaches are a short hop away. Tamarama, around the headland, is smaller, punchier and best left to experienced surfers. Bronte has a fun little break and a good post-surf café strip. Further south, Maroubra offers more consistent, powerful waves and room to spread out.

items.q: Can beginners surf at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - the northern end is one of the better spots in Sydney to learn, with a gentler sandbank and smaller waves. Stay well clear of the red-and-yellow flags, use a soft-top, and consider a lesson for your first go.

items.q: Where can I surf at Bondi without getting in trouble?
items.a: Surf to the side of the red-and-yellow flags, never between them - that's a swimming-only zone. Learners stick to the northern sandflats; stronger surfers head to the southern 'Backpackers' break.

items.q: Is the surf at Bondi dangerous?
items.a: It can be. The southern end has the biggest waves and the strong 'Backpackers' Express rip, which drives many rescues each summer. Check Beachsafe, surf near the patrolled area, and don't paddle out far unless you're a strong swimmer.

items.q: Where can I hire a board or take a surf lesson at Bondi?
items.a: Bondi's licensed surf school, Let's Go Surfing, offers beginner lessons and hires soft boards and wetsuits from the southern end of the promenade. Check their website for current times and prices.

items.q: What's the best time of year to surf Bondi?
items.a: Summer brings smaller, friendlier waves but big crowds; the cooler months are often more consistent and far quieter, so bring a wetsuit. Whatever the season, check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast on the day.

blocks.text: Surfing Bondi comes down to a few habits: pick the right end for your level, keep clear of the flags and the rips, respect the people around you, and check the forecast before you paddle out. Get those right and you've got one of the world's most iconic waves on the city's doorstep. See you out there.

blocks.text: Bondi Beach has free public toilets and showers at three points - the north end near North Bondi, the middle at the Bondi Pavilion, and the south end near the Icebergs and the skate park. The Pavilion is your best all-rounder, with free toilets, change rooms, baby-change tables and accessible facilities in one spot, plus paid lockers. Below, I'll show you exactly where each one sits so you never have to do the wet-towel shuffle up the promenade.

items.label: Cost
items.value: Free - all public toilets & beach showers

items.label: Accessible & baby-change
items.value: Yes - Pavilion ground floor & North Bondi

blocks.text: Where the public toilets are

Picture the beach as a long crescent with the toilets as three anchor points. In the middle sits the Bondi Pavilion - the big Mediterranean-style building set back from the sand. This is the one I send everyone to: public toilets on the ground floor and a straight walk up from the flags. If you're anywhere near the centre of the beach, aim here.

At the northern end, there's an amenities block near North Bondi, up by Brighton Boulevard and the surf club. It's the closest option if you've parked up north or you're with little ones at the shallow northern corner. At the southern end, near the Bondi Icebergs and the skate park, you'll find the closest toilets for anyone down that way - handy if you're starting the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk or watching the swimmers do laps at the pool.

The Pavilion is the only spot that reliably has everything - change rooms, lockers, baby-change and accessible facilities together. If you need more than a quick toilet stop, don't gamble on the end blocks; make a beeline for the middle.
Free beachfront showers

You don't need to pay a cent to rinse off at Bondi. There are free outdoor showers along the promenade near the toilet blocks at both ends, plus foot-rinse taps where the sand meets the concrete. They're cold-water rinse-offs for getting the salt and sand off before you head home - perfect after a swim between the flags.

blocks.title: Rinse first, change second
blocks.text: The promenade showers are for a quick sandy rinse in your swimmers - they're right out in the open. For a proper change into dry clothes, use the change rooms inside the Pavilion.
Change rooms, lockers & baby-change

For actually getting changed, the Bondi Pavilion is the place. It has male and female change rooms and showers on the beach side, plus lockers if you'd rather not leave your bag on the sand. The lockers run 6am-10pm daily: a small one is $6 for 4 hours and a large one $9 for 4 hours, or $10 and $15 for all day (verified August 2026). There's more detail - what fits, what doesn't - in my [full lockers & valuables guide](/bondi-blog/bondi-beach-lockers-where-to-leave-valuables). On a busy day it's a genuine relief - you can swim, rinse, change and stash your gear all in one building.
Travelling with a baby? There are baby-change tables in the Pavilion ground-floor toilets and at the North Bondi amenities, so you're covered at the middle or the northern end of the beach.
Accessible facilities

Bondi is better set up than most beaches here. There are accessible and ambulant toilets on the Pavilion ground floor, and again at the North Bondi amenities. The Pavilion also has an adult-change 'Changing Places' facility on the ground floor, with a height-adjustable change table, ceiling hoist and shower. It's secured with a Master Locksmith Access Key (MLAK); if you don't carry one, ask a staff member. For the full accessibility rundown, Waverley Council's 'Access Bondi!' page is the definitive source.

blocks.title: Opening hours can change
blocks.text: The Pavilion facilities - toilets, showers, change rooms and lockers - are open 6am-10pm daily (checked Aug 2026), events. Rather than trust a number that might be out of date, check the current times on the Bondi Pavilion or Waverley Council site before relying on a late-night stop.

items.q: Are the toilets and showers at Bondi Beach free?
items.a: Yes. All the public toilets, the outdoor beachfront rinse-off showers and the foot taps along the promenade are free, and so are the Pavilion change rooms. The Pavilion lockers are the exception - they're paid (from $6 for 4 hours, as at August 2026).

items.q: Where are the closest toilets to the flags?
items.a: The Bondi Pavilion, in the middle of the beach, is a straight walk up from the flagged swimming area and is your best bet for toilets, showers and change rooms in one spot.

items.q: Is there somewhere to get changed at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes - the Bondi Pavilion has male and female change rooms and showers on the beach side, plus lockers. The promenade showers are just for rinsing salt off in your swimmers, not for changing.

items.q: Are there baby-change and accessible toilets?
items.a: Yes. Baby-change tables are in the Pavilion ground-floor toilets and at the North Bondi amenities. Accessible toilets are at both spots, and there's an adult-change Changing Places facility (MLAK-operated) on the Pavilion ground floor.

items.q: What are the opening hours?
items.a: The Pavilion facilities run 6am-10pm daily (checked Aug 2026), though one-off closures happen for events andts. Check the current times on the Bondi Pavilion or Waverley Council website before relying on a late stop.

blocks.text: That's the whole map in your head now: the middle of the beach for the full setup, the north and south ends for a quick stop, and free showers to rinse off before you go. Aim for the Pavilion when you need to change, and you'll spend your Bondi day in the water - not hunting for a bathroom.

If you've only got a day or two at Bondi and you're wondering which tour is actually worth your time, here's my honest local take: the best way to see Bondi isn't from a tour bus at all - it's on a surfboard, on foot along the clifftops, or from the air. I've lived and worked around this beach long enough to have tried most of what's on offer, so here's how I'd spend the time and money.
Learn to surf where it all started

You can't come to the home of Australian beach culture and not at least try to stand up on a board. The name locals point newcomers toward is Let's Go Surfing, a long-established surf school operating from Ramsgate Avenue at the north end of the beach. Lessons run in small groups with soft, beginner-friendly boards, wetsuits and rashies included, and the instructors are trained lifesavers who know exactly which patch of the beach is safest for learners on the day.

Don't stress about being hopeless - most people catch a wave (on their belly at least) inside the first session. Book ahead in summer, and check current session times and prices directly on the Let's Go Surfing website, as these shift with the seasons.

Always swim and surf between the red-and-yellow flags, and if you're learning, the gentler northern end is usually kinder than the southern corner near the rocks below Icebergs - that's where the notorious rip runs. The lifeguards move the flags for good reason - follow them.
The coastal walk: the tour I recommend to everyone

If you do one thing here, make it the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. It's around 6 km of clifftop path stitching together Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee, and it is completely free. Waverley Council maintains the Bondi-to-Bronte section, and you genuinely don't need a guide - the path is well signed and hugs the coast the whole way. Allow two to three hours if you stop for photos, a swim or a coffee, which you absolutely should.
You can book a guided version if you'd rather have the stories told to you, but honestly, half the joy is setting your own pace.

items: Start early to beat the midday sun and the crowds.
Wear proper shoes - there are stairs and uneven rock in places.
Detour down to Bronte or Clovelly for a swim (Clovelly's sheltered channel is my favourite).
If you visit in late October or early November, the walk hosts the Sculpture by the Sea outdoor exhibition - check its official site for exact dates each year.

blocks.text: See Bondi from the air (and other splurges)

For a genuine once-in-a-trip moment, a scenic helicopter or seaplane flight over Bondi and Sydney Harbour is hard to beat - that first glimpse of the beach as a perfect gold crescent against turquoise water is something photos never quite capture. These leave from Sydney's airfields rather than the beach itself, so factor in travel, and book with a licensed operator; compare current flight lengths and prices on the operator's own site before you commit.

blocks.title: A note on booking
blocks.text: Tour prices, departure points and operating hours change constantly. I've deliberately not quoted figures here - always confirm the latest details and availability on the official operator's website before you pay, especially in peak summer when popular experiences sell out days ahead.

Rounding out the options: private day tours that pair Bondi with the Opera House, Harbour Bridge and The Rocks are great if your time is tight and you'd rather not navigate public transport, and small-group local tours will walk you through Bondi's cafes, street art and swimming spots with someone who actually lives here. Both are worth it for the context; neither is essential if you're happy to explore under your own steam.

items.q: Do I need to book Bondi tours in advance?
items.a: For surf lessons, helicopter flights and private day tours, yes - especially over summer and on weekends, when they book out. The coastal walk needs no booking at all; just turn up.

items.q: Is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk free?
items.a: Yes, it's completely free and open all year. It's roughly 6 km one way, and most people take two to three hours with stops. You can walk it in either direction.

items.q: Can complete beginners take a surf lesson at Bondi?
items.a: Absolutely - that's most of who the schools teach. Lessons include a board and wetsuit, and instructors pick the safest, gentlest part of the beach for learners on the day.

items.q: What's the best free thing to do at Bondi?
items.a: The coastal walk, hands down. Add a swim between the flags and a wander past the Bondi sea-wall street art and you've had a brilliant day without spending a cent.

items.q: Where do the helicopter and seaplane tours leave from?
items.a: Not from the beach - scenic flights depart from Sydney's airfields and harbour bases, so allow travel time and confirm the exact departure point with the operator when you book.

blocks.text: My advice? Do the walk, have a surf, and if the budget stretches, get in the air. Skip anything that promises to 'do' Bondi in twenty minutes - the whole point of this place is to slow down and stay a while.

blocks.text: After years of pointing lost visitors toward the sand, I've heard just about every Bondi question there is. So here's my local cheat sheet: the quickest way in is the 333 bus from the city or the train to Bondi Junction, the beach is patrolled by professional lifeguards, and the single most important rule is to always swim between the red and yellow flags. Everything else - the coastal walk, the Icebergs pool, dogs, parking - I've rounded up below.

items.label: Getting here
items.value: 333 bus from the CBD, or train to Bondi Junction + bus

blocks.text: Getting to Bondi and getting around

The easiest way in from Sydney's CBD is the 333 bus, which runs from the city down Oxford Street and drops you right at Campbell Parade beside the beach - it's the express of the Bondi bus routes. If you'd rather take the train, ride the T4 line to Bondi Junction, then jump on the 333 or 380 bus for the last stretch down to the water. Because timetables shift, I always tell people to check the live times in the Transport for NSW trip planner before they set out.
Driving? It can be done, but parking near the beach is metered, tightly timed and brutal on a sunny weekend. My advice: skip it and let public transport do the work.
Swimming, safety and the Icebergs pool

Yes, Bondi is patrolled by lifeguards, and yes, it's one of the safest beaches in Sydney to swim at - but only if you play by the flags. The red and yellow flags mark the supervised zone where lifeguards are actively watching, and it's the one part of the beach they can reach you fastest. Bondi is famous for its rips, so this genuinely matters.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: If you're caught in a rip, don't fight it - stay calm, raise an arm to signal for help, and float. Never swim outside the patrolled flagged area, and if in doubt, ask a lifeguard where it's safe to go in that day.

At the southern headland you'll find the Bondi Icebergs - the ocean pool you've seen in a thousand photos, with waves crashing over the edge of a 50-metre lap pool. It's a public pool, not a private club-only affair, so visitors are welcome to swim for an entry fee. It closes periodically for cleaning, so check the Icebergs website for current session times and prices before you go.

Early morning is my favourite window at Bondi - the light is gorgeous, the crowds haven't arrived, and the lifeguards are already on duty. For a swim without surf, the calmer northern end near the kids' pool is gentler than the wave-battered south.
The coastal walk, dogs and the everyday essentials

The Bondi to Coogee coastal walk is the walk everyone means when they say "the walk" - a clifftop path of roughly six kilometres that strings together Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee, with ocean pools and cafés along the way. Take your time; the views are the whole point. You don't need the full length either - Bondi to Bronte is a lovely shorter taste.
A few of the rapid-fire ones I get asked constantly:

items: Dogs on the beach? Not on the Bondi sand - it's off-limits to dogs. Check Waverley Council for the nearest designated off-leash areas.
Toilets and showers? Yes - there are public amenities and rinse-off showers around the Bondi Pavilion and along the promenade.
Surfboard hire? Several surf shops and surf schools operate along and just off Campbell Parade - you can hire a board or book a lesson easily.
Best time to visit? I love the shoulder seasons - spring and autumn - for warm days without the peak-summer crush.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach from Sydney city?
items.a: The simplest route is the 333 bus from the CBD straight to the beach. Alternatively, take the T4 train to Bondi Junction and transfer to the 333 or 380 bus for the final leg. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for live times.

items.q: Are there lifeguards at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes. Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards, and it's one of Sydney's most closely watched beaches. Always swim inside the red and yellow flags, which mark the supervised zone.

items.q: Can the public swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes - the Icebergs ocean pool is open to the public for an entry fee, not just to club members. It closes at times for cleaning, so check the Icebergs website for current opening hours and prices before you go.

items.q: Are dogs allowed on Bondi Beach?
items.a: No, dogs aren't permitted on the sand at Bondi. There are designated off-leash areas elsewhere in the Waverley area, so check Waverley Council for the closest one.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: It's roughly six kilometres one way along the clifftops, linking Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee. Allow a couple of hours if you want to stop for the views, a swim or a coffee.

blocks.text: That's the short version of the Bondi bible. Whatever brings you down here - a swim, the walk, or a coffee with a sea view - come early, respect the flags, and you'll have a Bondi day worth coming back for.

The short version: the best Bondi Icebergs brand takeover I've ever seen is the Hennessy x NBA basketball court, with the Barbie movie's all-pink invasion a close second. I've lived a stone's throw from that pool for years, and nothing gets the neighbourhood buzzing like waking up to find our famous ocean baths transformed overnight into a stadium, a tennis court, or a wall of pink. Here's my ranking of the ones that earned it.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Icebergs, 1 Notts Ave, Bondi Beach

items.label: Best photo spot
items.value: The Notts Ave lookout above the pool

blocks.text: What makes a great Icebergs takeover

The bar is high because the setting does half the work: that turquoise pool clinging to the rocks, waves crashing over the edge, the sweep of Bondi behind it. So a lazy logo on the pool floor doesn't cut it. The takeovers I remember used the space rather than just borrowing it - they built something you'd never expect to see hanging over the ocean, and gave walkers on the coastal path a real reason to stop.
My ranking, best to most memorable
1. Hennessy x NBA - the floating basketball court (2021)

For my money, nothing has topped this. Hennessy and the NBA drained the pool and dropped a full black court into it for their 'Courts Beyond Limits' launch - Bondi was the debut, before London and Shanghai. That monochrome court against the turquoise water and the ocean beyond was ridiculous in the best way, and half of Sydney spent the week wondering how you got a game there.
2. Barbie - the all-pink press blitz (2023)

When Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig brought the Barbie press tour to Icebergs, the whole precinct went Barbie-pink. What I loved was that they made the space around the pool the hero rather than tinting the water - it felt like a set, not an ad. If that didn't stir up childhood Dreamhouse memories, nothing would.
3. Adidas x Parley - the tennis court (2019)

Adidas emptied the pool and laid down a tennis court to launch their Parley range made from recycled ocean plastic, timed to the Australian Open. Clever concept, clever timing, and a real message underneath it about the plastic ending up in exactly the ocean you were looking at.
4. American Express 'Shop Small' - the OG

Amex was the first to treat the pool floor as a canvas, sinking a giant 'Shop Small' banner into the baths and setting up a local traders' market for the day. Every brand that has dressed the pool since builds on that idea. It's not the flashiest here, but without it the rest might never have happened.

The best free view of any takeover isn't from inside the club - it's from the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk just above the pool on Notts Avenue. Come at first light: the sun lights the water, the crowds haven't arrived, and the overnight transformations look their most surreal.

blocks.title: These are temporary - check before you trek
blocks.text: Brand takeovers usually last a day or two, then the pool goes back to being a working ocean bath. There's no public calendar of them. If you're hoping to catch one, follow Bondi Icebergs' own channels, and check the official site for pool hours and closures before you visit.

Plenty of other brands have had a crack at the pool - some inventive, some just a logo in the deep end - but these four are the ones I'd send a visitor chasing. They're unpredictable and fleeting by design. The pool itself is here every day, and it's a stunner even with nothing in it but a few early-morning lap swimmers.

items.q: What was the best Bondi Icebergs brand takeover?
items.a: The Hennessy x NBA floating basketball court from 2021 is the standout - they dropped a full black court into the drained pool for the launch of their 'Courts Beyond Limits' series, and Bondi was the first stop. The Barbie movie's all-pink 2023 takeover runs it a close second.

items.q: Can I visit or use the pool during a brand takeover?
items.a: Usually not - the pool is typically drained or dressed for the activation and closed to lap swimming while it's on. You can almost always still see it for free from the coastal walk on Notts Avenue above the baths. Check the official Bondi Icebergs website for current pool hours and closures.

items.q: How often do brands take over Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: There's no fixed schedule - they pop up occasionally when a brand books the space, and each usually lasts only a day or two. Because they're not announced far in advance, following Icebergs' own channels is the only reliable way to hear about one.

items.q: Was American Express really the first brand to take over the pool?
items.a: Amex's 'Shop Small' activation is widely credited as the first to turn the bottom of the Icebergs pool into a branded canvas, sinking a large banner into the baths. It set the template that later brands built on with courts, sets and full precinct makeovers.

items.q: Where's the best place to photograph an Icebergs takeover?
items.a: The lookout on Notts Avenue, on the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk directly above the pool, gives you the classic elevated shot of the baths against the ocean. Go early in the morning for soft light and far smaller crowds.

AdNews - Adidas takes over Bondi Icebergs (Parley)
Fourth Wall - American Express 'Shop Small' at Icebergs

blocks.text: If you're looking for Bondi's answer to Venice Beach's Muscle Beach, you'll find it at the free outdoor gym in Bondi Park, up the northern end of the beach near the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club. It's an open-air calisthenics station - pull-up bars, parallel bars and benches rather than a rack of dumbbells - and it's completely free, all day, every day. No membership, no booking, no lock on the gate. Just turn up.

I walk past it most mornings and I've never seen it empty. It's one of my favourite corners of Bondi precisely because it's so democratic: the same set of bars gets used by shirtless gym junkies chalking up for muscle-ups, personal trainers running early bootcamps, backpackers doing a few casual chin-ups, and the odd acro-yoga pair balancing in the grass beside it. Everyone shares. That's the whole spirit of the place.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Park, northern end, near North Bondi SLSC

items.label: Access
items.value: Off Campbell Parade / the beach promenade

blocks.text: What's actually there

This is a bodyweight setup, so come expecting bars rather than barbells. The station is built around the classic calisthenics kit: pull-up and horizontal bars at different heights, parallel and dip bars, and benches for core work - the council has tweaked the exact line-up over the years. It's ideal for pull-ups, dips, muscle-ups, L-sits, leg raises and the endless variations calisthenics people love.

blocks.title: It's not a weights gym
blocks.text: You won't find free weights or dumbbells here - the loose weights that once floated around the site were removed on public-safety grounds. If lifting heavy is your thing, bring your own resistance bands, or head to one of Bondi's indoor gyms instead.

Because it sits right on the grass above the sand, the view is the real draw. There aren't many places where you can knock out a set of pull-ups with the whole sweep of Bondi Beach in front of you. It's the reason the spot has a genuine community around it - Bondi has produced some well-known street-workout and calisthenics athletes, and this is one of their home bars.
When to go, and the unwritten etiquette

Timing changes the whole feel of the place. Early morning - say, sunrise to about 8am - is the calm, focused window: trainers with clients, regulars doing their routines, plenty of room. Mid-morning to afternoon on a sunny weekend it becomes a scene, busier and more social, and you may wait your turn on the popular bars.
If you want the bars mostly to yourself, come at first light. You'll get an empty station, the best light on the water for photos, and a swim straight afterwards while the beach is still quiet.

items: Share the bars - don't camp on one station between sets; let people work in.
Wipe down benches after a sweaty session; bring a small towel.
Bring your own water - there's no kiosk at the equipment itself.
Chalk sparingly and clean up after yourself; it's a shared public space.
Mind your gear and go easy on volume - it's a family park, not a private studio.

blocks.text: None of this is signposted, but it's how the regulars keep the place friendly. Follow it and you'll fit right in, even on your first visit.
Making a morning of it

The gym's location is half the appeal. You're a two-minute walk from the sand, so I'd pair a session with a cool-down swim between the flags - the North Bondi end is patrolled by Surf Life Saving in season, so check the flags and the conditions before you dive in. Afterwards, the cafés along Campbell Parade and around North Bondi are right there for a coffee or a post-workout breakfast. It makes for a properly Bondi morning: train, swim, eat, repeat.

items.q: Where exactly is Bondi's outdoor gym?
items.a: It's in Bondi Park at the northern end of the beach, near the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club, just up from the sand off Campbell Parade and the promenade. Look for the cluster of steel pull-up and parallel bars on the grass.

items.q: Is the Bondi outdoor gym free?
items.a: Yes - it's a free, public outdoor gym. There's no membership, no booking and no staff. Just turn up and use it, and share the equipment with whoever else is there.

items.q: Does it have weights and machines?
items.a: No. It's a calisthenics (bodyweight) station - pull-up bars, parallel bars, dip bars and benches. There are no free weights or resistance machines, so it suits bodyweight training. Bring resistance bands if you want extra load.

items.q: What are the opening hours?
items.a: It's an unstaffed open-air park facility, so there are no set hours - you can use it any time. For the quietest, coolest session, early morning is best; sunny weekend afternoons are the busiest.

items.q: Can beginners use it?
items.a: Absolutely. The equipment suits all levels, from casual chin-ups and assisted dips to advanced muscle-ups. Don't be put off by the strong crowd - the bars are there for everyone, and the regulars are more welcoming than they look.

blocks.text: So don't be intimidated by the hulks mid-muscle-up. Bondi's Muscle Beach is one of the friendliest free workouts in Sydney, with a view you'd normally pay a fortune for. Grab a bar, wait your turn, and enjoy it - that's exactly what it's there for.

PedestrianTV - Bondi fitness community and Council

blocks.text: If you've only got time for one of Sydney's two most famous beaches, here's my honest short answer: choose Bondi for surf culture, a buzzing café and bar scene and the iconic clifftop coastal walk; choose Manly if you'd rather ride a harbour ferry to a calmer, more laid-back beach town with a sheltered swimming cove. Neither is a mistake - they're genuinely different days out. Below I compare them on getting there, vibe, surf and things to do, so you can pick the one that suits your trip.

items.label: Bondi
items.value: Eastern suburbs; surf beach, Icebergs pool, Bondi to Coogee walk

items.label: Manly
items.value: Northern beaches; reached by ferry, sheltered Shelly Beach nearby

items.label: Best for Bondi
items.value: Surf, people-watching, café and bar scene

items.label: Best for Manly
items.value: The ferry ride, a mellower pace, easy swimming

items.label: Getting there
items.value: Plan both with the Transport for NSW Trip Planner

blocks.text: Getting there is half the decision

How you arrive shapes each day. Manly's big drawcard is the ferry from Circular Quay - gliding out past the Opera House and Harbour Bridge across open water is one of Sydney's great cheap thrills, and a reason to visit on its own. Bondi has no ferry; the usual route is a train to Bondi Junction and then a bus down the hill, with the 333 and 380 the services most visitors use. Both trips are straightforward on an Opal card or contactless tap. Because times shift with the day and any events on, I always check current departures in the Transport for NSW Trip Planner rather than trusting a fixed number.
The vibe: buzzing versus breezy

This is where they split most clearly. Bondi is Sydney's showpiece beach - busy, glamorous and a little on-show, with a dense strip of cafés, restaurants and bars behind the sand and a steady parade of surfers, joggers and sunbathers. Manly feels more like a relaxed beach town: a walkable village of shops and eateries along the palm-lined Corso from the ferry wharf to the ocean, with a slower, family-holiday air. If you want energy and a scene, lean Bondi. If you want to exhale, lean Manly.
Surf and swimming

Both are proper ocean surf beaches patrolled by lifeguards, and both catch out visitors with rip currents. Bondi faces the open Pacific and usually has something to ride, plus the famous Bondi Icebergs ocean pool in the southern rocks. Manly has consistent surf too, but its ace is nearby Shelly Beach - a small, sheltered cove inside Cabbage Tree Bay, calm enough for easy swimming and snorkelling. If a gentle dip matters more than waves, that cove tips things toward Manly.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi and Manly both have real rip currents. Always swim inside the red-and-yellow flags, which mark the zone lifeguards are actively watching, and never off at the quiet, unpatrolled ends of the beach.
Walks and things to do

Each beach anchors a walk worth doing. From Bondi you can pick up the coastal path running south past Tamarama and Bronte toward Coogee - clifftops, ocean pools and hidden sand the whole way, and each spring it hosts the free Sculpture by the Sea exhibition (check the official sources for current dates). From Manly the easy stroll to Shelly Beach hugs the water, while the longer Manly to Spit Bridge track heads through bushland and harbour beaches. Both towns are full of places to eat and drink, though Bondi's after-dark scene is livelier.
Manly early, when the ferry is quiet and Shelly Beach is glassy, then Bondi for a late lunch and a sunset drink, makes a brilliant one-day Sydney combo.
So which should you visit?

My rule of thumb: if this is your one big Sydney beach day and you want the postcard - surf, the Icebergs, the coastal walk and a proper café strip - go to Bondi. If you'd trade a little of that buzz for a memorable harbour ferry, a calmer pace and an easy swimming cove, go to Manly. If you have two days, do both. Whichever you choose, swim between the flags and plan your transport before you set off.

items.q: Should I visit Bondi or Manly?
items.a: Pick Bondi for surf culture, the Icebergs ocean pool, the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk and a lively café and bar scene. Pick Manly for the harbour ferry ride, a more relaxed pace and the sheltered swimming at nearby Shelly Beach. Both are excellent - they just offer different days out.

items.q: Which is easier to get to from the city?
items.a: Manly is reached by ferry from Circular Quay, a highlight in itself. Bondi is a train to Bondi Junction followed by a bus (the 333 or 380). Both are simple on an Opal card or contactless payment - check current times in the Transport for NSW Trip Planner.

items.q: Which beach is better for families?
items.a: Many families lean toward Manly for its calmer village feel and the sheltered Shelly Beach cove. Bondi is family-friendly too but busier. Either way, keep young swimmers between the patrol flags.

items.q: Can I visit both in one day?
items.a: Yes. They're on opposite sides of the city, so it takes some travel, but doing Manly in the morning and Bondi in the afternoon (or the reverse) is a popular way to see both. Plan the connections with the Transport for NSW Trip Planner.

blocks.text: Still torn? You can't lose here - both are free, beautiful and quintessentially Sydney. Match the beach to your mood and enjoy.

The crew you know from Bondi Rescue are real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council - not actors, and not the volunteer surf lifesavers in the red-and-yellow caps. They're the same team in blue and yellow you'll see working the sand any day of the year. The show made them famous; the day job is keeping one of the world's busiest beaches safe. Rosters rotate season to season, so I treat the bios below as the well-known regulars rather than a live line-up.
The lifeguards you'll recognise
Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins - head lifeguard

Hoppo is the show's steady centre of gravity. He joined the Bondi lifeguard service in 1991 and was appointed head lifeguard in 2000, and on screen he's the calm, experienced voice coordinating the team through the busy days and the serious rescues. If one name is fused to Bondi Rescue, it's his.
Anthony ‘Harries’ Carroll

One of the most recognisable and charismatic faces of the team - high-energy, relentless on a rescue, and known for his fundraising and community antics off the sand. He's among the longest-serving lifeguards on the show.
Andrew ‘Reidy’ Reid
A seasoned member of the crew known for his humour, his fitness and a big social-media following - one of the regulars viewers have followed across many seasons.
Trent ‘Maxi’ Maxwell

Maxi came through as one of the younger lifeguards and became a fan favourite. He's also widely known for working as a firefighter, splitting his time between saving lives on the beach and in the city.
Ryan ‘Whippet’ Clark

Whippet has the most unusual back story on the tower: before lifeguarding he worked as a child actor, and he's now far better known by the nickname than the name on his birth certificate. He's one of the crew viewers most often try to look up after an episode - usually spelled ‘Whippy’ in the search box, which is why it takes people a while to find him.

Plenty of others have featured across the seasons, and because viewers usually meet them by nickname first, here's the roster with the names behind them. The team rotates, so treat this as the recognisable faces of the show rather than today's shift list.

items: **Chris ‘Chappo’ Chapman** - also turns up on screen as ‘Chips’.
**Dean ‘Deano’ Gladstone**
**Tom ‘Egg’ Bunting**
**Matt ‘Matty’ Dee**
**Terry ‘Tezz’ McDermott**
**Dunstan ‘Dunno’ Foss**
**Kobi Graham**, and **Aaron**, known on the beach as ‘Azza’.

blocks.text: About the show

items.label: Who they work for
items.value: Waverley Council - the lifeguards are council employees, not cast

items.label: Where they patrol
items.value: Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte, 365 days a year

blocks.text: Bondi Rescue is a documentary series, not scripted drama - the rescues are real. It first aired on Network 10 on 15 February 2006, is made by Sydney production company Cordell Jigsaw (CJZ), and has run for around 18 seasons, making it one of Australia's longest-running and most-exported factual shows. It was rested in 2025 with no new season that year and, its producers say, is expected to return, subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. Either way, the lifeguards keep patrolling.

Much of the drama comes from one stretch of water: the notorious rip at the southern end, nicknamed the ‘Backpackers Express’ for the hostels above that end of the beach and the steady stream of visitors it catches. It's a big reason Bondi is one of the most rescue-heavy beaches in the country. For more, see our companion pieces on [20 obscure facts about Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2023/9/5/20-obscure-facts-about-bondi-rescue) and [the most dramatic moments on the show](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).
Seeing the team at Bondi

The lifeguards are on the beach every day, based around the lifeguard tower towards the southern end near the flags, and you'll often spot the Bondi Rescue crew there in season. Keep in mind they're working - their first job is watching the water - so give them room on busy days and never interrupt a rescue for a photo. The simplest way to respect (and benefit from) their work is to swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where they've judged it safest and are actively watching.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Set up and swim inside the red-and-yellow flags - the patch the lifeguards have chosen and are watching. Our guide to [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) covers the safest spots and how to spot a rip.

items.q: Are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards real?
items.a: Yes. They're professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council who patrol Bondi year-round. The show is a documentary and the rescues are real.

items.q: Who is the head lifeguard at Bondi?
items.a: Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins. He joined the Bondi lifeguard service in 1991 and was appointed head lifeguard in 2000, and he's the most recognisable figure on the show.

items.q: Is Bondi Rescue still on?
items.a: It was rested in 2025 with no new season that year, but its producers say it's expected to return, subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. The lifeguards continue to patrol regardless.

items.q: Are Bondi lifeguards the same as surf lifesavers?
items.a: No. The Bondi Rescue lifeguards are paid council professionals. The volunteer surf lifesavers in the red-and-yellow caps are a separate service that also patrols, typically on weekends and public holidays.

items.q: What is Chappo's real name?
items.a: Chris Chapman. He also appears on the show under the nickname ‘Chips’, which is why searching one name sometimes turns up nothing.

items.q: Was Whippet a child actor?
items.a: Yes - Ryan ‘Whippet’ Clark worked as a child actor before becoming a Bondi lifeguard, and is now much better known by the nickname.

items.q: How old are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards?
items.a: Neither Waverley Council nor the producers publish the lifeguards' ages, so any specific number you find online is someone's guess rather than a confirmed fact. What is on the record is service length - Hoppo, for instance, joined in 1991 and became head lifeguard in 2000.

items.q: Which beaches do the Bondi lifeguards patrol?
items.a: Waverley Council's professional lifeguards patrol Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte, 365 days a year. They wear blue and yellow; the volunteer lifesavers in red and yellow are a separate service.

blocks.text: However you know them - from the tower or the TV - Bondi's lifeguards are a huge part of what makes the beach what it is. For more, see the [Bondi Rescue hub](/bondi-rescue) and the rest of [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).
